output: President Donald Trump held a news conference Wednesday that began as a soliloquy. He addressed the party's losses in congressional races held Tuesday, when Democrats regained control of the U.S. House. He criticized Republicans who distanced themselves from the president and lost. Regarding Rep. Mike Coffman (R-Colo.), Trump said: "Too bad, Mike. Mia Love gave me no love. And she lost. Too bad. Sorry about that, Mia." Rep. Barbara Comstock (R-Va.) lost to Democrat Jennifer Wexton, who partially ran her campaign by tying Comstock to Trump. Trump said of Comstock: "She didn't go on to have any embrace. For that, I don't blame her. But she lost, substantially lost." He added: "Those are some people that decided for their own reason not to embrace, whether it is me or what we stand for. But what we stand for meant a lot to most people." Trump did not mention other House incumbents who lost their races despite embracing him, including Reps. Dave Brat (R-Va.), Pete Sessions (R-Texas), Claudia Tenney (R-N.Y.) and Dan Donovan (R-N.Y.) or other pro-Trump Republicans who lost their state or national races. On Wednesday, he also blamed retiring GOP representatives for creating "very tough" conditions for Republicans. Many of those incumbents retired in part because of Trump.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on Thursday deleted a tweet in which she mocked a Democratic lawmaker she wrongly identified as a Republican. Ocasio-Cortez posted a picture in which Rep. John Yarmuth (D-Ky.) posed alongside a cardboard cutout of Ocasio-Cortez. Her tweet referred to him as one of the GOP's "older male members." Instead, she misfired at a fellow Democrat who said he took the picture because he "wanted everyone to know" he welcomed Ocasio-Cortez in Kentucky. Twitter users quickly spotted Ocasio-Cortez's mistake. She removed the post within minutes, and has not offered an explanation. Her office did not immediately return HuffPost's request for comment. The Republican Party of Kentucky shared the cutout photo earlier on its Twitter account, saying it "looks like" Ocasio-Cortez is "calling the shots" for the state's Democrats. That was what sparked Ocasio-Cortez's tweet. Yarmuth, chair of the House Budget Committee who has served in Congress since 2007, later explained the cutout photo on Twitter, saying he wanted everyone to know he welcomes Ocasio-Cortez in Kentucky "regardless of what old white male Republicans think." Some conservatives commented on Ocasio-Cortez's error. Other tweeters pointed out that President Donald Trump tweets multiple mistruths on most days, almost all of them ignored.

Congressman Sean Maloney asked Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman why he told his father not to worry, stating, "Because this is America." Maloney said Republicans had kicked up, saying, "Let's do it again. Let's do the substance." Maloney ran through facts: Williams heard Donald Trump say "unusual and inappropriate" things to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about investigating the Bidens. Vindman was in a meeting in which Ambassador to the European Union Gordon Sondland talked about conditioning White House meetings on Ukraine launching the investigation Trump wanted, and he reported it to the National Security Counsel lawyer. Vindman heard Trump's voice on the call. Vindman said he "couldn't believe what I was hearing" and worried about national security implications, so he reported that, too. Maloney emphasized that these facts were presented by the fact witnesses, people who were listening to the Trump-Zelensky call. Maloney also asked, "Why do you have confidence that you can do that, and tell your dad not to worry?" Vindman replied, "Congressman, because this is America. This is the country I've served and defended. That all of my brothers have served. And here, right matters."

Former Republican Rep. David Jolly has publicly declared that he voted for Andrew Gillum for Florida Governor. Jolly, who at one point considered a split ticket for governor with Democratic former congressman Patrick Murphy, has already voted. "I've turned in my ballot. I voted for Andrew Gillum," Jolly said. "The reason is simple: it's because I've served with Ron DeSantis." DeSantis is a disciple of Trump who played up his similarities with the Republican leader to win the nomination. He starred in a television advertisement where he told his children to "build the wall," a reference to Trump's platform. In exchange, Trump endorsed DeSantis in the primary and pushed him in the general election. DeSantis recently endorsed Trump's proposal to end birthright citizenship. Gillum responded, "Floridians deserve a Governor who will stand up for everyone in our state, not bow down to Donald Trump's every unconstitutional whim." During their debate, Gillum said, "I'm not calling Mr. DeSantis a racist — I'm simply saying the racists believe he's a racist."

Trump said President Obama "outsmarted him" because Obama thought it was not a good thing to have Russia in, so he wanted Russia out, referring to Obama's push for a united stand against Russia after it annexed Ukraine's Crimea region. Trump said he thinks it is much more appropriate to have Russia in. He added that "if somebody would make that motion, I would certainly be disposed to think about it very favorably." Russia was expelled from the group in 2014 and has since been criticized by U.S. lawmakers and foreign powers over interference in the U.S. presidential election, among other actions. Trump broke with most other G-7 leaders in June 2018 by calling for Russia to be readmitted. "Whether you like it or not, and it may not be politically correct, but we have a world to run. . . . They should let Russia come back in," he said at the time. He has also repeatedly blamed Obama for the annexation of Crimea, saying that Obama allowed it to happen and that Russian President Vladimir Putin "didn't respect" him. On Tuesday, Trump said Russia should be allowed to rejoin "because a lot of the things we talk about have to do with Russia." "As you know, for most of the time, it was the G-8," he said. "It included Russia. And President Obama didn't want Russia in because he got outsmarted. Well, that's not the way it really should work."

Former Redskins tight end Clint Didier has announced his candidacy for the U.S. House seat being vacated by Doc Hastings (R-Wash.). Didier's past attempts at political positions include a failed Senate campaign in 2010 and a losing race for Washington state land commissioner in 2012. "You have seen my Senate run, you have seen my lands commissioner run and my message has not changed," Didier said in a news conference. "It's the same. We have to get government under control." The Seattle Post-Intelligencer reported that Didier has previously expressed skepticism over climate change and has accused some of President Obama's appointees of having "communist ties." On Tuesday night, a report from ESPN stated that Didier appeared the same watching the Wizards lose as he watched the Caps lose. ESPN reported that Harper wore a "PED FREE" shirt but said the shirt was not meant to send a message.

North Korea said it is preparing a "Christmas gift" for America. Trevor Noah, host of "The Daily Show," commented on the development on Thursday after President Donald Trump made comments at the NATO summit on Tuesday. Trump had been asked about the status of nuclear talks with North Korea given its recent uptick of missile tests. Trump had said: "We have the most powerful military we've ever had and we're by far the most powerful country in the world. And, hopefully, we don't have to use it, but if we do, we'll use it." Trump had also referred to Kim as a "rocket man," a nickname he used in 2017 during the war of words between the pair. Kim replied with his own insult, labeling Trump a "dotard" in a statement from Choe Son Hui, first vice minister of foreign affairs for North Korea. Earlier this week, a North Korean foreign ministry official stated that Pyongyang was preparing a "Christmas gift" for Washington and that "it is entirely up to the U.S. what Christmas gift it will select to get," increasing pressure on the U.S. government to offer a deal North Korea finds acceptable by the end of the year. Noah recap the remarks from North Korea and suggested what Trump might expect for Christmas.

Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels will deliver the Republican response to President Obama's State of the Union address Jan. 24, congressional GOP leaders announced Thursday. In a statement, House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) described Daniels as "a fierce advocate for smaller, less costly and more accountable government" and said he "has the record to prove it." Boehner added, "For making tough choices and keeping his promises, Mitch Daniels is the right choice at the right time to deliver the Republican response to President Obama's address." Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) called Daniels "an eloquent spokesman for limited government" and said he "knows that President Obama's three-year experiment in big government has made our economy worse and our future more uncertain, and he knows that Americans want a government that's simpler, streamlined and secure." McConnell said, "He is a forceful advocate of pro-growth policies like fundamental tax reform, regulatory reform and energy security. And he is the right choice to explain the challenges we face and to outline a hopeful, common-sense vision for moving America forward by growing the economy, not the national debt." Obama's latest State of the Union address comes as the White House is ramping up its effort to cast the 112th Congress — where Republicans control the House and Democrats hold the Senate — as a "do-nothing" institution ahead of the 2012 election. Last year, House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) delivered the GOP response to Obama.

U.S. President-elect Donald Trump said on Sunday that he fully understands the "one China policy" but does not know why the United States has to be bound by a "one China policy" unless it makes a deal with China on other things, including trade. The congratulatory call from Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen was the first such contact with Taiwan by a U.S. president-elect or president since President Jimmy Carter switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 1979, acknowledging Taiwan as part of "one China." Taiwan is one of China's most sensitive policy issues, and China generally opposes any form of official contact by foreign governments with Taiwan's leaders. In the Fox interview, Trump criticized China over its policies on issues such as currency, the South China Sea and North Korea and said it was not up to Beijing to decide whether he should take a call from Taiwan's leader. "I don't want China dictating to me and this was a call put into me," Trump said. "It was a very nice call. Short. And why should some other nation be able to say I can't take a call?"

President Obama held a news conference Friday. During the event, he said some people had expected him to force Republicans to accept his terms. "Even though most people agree... I'm presenting a fair deal, the fact that they don't take it means that I should somehow do a Jedi mind-meld with these folks and convince them to do what's right," he said. The phrase "Jedi mind meld" was used during extemporaneous remarks during the question-and-answer portion of the news conference. The phrase "mind meld" is a phenomenon from "Star Trek" and is a method of communication used among Vulcans, like Spock. The phrase "mind meld" was reported to have inspired the Twitter hashtag #ObamaSciFiQuotes, which combined lines from the two. The White House subsequently tweeted a photo and a link to wh.gov/jedimindmeld.

Donald Trump proposed a ban on Muslims entering the United States that would have exceptions, including London Mayor Sadiq Khan. In an interview on Monday, Trump said, "There will always be exceptions." He said of Khan's election, "I was happy to see that. I think it's a very good thing, and I hope he does a very good job because frankly that would be very, very good." Khan tweeted that "Trump's ignorant view of Islam could make both our countries less safe." He added, "This isn't just about me—it's about my friends, my family and everyone who comes from a background similar to mine, anywhere in the world."

On Sunday, Donald Trump appeared on "Meet the Press" and said he would raise taxes on the wealthy. When asked about taxing the rich, Trump said: "For the wealthy, I think, frankly, it's going to go up. And you know what? It really should go up." Trump initially said the new top rate would cost him "a fortune." He later said the rate would go down and he would pay less, but he would not reveal what rate he is currently paying. The presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump continued to refuse to release his tax returns and today declined to reveal his tax rate. On "Good Morning America," ABC News' George Stephanopoulos asked Trump what his tax rate is. Trump replied, "It's none of your business." As president, Trump would cut his own tax rate. Trump said: "You'll see it when I release but I fight very hard to pay as little tax as possible."

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) admitted on Tuesday that he mishandled his health before being hospitalized last week with a heart attack. He told reporters outside his home in Vermont ahead of a cardiologist appointment that he must confess that he was dumb. Sanders noted that at some points on the campaign trail he was leading three to four rallies in a single day, adding that "in the last month or two, [I] just was more fatigued than I usually have been, and I should have listened to those symptoms." He said that if there is any message that he hopes can get there, it is that he wants people to pay attention to their symptoms. He said that when you're hurting, when you're fatigued, when you have pain in your chest, listen to it. On Oct. 1, the 78-year-old underwent an emergency heart procedure in Las Vegas to treat a blocked artery with two stents after he experienced chest discomfort. Hours after his release on Friday, Sanders shared a taped statement on Twitter, announcing that he was "feeling so much better" and thanking his supporters "for all of the love and warm wishes that you sent me." The campaign has no scheduled events until his planned appearance at the fourth Democratic debate on Oct. 15 in Westerville, Ohio.

Actor Rosario Dawson said she voted for Bernie Sanders in the primary on Monday, the same day former presidential candidate Cory Booker endorsed Joe Biden. Dawson, who also supported Sanders in 2016, wrote on Instagram: "I got to vote for Bernie again and I did. Whoever it is that you're supporting I hope that you are doing it consciously, with heart and with a ballot." Booker dropped out of the Democratic race in January. On Monday, Booker tweeted: "Joe Biden won't only win – he'll show there's more that unites us than divides us." Booker told a CNN town hall in March 2019: "She is an incredible girlfriend. I'm very lucky to be in a relationship with someone who is just so incredibly special, but more importantly has taught me so much in a very short period of time." Dawson, known as "Rent," called Booker a "wonderful human being." In September 2019, when questions from conservative outlets about her candidate allegiance were raised, Dawson said she endorsed Booker. Dawson co-founded Voto Latino, a group that encourages Hispanic voting and political involvement, and presumably voted in the California primary on Super Tuesday.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Zeid Ra'ad al-Hussein, the United Nations high commissioner for human rights, spoke out against the policy during an address in Geneva, The New York Times reported. "The thought that any state would seek to deter parents by inflicting such abuse on children is unconscionable," al-Hussein said. The United States plans to withdraw from the UN Human Rights Council, two U.S. officials confirm. The announcement is expected to be made by Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and Ambassador Haley at 5 p.m.

White House press secretary Robert Gibbs speaks thousands of words in public every week as he promotes and defends President Obama. On NBC's "Meet the Press," Gibbs was asked if Democrats could lose the House in the fall mid-term elections. Gibbs answered, "There's no doubt there are enough seats in play that could cause Republicans to gain control." The White House had admitted it might lose the House. Gibbs said he was not saying he wanted the other side to win or thought they would. Dick Morris, a Maryland Democrat, said on Fox News: "They're trying to distance Obama from it." Representative Elijah Cummings, a Maryland Democrat, said on MSNBC: "He probably was trying to stir up the troops."

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) said Wednesday he wants the imminent Senate impeachment trial of Donald Trump over the Ukraine scandal to be concluded swiftly because "the best is yet to come" from the president. Graham, who had expressed skepticism about Trump before the 2016 election, told Fox News host Sean Hannity that the best thing for the American people is to end the matter as quickly as possible. He said the Senate should have a trial in the Senate, citing bipartisan acquittal of the president and the president's appearance in the House chamber on Feb. 4 to deliver the State of the Union, where he will be acquitted by the Senate, and will be the strongest he has ever been politically. Graham added that when it comes to Trump, all that stuff is yet to come. Members of the House formally marched the two articles of impeachment — abuse of power and obstruction of Congress — to the Senate on Wednesday. Graham had earlier predicted that a backlash to Trump's likely acquittal in the GOP-controlled Senate could boost Republicans. He said of House Democrats: "We're going to get the House back, we're going to keep the Senate majority and President Trump's gonna be reelected, and one of the reasons is the way they've conducted themselves."

Donald Trump is heading back to the White House after three days in the hospital. According to reports, Trump's Sunday ride outside Walter Reed National Military Medical Center was a compromise over his wish to return to the White House. On Monday, CNN's Dana Bash tweeted: "He's being warned that if he rushes to leave the hospital and has a setback it would be bad for not just his health, but his re-election campaign." With Trump's doctors scheduled to give an update on his condition in the 3 p.m. hour, Trump posted on Twitter: "I will be leaving the great Walter Reed Medical Center today at 6:30 P.M. Feeling really good! Don't be afraid of Covid. Don't let it dominate your life. We have developed, under the Trump Administration, some really great drugs & knowledge. I feel better than I did 20 years ago!" The article reported that the weekend showed the public cannot believe anything Trump's doctors say about his condition or the basic facts of when he was diagnosed and became symptomatic, which the article said will be a problem throughout his illness. The article also stated that Trump will returnto a White House that has become a COVID-19 hot spot, with multiple aides testing positive.

A critic's notebook on Wednesday about restaurant tipping misstated the location of the French Laundry, a California restaurant that includes the cost of service in its prices. It is in Yountville, not Healdsburg. An article on Tuesday about Diana Nyad's swim from Cuba to Florida misquoted part of the comments she made after completing it. Nyad said: "I have three messages. One is we should never, ever give up. Two is you never are too old to chase your dreams. Three is it looks like a solitary sport, but it's a team." She did not say, "but it takes a team." An article on Aug. 28 about changes in spice-growing methods undertaken in India to address the United States' concerns that imported spices are a potent source of salmonella poisoning misstated the amount of spices imported by the United States in 2012, according to the Department of Agriculture. The imports totaled 326,000 metric tons, not 326. A headline in some editions on an article on Aug. 27 about the contest between two New York City mayoral candidates, William C. Thompson Jr. and Bill de Blasio, to capture the African-American vote in the Democratic primary incorrectly characterized the number of candidates who a poll indicated could receive the largest share of that vote. Three candidates, Mr. Thompson, Mr. de Blasio and Christine C. Quinn, were all within the statistical margin of error to receive the largest bloc of black votes; it was not a "2-Way Fight."

Senators Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) criticized Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau on Saturday for releasing a statement praising Fidel Castro after the Cuban leader's death. Cruz, who was born in Canada and whose father fled Cuba for the United States after participating in the early days of the revolution, called Trudeau's statement "disgraceful." Cruz had more to say about Cuba and Castro in the hours following his death. Trudeau called Castro a "legendary revolutionary and orator" while acknowledging the late Cuban leader was "a controversial figure." He added, "both Mr. Castro's supporters and detractors recognized his tremendous dedication and love for the Cuban people who had a deep and lasting affection for 'el Comandante.'" The statement made no reference to Castro's dictatorial rule, squashing of dissent, or human rights abuses. Canadian politicians also denounced Trudeau's comments. Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, described Trudeau's statement as "shameful and embarrassing." In his own statement, President Barack Obama offered condolences to Cubans without directly praising Castro. President-elect Donald Trump addressed the pain Castro caused. "Though the tragedies, deaths and pain caused by Fidel Castro cannot be erased, our administration will do all it can to ensure the Cuban people can finally begin their journey toward prosperity and liberty," Trump said in a statement.

Stephen Colbert said he promised Anthony Scaramucci he would not ask any "gotchya questions" during the Monday night interview. The "Late Show" host asked Scaramucci, aka "the Mooch," the one question he likely was not expecting. The pair were discussing the interview the former White House communications director gave days before his resignation 10 days into the job. The interview with The New Yorker's Ryan Lizza provided quotes about President Donald Trump's administration. Scaramucci called Trump's former Chief of Staff Reince Priebus "a fucking paranoid schizophrenic, a paranoiac." Scaramucci's description of why he was not behaving like senior White House Chief Strategist Steve Bannon caught Colbert's attention. "I'm not trying to suck my own cock," Scaramucci said of his former colleague during the interview. "Here's the deal," Colbert said. "Are you telling us that you never even tried? Because as an adult male, it does not pass the smell test." Scaramucci paused before answering Colbert's question and eventually shared that he "is not capable of doing it." "Let's just put it that way," he added.

California Attorney General Xavier Becerra said in a statement Monday that the state will take President Trump to court to block his national emergency declaration. The lawsuit states that the declaration uses a "pretext of a manufactured 'crisis" with "no national emergency at the southern border that warrants construction of a wall." The 16 states are suing to stop Trump from unilaterally robbing taxpayer funds lawfully set aside by Congress for the people of the states. The lawsuit states that the national emergency declaration uses a "pretext of a manufactured 'crisis," with "no national emergency at the southern border that warrants construction of a wall." The article reports that Trump's comment that "I could do the wall over a longer period of time. I didn't need to do this, but I'd rather do it much faster" is likely to figure prominently in showing he does not truly consider it an emergency. Legal experts suggest courts may defer to a sitting president's analysis of national security. NPR's Nina Totenberg wrote that the big, ultimate constitutional question is whether the president has the constitutional power to ignore a congressional vote that did not provide him all the money he wanted for a Southern border wall. California is joined by Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, and Virginia in suing.

Donald Trump and former Vice President Joe Biden will both visit Iowa on Tuesday. Biden will criticize Trump. According to prepared remarks his campaign shared with reporters, Biden will say: "How many sleepless nights do you think Trump has had over what he's doing to America's farmers?" He will also call out Trump's "crude language" and "embarrassing behavior." Biden will also call out Trump's "crude language" and "embarrassing behavior." The comments follow another set of Biden comments suggesting congressional Republicans will work with Democrats post-Trump.

During Thursday evening's Democratic primary debate in Los Angeles, PBS correspondent Amna Nawaz questioned former Vice President Joe Biden about recent Washington Post reporting showing that U.S. officials misled the public about how badly the war in Afghanistan was going. Biden, who is currently a front-runner in the contest for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination, interjected mid-question. "Afghanistan, you said?" Biden asked, using the common American pronunciation. "Yes, sir. Afghanistan," Nawaz responded, sticking to her pronunciation. Once Nawaz confirmed she said what he thought she did, Biden went into an answer about his track record of opposing increased U.S. military intervention there. Political commentator and podcaster Tommy Vietor, who served with Biden in the Obama administration, noted that Biden "broke hard from Obama on Afghanistan." Vietor wrote on Twitter: "It's true that he opposed the 2009 surge and was skeptical of the Pentagon's hard sell about [counter-insurgency] strategy." Biden has similarly diverged from former President Barack Obama's approach to taking responsibility for approving U.S. support for a Saudi-led campaign in Yemen. The candidate's answer won him praise from commentators. His reaction to an accurate pronunciation by a person of color is not likely to go down quite as well.

On Monday morning, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker officially declared his expected candidacy to become president of the United States. Richard Trumka, head of the AFL-CIO labor federation, issued a six-word statement in response to the announcement. "Scott Walker is a national disgrace." The statement was brief. For years, Walker has been a political adversary to organized labor. As governor of Wisconsin, he ushered into law the Act 10, which stripped most public-sector workers in the state of their collective bargaining rights, then survived a recall election pushed by unions. Earlier this year, he signed a right-to-work bill into law, further weakening the state's labor movement. His relationship with unions has made Walker a conservative hero. In the runup to his announcement, Walker has cast himself as a politician willing to take on the hard battles, pointing to his match with public-sector unions as evidence of his courage. Walker's own announcement tweet reflected the tough-guy image he is cultivating. A Walker campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trumka's statement. Asked if the statement had been accidentally truncated, an AFL-CIO spokesman said Trumka "said what needed to be said."

During a speech in El Paso, Texas, yesterday on border security, President Donald Trump said, "We're only getting stronger together." The phrase was a riff on Hillary Clinton's "Stronger Together." On Monday evening, Twitter users pointed out the phrase. The Republican National Committee posted a graphic with superimposed text reading "We're only getting stronger together" on social media. Republican National Committee spokesperson Steve Guest told The Hill, "When you lose your campaign, you lose your monopoly on any slogans." Clinton and Tim Kaine, her running mate, wrote a book with the title Stronger Together.

President Donald Trump said he tried to watch former President Barack Obama's speech on Friday but could not stay awake. "I'm sorry, I watched it, but I fell asleep," Trump said while speaking at an event in North Dakota. "I found he's very good, very good for sleeping." During the speech on Friday, Obama called out Trump directly for the first time since leaving office in January 2017. Obama criticized the current president's policies as well as some of his more contentious remarks, including when Trump said there were "some very fine people on both sides" of the rally last year in Charlottesville, Virginia, that saw white supremacists fighting anti-racism protesters. "How hard can that be, saying that Nazis are bad?" Obama asked Obama, speaking at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Obama also criticized those in Trump's administration, including the anonymous author of a New York Times op-ed published Wednesday, who said they are trying to keep Trump from implementing damaging policies while still working for him. "They're not doing us a service by actively promoting 90 percent of the crazy stuff that's coming out of this White House and then saying, 'Don't worry, we're preventing the other 10 percent,'" Obama said. "That's not how things are supposed to work. This is not normal."

"How hard can that be, saying that Nazis are bad?" Obama asked Obama, speaking at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Obama also criticized those in Trump's administration, including the anonymous author of a New York Times op-ed published Wednesday, who said they are trying to keep Trump from implementing damaging policies while still working for him. "They're not doing us a service by actively promoting 90 percent of the crazy stuff that's coming out of this White House and then saying, 'Don't worry, we're preventing the other 10 percent,'" Obama said. "That's not how things are supposed to work. This is not normal."

Steele said during a Tuesday morning interview on "CBS This Morning" that leading into the presidential debate in two weeks, frustration on the stage would be high enough that "you will cut it with a knife." Steele said, "And anything could happen, the explosion could be monumental." The interview followed a previous incident in which South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham called Trump a "jackass" several times during a Tuesday morning interview. Graham said, "I don't care if he drops out. Stay in the race, just stop being a jackass." Later that day at a rally in South Carolina, Trump said, "Give it a shot. Your local politician, you know? He won't fix anything but at least he'll talk to you."

The Trump administration is using the military to house migrant families it detains and prosecuting at great expense and is currently under court order to reunite. The plan calls for 2,000 people to be held at military facilities within 45 days and for more capacity to be added going forward. The Defense Department said it was asked to identify any of its facilities that could house 12,000 people, and if those spaces are not available it has been asked to build "semi-separate, soft-sided camp facilities" capable of housing 4,000 people each at three separate locations. A retired Air Force colonel said recently that the whole plan "smacks of totalitarianism," while other observers pointed to the likelihood of abuses. The administration has resisted accepting legitimate asylum applications.

On Tuesday afternoon, MSNBC released a clip of an upcoming interview with former White House advisor Valerie Jarrett. Jarrett, an attorney who worked with President Obama, was the main target of actress Roseanne Barr's racist tweet. Barr made the comment Tuesday morning. By Tuesday afternoon, Barr was fired and the sitcom "Roseanne" was cancelled. ABC issued a statement early Tuesday afternoon. Jarrett responded via an MSNBC video, followed by a transcript. Jarrett said she was worried about people who do not have a circle of friends and followers who come right to their defense. Jarrett said she saw someone cling to their purse or run across the street, and that every black parent she knows has a boy who has to sit down and have a conversation, the "talk." When asked if ABC made the right call in canceling the sitcom "Roseanne," Jarrett said the network did and that Bob Iger, the chief executive officer of Disney, had called her before the announcement. Disney is the corporate owner of ABC. Iger apologized, Jarrett said, adding that he told her there would be zero tolerance for that type of comment. Jarrett said he wanted her to know before he made it public that he was canceling the show.

On Monday, Fox News personalities Sean Hannity and Jeanine Pirro joined President Donald Trump on stage at a campaign rally in Missouri. Hannity had described the media as "fake news" hours before the event. He denied reports that he would join Trump on stage. "To be clear, I will not be on stage campaigning with the president," he said. "I am covering the final rally for my show." Hannity had faced criticism from his network in 2016 for appearing in a video endorsing Trump. Twitter users commented on the two hosts' actions. Fox News labeled the hosts' actions an "unfortunate distraction." In an emailed statement to HuffPost on Tuesday, Fox News said: "FOX News does not condone any talent participating in campaign events. We have an extraordinary team of journalists helming our coverage tonight and we are extremely proud of their work. This was an unfortunate distraction and has been addressed." Hannity said on Tuesday that getting on stage to praise the president during a campaign rally was not a problem because it "was NOT planned." He clarified his comments on the media to say he did not mean to include his Fox News colleagues.

Former Vice President Joe Biden won four states on Tuesday as he continued his path toward the Democratic nomination. Six states voted. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Biden competed in the two-man race. Biden was declared the winner in Missouri and Mississippi immediately after polls closed. Shortly after, he was declared the winner in Michigan, a state Sanders won in 2016 and the state with the most delegates up for grabs this week. He later went on to take Idaho. Biden thanked Sanders and his supporters in a speech Tuesday to a small group of reporters in Philadelphia after both candidates canceled campaign events due to concerns over coronavirus. "To all those who have been knocked down, to all those who have been counted out, left behind, this is your campaign," Biden said. "Just over a week ago many of the pundits declared that this candidacy was dead. Now we're very much alive." Rep. Tulsi Gabbard (Hawaii) is still campaigning despite having won two delegates so far. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg dropped out last week after poor showings in the Super Tuesday primaries. Former South Bend, Indiana, Mayor Pete Buttigieg and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (Minn.) exited the race just before Super Tuesday, throwing their support behind Biden. The states with primary elections Tuesday included: Follow results here as they come in. Live updates on the March 10 primaries were available.

President Obama had promised on his 2009 inauguration to close the facility opened by his predecessor and once housing around 700 inmates accused of terrorism charges. Congress prevented Obama's efforts by refusing to allow any inmates to be transferred to U.S. soil, forcing the search for countries abroad to take them. Under Obama, 179 prisoners were resettled. The Omani Foreign Ministry said that the men released from Guantanamo would "temporarily reside" in the country. The move was in response to a request by the U.S. government and "out of consideration for their humanitarian situation." The statement did not identify the prisoners names or nationalities. There has been no official announcement by the U.S. government, but a U.S. defense official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the transfer of the 10 detainees. An estimated 40 inmates will remain in the facility, which President-elect Donald Trump has pledged he would keep open and "load it up with some bad dudes." The detention facility operates outside the U.S. legal framework and has been criticized by human rights and legal experts. Prisoners first arrived in Guantanamo in January 2002 and it became a depository for those accused of plotting terrorism against the United States. 16 years later, the main suspects in the 9/11 attack, including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, have yet to be tried. Additional reporting by Missy Ryan and Julie Tate from Washington, D.C.

Harley-Davidson motorcycles have been affected by tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump. The company announced it is shifting some production overseas in response to European Union tariffs on motorcycles. The tariffs were imposed in retaliation for Trump's tariffs on the EU. In prepared remarks, the company said: "Harley-Davidson maintains a strong commitment to U.S.-based manufacturing which is valued by riders globally. Increasingasing international production to alleviate the EU tariff burden is not the company's preference, but represents the only sustainable option to make its motorcycles accessible to customers in the EU and maintain a viable business in Europe. Europe is a critical market for Harley-Davidson." The announcement comes months after a Missouri nail company announced it had laid off 60 temporary workers due to Trump's tariffs, with more jobs on the line.

The Senate will take up Donald Trump's impeachment next week, essentially halting the body's business. Majority Mitch McConnell has shut down legislating. Democratic Sen. Kamala Harris has intervened. The trial will include more Trump court-packing by McConnell and Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Lindsey Graham. There will not be committee hearings during the trial. The three-day MLK holiday weekend will be a busy one for the prosecution and defense. As of Thursday afternoon, McConnell had not shared the text of the trial procedures with Senate Democrats. Democratic leader Chuck Schumer plans to force votes for calling witnesses at the outset on Tuesday. They want a minimum of four witnesses, including former national security adviser John Bolton and acting White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney. McConnell has a plan, aided by Sen. Susan Collins, to defeat that vote by postponing any votes on witnesses or documents until after the presentation of the case by the House and the rebuttal by Trump's lawyers.

The English Twitter account of Iranian President Hassan Rouhani used the hashtag #RouhaniCare on Wednesday to refer to a new health care initiative that will extend medical insurance to all Iranians. The hashtag is a reference to the Affordable Care Act, commonly dubbed "Obamacare." According to Your Middle East, the website's Iran correspondent Alborz Habibi said on the website: "Rouhani hinted at an insurance and health care program. Then I joked and used RouhaniCare hashtag on Twitter." According to Bloomberg News, Rouhani announced the new health care plans in a televised address to the nation on Wednesday night. The speech also covered topics such as the Geneva accords on Iran's nuclear program and the country's economy. Experts and pundits responded to the #RouhaniCare tweet, with many referring to obstacles the Affordable Care Act has faced in the U.S. The Iranian president told reporters at the World Economic Forum in Davos last January that he does not run his English Twitter account himself but trusts "friends" to post frequent updates. The headline on the story was changed to highlight that Iranian President Rouhani does not manage his English Twitter account personally and did not originate the phrase "Rouhani care."

Rumors and conspiracies have proliferated following the Sunday night shooting at a Las Vegas music festival that left at least 59 dead. The false allegations include false allegations about the gunman, a person of interest, and Nevada's gun control laws. Before police named Stephen Paddock as the gunman, some bloggers and social media users incorrectly pointed to a man named Geary Danley as the "murderer." In a now deleted post, the blog The Gateway Pundit called Danley "a far left loon" and noted that he had followed several pages dedicated to liberal politics on Facebook. All of these claims are untrue. The unfounded rumors appear to have originated on the anonymous messaging board 4chan. ISIS claimed responsibility for the attack and said the gunman had recently converted to Islam. An FBI spokesman said there is no proof so far that Paddock had any ties to international terrorist groups. Some social media accounts spread the unfounded claims that Paddock has been radicalized. New York Times reporter Rukmini Callimachi, who has covered ISIS for several years, noted on Twitter that the organization has incorrectly claimed responsibility for two recent attacks, casting further down on any assertion of an ISIS connection. Additionally, Graeme Wood, who has reported on ISIS for The Atlantic, noted that Paddock was a gambler and had committed suicide, actions that are at odds with ISIS' ideology.

President Obama has sometimes watched events around the White House only on television. Throughout his presidency, he and his wife Michelle have complained to friends about how isolated their lives have become: no trick-or-treating, quick shopping trips, or date-nights out. The two have mostly refrained from publicly complaining publicly about how security concerns have hurt their freedom and friendships, for fear that they would be seen as ungrateful for the extraordinary opportunities they have been given as the first family. On Tuesday, President Obama expressed regret that he was not able to celebrate with crowds outside the White House that had gathered on Friday hours after the Supreme Court struck down limits on same-sex marriage. The administration lit up the White House in rainbow colors that evening in celebration of the ruling. "To see people gathered in an evening outside on a beautiful summer night and to feel whole and to feel accepted and to feel that they had a right to love, that was pretty cool. That was a good thing," Mr. Obama said when asked to talk about the week. "And the only bad part about it was I couldn't go out and peek at it myself, because then I would have had to clear out all the people, or the Secret Service would have. So I — I could only reflect on it from a television screen. That's a moment worth savoring."

On Friday's "Late Night with Jimmy Fallon," former Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney, whose documentary "Mitt" is available on Netflix, "slow jammed the news." Fallon pairs a serious-facer–a Brian Williams or a Barack Obama–and ad-libs Barry White-style as his guest sums up the week's headlines. Romney, dubbed "Roma lama ding dong" by the "Late Night" crew, offered the audience a primer on Tuesday's State of the Union speech. On the menu? Unemployment, debt, immigration reform and "wide spread wire tapping." Fallon said, "Ah yeah. President Obama looked at the American people up and down and said, 'I'd tap that.'" Romney kept a straight face for the next two minutes. On his way out of New York, Romney ran into "Scrubs" star Zach Braff at JFK airport. A selfie ensued. The article included the phrase "The Hunger Games" reference.

The Democratic Party is holding a debate in South Carolina tonight. Candidates are seeking to stand out and gain votes needed for Super Tuesday. Mike Bloomberg has been criticized for his history of bad work practices and his standing as a billionaire in an era of extraordinary income inequality. Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized Bloomberg for his financial support of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham. Bloomberg said he also spent lots of money on Democratic campaigns. Michael Bloomberg said he bought the Democratic Party. Bloomberg said he had difficulty sticking the landing, offering what he called the kind of Freudian slip only a billionaire could make. Bloomberg said: "Let's just go on the record. They talk about 40 democrats. 21 of those were people they spent $100 million to help elect. All of the new Democrats that came in, put Nancy Pelosi in charge, and gave the congress the ability to control this president, I bought--Igot them."

An NBC/WSJ/Marist survey released Thursday found 58 percent of likely Democratic voters in New Hampshire support Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, while 38 percent support Hillary Clinton. The poll was conducted after the Iowa caucuses. Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist College Institute for Public Opinion, said Clinton continued to face an "uphill fight" in New Hampshire as Sanders remained popular in his neighboring state. Sanders is leading by a large margin with independents, men and younger voters, while Clinton is also doing better with women. Clinton has an edge with voters older than 60. Clinton overcame a polling deficit in 2008 and defeated Senator Barack Obama in New Hampshire. Clinton and Sanders will also face off for their first one-on-one debate on Thursday night in Durham, N.H., giving voters a last chance to judge them against each other in person. The poll released Thursday had a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points.

Nearly three weeks after the shooting of Michael Brown prompted widespread protests in a St. Louis suburb and a national examination of race and police tactics, Hillary Rodham Clinton on Thursday praised President Obama's response to the episode and called for a swift investigation into the circumstances that led to the unarmed black teenager's death. In a paid speech at a technology conference in San Francisco, Clinton said she watched the funeral of Mr. Brown, the 18-year-old who was shot by a white police officer in Ferguson, Mo. "As a mother, as a human being, my heart just broke for his family," she said. "But I also grieve for that community and for many like it across our country. Behind the dramatic, terrible pictures on television are deep challenges that will be with them and with us long after the cameras move on." On Sunday, as Clinton finished a book signing for her memoir "Hard Choices" in the beach community of Westhampton, N.Y., she declined to respond to news media inquiries about Ferguson. Clinton had been criticized for not speaking out on the subject. On Thursday, she weighed in with extended remarks that included praise of Obama for deciding to send Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. to Ferguson and for having demanded a swift investigation into the circumstances that led to Mr. Brown's death.

Since the publication of her book Unhinged last month, former White House aide Omarosa Manigault Newman has been releasing audio clips that she argues are damning to President Donald Trump and his administration. While dropping one of her audiotapes on Monday's "The View," Manigault Newman said she thinks a rumored "racial slur" tape, featuring Trump using the n-word during the making of "The Apprentice," not only exists but will be released before the midterm elections. "I don't hold the tape," Manigault Newman said. "I've heard the tape." Several people associated with the "Apprentice" and "Celebrity Apprentice" series have said they heard Trump use racist or other offensive language, but no one has provided concrete evidence. Former "Apprentice" producer Bill Pruitt tweeted in 2016 that such tapes exist, but in subsequent posts admitted he does not know where. In Monday's interview, Manigault Newman also introduced new audio that she had recorded while sitting in on meetings with the president and other White House staff last year. In this tape, Trump rants that Hillary Clinton is "getting killed now with Russia" and that the "real Russia story is Hillary and collusion."

Rep. Michele Bachmann (Minn.) and four other House Republicans sent letters to the inspectors general of the departments of Homeland Security, State and Justice asking them to investigate whether the Muslim Brotherhood has tentacles within the U.S. government. The letter concerned Abedin. Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) spoke on the Senate floor and criticized his House colleagues. He called the attacks "sinister" and described Abedin as "an intelligent, upstanding, hard-working and loyal servant of our country and our government." House Speaker John A. Boehner (R-Ohio) said Thursday that "accusations like this being thrown around are pretty dangerous." CNN's Wolf Blitzer described the allegation against Abedin as "an outrageous McCarthy-like charge." Bachmann, who is typically ubiquitous on the cable chat circuit, did not respond to the criticism.

Turkey's leading press organization and two experts in Internet law filed a complaint Monday to overturn a government ban on Twitter. The organization, the Turkish Journalists' Association, which represents 3,300 journalists, filed the complaint in a local Ankara court, arguing that the ban violated freedom of information protected by the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. Using a similar argument to challenge the ban's legality, two lawyers specializing in Internet regulation filed a case at the Constitutional Court of Turkey, which has the authority to revoke the ban. Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan moved to ban Twitter on Thursday after a series of leaks on social media helped fuel a corruption scandal in his government. The scandal is one of the biggest challenges to Erdogan's authority since he came to power 11 years ago. Despite international outcry over the ban, the government has remained undeterred. Over the weekend, The Hurriyet Daily News, a Turkish newspaper, reported that the government had moved to make it more difficult for Twitter users to try to circumvent the ban. Thousands of users have been altering the Domain Name System settings on their devices to allow them to use Twitter. The United States has criticized the ban. On Friday, Douglas Frantz, the assistant secretary of public affairs at the State Department, described it as "21st-century book burning."

Senate Republican leaders said Tuesday that there would be no confirmation hearings, no vote, and no courtesy meeting with President Obama's nominee to replace Justice Antonin Scalia, all but closing the prospects for an election-year Supreme Court confirmation. The pledge came together with a written vow from Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee that they would not hold any confirmation hearings. The pledge was the clearest statement yet from the Senate's majority party that it would do everything it can to prevent Obama from shifting the ideological balance of the nation's high court. Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, the majority leader, urged Obama to reconsider even submitting a name. "This nomination will be determined by whoever wins the presidency in the polls," McConnell said. "I agree with the Judiciary Committee's recommendation that we not have hearings. In short, there will not be action taken." Their first full day back at the Capitol since Justice Scalia's death afforded Senate Republicans the opportunity to unite around a message and strategy to thwart Obama. Huddles in McConnell's Capitol suite and a lunchtime conclave appeared to stem any wavering and push Republican troops into line. They had the ammunition in a June 1992 floor speech by Joseph R. Biden Jr., then a senator, urging President George Bush against any nomination to the Supreme Court until after that year's presidential election.

President Trump criticized Nordstrom department store chain on Wednesday for dropping his daughter Ivanka Trump's accessories and clothing line. The decision to stop carrying Ivanka Trump's products, based on sales, prompted criticism from Boeing, Lockheed Martin, automakers, and news organizations. The criticism sometimes caused stock prices to spike and prompted debates about whether corporations would tailor their conduct to suit a president. In those cases, Trump's criticism targeted government contracts, departing American jobs, and news coverage, not his family's personal fortunes. Six days after Nordstrom announced that, based on sales, it would no longer carry Ivanka Trump's products, a decision that prompted some Trump supporters to call for a boycott of the stores. The president posted on Twitter that "Ivanka has been treated so unfairly" by the company. He first posted the message from his personal account and then re-sent it from his official White House account. The complaint also raised questions about how he might handle the moves of numerous other companies as their relationships with Trump brands change. The large national discount retailers T. J. Maxx and Marshalls, and Neiman Marcus, the luxury department store, have recently taken steps to give less prominence to Ivanka Trump's products.

On Monday, Rep. Ben Ray Luján became the first major Democrat to announce a bid to succeed New Mexico Sen. Tom Udall, a Democrat who announced last week that he would retire. Luján served as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee during the last two election cycles, including during the party's 2018 election year. He has represented the northern third of New Mexico in the House since his 2008 win and also hails from a prominent local family. In 1989, then-GOP Sen. Pete Domenici joked that New Mexico may as well have three parties: The Democrats, the Republican, and The Lujáns. Ben Ray Luján's late father served as speaker of the state House from 2002 until his death in 2012. Democratic Gov. Michelle Luján Grisham and the congressman are distant cousins by marriage. Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver is eyeing the race and reportedly told Luján last week that she would be willing to run against him. Freshman Rep. Deb Haaland and Valerie Plame, the CIA agent whose identity was leaked by the Bush administration, are also considering running in the Democratic primary.

The Senate is scheduled to vote Tuesday on Trumpcare. The vote is scheduled for Monday at 4 PM. Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has a day to bribe Republicans into voting yes on the motion to proceed to an Obamacare repeal motion. The bill's contents are not known. The bill could be rewritten or could be voted on TOMORROW. The problems present in the bill could take weeks rather than hours. McConnell could still seek a commitment from 50 senators to vote on repeal and delay, with a vague promise to figure out what is needed to replace Obamacare in the next two years. The next 24 hours are key. The article urges Republican senators to call their office at (202) 224-3121 to demand they vote against repealing Obamacare and to stop what the article describes as ripping health care away from millions of Americans.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) said in Austin, S.C., that Donald Trump would appoint liberal justices to the Supreme Court, like his sister, Maryanne Trump Barry, a federal appeals court judge. Trump had said last year that his sister would be a "phenomenal" Supreme Court justice, but he has now said he was kidding. Cruz said, "Now it's good to stand with your sister, but Donald's sister was a Bill Clinton-appointed federal appellate judge who is a radical pro-abortion extremist." In July 2000, Barry wrote the majority opinion on a panel that ruled that New Jersey's ban on late-term abortions was "constitutionally vague" and "unduly burdened a woman's constitutional right to obtain an abortion." One of the other judges on the panel was now-Supreme Court Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. The case involved Planned Parenthood, which Trump said in Saturday night's debate is doing "wonderful things" for women's health. Cruz said, "Even among liberal judges that position is extreme and Donald said his extreme abortion-supporting sister would make a terrific Supreme Court justice." Cruz said Trump is a liberal. Cruz said, "A vote for Donald Trump is a vote to write the Second Amendment out of the Bill of Rights."

Multiple media outlets reported that Russians accessed a single laptop computer belonging to the Burlington Electric Department (BED), a municipal-owned electrical utility company serving Burlington, Vermont. The Burlington Electric Department issued a statement: "Last night, U.S. utilities were alerted by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of a malware code used in Grizzly Steppe, the name DHS has applied to a Russian campaign linked to recent hacks. We acted quickly to scan all computers in our system for the malware signature. We detected the malware in a single Burlington Electric Department laptop not connected to our organization's grid systems. We took immediate action to isolate the laptop and alerted federal officials of this finding. Our team is working with federal officials to trace this malware and prevent any other attempts to infiltrate utility systems. We have briefed state officials and will support the investigation fully."

Former White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders apologized Thursday after mocking Joe Biden's stuttering during Thursday's Democratic debate. Biden responded: "It's called empathy. Look it up." Sanders' first message received negative responses. In a follow-up tweet, she said she "was not trying to make fun of anyone with a speech impediment." She deleted the tweet and apologized. Biden, who has battled to overcome stuttering, was demonstrating a stutter during the debate. He said he keeps in touch with people who have reached out to him for help. "The little kid who said, 'I-I-I can't talk. Wh-wh-what do I do?' I have scores of these young women and men who I keep in contact with," he said. Sanders initially posted: "I I I I I I I I I I I I I I I I I hhhave absolutely no idea what Biden is talking about." She said in a tweet minutes later that she was not "trying to make fun of anyone with a speech impediment." The article reported that Sanders apologized.

Iranian news service Fars News Agency, described as Iran's leading independent news agency, ran a story about a poll finding that the "overwhelming majority of rural white Americans said they would rather vote for Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad than U.S. President Barack Obama." The Fars story is a word-for-word reprint of an Onion piece. The article states that the agency might be guilty of what it calls unoriginality and gullibility. The article notes that the line between total absurdity and outrageous-but-true can be drawn. The poll identified 77 percent of rural Caucasian voters would much rather go to a baseball game or have a beer with Ahmadinejad, who has repeatedly denied the Holocaust and has had numerous political prisoners executed, than spend time with Obama. The article also states that according to the same Gallup poll, 60 percent of rural whites said they at least respected that Ahmadinejad doesn't try to hide the fact that he is Muslim.
