Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) will not block the Senate from moving ahead on a House-passed bill that would keep the government running and defund Obamacare, according to McConnell spokesman Don Stewart on Monday afternoon. "Senator McConnell supports the House Republicans' bill and will not vote to block it, since it defunds Obamacare and funds the government without increasing spending by a penny," Cruz said. The House-passed plan is exactly what Cruz has been calling for. Cruz wants his colleagues to join him to prevent the Senate from moving ahead on the measure. Because once the bill clears a procedural vote requiring the support of 60 senators, Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) intends to strip out the portion that would defund Obamcare. Because of Senate rules, the new measure could pass the Democratic-controlled Senate with a simple majority. Stewart said McConnell would vote against any amendments that add funding for Obamacare back into the House-passed bill. "If and when the Majority Leader goes down that path, Washington Democrats will have to decide — without hiding behind a procedural vote — whether or not to split with their leadership and join Republicans and their constituents in opposing the re-insertion of Obamacare funding into the House-passed bill," Stewart said.

Voters in San Diego will elect their next mayor today, months after Democrat Bob Filner resigned amid sexual harassment allegations. The outcome of the race will carry implications beyond San Diego's city limits. After a fall election whittled the field, the contest comes down to two city councilmen: Republican Kevin Faulconer and Democrat David Alvarez. The White House does not involve itself in any race. On Saturday, President Obama endorsed Alvarez. Obama said he is watching the campaign and believes it is winnable. If Alvarez wins, he will trigger an alliance between the White House and the new head of one of the nation's largest cities. One of the main reasons Alvarez has been able to compete is the strong backing of organized labor. The news Web site inewsource.org has a rundown of the seven-figure investment unions have put behind Alvarez. Polling shows the two candidates are running neck and neck.

President Trump criticized his own secretary of state on Sunday, calling his effort to open lines of communication with North Korea a waste of time and seeming to rule out a diplomatic resolution to the nuclear-edged confrontation with Pyongyang. A day after Secretary of State Rex W. Tillerson said he was reaching out to Pyongyang in hopes of starting a new dialogue, Mr. Trump belittled the idea and left the impression that he was focused mainly on military options. Mr. Trump was privately described by advisers as furious at Mr. Tillerson for contradicting the president's public position that now is not the time for talks. "I told Rex Tillerson, our wonderful Secretary of State, that he is wasting his time trying to negotiate with Little Rocket Man," Mr. Trump wrote on Twitter, using the nickname he has assigned to Kim Jong-un, the North Korean leader. "Save your energy Rex," he added, "we'll do what has to be done!" Some analysts wondered if the president was intentionally playing bad cop to the secretary's good cop. Veteran diplomats said they could not remember a time when a president undermined his secretary of state so brazenly in the midst of a tense situation, and the episode raised questions about how long Mr. Tillerson would remain in his job.

President Donald Trump confirmed Friday that State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert has been chosen as the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. The former Fox News host had been Trump's top pick for the spot since mid-October, shortly after Nikki Haley announced her departure by the end of the year. CNN reported that Trump was looking for a candidate who had a willingness to defend him. Trump called his U.N. pick "very talented, very smart and very quick" as he spoke to reporters in front of the White House, praising her work at the State Department. "I think she's going to be respected by all," he said. Haley had insisted that her ambassadorship be a Cabinet-level role, but Secretary of State Mike Pompeo reportedly has asked that Nauert's position not be so high-level. Nauert was criticized over an Instagram photo she shared in October depicting her smiling in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh shortly after Pompeo arrived there to discuss the disappearance of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a U.S. resident. The Saudi government later admitted that Khashoggi had been murdered. Sara Boboltz contributed to this report.

Georgia Representative John Lewis spoke on the House floor Tuesday. He declared that it is time to begin impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump. He said he is deeply concerned about the future of democracy and is not alone. He said, "We cannot delay. We must not wait. Now is the time to act. I have been patient while we tried every other path and used every other tool. We will never find the truth unless we use the power given to the House of Representatives and the House alone." He said, "We took an oath," to protect and defend the Constitution, and, he said, "I am afraid to go to sleep for fear I wake up and our democracy will be gone." He spoke of Trump's "disdain and disregard for the law and the constitution," concluding, "I truly believe the time to begin impeachment proceedings against this president has come. To delay or to do otherwise would betray the foundation of our democracy." The outcome of the Democratic caucus meeting on whether to move forward with impeachment proceedings is less in doubt. However, a delay on making it official until Thursday, when acting Director of National Intelligence Joseph Maguire appears before Congress, with or without the Ukraine whistleblower's complaint.

Anderson Cooper criticized President Donald Trump for failing as a dealmaker, calling it "the one thing he says he does better than anyone else." Trump is expected to sign a new border security deal that would avoid another partial government shutdown, but he has said he is not "thrilled" with it. Under the deal, $1.375 billion would be allocated to border barriers, less than a quarter of the $5.7 billion Trump has been demanding. Cooper said it came as no surprise that Trump was unable to secure a better agreement, especially given that "the president's record in the private sector is riddled with ill-fated deals." Cooper said: "The president is said to be angry, he's said to be upset, he's complained publicly about where things have ended up, but the reality is he could've had a better deal than this one. Whatever the lessons he preached in The Art of the Deal, they did not work out for him this time. This may not have been the legacy that he wanted, but it's hard to deny that it's the legacy he's earned in this case."

A new Quinnipiac University poll shows Hillary Clinton trails all the leading Republican contenders by 11 percentage points in Colorado, a swing state. Florida Sen. Marco Rubio leads Clinton 52% to 36%. Ben Carson wins a potential head-to-head matchup with 52% to 38% advantage. Donald Trump leads 48% to 37%. Tim Malloy, the assistant director of the Quinnipiac University Poll, described it as a "chilly if not frigid reception" in Colorado for Clinton. In the nominating contest, Colorado's Republican voters' preference carries little weight. The party's caucus does not count because it violates Republican National Committee rules that require states to bind their delegates to the winners of their votes. Carson is Republican voters' preference there, with 25% support. He is trailed by Rubio at 19%, Trump at 17%, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz at 14%, Carly Fiorina at 5%, Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul at 3% and former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush at 2%. Among Democrats, Clinton has 55% support to Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 27% and former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley's 2%. President Barack Obama captured the state in both 2008 and 2012.

Attorney General William Barr wrote in a letter to Congress on Friday that the Justice Department has "no plans" to submit Robert Mueller's nearly 400-page special counsel report to the White House for an executive privilege review before its mid-April public release. Barr wrote that although the President would have the right to assert privilege over certain parts of the report, he has stated publicly that he intends to defer to him and, accordingly, there are no plans to submit the report to the White House for a privilege review. Barr released a four-page letter on Sunday that reflected the principal conclusions of Mueller's report. He also wrote that it is inaccurate to describe that letter as a "summary" of the Mueller report. "The Special Counsel's report is nearly 400 pages long (exclusive of tables and appendices) and sets for the Special Counsel's findings, his analysis, and the reasons for his conclusions," Barr wrote. "Everyone will soon be able to read it on their own. I do not believe it would be in the public's interest for me to attempt to summarize the full report or release it in serial of piecemeal fashion."

The President gave a news conference today where he made a statement and took no questions. He was flanked by first responders. The news conference concerned the impending sequester, where cuts would be made to several social programs and arbitrary cuts to the military. The President's statement to the Republicans was simple, stark, and strong. President Obama said: "The Republicans in Congress face a simple choice. Are they willing to compromise to protect vital investments in education, healthcare, national security, and all the jobs that depend on them. - Or would they rather put hundreds of thousands of jobs and our entire economy at risk just to protect a few special interest tax loopholes that benefit only the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations." The President's message was short and succinct: "If the sequester goes into effect in March, $85 million will go into effect immediately. Cuts will be a self inflicting wound that depresses the economy." Cuts will include furloughed FBI agents and reduction in funds for police and fire personnel. Cuts will include the lay off of thousands of teachers. Head Start will be cut. Homeland Security cuts will cause severe delays at airports. A carrier group scheduled for the Persian Gulf will not be deployed.

Federal law requires that Medicaid beneficiaries may obtain services, including family-planning care, from any qualified provider. Terminating Planned Parenthood's Medicaid provider agreements restricts access by not permitting them to get services from providers of their choice, according to the Department of Health and Human Services. Planned Parenthood has not committed fraud or a criminal act. In Louisiana, Planned Parenthood does not provide abortions. In some previous attempts by states to cut off funding, Planned Parenthood has prevailed in court. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a unit of HHS, has notified Louisiana and Alabama, which have taken action to terminate their Medicaid provider agreements with Planned Parenthood, that they may be in conflict with federal law, according to HHS. CMS said that by restricting which provider a woman could choose to receive care from, women could lose access to critical preventive care, such as cancer screenings. The agency reached out to Louisiana's Medicaid director on Aug. 5 and spoke with Alabama's Medicaid agency on Aug. 7. CMS said it provided both states with guidance it released in 2011 on this issue. The June 2011 memo says states are not permitted to exclude providers from Medicaid solely on the basis of the range of medical services they provide. The memo says states may exclude providers under certain circumstances, such as when providers commit fraud or certain criminal acts.

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs steps down from the post Friday after two years as President Barack Obama's top spokesman. Jay Carney, the current communications director for Vice President Joe Biden, will succeed him at the podium. Gibbs announced his decision to leave in January. Gibbs called it a "remarkable privilege" to serve the president. He said he wants to "step back a little bit and recharge some" after four years of campaigning and a hard-fought first half of the Obama administration, which he called "probably the busiest years that Washington and the White House have seen in a couple of decades." Gibbs said he will remain in the Washington area as a pundit, supporting White House positions on cable television and in speeches. "It's a remarkable privilege. It is in many ways the opportunity of a lifetime," he told reporters at the White House briefing announcing his decision. He added, "We've been going at this pace for four years." In a written statement, Obama described Gibbs as "a close friend, one of my closest advisers and an effective advocate from the podium." He said it was "natural" for his longtime aide "to want to step back, reflect and retool." Gibbs was Obama's spokesman during the 2008 presidential campaign, having joined the future president's team when Obama ran for U.S. Senate in 2004.

A letter to the editor responded to the article "A 'New Day' of Openness, Taxed by Old Grievances" (front page, March 22). The letter writer stated President Obama referred to the First Amendment, free speech, freedom of assembly, and religious freedom. The writer also referenced Cuba's universal health care, free education, and equal pay. The writer suggested both are lofty human rights that could someday emulate in each other. The letter writer from Pompton Plains, N.J., said: "I actually welcome President Castro commenting on some of the areas where he feels that we're falling short, because I think we should not be immune or afraid of criticism or discussion as well." The writer stated: "I cannot be the only person who recognizes the maturity, honesty and statesmanlike nature of that remark. Our country so desperately needs this kind of grown-up behavior in our elected officials. The mindless 'we're No. 1!' attitude does nothing to help us at home or improve our standing in the world. We are not faultless. It is not weakness to acknowledge mistakes. Will we ever mature to the point at which we welcome and praise a leader willing to voice our awareness of error and pledge to do better?" The letter writer from Santa Fe, N.M., asked: "Will we ever mature to the point at which we welcome and praise a leader willing to voice our awareness of error and pledge to do better?"

President Obama will not re-nominate former Georgia legislator Michael Boggs to a lifetime position on the federal bench. Boggs was nominated last December as part of a deal with Georgia's two Republican senators. He did not receive a confirmation vote in the Senate before it adjourned. During his time in Georgia's House of Representatives, Boggs compiled a voting record that was described as conservative. Though nominally a Democrat, he campaigned on his "quality conservative Christian values," including opposing marriage equality, opposing "homosexual Boy Scout leaders," and supporting school prayer. Boggs drew opposition from Georgia Rep. John Lewis (D), another member of the Congressional Black Caucus, for his record, including a vote to keep the Confederate battle emblem as part of the Georgia state flag.

General Motors chief executive Mary T. Barra spoke at an investor conference on the sidelines of the Detroit auto show on Tuesday. Barra said any changes in the North American Free Trade Agreement should account for the effect on American automakers and workers. "There could be unintended consequences, changes made, that would directly impact jobs in the United States," she said. "Nafta needs to be modified," she added, but she rejected the idea that "we need to walk away from it." President Trump has said that Nafta should be renegotiated and has at times suggested that the United States could withdraw from the agreement or tax vehicles imported from Mexico, where G.M. makes certain small cars, sport-utility vehicles and pickup trucks. Barra said she favored steps to modernize the agreement and added, "We are completely aligned with the administration on job preservation." She said G.M. had had discussions with officials from the United States, Mexico and Canada "to make sure everybody understands the complexity" of how the pact affects automakers and the flow of parts and vehicles across borders within North America.

Three days after Victory Day, Secretary of State John Kerry visited Sochi, the Black Sea resort city, three days after the seizure of Crimea. The seizure of Crimea occurred more than a year ago. Since then, President Obama has sought to isolate Russia and its president, Vladimir V. Putin, portraying him as a lawless bully atop an economically failing, increasingly irrelevant petrostate. Obama led the charge by the West to punish Putin for his intervention in Ukraine, booting Russia from the Group of 8 economic powers, imposing sanctions on some of Putin's closest confidants, and delivering financial and military assistance to the new Ukrainian government. In recent months, Russia has not only weathered those attacks and levied countersanctions on America's European allies, but has also proved stubbornly important on the world stage. That has been true especially in regard to Syria, where its proposal to confiscate chemical weapons has kept President Bashar al-Assad, a Kremlin ally, in power, and in the negotiations that secured a tentative deal on Iran's nuclear program.

An article titled "John McCain to Endorse Hillary Rodham Clinton in 2016" was published by Yahoo. The headline stated McCain said Hillary Clinton did a fine job as secretary of state, that she is a rock star, and that she has the aura of someone widely regarded throughout the world. The article said McCain thought it was interesting that issues where John Kerry engaged were issues where Hillary Clinton did not engage, and that those decisions were left to the White House and the National Security Council. The article also included a nugget stating McCain would vote for Rand Paul in 2016. The author of the piece wrote that McCain thinks Rand Paul represents a segment of the GOP, just like his father, and that McCain is trying to expand that segment intelligently to make it larger. The author asked McCain whether he was happy and whether he would like to be president.

Former President Bill Clinton said in an interview with Town & Country magazine that he is less angry now that he has a granddaughter, Charlotte Clinton Mezvinsky, born in September 2014. Clinton said Charlotte keeps him from harboring bad feelings. "I've told Hillary that I don't think I'm good [at campaigning] anymore because I'm not mad at anybody," Clinton said. "I'm a grandfather, and I got to see my grand daughter last night, and I can't be mad." Clinton also noted he will likely be a "backstage adviser" to his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, in her potential 2016 presidential run. Hillary Clinton is expected to make an announcement on her 2016 plans in the coming weeks. "I think it's important, and Hillary does too, that she go out there as if she's never run for anything before and establish her connection with the voters," Bill Clinton told T&C. In the interview, Clinton also defended work done by the Clinton Foundation, which he said is, "by a good long stretch, the most transparent of all the presidential foundations and more transparent than a lot of other major foundations in the country."

North Korea neared completion of the transition to its new leader, Kim Jong-un, on Thursday as a confrontation with the United States continued over the North's intent to launch a long-range rocket. The governing Workers' Party, during the country's first major political gathering in a year and a half, declared Kim "supreme leader" on Wednesday and awarded him the title of first secretary. On Thursday, North Korea also said that Kim had been elevated to chairman of the party's central military commission and granted membership in the Politburo and its presidium. The inevitable elevation of Kim later this week to the top defense commission post will cap his rise to the pinnacle of party, military and state leadership. Analysts in the region said the speed of his elevation reflected insecurity of the young leader's status as much as it did the leadership's need to have a solid power center in place immediately. The country's Unha, or Galaxy, rocket is expected to blast off within days. The North says the rocket's purpose is peaceful — to put a satellite in orbit — but the United States and other countries see the event as a test of long-range missile technology.

The Republican-led House of Representatives voted Wednesday to extend expiring George W. Bush-era tax cuts at all income levels for another year. With Congress leaving Washington on Friday for a month-long recess, the vote was a pre-election statement of the GOP's opposition to raising taxes for any taxpayer. It also earned support from a handful of Democrats facing difficult reelection campaigns this fall. The final vote count was 256-171, according to The Washington Post Congressional Votes Databse. 19 Democrats voted with Republicans to approve the bill. Collectively, these 19 Democrats vote with their party 72 percent of the time. Donnelly, who is running for the U.S. Senate and has described his moderate record, votes with Democrats 67 percent of the time, according to the votes database. Of these 19 Democrats, several have consistently abandoned the party on high-profile votes, including Boren, Kissell, McIntyre and Matheson, who face difficult reelection bids, and Ross, who is retiring but many one day run for statewide office.

Montana is home to one of several incumbent Democrats across the country seeking to maintain their statewide positions in a state President Trump won by double digits. The White House has visited Montana with visits by high-profile figures, several headlined by the president himself. The visits are intended to defeat Democratic Senator Jon Tester and replace him with Republican state auditor Matt Rosendale, described as a Trump ally. Tester is described as a "pro-gun, anti-big-business prairie pragmatist." Tester is seeking to keep the race local, while Rosendale is using his association with the president. A former rancher and teacher, Tester is one of two Democrats in Montana who have held statewide office. The other is Gov. Steve Bullock, who won in 2016 on a platform that included expanding Medicaid, raising the minimum wage and opposing the Citizens United decision. Taxes would be increased on all tobacco products, including electronic cigarettes, with the revenue used to expand eligibility for Medicaid coverage under the Affordable Care Act. This measure would ban people from collecting election ballots filled out by others, unless they are relatives, members of the same household as the voter, election officials, postal workers, or the like.

Top White House aide Dan Pfeiffer said Sunday that President Obama is not threatening Congress by promising to take more actions on his own in 2014. Obama's use of "a pen and a phone" — the pen being the use of so-called executive actions, a.k.a. generally limited policy declarations that a president takes unilaterally — is expected to be a major theme of his State of the Union address Tuesday. The White House has been telegraphing this strategy for weeks. Some see this strategy as threatening Congress that, if it does not act, Obama will. "I don't think it's confrontational," Pfeiffer said on CNN's "State of the Union." "Let's find some areas we can work together." Pfeiffer said Obama "is not going to tell the American people that he's going to wait for Congress." Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), appearing on the same program, said the White House's comments do indeed sound like a threat. "It sounds vaguely like a threat, and I think it also has a certain amount of arrogance in the sense that one of the fundamental principles of our country were the checks and balances -- that it wasn't supposed to be easy to pass legislation, that you have to convince people," Paul said.

A House panel voted Wednesday to place a five-year moratorium on bonuses to senior executives at the Department of Veterans Affairs. The sponsor, Rep. Jeff Miller, Republican chairman of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, said the legislation was in response to media reports about various executives who received performance bonuses despite significant problems at the VA during their watch, such as the increase in the number of disability claims pending longer than 125 days. The VA had already halted bonuses for executives overseeing disability claims, but Miller's legislation extends the ban to other divisions within the government's second-largest department. The VA did not respond to a request for comment, but has stressed previously that bonuses have been reduced in recent years. In 2009, the department awarded executives $3.3 million in bonuses. Last year, the amount of bonuses fell to $2.3 million. The bonuses go to career professionals and not to political appointees. The Florida lawmaker's amendment was part of a larger bill requiring states to charge in-state tuition rates for veterans using their Post 911 GI Bill benefits. No lawmakers spoke in opposition to the amendment. "Until we have complete confidence that VA is holding executives accountable rather than rewarding them for their mistakes, no one should get a performance bonus. Period," Miller said in a prepared statement sent after the vote.

The House on Thursday rejected a measure that would have withdrawn funding for U.S. military operations in Libya. The amendment was offered as an amendment to a defense appropriations bill and failed on a 199 to 229 vote. It was sponsored by Reps. Dennis J. Kucinich (D-Ohio) and Justin Amash (R-Mich.) and co-sponsored by a bipartisan group of 13 other critics of U.S. involvement in Libya. The measure states that "none of the funds made available by this Act may be used for the use of military force against Libya." The vote gave members of the House another opportunity to express dissatisfaction with U.S. participation in the NATO-led effort against Libyan leader Moammar Gaddafi's regime. Two weeks ago, the House rejected a measure to authorize the U.S. mission in Libya and a bill that would have limited funding of U.S. operations in that country. On Thursday, another Libya-related amendment, sponsored by Rep. Tom Cole (R-Okla.), passed on a 225 to 201 vote. That measure would prevent funds from being used for equipment and training related to the Libyan operation.

Secretary of State John Kerry addressed critics of a potential nuclear deal with Iran on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, a week before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel is scheduled to deliver an address to Congress criticizing the emerging accord. Kerry said: "Anybody running around right now, jumping in to say, 'Well, we don't like the deal,' or this or that, doesn't know what the deal is. There is no deal yet. And I caution people to wait and see what these negotiations produce." At another point, Kerry said Netanyahu had been wrong about the Obama administration's policy toward Iran in the past. Kerry said Netanyahu had denounced a 2013 interim accord to freeze much of Iran's nuclear program, only to acknowledge belatedly that it was in Israel's interest. Kerry said: "I don't know anybody who looks at the interim agreement and doesn't say, 'Wow, this has really worked' — including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who would like to see it extended, having opposed it vehemently in the beginning, calling it the deal of the century for Iran."

Senator Rob Portman will not run for re-election in 2022. The announcement came via the Columbus Dispatch. Portman cited "partisan gridlock" as the reason he was retiring. The Republican side of the race could feature a primary between the Trumpist wing of the party and more moderate Republicons. Former congressman Jim Renacci ran against incumbent senator Sherrod Brown in 2018. Rep. Jim Jordan might also enter the race. Other Trumpist tools, including Rep. Jim Jordan, could also enter the race. Lt. Gov. John Husted might enter the race. On the Democratic side, there is a lack of statewide officeholders with the same kind of name recognition as Brown. The Democratic candidate may have a better shot at the seat than one might expect given the division in the GOP and the likelihood that it will be more divided by the election. One additional thought is whether Portman will use the announcement to distance himself from the Trumpists and possibly align with the Trumpist line on impeachment and votes on Biden's legislative agenda.

President Donald Trump posted a video on Twitter that appeared to endorse violence against the press, particularly CNN. CNN commentator Ana Navarro said on ABC News' "This Week" that the president took things too far and his tweet was inciting violence. "He is going to get somebody killed in the media," she said. "Maybe that will stop him." Days earlier, Deputy White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the president has never incited violence. CNN posted its official response to Trump's tweet by quoting the comments Sanders made two days prior. Navarro, a Republican strategist, has criticized the president since he launched his candidacy for the nation's highest office. Last week, she called Trump a "lunatic man baby" for attacking MSNBC's Mika Brzezinski. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that the president's son-in-law and top advisor, Jared Kushner, complained about Navarro's coverage to a senior executive at CNN's parent company, Time Warner. Navarro has criticized the president and his administration.

House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan (R-Wisc.) appeared on CNN's State of the Union on Sunday to discuss his federal budget proposal and whether he would run for Senate. When asked if the Bush administration bore some responsibility for the nation's fiscal woes, Ryan said, "Both parties messed this up." Ryan also said President Obama had offered some ideas regarding cutting spending and addressing entitlements, but said a formal plan had not been released by either the president or Senate Democrats. "My townhall meetings went phenomenally well," Ryan said, despite reports of constituents appearing at townhalls in his district. "I would argue that's really a non-sequitur," Ryan said when asked to address the line he and other Republicans were attempting to walk — specifically, calling for the preservation of oil industry tax breaks at a time of rising gas prices, while asking seniors-to-be to accept cuts in Medicare benefits. Asked if he would run for the Senate to replace retiring Senator Herb Kohl (D-Wisc.), Ryan said, "We just started digesting this. I plan on making an announcement very quickly." He said he would announce his intentions this week.

Secretary of State John Kerry toured miles of roofless homes and shantytowns destroyed by Typhoon Haiyan last month and announced on Wednesday that additional American humanitarian aid would be sent to the Philippines. Kerry called the storm a warning of extreme weather in a warming world. "No words can do justice to the level of destruction we've seen in this entire community," he said. For the most part, severe shortages of food and clean water in the two weeks after the typhoon made landfall on Nov. 8 have ended. Four million people lost their homes to the tsunami-like storm surges or gusts that reached 200 miles an hour, and the effort to rebuild has barely begun. The Philippine government raised the official death toll to 6,092 on Thursday, with 27,665 injured and 1,779 missing. Local officials said the number of dead will continue to rise as more bodies are found. Running water has been restored in some central areas of Tacloban, but large areas of Leyte and Samar Islands still have none. "Looking around here," Kerry said, "you see an unmistakable example of what an extreme weather event looks like, and a reminder of our responsibility to act to protect the future."

President Donald Trump posted a video on Twitter that appeared to endorse violence against the press, particularly CNN. CNN commentator Ana Navarro said on ABC News' "This Week" that the president took things too far and his tweet was inciting violence. "He is going to get somebody killed in the media," she said. "Maybe that will stop him." Days earlier, Deputy White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the president has never incited violence. CNN posted its official response to Trump's tweet by quoting the comments Sanders made two days prior. Navarro, a Republican strategist, has criticized the president since he launched his candidacy for the nation's highest office. Last week, she called Trump a "lunatic man baby" for attacking MSNBC's Mika Brzezinski. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that the president's son-in-law and top advisor, Jared Kushner, complained about Navarro's coverage to a senior executive at CNN's parent company, Time Warner. Navarro has criticized the president and his administration.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) told MSNBC's Rachel Maddow on Wednesday that he would end the Republican Party if he did not care so much about it. "If I didn't care so much about our country, I would hope that [Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas)] would get the Republican nomination for president, because that would be the end of the Republican Party," Reid said. "He stands for everything America doesn't." The Democratic leader criticized the right for what he described as offending women, the gay community, the poor, and just about every other minority group through recent legislation, such as food stamp cuts and the Employment Non-Discrimination Act, known as ENDA. "The Republican Party is staggering right now," Reid said. On Wednesday, the Democratic caucus reached unanimous support for the bill. Reid said he is "comfortable" it will get enough support from the right to pass the Senate. "Why in the world should someone in modern day America be allowed to be fired or have their employment in any way discriminated against because their sexual orientation? They shouldnt be," Reid said. "We are calling for fairness."

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) is traveling to Canada to have hernia surgery, the Louisville Courier Journal reported Monday. The surgery is because of injuries Paul sustained in 2017 when he was attacked by his neighbor, Rene Boucher, in a dispute over lawn debris, according to court documents cited by the Courier Journal. Boucher pleaded guilty to attacking Paul and was sentenced to 30 days in jail. Paul has also filed a lawsuit against Boucher over the incident. The Courier Journal reported that Paul is scheduled to have surgery next week at the Shouldice Hernia Hospital in Thornhill, Ontario. Paul has been an opponent of universal health care. His office said Monday that critics attacking the senator for seeking medical care in a country with such a system were out of line, noting that the hospital where the surgery will be performed is privately run. "This is more fake news on a story that has been terribly reported from day one — this is a private, world renowned hospital separate from any system and people come from around the world to pay cash for their services," Sergio Gor, Paul's deputy chief of staff, said in a statement. "The Courier Journal should know better!" Gor did not respond to a request for comment on why Paul was seeking medical care outside the United States.

The Obama administration intensified its objections on Tuesday to Iran's nomination for United Nations ambassador, Hamid Aboutalebi, a former translator whose role in the 1979-81 Tehran hostage crisis. White House press secretary Jay Carney said the choice was "not viable" in what seemed as close as possible to ruling it out. The assertion came hours after the Senate voted unanimously on Monday night on a bipartisan measure that would bar the nominee, Hamid Aboutalebi, from taking the United Nations post by denying him a visa. House passage of the measure was considered a near certainty. The administration's objections could turn into a new confrontation with the Iranian government at precisely the time when it is seeking to improve the diplomatic climate for talks on Iran's disputed nuclear program, which resumed on Tuesday in Vienna. The United States is obliged to grant visas to United Nations diplomats from all countries, even those it finds objectionable, and has reserved the right to disallow anyone known to have played a role in the Iranian student revolutionary movement that seized the American Embassy in Tehran in 1979, holding American hostages for 444 days. The hostage crisis was the defining event that to this day has helped shape the estranged relations between Iran and the United States.

Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz said he would move to Canada if elected president. Cruz, a Canadian-born citizen, said, "America's voters are telling us they want an outsider as president. Therefore, if I am elected as your president I will move to Canada to be as outside as I can get." He plans to move the White House to Calgary, Alberta. Cruz said, "I own a home there, my kids still go to school there, and all my CanadaCare doctors are there. It'll be like I never left." Republican political strategist Fern Bronwin said, "This canny strategy nicely refutes Donald Trump's complaint that none of Cruz's colleagues in the Senate have endorsed him." Bronwin said, "By demonstrating that he has indeed been rejected by his peers, Cruz hopes to appeal to the hundreds of millions of American voters who also reject him." Cruz said he is confident this strategy will work. He said, "So many people hate me now, maybe they'll vote for me just to get me to leave." Cruz concluded, "To be perfectly candid with you, I wouldn't want to live in a country that would elect someone like me President. So if I wind up back in Canada, it;s a win-win, Eh?"

On Friday, members of the United Nations Security Council used a special session called by the United States to address the American ambassador's role in the body's response to Iran's crackdown on anti-government protesters. The session addressed the ambassador's role and reaffirmed support for the Iran nuclear agreement. The session began with a denunciation of Iran's "oppressive government" by American ambassador Nikki R. Haley and ended with the Iranian ambassador delivering a history of popular revolt in the United States, including demonstrations at the Democratic National Convention in 1968 and Occupy Wall Street protests in 2011. Council members condemned the Iranian government's response during more than a week of protests. As of Friday, more than 20 people had been killed and hundreds had been arrested. Authorities have blocked access to social media and have blamed foreign "enemies" for instigating the unrest. In her remarks, Haley said the United States would remain steadfastly behind the Iranian protesters.

In a digital advertisement that begins Friday morning, Hillary Clinton's aides presented a hypothetical that campaigns often avoid: the possibility that the opposition could win. The advertisement, which an aide said is being promoted on social media and through paid digital advertising, imagines cable news headlines of a future under President Donald Trump. The article states that fear of the GOP presidential nominee has been a primary motivating factor for many Clinton voters. The advertisement appears to target voters who are nonchalant over the significance of their vote or about the election entirely. The article notes that the ad's creators had the Brexit referendum in mind when putting it together. In June, most people voted for the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union. That was followed by news reports of "leave" voters regretting their decision. Several were quoted as saying they had assumed the "remain" camp would prevail and wanted merely to send a message. The Trump campaign has often pointed to the Brexit result as proof that an unanticipated surge in support — not caught by pollsters — could come for the Republican nominee. The Clinton campaign is telling voters to recognize the consequences of not taking that seriously.

President Donald Trump wrote on Twitter early Friday morning: "Looking forward to straightening out unfair Trade Deals with the G-7 countries. If it doesn't happen, we come out even better!" On Thursday, Trump exchanged criticisms with French President Emmanuel Macron after Macron suggested the G7 nations would band together without the US. On Twitter, Trump also called Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau "indignant" for his country's trade practices. The summit comes amid tariffs the US imposed last week on Canada, Mexico and the European Union. France and other US allies have also criticized Trump's decision to withdraw from the Paris climate agreement. The President has questioned privately why he should attend the G7 at all, according to a person familiar with the conversations, but was advised that skipping the meeting would appear as though he is backing down. He plans on cutting his trip short to fly to Singapore for his upcoming summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The White House announced Thursday that the President would depart the G7 mid-morning on Saturday, skipping sessions on climate change and the environment.

Seth Meyers said every day with Trump is like "Fight Club." The article presents a rundown of the previous night's highlights and provides recommendations for future shows. It also includes a link to a Watching newsletter for recommendations. Last Thursday night, The New York Times reported that President Trump had canceled an airstrike on Iran with 10 minutes to spare. Trevor Noah said Vice President Mike Pence was reported to have backed both of Trump's decisions. In a tweet last week, Trump said the military had been "cocked and loaded" when he called off the Iran strike. "The Late Show" parodied Trump's interview with Chuck Todd in "Meet the Colbert." Desus & Mero discussed the Democratic candidates and their "swaggerless" favorite comfort foods. Olivia Munn will appear on "The Daily Show" to discuss a new season of "The Rook." The New York City Opera commissioned a new work based on the Stonewall Riots, the event that took place 50 years ago this week.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 81, underwent heart surgery Wednesday morning at the MedStar Heart & Vascular Institute in Washington, D.C. According to a release from the high court, Ginsburg began experiencing discomfort after doing routine exercise Tuesday night and was taken to the hospital. She is expected to be discharged in 48 hours. Ginsburg told The New Republic in September she still works out with her trainer, who she shares with fellow Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan, twice a week. "I do a variety of weight-lifting, elliptical glider, stretching exercises, push-ups," Ginsburg said. "And I do the Canadian Air Force exercises almost every day." Ginsburg has had her share of health problems, including two broken ribs in June 2012 and bouts with both colon and pancreatic cancer. Despite setbacks to her health and calls from many who want her to retire so that President Barack Obama can appoint a new Supreme Court justice before the end of his term, Ginsburg told Elle in September she will remain in her position as long as she feels she "can do the job full steam."

Days before Friday's filing deadline for the Florida Senate race, Marco Rubio said he still had not decided whether to run for re-election. In an interview with CNN outside his office, Rubio said he was still weighing whether to make a decision that could affect the balance of power in the Senate and impact his own future political ambitions. "I'll let you know when I'm ready for it," Rubio said. Asked if he had made up his mind, he responded, "When I make a decision and I'm ready to announce, I'll tell you." Rubio would not say if he would commit to serving a full six-year term if he were to keep his seat. "Well, when I make my decision, if that's a pertinent question, we'll answer it. But we're not ready to announce anything yet," Rubio said. Asked if he were struggling with the decision, Rubio said: "When -- look, I hope we have a chance to talk about all these things when the time comes to do that. Right now, we're focused on some other things here regarding our work, OK?" Republican leaders have been pressuring Rubio to run, saying he is the only one who can keep the seat in GOP hands.

Former President George W. Bush appeared on "Ellen" yesterday to discuss politics, friendship and the poncho. Host Ellen DeGeneres began by asking Bush whether he had put one on the first time he had worn it at President Donald Trump's inauguration in January. Bush attempted to stay dry and took photographs of himself wearing the poncho. DeGeneres asked, "Had you put one on? Was that the first time?" Bush replied, "It looks like it, that's for sure." The interview included a segment in which DeGeneres suggested poncho wearing must run in the family, showing a photo of Bush's mother, Barbara Bush, struggling with one. Bush said, "It's genetics!" The segment concluded with a gift from DeGeneres: a poncho.

A billionaire, a queen and an American first lady walked into Excel Academy, an all-girls charter school, on Wednesday. Education Secretary Betsy DeVos, Queen Rania of Jordan, and Melania Trump, the first lady, accompanied the visit. The visit was intended to emphasize the Trump administration's stance on school choice. It was also part of a day of photo ops intended to cast a softer lens on a presidential administration grappling with several international crises and provide another glimpse of a first lady whose sporadic appearances in Washington have revealed relatively little about her own leadership style. Earlier in the day, Mrs. Trump and Queen Rania stood behind President Trump and King Abdullah II of Jordan at the White House. It was one item on Wednesday's agenda, which was also packed with a news conference to condemn a chemical attack in Syria and meetings to discuss brokering a peace agreement between Israel and the Palestinians. At the news conference in the Rose Garden, Mr. Trump said his position on the civil war in Syria and his opinion of the country's president, Bashar al-Assad, had changed. Mr. Trump did not offer details on any shift in policy.

President Obama said Thursday evening that there was "a possibility" that a terrorist bomb was responsible for the destruction of a Russian passenger plane that broke apart last Saturday over the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt. In a radio interview broadcast Thursday afternoon, Obama said there may have been a bomb on the plane. He did not go as far as his counterparts in Britain, who have suggested that the destruction of the plane and the death of all on board, was most likely the result of a terrorist explosion. "I don't think we know yet," Obama told the Seattle radio station KIRO during an interview broadcast Thursday afternoon. "Whenever you've got a plane crash, first of all you've got the tragedy, you've got making sure there's an investigation on site. I think there is a possibility that there was a bomb on board. And we are taking that very seriously." "We are going to spend a lot of time making sure our own investigators and our own intelligence community figures out exactly what's going on before we make any definitive pronouncements," Obama added. "But it is certainly possible that there was a bomb on board."

Kevin McCarthy, the House majority leader, said he would stop quoting him accurately and pointed out ways the $4.5 million Benghazi Committee has played all kinds of politics. McCarthy said, "Everybody thought Hillary Clinton was unbeatable right? But we put together a Benghazi Special Committee, a select committee. What are her numbers today? Her numbers are dropping." He added, "Let's be very clear: Benghazi is not political. It was created for one purpose and one purpose only: to find the truth on behalf of the families of the four dead Americans. Period."

The Supreme Court ruled on Friday that state bans on marriage among same-sex couples are unconstitutional. The decision caps off a rapid change in public opinion on gay marriage. In a 5-4 decision, the court decided that states can no longer limit the right to marry to heterosexual couples. Before the decision, 13 states banned same-sex marriage, mostly in the Midwest and South. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote in the majority opinion: "The court now holds that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry. No longer may this liberty be denied to them." Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen G. Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan joined Kennedy in the majority opinion, while Chief Justice John G. Robert Jr. and Justices Antonin Scalia, Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito Jr. dissented. State-by-state legalization of same-sex marriage has spread rapidly around the U.S. in the last few years. Eleven years ago, Massachusetts became the first state to legally recognize same-sex marriage. As of earlier this week, same-sex couples could marry in 37 states and the District of Columbia. Recent surveys by the Public Religion Research Institute showed that over half of the states expressed majority support for same-sex marriage.

Bernie Sanders said on CBS' "Face the Nation" that many of Donald Trump's supporters are working longer hours for lower wages and are angry because their jobs have left the country and gone to China or other low-wage countries. Sanders added that Trump has said he thinks wages in America are too high. Sanders responded to Trump's statement in a tweet, to which Trump replied: "Trump isn't used to people not backing down from him. Isn't going to happen with Bernie. So Donald did what all bullying cowards do: HE BACKED DOWN!" The article reported that Trump is off-balance and unhinged. Comments on the story were closed.

Karen Handel, a veteran Republican officeholder, won a special House election in Georgia on Tuesday. Handel, 55, defeated Jon Ossoff, a 30-year-old Democrat and political newcomer who raised $25 million from progressives across the country. The race was described as a referendum on President Trump and the most expensive House campaign in history. Handel, a former Georgia secretary of state and Fulton County official, averted an upset for Republicans in Georgia's Sixth congressional district, which Republicans have controlled for nearly 40 years. Republicans who had previously opposed Trump supported more conventional candidates from their party. The results reflected Republican attacks linking Ossoff to House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and her "San Francisco values."

The U.S. Senate confirmed on Tuesday President Donald Trump's choice to lead the U.S. Cyber Command and National Security Agency, Army Lieutenant General Paul Nakasone, 54. Nakasone has a background in cyber issues, having held positions including serving as chief of the U.S. Army's cyber command since late 2016. He replaces Admiral Mike Rogers, who is retiring after nearly four years in the "dual-hat" position leading the NSA, the country's largest spy agency, and the military's cyber warfare division. During his confirmation hearing, Nakasone said he did not think Russia, China and other countries had seen enough of a U.S. response to cyber attacks to change their behavior. He also said he had not come to a decision on whether the NSA and Cyber Command should be separated. They have been combined since the cyber operation was created in 2009, but there has been debate recently over whether they would be more effective as separate entities. Opponents of the idea say it is essential that they work closely together against a growing threat. Nakasone's confirmation also means he becomes a four-star general.

Deputy national security adviser Ben Rhodes said Sunday that the United States and Europe are likely to develop stronger sanctions this week against Russia for its involvement in the Ukraine crisis. "We still think that the best thing the United States can do is send a message to Russia through very strong sanctions coordinated with the Europeans, and I'd expect in the coming days you will see the Europeans move out on stronger sanctions," Rhodes said on CNN's "State of the Union." Rhodes also said European leaders were open to sanctions against Russia's energy, arms and financial sectors during talks with President Obama in the past week. The discussions came after a commercial jet was shot down by a surface-to-air missile over territory controlled by Russian separatists. U.S. authorities have suggested that Russia is partly responsible for the incident because it provided weapons and training for the separatists. Sen. Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.) said during an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he supports stronger sanctions against Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin "has shown he has no conscience," Schumer said. "He takes advantage of this horrible downing of the airliner and then just redoubles his efforts and rearms the rebels. It's about time we took tougher action against Putin. He's a schoolyard bully."

Representative Robert E. Andrews announced on Tuesday that he would resign from Congress after more than two decades. In an interview at his Haddon Heights office, Andrews said he loved Congress but loved his family more. He said he would leave office on Feb. 18 to lead the government relations practice of Dilworth Paxson, a law firm that once employed his wife and is run by partners who attended his wedding. "It's an offer that won't be there at the end of my term," Andrews said. He added that he joined the firm, which has offices in Washington, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, to "help my family be financially secure." He has two college-age children. The resignation coincided with Democrats' view that their chance of recapturing the House was slipping away. His move followed the decision to retire by Representative George Miller, Democrat of California and another key ally of House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia died on Saturday at a resort in Texas. His death prompted debate over a new nomination, with prominent Republicans calling for the next president to make a nomination. President Obama said he would nominate a new justice despite objections. House Speaker Paul Ryan, Republican of Wisconsin, remembered Scalia in a statement released Saturday as a man of towering intellect and deep faith. Ryan said: "Justice Scalia did more to advance originalism and judicial restraint than anyone in our time, and it all started with just two words: 'I dissent.' The passing of this brilliant jurist is a great loss, but his writings — with their plain language and constitutional moorings — will guide generations to come." Ryan did not join other Republicans, including presidential candidates Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz, in arguing that Scalia's seat on the court should remain vacant until after President Obama leaves office in 2017. Ryan added: "I learned so much from this man. I knew him. I respected him. I looked up to him. We all did. Tonight, Janna and I offer our sympathy and prayers to Justice Scalia's family."

Russian President Vladimir Putin said during an interview with French journalists on Tuesday that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has never been too graceful in her statements. Putin made the comments in response to questions about remarks Clinton reportedly made earlier this year in which she compared Russian aggression in Ukraine to Adolf Hitler's tactics in the 1930s. "It's better not to argue with women," Putin said, per a transcript posted online by the Kremlin. "But Ms. Clinton has never been too graceful in her statements. Still, we always met afterwards and had cordial conversations at various international events. I think even in this case we could reach an agreement. When people push boundaries too far, it's not because they are strong but because they are weak. But maybe weakness is not the worst quality for a woman." The interview, the Kremlin writes on its website, was conducted on Jun. 3 in Sochi. Clinton, a potential Democratic 2016 presidential contender, has been criticized for comparing him to Hitler. Last month, Reuters reported that the Russian president had accused Prince Charles of unroyal and unacceptable behavior after the royal allegedly compared him to the Nazi dictator.

Sen. Max Baucus (D-Mont.) will serve as the next U.S. ambassador to China after his colleagues confirmed him Thursday for the diplomatic position. Senators voted 96 to 0 to confirm Baucus; he voted "present." He replaces Gary Locke, who is stepping down to return to Washington state to be with his family. Baucus had already announced plans not to seek reelection when President Obama tapped him in December for the new role. The appointment will allow Montana's Democratic governor to choose a new senator. It is widely assumed that Baucus's successor would run for the seat in November as an incumbent, with the hope of helping Democrats hold on to a narrow majority in the Senate. As chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, Baucus played a key role in crafting Obama's health-care law and was among the first Democrats to publicly criticize the law's implementation. Baucus's impending departure will set off a round of musical chairs among Senate committee chairmen. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) is expected to assume control of the finance panel, a move that likely will lead to Sen. Mary L. Landrieu (D-La.) taking the top spot on the Senate Energy Committee.

A traffic stop Wednesday in the St. Paul suburb of Falcon Heights, Minnesota, left 32-year-old Philando Castile shot and killed by police. The death sparked outrage around a nation already reeling from a string of high-profile deaths of black men at the hands of police officers, the most recent less than 48 hours earlier in Louisiana. A Facebook Live broadcast of the aftermath captured by Castile's girlfriend circulated on social media. Protests occurred in St. Paul. Early Thursday morning, crowds began gathering at the scene of the shooting and in front of Minnesota Gov. Mark Dayton's (D) mansion to protest the shooting, according to the Minneapolis Star Tribune. Dayton said Thursday that he has asked federal authorities to launch an investigation into Castile's death. The Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension has already begun an investigation of the shooting, Dayton added. This is the second police-involved shooting death of a black man to gain national attention in as many days. The early Tuesday morning fatal shooting of 37-year-old Alton Sterling by police in Louisiana prompted a U.S. Department of Justice investigation.

In transcripts from the debate that have been released thus far, Megyn Kelly asked Jeb Bush about his service on the Bloomberg Foundation at a time when it supported Planned Parenthood. The exchange has been scrubbed. The exchange has not appeared in the transcripts. The Washington Post version, which appears identical to the CBS version, has not appeared. Fox News appears to be releasing selected clips of the debate and the exchange is not included. A transcription error may have taken out an entire question, answered a follow-up question, and then a follow-up question.

Liz Cheney ran unsuccessfully for a U.S. Senate seat in 2013 but did not gain traction among Wyoming's political establishment. Cheney cited personal reasons in 2014 for abandoning her Senate campaign. At the time she hinted at another future campaign: "At some point, I will be running for something else. This isn't the right time for my family." Her sister, Mary Cheney, criticized Liz Cheney's stance on gay marriage. Cheney said that Obama has "literally declared war" on the First and Second amendments to the United States Constitution as well as the interests of Wyoming ranchers and energy workers who face regulations from the United States Environmental Protection Agency. In August 2013, conservative Newsmax magazine named Cheney among the "25 most influential women in the GOP." Cheney's campaign was characterized by criticisms from her past championing of hawkish foreign policy positions to her public disagreement with Mary Cheney over her refusal to support same-sex marriage. Enzi's continuing popularity made it difficult for Cheney to make inroads with Wyoming Republican voters. On January 6, 2014, Cheney announced she had withdrawn from the race, citing family health issues.

Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel released his first television advertisement of the cycle on Sunday. The advertisement, announced via the Twitter account of top aide Ben LaBolt, emphasizes Emanuel's candidacy as an opportunity for the city to rescue itself from crisis. In the self-narrated spot, Emanuel says: "We have to make city government more accessible to everybody, and I think we are at a crossroads. We have got to decide whether we are going to continue to be a great city or become a second-tier city. And I think it is time to make that choice and make the tough decisions that are necessary." Emanuel has a national profile and a stint in Congress. Politico reported on Sunday that Emanuel is aiming to raise $6 million to $8 million before the Feb. 22 Chicago elections.

During an appearance on CNN on Monday, Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain said another woman is prepared to go public with allegations of "an affair for an extended period of time." Cain denied the accusation. Addressing the identity of the woman, he said, "It is someone that I know who is an acquaintance that I thought was a friend." Atlanta-based station Fox 5 is expected to run a report on the charges early Monday evening. Cain said he wanted to act preemptively before the claims came to light. "I wanted to get out in front of it," he said. "I have nothing to hide, I have done nothing wrong." The presidential contender suggested that "an infinite number of people" could come forward with similar allegations against him. Cain said he has no intention of abandoning his campaign for the White House. He said as long as his wife is behind him, he is in it to win it. An Atlanta businesswoman named Ginger White sat down with FOX News to tell her side of the story. "It wasn't complicated," she said. "I was aware that he was married. And I was also aware I was involved in a very inappropriate situation, relationship."

Senator Joe Manchin said in an interview that he will support Jeff Sessions for Attorney General. This is the second time in 10 days that Manchin has broken with party leadership, the first being when he criticized Senator Harry Reid (NV) for criticizing Trump. The article states this pattern has been familiar for Democrats, as it has been done during the years of Joe Liebermann. The article states that the Democratic Party's 47-seat majority would be unfortunate if Manchin is not a part of party leadership and does not buck it at the same time. The article also states that Manchin is not helpful to the Democratic Party in 2018, where he is sure to face stiff competition in his re-election in West Virginia. The article states that party purity is not something Democrats should strive for and is something they do not support, but that when you signal to the base that you are okay with a racist, KKK supporting, homosexual bashing AG, you are no friend to Democrats or progress. The article calls for Manchin to be out of party leadership and not be sent a single dime in his re-elect. It also recommends he run as a Republican, stating he seems to prefer to vote like one. Ted Cruz, the Republican senator from Texas, has not been identified as the Zodiac killer. The serial killer's last confirmed murder occurred in 1969, while Cruz was born in 1970. On Wednesday, Cruz posted on Twitter: "You might recognize the image as a coded letter the Zodiac killer once sent. This does not, any reasonable person would conclude, offer definitive proof that Mr. Cruz is the Zodiac killer, who was blamed for at least five murders in the San Francisco Bay Area and has never been identified." The tweet drew reactions on Twitter.

Parkland school shooting survivor David Hogg is starting a pillow company with software entrepreneur William LeGate to compete with Mike Lindell's MyPillow. Hogg, who has become a gun control activist, posted on Twitter on Thursday: "This pillow fight just got very real." Hogg and LeGate insist the venture is not a hoax and aims to be a progressive alternative to bedding produced by Lindell. Hogg and LeGate revealed their plans via multiple tweets. Hogg wrote: "It's going to take a couple of months though because we're not going to sacrifice quality for time." Hogg added: "The company's website will be live soon." He also wrote: "I never have been so excited about a pillow in my life. This kinda feels like a fever dream." Lindell, who continues to promote the conspiracy theory that the 2020 election was stolen from Trump, said: "Good for them. ... nothing wrong with competition that does not infringe on someone's patent."

President Trump has frequently criticized the "fake news" media for what he calls an imagined offense or an imagined offense. The article states that people respond with clapping and nods. It states that when Trump positions himself in front of men and women entrusted with protecting "the American way of life" — including the First Amendment — the same calculus prevails. In an address to service members at the Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in San Diego on Tuesday afternoon, Trump discussed creating a "Space Force." He said: "I said 'maybe we need a new force, we'll call it the space force.' And I was not really serious, and then I said 'what a great idea, maybe we'll have to do that.'" He added: "That could happen, that could be the big breaking story." Trump said: "Look at all those people back there, look at that. Ahhhh, that fake news." The crowd applauded.

The Senate voted Thursday by a unanimous voice vote to keep the government open for five more days, preventing a shutdown for now at least. The Senate will have until the middle of next week to reach an agreement on a year-end omnibus spending and tax extenders package. The House is expected to pass a continuing resolution on Friday to extend the funding deadline, originally set for Dec. 11, into next week. The House has repeatedly voted on last-minute spending measures. Lawmakers are hopeful they can pass a omnibus bill that sets spending levels well into 2017 and a tax package that permanently renews expired or expiring tax breaks. The hold-up centers on a provision to end a crude oil export ban. Republicans are trying to figure out what else they are willing to concede to get Democrats on board with the oil idea. All signs indicate that congressional leadership is close to a deal, but talks are fluid and there are a number of riders that lawmakers want to see attached to the legislation. Negotiations are expected to go into the weekend. Depending on how those play out, final votes should be held by Dec. 16.

President Petro O. Poroshenko of Ukraine headed to North America on Tuesday. He faces questions from both the United States and abroad about the pace of change. A White House meeting with President Obama and an address to a joint session of Congress on Thursday are likely to generate moral support, if little else, for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia. "It is a clear sign of solidarity and support from the United States," Foreign Minister Pavlo Klimkin said in a brief interview before leaving. Photo opportunities alone are enough to help Poroshenko domestically, although given its problems, Ukraine would like more. Winter looms with gas supplies from Russia cut off; it is unclear that limited self-rule for Russian-backed separatists regions is enough to satisfy the Kremlin; and the country is spending itself toward bankruptcy. Ukraine's leaders pushed through new laws through Parliament on Tuesday, even if they were mostly symbolic at this stage. One ratified closer economic and political ties with Europe, while the second supported temporary self-rule for the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk.

The White House announced that President Obama will make no further foreign policy-related decisions for the rest of his time in office. Global Uselessness spokesperson Leonard B. Tullock said the president is justifiably exhausted from having to make a decision about anything at all and will spend some much needed down time in Martha's Vineyard while he determines bolder, more specific ways to delay and/or avoid facing all realities in the world. State Department officials said this should in no way affect how the United States is currently ignoring allies and enemies or confusing which is which. Tullock said the president's non-decision decision will not alter foreign policy in the slightest. On an unrelated note, if anyone has a working foreign policy, they are invited to send it to JV Team, 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington D.C. 20500 or email it to notdoingstupidshit@gov. Winners will receive a ready-to-eat meal as a prize. A warning is provided that the prize may explode on impact.

Iowa state Sen. Joni Ernst (R) appears in a new campaign advertisement for the Senate. In the advertisement, Ernst says she grew up castrating hogs on an Iowa farm and will know how to cut pork. Campaign aides told the Des Moines Register that the advertisement will air on cable television in the Des Moines area starting Tuesday. Ernst says later in the advertisement: "Washington's full of big spenders. Let's make 'em squeal." The advertisement shows baby hogs sleeping in pens. Ernst says: "My parents taught us to live within our means. It's time to force Washington to do the same -- to cut wasteful spending, repeal Obamacare and balance the budget." Ernst is running for the Senate seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Tom Harkin (D-Iowa). The Republican nominee will challenge Rep. Bruce Baley, the lone Democrat running for the seat. Ernst has the backing of former GOP presidential nominee Mitt Romney, who sent a fundraising email on her behalf in early March.

The Trump administration said on Monday that it is resuming the admission of refugees from 11 countries with additional screening that it said will increase security but which refugee groups say will make it harder for Muslims to find safe haven in the United States. In late October, after a pause in admissions, the administration began accepting new refugees except for those from the 11 countries, citing the need for a 90-day security review. Officials did not name the countries, but they were widely reported to be Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Mali, North Korea, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria and Yemen. Those countries have accounted for more than 40 percent of all refugee admissions in recent years. Refugees from those countries will now be admitted again, but only after additional screening. "These additional security measures will make it harder for bad actors to exploit our refugee program, and they will ensure we take a more risk-based approach to protecting the homeland," the secretary of homeland security, Kirstjen Nielsen, said in a statement. Officials from refugee resettlement agencies said that while they welcomed the resumption of admissions, the announcement reinforced their view that the administration was determined to quash arrivals from Muslim countries by making it harder for them to qualify for approval.

Former Goldman Sachs executive Steven Mnuchin, a graduate of Yale University, worked for 17 years at Goldman Sachs, a Wall Street investment bank targeted by Trump during the campaign. He left in 2002 to start Dune Capital Management, a hedge fund, and has invested in the entertainment industry and housing. At Treasury, Mnuchin would oversee Trump's economic policies, including proposed tax cuts, an infrastructure spending plan, and sanctions against nations around the world, including Cuba and Iran, which Trump has targeted for criticism in recent days. Trump supporters should be over the moon—a guy with Goldman Sachs plus hedge fund pedigree will be looking out for the needs of the working man. The New York Times reported that Trump, in a campaign ad intended as a closing argument, portrayed the chief executive of Goldman Sachs as the personification of a global elite that the ad said had "robbed our working class."

Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) said President Obama should negotiate on the debt ceiling, but not with him. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) said Boehner was not doing that. Boehner told reporters the House would pass a bill and the Senate would pass a bill. Boehner added that he would guess Obama would engage with the majority leader if he so desires, referring to Reid. Boehner said it is wrong for Obama to refuse to negotiate over the debt limit with House Republicans, but that Obama should negotiate with Senate Democrats because House Republicans are not going to negotiate with Obama. White House spokesman Jay Carney said the video demonstrated an odd bit of Putin envy on behalf of the speaker. Carney said Obama might explain that.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said in an interview Tuesday night that sexism was a "major, major factor" in Hillary Clinton's loss to Donald Trump last November. Appearing before an audience at New York City's 92nd Street Y, CBS journalist Charlie Rose asked whether sexism played a role in the presidential election results. Ginsburg replied, "I have no doubt that it did." Rose asked whether sexism was the decisive factor, meaning if Clinton were a man, she would have won "going away." Ginsburg responded, "There are so many things that might have been decisive. But that was a major, major factor." In interviews in summer 2016, Ginsburg said she worried about Trump being elected, saying she worried about what it would mean for the Supreme Court and for the country. Trump responded she had overstepped boundaries and should retire. Ginsburg later issued a statement saying she regretted commenting on the election, and she has declined to answer questions about Trump since then. Ginsburg, 84, begins her 25th term on the court Monday.

Tommy G. Thompson, the 70-year-old former governor of Wisconsin, performed 50 push-ups for a local newspaper editorial board in the final week of his primary campaign. Thompson has campaigned extensively in the state for months, visiting with voters and receiving high-profile endorsements. The Republican Party has endorsed Thompson in the statewide primary. Thompson received the endorsement from his party in a race that pitted him against three fellow conservatives and splintered the Tea Party vote. "People doubted whether or not I had the stamina," Thompson said to a packed room of supporters at a hotel in Milwaukee, adding that he has been "shaking hands like I've never shaken before." Thompson was elected governor four times and served as health and human services secretary under President George W. Bush.
