Former Sen. Scott Brown won the Republican nomination to challenge incumbent Sen. Jeanne Shaheen to represent New Hampshire in the U.S. Senate, the Associated Press reports. The former senator defeated nine other Republican candidates in the Tuesday primary, including former state Sen. Jim Rubens. Brown will face Shaheen in the November general election. Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 2010 to 2013, lost his 2012 re-election bid to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.). He moved to New Hampshire in December 2013 and began his senatorial campaign in March. Before entering the Senate race in New Hampshire, Brown had weighed running for governor of Massachusetts. He announced his decision not to seek the governorship last August, citing his fulfillment in the private sector and saying he wanted "to continue with that process." Brown gained support from Massachusetts on the campaign trail but left the state to seek a seat in New Hampshire. Former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney endorsed Brown in July, calling him "a terrific American, an independent voice, an independent thinker." HuffPost Pollster, which aggregates all publicly available polling data, shows Shaheen with a safe lead over Brown with just under two months to the general election.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand spoke in Georgia on Thursday against Georgia's new anti-abortion law. She described the law and similar laws in Alabama, Ohio, and other states as part of "a nationwide assault on women's constitutional rights by ideological extremists." In an interview with The Washington Post before her Georgia trip, Gillibrand said: "If our party cannot support women's basic human rights, their fundamental freedoms to make decisions about their bodies and their futures, then we are not the party of women. I will not compromise on women's reproductive freedom." In Georgia, Gillibrand called for the protections of Roe v. Wade to be written into federal law, saying that "Federal law should supersede harmful state laws that take away women's reproductive freedom." She also advocated the repeal of the Hyde Amendment, which prevents the use of federal funds for health coverage that includes abortion. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Gillibrand's competitor in the 2020 Democratic primary, has also called for similar changes to federal law. Gillibrand reiterated a pledge to nominate only Supreme Court justices who would vote to uphold Roe v. Wade.

The parents of Republican Senate candidate Kevin Nicholson in Wisconsin have donated $2,700 to the primary campaign of the Democrat he hopes to unseat, CNN reports. The donation occurred months after Nicholson announced his candidacy for the seat in 2018. Nicholson's parents, Donna and Michael, reportedly donated $2,700 to Baldwin's primary campaign in December 2017. Nicholson had announced in July that he was seeking the Republican nomination for the Senate seat. Nicholson, a former Democrat, told CNN, "My parents have a different worldview than I do. It is not surprising that they would support a candidate like Tammy Baldwin who shares their perspective." Democrats have expressed concern about Baldwin's seat, with the incumbent targeted by outside spending from conservative groups. Democratic Party leaders have said the odds remain in Baldwin's favor. By early January, nine groups had spent more than $4.7 million on ads that attack Baldwin or boost one of the Republicans vying to oppose her, according to her campaign.

Four days after his announcement as Mitt Romney's running mate, Representative Paul D. Ryan traveled to Las Vegas for a meeting hosted by Sheldon Adelson, the billionaire casino mogul who has pledged to spend as much as $100 million this year to defeat President Obama. Adelson has contributed more money to defeat Obama than anyone: over $50 million has gone to the 2012 campaign, including $10 million to a super PAC backing Romney and $10 million to Crossroads GPS, which has run millions of dollars of advertisements against Obama. Romney aides declined to say who attended the meeting with Ryan. The location — a private room at one of Adelson's hotels — and leaks from the Romney campaign indicated the meeting was not a fundraiser. Aides to Romney said before the event that the meeting was not a fund-raiser.

Former FBI Director James Comey tweeted Sunday that he hoped the new year would bring "more ethical leadership focused on the truth and lasting values." Trump fired Comey in May, months after Comey said he and the president had an "uneasy" conversation in which the president demanded his "loyalty." Comey also testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee that Trump asked him to end the investigation into former national security adviser Michael Flynn. Flynn has since pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about contacts with Russian officials. Trump has denied that he asked Comey for his loyalty or asked him to drop the Flynn investigation. The New York Times reported that Trump called Comey a "nut job" while meeting with Russian officials in the Oval Office the day after the firing. "I faced great pressure because of Russia," Trump said, according to the Times, apparently referring to an investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. "That's taken off." Comey is currently working on a book titled A Higher Loyalty: Truth, Lies, and Leadership, due out in the spring.

The House impeachment investigation has moved past the first stage of witness testimony as the focus shifts from the Intelligence Committee's evidence gathering to the Judiciary Committee and the crafting of articles of impeachment. The Intelligence Committee released a report on Tuesday stating that Trump had "compromised national security to advance his personal political interests" in his dealings with Ukraine. The Judiciary Committee held a hearing the next day to consider historical and constitutional standards for impeachment and will hear evidence about Trump's conduct from House Intelligence lawyers on Monday. The hearings follow closed-door depositions with 17 government witnesses and televised public hearings with many officials relating to the president's July 25 phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. There is no clear indication of how long the process will take, but many Democrats have said they would like a vote by the full House before the end of the year. A list of scheduled events, followed by what has happened since the inquiry began, was published Oct. 2, 2019. Event and administration reaction information comes from House committee and White House documents and news reports.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (Ky.) on Tuesday publicly congratulated President-elect Joe Biden after weeks of refusing to recognize his presidential win. "Our country has officially a president-elect and a vice-president elect," he said. McConnell's acknowledgement came in a speech on the Senate floor after the Electoral College made Biden's win official on Monday. "Our system of government has processes to determine who will be sworn in on January the 20. The Electoral College has spoken. So today I want to congratulate President-elect Joe Biden," McConnell said, while recognizing Biden's decadeslong work in the U.S. Senate. "I also want to congratulate the vice president-elect, our colleague from California, Sen. Kamala Harris," McConnell continued. "Beyond our differences, all Americans can take pride in that our nation has a female vice president-elect for the very first time." McConnell was one of several Senate Republicans who had refused to acknowledge Biden's win. His recognition comes as President Donald Trump continues to contest the results of the Nov. 3 election, with him claiming, without supporting evidence, that the election was rigged and stolen from him.

President Obama has so far struck the right note on Iraq, where Sunni extremist militants are seizing territory and threatening the existence of the state. He has emphasized the need for political reform in Iraq and reached out to other countries that could have an impact on its fate. His opening to Iran has been the most controversial and potentially the most important move. Iran has the most leverage with the Shiite-led government in Baghdad and its prime minister, Nuri Kamal al-Maliki. The United States has been negotiating with Iran for months over Iran's nuclear program, but the agenda had not gone beyond that until Obama sent a senior State Department official to discuss Iraq with an Iranian official in Vienna this week. The two countries cooperated on Afghanistan in 2001 against the Taliban, and, in theory, they should be able to find common interest in stabilizing Iraq. Obama has called on Maliki to form a broadly representative government of Shiites, Sunnis and Kurds as a condition of any military action by the United States. The American ambassador in Iraq and a senior State Department official have been pressing that issue in Baghdad. Maliki on Tuesday refused to reach out to Sunnis.

A new NBC News/Marist poll released Wednesday shows Rep. Bruce Braley (D) and state Sen. Joni Ernst (R) tied at 43 percent in the Iowa Senate race. The poll also shows Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) leading former senator Scott Brown (R-Mass.) 50 percent to 42 percent, in line with other recent polls showing her leading. President Obama's approval rating is 37 percent in Iowa and 39 percent in New Hampshire. About half of voters in both states say the president's signature health-care law is a bad idea. In Iowa, a seat Democrats are defending, Braley is winning women by eight points while Ernst is winning men by the same spread. Shaheen is more personally popular than Brown is in New Hampshire, with more than half of voters saying they have a favorable opinion of her. Voters are split on their opinions of Brown. The poll comes as other recent surveys have shown Shaheen up by between 10 and 12 points. The NBC/Marist surveys of registered voters in each state were conducted from July 7 to 13.

Bernie Sanders supporters who have worked or volunteered for his campaign have come up with a draft proposal calling for the Vermont senator to suspend his presidential bid after the June 7 California primary, concede to Hillary Clinton, and build an independent organization aimed at defeating Donald J. Trump. The three-page document addresses a question facing Sanders's supporters: how to harness the energy of a movement now that his presidential bid appears to be bowing to the reality that Clinton will capture the Democratic nomination. The document suggests building "an organization, completely independent of the Clinton campaign," to defeat Trump before focusing on other goals after the November election. About a dozen current and former Sanders staff members and volunteers have been collaborating on the draft proposal, which was obtained by The New York Times and first reported by Politico. The authors believe Sanders will win the California primary, but write that "barring a miracle," he will not become the party's nominee. Two of the authors, who are former campaign staff members, confirmed the authenticity of the document. The authors all spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were working without the campaign's authorization.

Republican National Committee chair Michael Steele reacted to the news that Sen. Arlen Specter (R-Penn.) would switch parties. Steele said, "Some in the Republican Party are happy about this. I am not." He added, "Let's be honest -- Senator Specter didn't leave the GOP based on principles of any kind. He left to further his personal political interests because he knew that he was going to lose a Republican primary due to his left-wing voting record. Republicans look forward to beating Sen. Specter in 2010, assuming the Democrats don't do it first." Steele also said Specter "flip[ped] the bird" at the GOP leadership. He said, "For the senator to flip the bird back to Senator Cornyn and the Republican Senate Leadership, a team that stood by him, who went to the bat for him in 2004, to save his hide is not only disrespectful but down right rude." Steele added, "I'm sure his mama didn't raise him this way." Steele also said, "If Sen. Specter survives in the fall -- get ready to go to the mat, baby, because we're coming after you and taking you out."

CNN's Jake Tapper made a request during an appearance on "State of the Union" on Sunday: The president should tell the truth. During the appearance, Conway disagreed with Tapper over the state of President Donald Trump's credibility. Tapper asked, "Does his job include lying to the American people?" and "Because he continually does so and he undermines his own administration when he does so." Conway responded, accusing Tapper of wanting to go viral by using the words "Trump" and "lie" in the same sentence. Tapper said, "No, I would like him to stop lying, quite frankly." The two continued to discuss Trump's record. Conway denied there was any sort of "credibility crisis" within the current White House administration. Tapper referenced specific instances in which the president has lied to the American public and failed to correct the record. Tapper said, "It matters to people that the president tell them the truth."

White House Chief of Staff John F. Kelly criticized Rep. Frederica S. Wilson (D-Fla.). Sanders said he did not believe Kelly mischaracterized and gave his account of what took place. Sanders said Kelly and his family have made the ultimate sacrifice for the country and have led with honor and integrity. Sanders said Kelly is doing a great job as chief of staff and that he does not think Kelly has anything to correct or apologize for. Sanders said Kelly gave his account of what took place. A videotape of Wilson's speech at the 2015 dedication of a new FBI building in South Florida emerged. Kelly was angry at Wilson's criticism of President Trump for his handling of a phone call to a widow of a U.S. soldier who died in Niger. Kelly called Wilson an "empty barrel."

Senators Jeff Flake (R-AZ), who will leave the Senate this year, and Chris Coons (D-DE) brought their bill to the floor under unanimous consent. Majority Leader Mitch McConnell objected. Flake said he would not vote to advance any of the 21 judicial nominees pending in the Judiciary Committee or vote to confirm the 32 judges awaiting a confirmation vote on the floor until S. 2644 is brought to the full Senate for a vote. Flake has made similar statements before. In June, dozens of judges, including a Supreme Court justice, had been sent through committee with his consent and his vote. The vote is required to get nominees through the Judiciary Committee. There are 11 Republicans and 10 Democrats. Flake's refusal will make it more difficult to get nominees out of committee and to the floor. Fifty-three of them have refused.

President Obama will nominate Loretta E. Lynch, the top federal prosecutor in Brooklyn, to be the next attorney general, the White House said Friday. If confirmed, Lynch, 55, would be the first African-American woman to be the nation's top law enforcement official. Obama will announce her selection at a ceremony Saturday in the Roosevelt Room. He will be joined by Lynch and Eric H. Holder Jr., the current attorney general, who has announced his plans to step down. "Ms. Lynch is a strong, independent prosecutor who has twice led one of the most important U.S. attorney's offices in the country," Josh Earnest, the White House press secretary, said. He said Holder's tenure has been marked by historic gains in the areas of criminal justice reform and civil rights enforcement. The decision to announce Lynch's nomination came after days of speculation in the news media that she was a leading contender to replace Holder, an Obama confidant who has been a central figure in his cabinet since the start of his presidency.

During a virtual commencement speech for historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs) on Saturday, former President Barack Obama said the coronavirus pandemic has exposed a lack of leadership in the U.S. government. "More than anything, this pandemic has fully, finally torn back the curtain on the idea that so many of the folks in charge know what they're doing," Obama said, without naming specific officials. "A lot of them aren't even pretending to be in charge," he added.

Secretary of State John Kerry made an unannounced visit to Jordan on Friday to consult King Abdullah II about the Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas reiterated positions that highlighted the challenge Kerry faces in trying to shrink gaps between the two sides. Abbas told student activists from his Fatah faction that he would "not accept Israel's demands to recognize it as a Jewish state despite pressure put on us." He said he considers illegal all homes Israel built in the West Bank and East Jerusalem after it seized the territories in 1967. He said he considered all of East Jerusalem to be the capital of his future state and would not accept a single neighborhood, like Beit Hanina or Abu Dis, as some have suggested. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said in an interview broadcast Friday night on Israeli television that some Jewish settlements in the West Bank would not be part of his state if an agreement was reached. "Everyone understands that," he said, though it was a rare concession for him to make publicly to a domestic audience. "I'm going to make sure that that will be very limited."

Around the same time, a building at the Highlander Education and Research Center in New Market, Tennessee, an 80-year-old civil rights institution, was burning down. Hate-filled graffiti was being painted on buildings in Oklahoma. Specifically, Nazi-inspired swastikas, anti-Semitic phrases, and anti-LGBTQ and racist graffiti was left in front of the offices of the Oklahoma Democratic Party and the Chickasaw Nation in Oklahoma City. On March 29, Oklahoma City police released a security-camera image to the public of a potential suspect. On Wednesday, the Cleveland County Democratic Party headquarters, the Firehouse Art Center, and McKinley Elementary School, all in the Oklahoma city of Norman, were vandalized with similar graffiti. Law enforcement said they believed the incidents in the two cities were related. On Thursday, Norman police announced they had arrested a suspect, Allison Christine Johnson. The 45-year-old was taken into custody and booked on making "terrorist threats." According to the Oklahoman, Johnson is a registered Republican.

A man who was placed in isolation and tested for Ebola at New York's Mount Sinai Hospital this week has tested negative, according to the hospital. In a statement Wednesday afternoon, Mount Sinai said the Centers for Disease Control and Protection determined the patient kept in isolation since Monday is not infected with the disease. The man, according to the statement, "is in stable condition, is improving, and remains in the care of our physicians and nurses." The male patient had come to the Manhattan hospital's emergency room early Monday morning with high fever and gastrointestinal problems. He had recently returned from a West African country where Ebola has been reported. Early Monday evening, city health officials announced the patient was "unlikely to have Ebola," but that CDC test results were still pending. The confirmation of a negative test came hours after the World Health Organization announced that the worst Ebola outbreak in history has killed at least 932 people in four West African countries. The WHO also said Wednesday that it will convene a panel next week to discuss the use of experimental Ebola drugs to combat the outbreak that is ravaging Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea and has now spread into Nigeria.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz dominated the social media conversation during the Republican debate on CNBC last night, largely for using the media as a punching bag. The third GOP debate lacked some of the fire of the previous two contests and faced criticism from the media. Analytics partners at Zignal Labs tracked more than 650,000 mentions of the GOP field during the two-hour debate, down from the chatter in the previous debates. Cruz received the night's biggest moment with his criticism of the media's questions. In that one moment, Cruz captured a majority of the social and traditional media mentions of any candidate throughout the two-hour debate. In all, Cruz commanded 20 percent of the overall candidate chatter followed by Trump at 15 percent, Carson at 13 percent and Rubio at 12 percent. Jeb Bush commanded 8 percent of the media chatter during the debate, while Carly Fiorina, who turned in two previous debate performances, drew 7.5 percent of the mentions — the same share as Christie. The article also included a look at the top emojis used in tweets with the five most-frequently-mentioned GOP candidates Wednesday night.

A series of tweets by President Donald Trump resurface as tensions rise between the United States and Iran. Iran this week shot down a U.S. drone, which Tehran claims was flying over its territory. Washington called the attack an "unprovoked attack" and said the drone was in international airspace. Lawmakers from both parties have urged caution. The New York Times reported that Trump authorized retaliatory strikes on Iran that were scheduled for Thursday evening but called them off at the last minute. The Times said it is not clear why they were called off or if they could still take place. Trump formally kicked off his reelection campaign amid sagging poll numbers. In still other tweets, however, he accused Obama of being weak on Iran and even a "friend" to the nation.

President Donald Trump criticized the press on Saturday morning, calling it "the seriously dishonest and unhinged Lamestream Media." In a single-tweet, Trump said "we are not fighting" the "easy" Democrats but instead the press, which he alleged has never been "more inaccurate, unfair or corrupt." "They have gone totally CRAZY!" Trump wrote. He followed it up with his 2016 campaign slogan "MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!" It is not clear which piece of recent critical media coverage Trump was taking issue with. He has been widely condemned this week for the way in which he responded to last weekend's mass shootings in El Paso, Texas, and Dayton, Ohio. Critics said Trump failed to explicitly blame the massacres on guns or his government's inability to tackle the country's gun violence epidemic. The president was also chastised for his conduct during visits to hospitals where victims of the shootings were receiving treatment — where he boasted about himself and attacked political rivals.

Seth Meyers criticized Donald Trump's personal attorney Rudy Giuliani on Thursday night after Giuliani and other members of the president's legal team held a news conference alleging widespread voter fraud in their efforts to overturn the results of the election. Meyers said: "After a string of embarrassing court losses and bumbling performances in front of exasperated judges, Rudy Giuliani, voted America's wettest lawyer for three years running, held a marathon performance/performance art piece that was honestly at times so incomprehensible I thought I had to put on the closed captioning. And even when I did, the closed captioning said, 'Your guess is as good as mine.'" Meyers said it would be pointless to wade through the misinformation Giuliani put forth in the 90-minute event. He offered a sampling of the "televised therapy session" in which Giuliani described a scene from the 1992 film "My Cousin Vinny" to illustrate how GOP poll watchers were purportedly barred from monitoring vote counts.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie is set to seek re-election over his Democratic opponent Barbara Buono on Tuesday. Christie leads in polls by more than thirty points. Polls indicate that every demographic group is likely to support the winner. Christie's campaign has drawn attention from political observers, especially as attention shifts toward 2016. According to recent polls, Christie is running even or barely ahead of Buono among Latino voters. Buono chose labor leader Milly Silva as her running mate. Michael Duhaime, a top Christie advisor, said: "The governor has built inroads into the Latino community for the past 11 years going back to his days as a U.S. attorney. I think that as a party what we have done wrong is that we only talk to Hispanics in an election year, instead of doing it all the time. For us, there is dialogue and trust factor that we have built up."

On CNN's New Day, State Department spokesman John Kirby said, "We have said in the past, Chris that there was no policy prohibiting the use of a private email account here at the State Department, and that is still a fact." Kim Kardashian visited President Donald Trump at the White House on Wednesday to plead for a pardon for Alice Marie Johnson, a great-grandmother serving a life sentence for a nonviolent drug conviction. On Thursday, Trevor Noah said on "The Daily Show": "I know some of you were thinking, 'I can't believe this reality show moron is in the Oval Office.' But don't forget he was elected by the American people." Noah said he never saw coming Trump's follow-up move: pardoning Dinesh D'Souza, a "right-wing troll" and "brown Grand Wizard" who pleaded guilty to campaign finance violations and who is "known for saying things like, 'Obama is a gay Muslim' and 'Black people are thugs.'" Noah said he would have Kardashian write "racist Obama tweets and she'll be out in a week."

Donald Trump spoke to Fox News on Wednesday about dealing with "radical Islamic terrorism." Trump said he would consider naming former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani to head a commission on "radical Islam." "It's a real problem, so we'll figure it out and we will get it going but we have to be extremely careful," Trump said Wednesday. "In fact, I'm thinking about setting up a commission perhaps headed by Rudy Giuliani to take a very serious look at this problem. But this is a worldwide problem and we have to be smart." Giuliani was mayor of New York City during the September 11, 2001, terror attacks. The former mayor voted for Trump during April's New York primary but stopped short of officially endorsing the business mogul, distancing himself from the campaign. Giuliani criticized Trump's proposed ban on Muslims entering the United States in December, calling it a violation of the First Amendment. "It violates the First Amendment. You have no reasonable basis for it," Giuliani told Fox News at the time.

The United States on Friday targeted oil shipments from Venezuela to Cuba in its latest round of sanctions. The U.S. Treasury imposed sanctions on 34 vessels owned or operated by Venezuelan state-run oil company Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A., or PDVSA, and on two companies and a vessel that delivered oil to Cuba in February and March. Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin said in a statement: "Treasury is taking action against vessels and entities transporting oil, providing a lifeline to keep the illegitimate Maduro regime afloat. Cuba continues to profit from, and prop up, the illegitimate Maduro regime through oil-for-repression schemes as they attempt to keep Maduro in power." The latest round of U.S. sanctions, announced earlier by Vice President Mike Pence in a speech in Houston, aim to further undermine Maduro's government after the United States and most Western nations recognized opposition leader Juan Guaido as the rightful president of Venezuela. Guaido invoked the Venezuelan constitution to assume an interim presidency in January, arguing that Maduro's 2018 re-election was illegitimate.

Donald Trump gave an interview on Monday with Fox News' Sean Hannity. In the interview, Hannity said that the White House had treated him worse than Abraham Lincoln. Hannity also said: "Look, they gave out Pulitzer Prizes to people who got it wrong. All these people from The New York Times, which is a fake newspaper—we don't even want that in the White House anymore. We're gonna probably terminate that and The Washington Post—they're fake." Politico reported on Tuesday that the White House is planning to cancel subscriptions to the two papers. White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham confirmed that the White House would not renewing subscriptions.

During his re-election campaign this year, Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey hired a full-time director for Hispanic outreach, opened bilingual campaign offices, and secured key Latino endorsements. He also spoke out in favor of legislation allowing in-state tuition for unauthorized immigrants, which drew significant Latino and immigrant votes. For his efforts, about half of Hispanic voters cast ballots for him, which he won. Immigrants and their advocates accused the governor of waffling this week in his support of the in-state tuition legislation as he weighs a possible bid for president. "When he was running for election he was running to be able to say that, 'Look, I am the only Republican who can win the Latino vote,'" Giancarlo Tello, campaign manager for the New Jersey Tuition Equity for Dreamers Coalition, which has been lobbying for the bills, said on Wednesday. "Now that he already got the election, he's already flip-flopping."

President Barack Obama celebrated Thanksgiving at the White House on Thursday and called several members of armed forces to thank them for their service to the country. Many presidents have preferred to spend the holiday at Camp David, a Maryland mountaintop retreat, but the Obama family has more often chosen to have dinner at the Executive Mansion. The White House said Obama placed calls to several uniformed personnel. The White House said he talked to 10 service members — two each from the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force and Coast Guard. The White House said the president wished them and their families "a happy Thanksgiving." The guest list for the dinner was not made public, so it was not clear who would be joining the president, first lady Michelle Obama, daughters Sasha and Malia for the event. The menu was Thanksgiving, with turkey, honey-baked ham, cornbread stuffing, oyster stuffing, greens, macaroni and cheese, sweet potatoes, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole and dinner rolls. For dessert, the family had a choice of huckleberry pie, pecan pie, chocolate cream pie, sweet potato pie, banana cream pie or coconut cream pie.

Thousands of people are expected to visit Capitol Hill to pay respects to congressman and civil rights leader John Lewis, but President Donald Trump will not be among them. "No, I won't be going," the president told reporters Monday. "No." The president made the comment as he was leaving the White House for North Carolina. Lewis' American flag-draped casket was arriving at the Capitol and being carried into the building by a military honor guard. Lewis, who died July 17 at the age of 80, will be lying in state at the U.S. Capitol until Thursday's funeral at Atlanta's historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, which the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. once led. Trump did not say why he was declining to visit Lewis. Lewis was critical of Trump during his time in office. A week before the 2017 inauguration, Lewis said he did not consider Trump a legitimate president. Vice President Mike Pence and presumptive Democratic nominee Joe Biden are expected to pay their respects. One Twitter user said the president's decision was just another sign he is a racist. Others considered his presence inappropriate.

Trump tweeted an anti-Semitic photograph. Paul Ryan, who is supposed to be the intelligent one, said, "Look, anti-Semitic images - they've got no place in a presidential campaign. Candidates should know that." Ryan then said, "I don't know what flunky put this up there - they've obviously got to fix that." The article states that Ryan's statement was made because it cannot be the responsibility of the candidate who has been spewing racist bilge for the past year and cannot possibly have anything to do with him. The article also states that Ryan should stop trying to help Trump. Comments are closed on the story.

Former New York City Mayor Ed Koch has been placed in the intensive care unit at New York-Presbyterian Hospital, his spokesman George Arzt said Thursday. Arzt spoke to the former mayor this morning and told CNN affiliate WCBS that the mayor "was in obvious discomfort." "After I spoke to him ... his lead doctor and cardiologist decided that he should be put into the intensive care unit," Arzt said. Koch, 88, was hospitalized last September for anemia and underwent a blood transfusion at the same hospital. The lawyer-turned-public-servant was a U.S. congressman from 1968 until he ran for mayor of the city in 1977. He served three terms — from 1978 to 1989 — until he was defeated in a Democratic primary by David Dinkins. After leaving office, Koch practiced law, hosted a radio show, was a newspaper columnist, and made numerous appearances on television series as himself. His cameos included "Sex and the City," "Spin City," and "Picket Fences." For two years starting in 1997, he was the judge on the syndicated show "The People's Court."

Hillary Clinton addressed an audience in San Diego on Thursday. She said Republican opponent Donald J. Trump was hopelessly unprepared and temperamentally unfit to be commander in chief. Electing him would be a "historic mistake." Clinton said, "This is not someone who should ever have the nuclear codes. Because it's not hard to imagine Donald Trump leading us into a war just because somebody got under his very thin skin." The campaign had grappled for weeks over how to handle Trump. Clinton said the foreign policy pronouncements were "not even really ideas, just a series of bizarre rants, personal feuds and outright lies."

Senior U.S. intelligence officials told NBC News that they now believe with "a high level of confidence" that Russian President Vladimir Putin became personally involved in the covert Russian campaign to interfere in the U.S. presidential election. Two senior officials with direct access to the information said new intelligence shows that Putin personally directed how hacked material from Democrats was leaked and otherwise used. The intelligence came from diplomatic sources and spies working for U.S. allies, the officials said. A high-level intelligence source told NBC News that Putin's objectives were multifaceted. The official said what began as a "vendetta" against Hillary Clinton morphed into an effort to show corruption in American politics and to "split off key American allies by creating the image that [other countries] couldn't depend on the U.S. to be a credible global leader anymore." All 538 members of the Electoral College must be presented with an intelligence briefing detailing connections between the Russian Government and the Trump Campaign. There was a server in communication. President Obama must brief the country about the extent of Russian interference in the election and aid to the Trump campaign.

Eagle Forum President Phyllis Schlafly said she never urged Rep. Todd Akin (R-Mo.) to end his bid against Sen. Claire McCaskill (D), contrary to a BuzzFeed report. Schlafly has been a vocal supporter of Akin since he mused about "legitimate rape." Most prominent Republicans abandoned the congressman. Schlafly said it would be significant if she had private doubts about his electability. She said it is not so. "I criticized his campaign, but in no way was that meant to urge him to get out," she told The Post. "I was very critical of the staff and it was a strong statement to urge him to hire good people." She added that she believed Akin was following her advice; he recently hired Rick Tyler, a long-time aide to Newt Gingrich. The meeting in question happened in Tampa, shortly before the Republican National Convention, during a conference held by the conservative Center for National Policy. Schlafly said that anyone who claimed she wanted Akin to drop out must have misunderstood. She noted that at the same event, she held a fundraiser for Akin's campaign.

President Obama said on Wednesday that he believed the United States had "a credible way forward" in its nuclear negotiations with Iran. He suggested that after consultations with Congress, which has been threatening additional sanctions, he would seek an extension of the talks beyond Sunday's deadline. "There are still some significant gaps between the international community and Iran," he said in the White House press room, before announcing additional sanctions on Russia, "and we have more work to do." Iran has signaled it wants more time to negotiate. Obama is almost certain to face opposition on Capitol Hill if he agrees to the extension. Republicans and some Democrats have argued that Tehran is stalling. It is unclear whether Iran will demand more sanctions relief in return for an extension. In Vienna over the past two weeks, as Iran and the West began to define what a deal might look like, Obama's aides have debated a question that no longer seems theoretical: How much risk is the United States willing to take to reach a deal that will almost certainly leave Iran with some potential, over the long term, to make a nuclear weapon?

Mitt Romney said on Tuesday, "we have a good reason to believe that there's a bombshell in Donald Trump's taxes." Romney had not released his tax returns as the 2012 Republican nominee. Trump responded: "It's my honor, real honor, to endorse Mitt Romney," with Romney and his wife standing nearby. Trump called Romney "tough" and "smart" and said, "he's not going to continue to allow bad things to happen to this country." The article characterized Romney as a loser and a loser who was going after Trump's tax returns. According to Trump, "my returns are extremely complex" and "I'm in no rush to do it." Comments on the story were closed.

Outgoing Vice President Joe Biden said in an interview with PBS NewsHour's Judy Woodruff broadcast on Thursday, "Grow up, Donald." Woodruff asked about President-elect Donald Trump's tweets, including one this week calling Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) the "head clown." Biden urged Trump to focus on the issues instead. "Time to be an adult, you're president," Biden said. "You gotta do something, show us what you have." Biden said it is time for Trump to propose legislation, let the public decide and allow lawmakers to vote. "It's going to be much clearer what he's for and against, and what we're for and against now that it's going to get down to actually discussing in detail the issues that affect people's lives," Biden said. Biden also spoke about Trump's criticism of the U.S. intelligence community, the Affordable Care Act and his plans after leaving office.

President Trump said he would nominate Rep. John Ratcliffe, whom Republicans rejected last year as Director of National Intelligence. Trump had withdrawn the offer because Ratcliffe's resume was a lie. Trump tweeted in August that Ratcliffe was out of the running. In that tweet, Trump wrote: "Would have completed process earlier, but John wanted to wait until after IG Report was finished. John is an outstanding man of great talent!" The nomination was withdrawn because Republicans opposed Ratcliffe, including Richard Burr, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee and would be the nominee. Burr had warned Trump last time around not to tap Ratcliffe for the job because he was partisan.

President-elect Donald Trump wished a happy new year Saturday morning to all, including his "many enemies." Trump tweeted: "Happy New Year to all, including to my many enemies and those who have fought me and lost so badly they just don't know what to do. Love." The tweet recalled a 2013 tweet from Trump extending best wishes to "the haters and losers" on September 11, 2013: "@realDonaldTrump: I would like to extend my best wishes to all, even the haters and losers, on this special date, September 11th." Trump has continued to criticize opponents and the media during his transition, and has been at odds with the Obama administration over its belief that Russia meddled in the 2016 election to aid his campaign. The President-elect has spent the holidays at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. Later Saturday, Vice President-elect Mike Pence posted on Twitter: "Happy New Year! 2017 will be the year we Make America Great Again! We wish you every blessing for healthy & prosperous New Year! The Pences."

CNN correspondent Sanjay Gupta has withdrawn his name from consideration as the nation's next surgeon general, opting to continue his reporting and his medical career. Gupta will discuss his decision and the president's health care agenda on CNN's Larry King Live tonight. Fox News reported earlier Thursday that Gupta might be out. Jerry Farrell, who heads the Commissioned Officers Association, told FOXNews.com Thursday that CNN's chief medical correspondent is known to have taken himself out of consideration. "The general consensus from everybody is Gupta is no longer in contention ... it's more he's withdrawing himself," Farrell said, citing conversations he has had with "well-placed" individuals. According to Farrell, Gupta had misgivings about both the pay cut he would have to take and the fact that he could be reporting to two high-level bosses: both the health secretary and health reform office director. When Gupta's name surfaced, President Obama had planned to have former Sen. Tom Daschle fill both of those roles. After Daschle withdrew from consideration, the president named two separate nominees for the posts.

Donald Trump has named former World Wrestling Entertainment CEO Linda McMahon as his nominee to head the Small Business Association. McMahon is the co-founder of WWE along with her husband, Vince McMahon, and is twice a Republican Senate candidate from Connecticut. She stepped down from WWE in 2009 and ran two failed bids for the Senate in 2010 and 2012. She donated $6 million in August and September to Rebuilding America Now, a super PAC that supported Trump's presidential bid. McMahon is the single largest donor to the Trump Foundation, having given nearly as much as the total amount Trump and his companies have donated to the foundation.

On the day Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner were dining Xi Jinping and other Chinese dignitaries, Ivanka Trump received the go-ahead to promote her products in China. Georgia voters have one final chance to cast their ballots this week in two Senate races. Congress will certify Joe Biden's victory over President Donald Trump by counting Electoral College votes. Control of the U.S. Senate will be determined by runoff elections in Georgia on Tuesday. Republican David Perdue is running for reelection against Democrat Jon Ossoff, and Sen. Kelly Loeffler (R) is facing off against Democrat Raphael Warnock. Trump and Biden have both campaigned with their party's candidates ahead of the election. Trump has also repeatedly criticized the state's GOP election officials. He threatened Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger (R) with criminal prosecution unless he could "find" 11,780 votes in Trump's favor. On Wednesday, Congress will formally count the Electoral College votes from the 2020 presidential election, certifying Biden's win. At least 12 Republican senators have pledged to object to the vote certification, dragging out the process but ultimately not changing the result of the race.

Former FBI deputy Director Andrew McCabe will likely face federal criminal charges for allegedly misleading Justice Department investigators who were investigating the leak of an investigation into the Clinton Foundation during the 2016 campaign. McCabe's legal team received notice from a top Justice Department official indicating that the office had rejected their appeal of the decision by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia to move forward with the case, according to a person familiar with the matter. McCabe's team had asked the D.C. office's principal deputy attorney general to veto the D.C. office's decision to indict. USA Today first reported the news Thursday. An investigation found that McCabe lacked candor about whether he authorized media disclosures about the Clinton investigation during the 2016 campaign. McCabe filed suit last month over his 2018 dismissal, which came hours ahead of his planned retirement. President Donald Trump had targeted McCabe, a Republican, in part due to his wife's run for office as a Democratic candidate. McCabe went on to write a book about his experiences in the FBI, and recently joined CNN as a commentator.

Defense Secretary Ashton B. Carter will convene a meeting in Brussels on Thursday to urge about two dozen of his counterparts to contribute more to the American-led campaign against the Islamic State. President Obama told Carter in December that as the administration intensifies its efforts against the Islamic State, other countries — particularly Arab ones — need to do more. Carter said Tuesday he was confident he would leave the meeting this week with pledges of aid including air support, special forces, trainers and money. Foreign policy analysts and former American diplomats said the administration may gain some help from European allies but continues to miscalculate what the Arab countries are willing to do. Ryan C. Crocker, a former United States ambassador to Iraq, said: "The thing is, the Islamic State is nobody's top enemy. For the Turks, the enemy is the Kurds, and for the Sunni Arabs, it's Iran, followed by Assad," referring to President Bashar al-Assad of Syria.

The article stated that standard words for campaign mishaps — "flip-flop," "retreat," "walk-back" — do not apply to this candidate's spirals through unreality.

Hillary Clinton's campaign raised $63 million in July, its most successful month to date, according to campaign officials who said the campaign received $8.7 million in donations in the 24 hours after Clinton's speech Thursday accepting the nomination. Clinton also raised $26 million in July for the Democratic National Committee. Clinton began August with $58 million in the bank. At a rally on Monday, Donald J. Trump said his campaign had "raised with small donors $35.8 million. I believe it's 517K donors." The candidate did not specify whether that figure applied only to his campaign or to his joint fund-raising operation with the Republican National Committee. His campaign did not respond to a request for more information.

The husband-and-wife team of Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, now both senior federal government officials, has been alongside President Trump as the White House has hosted dozens of chief executives and a handful of world leaders in recent weeks. The crowd has included the top executives of some of the world's largest automobile, airline, chemical, pharmaceutical and tech companies. Mr. Kushner will continue to keep such select company now that he has helped create a new office that Mr. Trump is calling the White House Office of American Innovation. The financial disclosure report released late Friday for Mr. Kushner shows that he and his wife still benefit financially from a real estate and investment empire worth as much as $740 million. Several prominent experts on the subject said the couple is walking on perilous legal and ethical ground. Unlike Mr. Trump, who is exempt from conflict of interest laws, both Mr. Kushner and Ms. Trump — who took a formal White House position this past week — are forbidden under federal criminal and civil law to take any action that might benefit their particular financial holdings.

North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un proposed direct talks with South Korea on New Year's Day. The proposal came as sanctions appeared to be affecting the North, with reports of shortages in the North and pressure by Washington to intercept ships engaged in fuel smuggling. South Korea's president, Moon Jae-in, embraced the initiative. Moon sees his first concrete chance to carry out his campaign agenda of engaging with the North while also easing tensions as President Trump's threats have rattled the country. In a telephone message delivered through the restored cross-border hotline on Friday, North Korea accepted the South's proposal that the two sides begin talks on Tuesday, South Korean officials said. The talks, to be held in the border village Panmunjom, will be the first high-level inter-Korean dialogue in two years. Skepticism abounds in Washington and among South Koreans.

A number of political pundits expressed disapproval over the resignation of Mozilla CEO Brendan Eich after news of his support of a 2008 anti-gay marriage campaign came to light. Last week, Bill Maher suggested that Eich's resignation was the result of pressure from a "gay mafia." Maher's remarks sparked social media debate. Some lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) rights advocates said his words are ripe for misinterpretation. "What happened in the Brendan Eich situation was actually not as a result of pressure that came from within the LGBT movement," said Freedom to Marry's John Becker, who is also a HuffPost Gay Voices blogger. Noting that Maher has been an ally to the LGBT community in the past, he added, "This is all about internal pressure from within the Mozilla community itself." Activist and political consultant Scott Wooledge said that Eich's resignation was partly due to "pre-existing opposition" from within the Mozilla group, as evidenced by the fact that three board members stepped down ahead of the CEO's appointment.

Hillary Clinton's campaign raised $63 million in July, its most successful month to date, according to campaign officials who said the campaign received $8.7 million in donations in the 24 hours after Clinton's speech Thursday accepting the nomination. Clinton also raised $26 million in July for the Democratic National Committee. Clinton began August with $58 million in the bank. At a rally on Monday, Donald J. Trump said his campaign had "raised with small donors $35.8 million. I believe it's 517K donors." The candidate did not specify whether that figure applied only to his campaign or to his joint fund-raising operation with the Republican National Committee. His campaign did not respond to a request for more information.

President-elect Donald J. Trump invited the leading anchors and executives of television news to join him on Monday for a private meeting of minds. On-air stars including Lester Holt, Charlie Rose, George Stephanopoulos and Wolf Blitzer headed to Trump Tower for the off-the-record gathering, typically the kind of event where journalists and politicians clear the air after a hard-fought campaign. Trump said the television networks were dishonest in their reporting and shortsighted in missing signs of his upset victory. He criticized some in the room by name, including CNN's president Jeffrey A. Zucker, according to multiple people briefed on the meeting who were granted anonymity to describe confidential discussions. It is not unusual for journalists to agree to off-the-record sessions with prominent politicians, including President Obama, as a way to gain insights and develop relationships.

The Republican presidential debate was held this week. The event was the last until December. Donald Trump proposed boycotting Starbucks for changing its holiday coffee cup design. Trump also promised a crowd recently that when he is president, "we're all going to be saying 'Merry Christmas' again." Jeb Bush sent a mass email before the event began asking his friends to send him a dollar so he would "know you're at home cheering me on." The article reported that the debate was more issue-oriented than previous debates. The subject of the debate was the economy, and the article stated that when people talk tax plans, they will not hear anything except the word low and occasionally flat.

Among the 36 states in which same-sex couples can marry, 20 have invoked the Constitution to strike down marriage bans. The Supreme Court originally declined to hear a same-sex marriage case even though three federal appeals courts had already struck down marriage bans. The 6th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a ban, and the Supreme Court decided to intervene. Those rulings would conflict with the nation's highest court if the justices uphold the power of states to limit marriage to heterosexual couples. A decision is expected by late June in cases from Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and Tennessee. Top officials in some states, including California, seem determined to allow gay and lesbian couples to continue to marry no matter how the court decision comes out. Some county clerks, who issue marriage licenses, might not go along, experts said. In other states, a high court ruling in favor of state bans would prohibit any more such unions but could give rise to new efforts to repeal marriage bans through the legislature or the ballot.

Michelle Obama discussed White House chores during an appearance on "The View." Gayle King asked about Malia Obama's party clothes. Obama said she told the girls, "They will not live in the White House forever. And if they're 17, 18 and can't make a bed, they will be pretty pathetic." Obama said that Malia will have to start doing laundry soon, which is the order of the First Family. Obama also said that First Lady Sasha Obama and First Lady Malia Obama have had pooty duty before, but that Bo "goes in a private place" and is "really good about that." Obama also said Sasha Obama and Malia Obama take Bo out after dinner, during weekends when they are not in school, and that Malia Obama is in charge of Bo in the evenings so he has to do his last walk rain or shine, homework or no homework.

President Obama sent a plan on Tuesday to close the United States military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. The plan faces near-certain rejection by Congress. The prison has come to symbolize the darker side of the nation's antiterrorism efforts. Obama outlined a series of steps at the White House that he said were a practical blueprint for transferring prisoners. In presenting them, the president made little secret of his frustration that his quest to close Guantánamo, once regarded as a bipartisan moral imperative, had become a divisive political issue. "I am very cleareyed about the hurdles to finally closing Guantánamo: The politics of this are tough," Obama said during a 17-minute address. "I don't want to pass this problem on to the next president, whoever it is. And if, as a nation, we don't deal with this now, when will we deal with it?"

Hillary Clinton answered a question about Bill Clinton's alleged sexual impropriety on Thursday at a campaign stop in Hooksett, New Hampshire. A woman asked Clinton: "Secretary Clinton, you recently came out to say that all rape victims should be believed. But would you say that Juanita Broaddrick, Kathleen Willey and Paula Jones be believed as well?" Clinton responded: "Well, I would say that everyone should be believed at first until they are disbelieved based on evidence." She then moved on to the next question. Broaddrick in 1999 said on NBC's "Dateline" that Bill Clinton had raped her two decades earlier, during his campaign for Arkansas governor's office. Willey was a Democratic activist and White House volunteer who said that in 1993, Bill Clinton had grabbed and kissed her in the Oval Office's private study. Jones was an Arkansas state worker who sued Bill Clinton for sexual harassment, saying he had propositioned her for sex and exposed himself during a 1991 meeting in a hotel room. Bill Clinton's office declined CNN's request for comment.

Rep. Elijah Cummings, chair of the House Oversight and Reform Committee, is spending Wednesday in a hearing with Michael Cohen, Donald Trump's longtime personal lawyer and fixer. Hours before the hearing, Cummings sent letters to two additional Trump lawyers seeking information about Trump's legally mandated financial disclosures and payments. Cummings is seeking to depose Sheri Dillon, Trump's tax lawyer who participated in a January 2017 photo opportunity with Trump to settle concerns about conflicts of interest between his businesses and his official role. Cummings' questions for Dillon and former deputy White House counsel Stefan Passantino center on Trump's financial disclosure forms from June 2017 and May 2018. The former does not mention a debt to Cohen, while the latter covers a payment to him. Michael Cohen is providing information. The investigation into Trump's finances will not end on Wednesday.

Ukraine is experiencing a political crisis. Dozens of people died this week and hundreds more were injured as protesters fought police in the capital, Kiev. Lethal violence has been spreading to the rest of the country, and a truce announced early Thursday fell apart as the death toll kept growing. The protests began in November as peaceful protests favoring closer ties with the European Union and greater autonomy from the influence of Russia. The government and opposition alike must make the difficult but necessary choice to compromise and reconcile. European leaders should immediately schedule direct talks with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and his top officials to find a temporary solution to stop the bloodshed and a longer-term plan that would allow Ukrainians to determine their political destiny in a peaceful and democratic fashion. The West must make clear to Moscow that Ukraine — a bridge between East and West — should not be the object of geopolitical games. European leaders should back down from their threats of sanctions against Ukraine and its president, Viktor F. Yanukovych, which would only prolong the suffering of the Ukrainian people. Russian interference in Ukraine's internal affairs must not be tolerated.

The article presents the Democratic Party as working together in a "good cop/bad cop dynamic" regarding policy. It states that Republicans can adopt any extremist position they like, including an end to the New Deal, removing obstacles to corporations doing whatever they want, and making sure the rich pay little in taxes. The article argues that Democrats can adopt this approach, stating, "These nasty Republicans want to make things terrible for you. We're much more reasonable-- we'll only do those Republican things half as much, so you should support us." The article reports that the rich get richer while the poor get poorer, and the New Deal is slowly shredded. The article states it cannot believe progress can be made in the two-party system. It states that the "fiscal cliff" negotiations have resulted in keeping the vast majority of the Dubya tax cuts, guaranteeing deficits indefinitely, which gives the banksters ever more control over the entire economy. The article asks whether the Occupy movement can be heated up again, and states that without "class war" there is no hope of improvement.

NBC Universal said in a statement that after further review it recognized the insensitive nature of the advertisement and decided to cease airing it across its properties as soon as possible. NBCUniversal's decision to run the Trump campaign ad differed from CNN's, which publicly responded when Donald Trump Jr. criticized the network for refusing to run it. The network's public relations account posted on Twitter: "CNN has made it abundantly clear in its editorial coverage that this ad is racist. When presented with an opportunity to be paid to take a version of this ad, we declined." The advertisement was paid for by Donald Trump for President. The advertisement demonizes immigrants and gaslight his followers into believing the country is under threat of imminent invasion. Fox News pulled the advertisement. The advertisement was also pulled by Fox News. The network's statement: "Upon further review, the intended damage has been done and we're happy to pull the ad with less than 24 hours to the vote."

Former Florida Governor Charlie Crist, 57, announced Monday that he would run for the office again, this time as a Democrat. Crist, a former Republican, spoke to a crowd of about 250 supporters in a bayfront park in St. Petersburg. He said education, voting rights, the environment, and bipartisanship have been silenced by financial bullies and special interests. Crist said the reason is to put him back in charge. He spent much of his speech criticizing Gov. Rick Scott, who was elected in 2010 on a wave of Tea Party support. Crist described Scott as an extremist who cares more about big business than the lives of ordinary Floridians.

President Obama on Monday will take executive actions to ease the burden of college loan debt for potentially millions of Americans, in a White House event coinciding with Senate Democrats' plans for legislation addressing a concern of many voters in this midterm election year. Before an East Room audience, Obama is scheduled to announce "new steps to further lift the burden of crushing student loan debt," said a White House official who declined to be identified describing the actions in advance of the president's event. Despite past actions by the administration, borrowers' debt load is growing and retarding the ability to buy homes, start businesses, or otherwise spend to spur the economy, economists say. Obama's main action will be to expand on a 2010 law that capped borrowers' repayments at 10 percent of their monthly income. The intent is to extend such relief to an estimated five million people with older loans who are currently ineligible — those who got loans before October 2007 or stopped borrowing by October 2011. The relief would not be available until December 2015, officials said, given the time needed for the Education Department to propose and put new regulations into effect.

Donald Trump referred to Joe Biden as "Sleepy Joe" on Thursday night. The two presidential candidates held town halls on rival networks — Trump on NBC and Biden on ABC — after their events concluded. After the president's town hall, which lasted an hour, Trump stayed for a few photos but did not answer voter questions, according to USA Today. After the 90-minute broadcast ended, he stayed on at least 30 additional minutes to answer questions to voters who did not speak during the ABC broadcast. Topics ranged from whether the National Guard should quell protests to the Trump administration's Muslim travel ban. Mediaite noted that Biden received lots of praise for answering voter questions off-camera. ABC News showed the interactions in the background while pundits speculated on what it meant. Some social media viewers are asking ABC News to make the footage with sound available for viewing, according to Newsweek.

In November, Bob Filner became the first Democrat in two decades to be elected mayor of San Diego. He celebrated with his fiancée at his side in Old Trolley Barn Park, where he thanked hundreds of supporters who had showed up. After a week in which seven women publicly accused him of sexual harassment, it was all but impossible to find any Filner supporters in Old Trolley Barn Park. Democrats and Republicans have been united on an issue: their insistence that the mayor resign. On Friday, the mayor announced he would take two weeks away from City Hall to seek what he described as intensive behavior therapy. Many residents said he was dragging the city through the mud in hopes of salvaging his own career. Mona Mukherjea-Gehrig, 46, said: "I'm bummed. I voted for him. Can you change in two weeks? That's a joke. What are you going to do in two weeks?"

Kathleen Sebelius, the woman who provided the Obamacare rollout, said she is not considering a run for the Senate seat. The article reports that Senator Pat Roberts, a former friend, criticized Sebelius because he was afraid of a challenge from Sebelius. A spokeswoman said: "Secretary Sebelius is continuing her important work at H.H.S. and is not considering a run for the Senate." Some Democrats had told The Times' Jeremy Peters that they wanted to see Sebelius run. The idea initially appeared unusual, given the health care website's crash. Fox News reported that it has a new variation on "The Bachelor" in which 12 American women believe they are competing for the hand of England's Prince Harry.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate on Wednesday for the second time since the 2008 financial crisis. Economists have discussed the impact this will have on markets. The Fed's decision can affect the cost of housing, cars, student loans and interest on credit card interest, though not necessarily immediately. When the Fed raises rates, other expenses eventually tick up. The move is part of what will be a slow upward climb for the federal funds rate. Banks are ordered by law to have a certain amount of money in reserve, so they typically make overnight loans to each other to keep those balances up. The federal funds rate is the level of interest that applies to those short-term loans. Because the rate has been close to zero since 2008, as part of the Fed's strategy to bring the nation out of a recession, there is hardly anywhere for it to go but up. As the economy improves and President-elect Donald J. Trump unveils his stimulus package, economists expect rates to rise steadily over a period of years.

A DealBook Briefing was published on Tuesday covering the topic of National Champions having to deliver and how companies plan to spend tax savings. The briefing covered President Trump's block of Broadcom's bid for Qualcomm, Larry Page's flying taxi start-up, and the potential path for Goldman Sachs' presumptive heir. President Trump intervened to protect Qualcomm from Broadcom, a foreign company that wanted to buy the San Diego-based chip maker. The administration intervened because it had concerns about national security. In a March 5 letter, the administration stated that Broadcom would reduce Qualcomm's spending on research and development, causing Qualcomm to lose ground in the race to develop new technologies such as 5G, which is designed to make wireless networks faster and more reliable. Chinese companies may gain an advantage in 5G.

Former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell and his wife Maureen McDonnell are on trial for conspiring to use his office for personal enrichment. Their lawyers presented their legal defense on Tuesday. The defense was that their marriage was broken and they did not communicate enough to conspire about anything. In opening arguments in the couple's corruption trial in federal court in Richmond, their lawyers said they planned to rely on the details of their union as the basis of their legal defense. It was the first time the McDonnells' version of events had been heard in the case. The indictment against them charges the couple with accepting more than $165,000 in cash and luxury gifts from a Virginia businessman. Ms. McDonnell, her lawyer said, had a "crush" on the businessman, Jonnie R. Williams Sr., the prosecutors' star witness. The government said Williams would detail the designer clothing, vacations, golf rounds and cash he provided in exchange for the governor's help in promoting his company, which made a dietary supplement.

The Arkansas Democratic Party pointed out the irony of voter ID laws. The Arkansas Democratic Party said: "I wonder if he stills supports the law now." Asa Hutchinson was turned away from the polls because he did not have proper ID as required under Arkansas's Voter ID Law. Hutchinson's support for making it harder for Arkansans to cast a ballot was noted. The article stated Hutchinson's experience at the polls yesterday will cause him to reevaluate the burden the Voter ID law places on senior citizens, students, and those serving in the military. Arkansas's Voter ID law was ruled unconstitutional and is still under review.

Despite broad party support for Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) to continue as Speaker of the House on Wednesday, 19 Democrats cast votes for other candidates. Rep. Heath Shuler (D-N.C.), who had challenged and lost to Pelosi in a Democratic caucus vote, received 11 votes. Shuler voted for himself. Other Democrats received protest votes, as well, including Reps. Dennis Cardoza (Calif.), Jim Costa (Calif.), Jim Cooper (Tenn.), John Lewis (Ga.), Marcy Kaptur (Ohio), and the newly elected Minority Whip Steny Hoyer (Md.). Rep. Sanford Bishop (Ga.) chose to vote "present," while Rep. Peter DeFazio (Ore.), a Pelosi dissenter, missed the vote entirely. The Associated Press reported that under House rules, each party puts up a candidate to be the next speaker. All 241 in the new Republican majority voted for Boehner on Wednesday, except for Boehner himself, who did not vote, while 173 Democrats backed Pelosi. The full list, via The Hill, appears below.

Anheuser-Busch proposes selling Corona rights in the United States. A federal judge in Washington on Wednesday agreed to delay proceedings to allow Anheuser-Busch to revise its efforts to take over the Mexican brewers of Corona and Corona Light. Judge Richard Roberts put off any court proceedings until March 19. Last month Justice Department antitrust lawyers blocked Anheuser-Busch InBev from taking over Grupo Modelo of Mexico. The Justice officials argued that the merger of the nation's No. 1 brewer, makers of Budweiser and Bud Light, and the nation's third-largest brewer, Grupo Modelo, would be anticompetitive and harm consumers. The officials said beer prices would go up. Anheuser-Busch then agreed to sell the rights to Corona and other Grupo Modelo brands in the United States to an independent company, Constellation Brands, a large wine company. It is unclear whether that $3 billion deal to sell the Corona rights would be enough to satisfy the Justice Department. The Anheuser-Busch merger with Grupo Modelo is estimated to be worth $20 billion.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has informed the Obama administration that he will not attend President Obama's nuclear security summit in Washington next week, according to a senior U.S. official familiar with the situation. The move could indicate further tension between the United States and Israel and may distract from the Obama administration's attempts to highlight the nature of the 46-nation summit aimed at reducing nuclear weapons. The Israeli government is sending Deputy Prime Minister Dan Meridor in Netanyahu's place, U.S. National Security Council spokesman Mike Hammer announced Thursday. "Israel is a close ally, and we look forward to continuing to work closely with it on issues related to nuclear security," Hammer said Thursday. "This is a summit focused on addressing the security of nuclear materials and geared toward having the participants take practical measures to ensure that terrorists cannot get access to those materials." The news comes after Obama and Russian President Dmitry Medvedev signed a major nuclear arms treaty in the Czech Republic earlier Thursday. The new Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty -- known as START -- reduces the number of nuclear weapons held by the United States and Russia by about one-third, among other provisions.

A new Quinnipiac University poll shows Cory Booker leads GOP nominee Steve Lonegan by 12 points among likely voters in the Oct. 16 New Jersey special election. Booker is at 53 percent, while Lonegan is at 41 percent. Before the primary, a pollster showed Booker led Lonegan by 25 points. That poll was among registered voters rather than likely voters. The poll shows Booker's lead is due almost completely to women, who back him by a 60-34 margin. Among men, the two candidates are split, with 48 percent choosing Lonegan and 46 percent choosing Booker. The poll shows Booker remains popular, though not as much as other polls. His favorable rating is 53 percent favorable and 30 percent unfavorable. Lonegan is less well-known, with 35 percent viewing him favorably and 22 percent unfavorably. The two are running for the seat of the late-Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D-N.J.). National Republicans have not yet endorsed Lonegan's candidacy.

Republican vice presidential nominee Mike Pence said on "Fox News Sunday" that New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie will still lead Donald Trump's transition team despite the Bridgegate controversy. Pence said Christie has continued to state his position that he had no knowledge of the actions taken. He said Christie said late in the week that what the convictions proved proved was right to immediately fire those people for the actions taken. Pence, the governor of Indiana, said he and Trump are "grateful for Chris Christie's role in the campaign." He said there are no plans to alter Christie's role, particularly on Election Day. Pence said there are no changes in personnel in the waning days of the campaign. He said they are 100% focused on bringing home a great victory for the American people. Two former Christie aides were convicted last week of charges tied to the closure of the George Washington Bridge in what they described as political retribution. Testimony during their trial indicated Christie knew what was happening.

Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) won reelection against State Treasurer Josh Mandel on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press. Recent polls showed Brown with a consistent but narrow lead in his bid for a second term. Mandel received over $22 million in outside spending, according to the Center for Responsive Politics. Brown has had over $14 million in outside help. The Karl Rove-linked Crossroads GPS has boosted Mandel by $6.3 million, in addition to his $4.3 million from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and over $1 million from the National Federation of Independent Business, none of which are required to disclose their donors. Brown had millions more spent against him in issue ads, which are not counted in Federal Election Commission data compiled by CRP. Mandel had also said he would have opposed the auto bailout, which hurt him in the state. Brown first won election to the Senate in 2006. He served in the U.S. House from 1993 to 2007.

More than six weeks after killing nine members of Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, in 2015, Dylann Roof wrote in a journal about his purpose. The then 21-year-old white supremacist wrote: "I did what I thought would make the biggest wave, and now the fate of our race is in the hands of my brothers who continue to live freely." Page after page from the journal was read aloud on Thursday afternoon in Federal District Court, where jurors will decide, perhaps as early as next week, whether to sentence Roof to death. The journal provided an extension of the manifestoes Roof wrote before he opened fire in the fellowship hall on June 17, 2015. Roof wrote that he "would rather live in prison knowing I took action for my race than live with the torture of sitting idle."
