Scott Pruitt received pay raises from the Clean Water Act budget this week. The EPA administrator is allowed thirty hires that do not require White House approval. The article reports that at least two additional stories broke about Pruitt's EPA. The article states that Pruitt paid for pay raises for two employees from money dedicated to the Clean Water Act. It also states that Pruitt lived for the first part of last year in a condo provided by a lobbyist and his wife. The article reports that Pruitt paid fifty bucks a night for the nights he stayed in the Capitol Hill condo. The condo remained open for the other nights. The article also reports that one of the lobbyist's clients received EPA approval for a pipeline.

House Republicans said Friday they would agree to lift the federal government's statutory borrowing limit for three months, with a requirement that both chambers of Congress pass a budget in that time to clear the way for negotiations on long-term deficit reduction. The proposal came from closed-door party negotiations at a retreat in Williamsburg, Va. The White House press secretary, Jay Carney, said he was encouraged by the offer. Senate Democrats, who had opposed the demand for a budget, were also reassured and viewed it as a de-escalation of the debt fight. Speaker John A. Boehner of Ohio had previously said he would raise the debt ceiling only if it were paired with immediate spending cuts of equivalent value. The new strategy is designed to start a more orderly negotiation with President Obama and Senate Democrats on ways to shrink the trillion-dollar deficit.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democratic congresswoman from New York, tweeted a link to a story about a large number of former lawmakers working as lobbyists and suggested the laws be changed to stop it. Cruz responded to the tweet and said he agreed with the congresswoman and suggested some "bipartisan cooperation" might be in order. Ocasio-Cortez suggested what she thought would be needed to make a good bill with some teeth in it. Cruz responded: "You're on." Twitter users reacted cautiously to the tweet exchange. Some users expressed skepticism.

According to a new Washington Post-ABC News poll, Republicans are overwhelmingly confident about taking back the White House in 2012. Democrats are less confident. Overall, 55 percent of Americans expect a Republican victory next year. Thirty-seven percent predict President Obama will win reelection. A majority of independents sense the GOP nominee will prevail. The poll found that 83 percent of Republicans say the GOP nominee — whoever he or she may be — is likely to claim the presidency next year. Among Democrats, 58 percent say they think Obama will win a second term. A third of Democrats expect a GOP win; 13 percent of Republicans sense a repeat for Obama. Republicans who "strongly support" the tea party political movement are particularly confident: 91 percent of these Republicans say they think the GOP candidate will win the general election. The poll was conducted Sept. 29 to Oct. 2 and has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus four percentage points. More from the new poll will be available in tomorrow's Washington Post.

The Republican National Committee voted unanimously Friday at its summer meeting in Boston for a resolution banning CNN and NBC from hosting 2016 primary debates if they proceed with proposed programs about former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. The RNC tweeted the news Friday: "BREAKING: RNC resolution to stop CNN & NBC from hosting GOP primary debates in 2016 PASSES!" Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus had said that if CNN and NBC did not scrap their Clinton programs, he would seek an RNC vote saying the Republican Party would not work with the two networks on its 2016 primary debates or sanction the debates sponsored by them. In preparation for the next presidential election, Priebus said the party would consider holding its 2016 nominating convention in June or July, rather than August, to reduce the amount of time Republican candidates spend competing against one another. An earlier convention also would allow the Republican nominee to focus on the Democratic opponent. "Our party should not be involved in setting up a system that encourages the slicing and dicing of candidates over a long period of time with moderators that are not in the business of being at all concerned about the future of our party," Priebus told reporters this week.

President Donald Trump signed a measure Monday creating a new national historic park for Martin Luther King Jr. during a trip to the college football national championship game in Atlanta. The President performed the signing on Air Force One with Alveda King, the niece of the late civil rights leader, looking on. The law creates the first national historic park in the state of Georgia. It was sponsored by Democratic Rep. John Lewis, a Trump critic who recently boycotted the opening of the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum because the President spoke at the event. The legislation expands the boundaries of the former Martin Luther King Jr. National Historic Site in Atlanta to include the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, a site that King used as the headquarters for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, according to a White House spokesman. White House deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley told reporters on Monday afternoon: "Through his life and work, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. made America more just and free. This important historical park tells his story, and this bill will help ensure that the park continues to tell Dr. King's story for generations to come."

A senior U.S. military official visiting Seoul warned Pyongyang over recent threats and reassured South Korea that military backing would not be hurt by a U.S. budget debate. Deputy Secretary of Defense Ashton Carter told reporters Monday that Pyongyang's threats would deepen Washington's defense commitment to Seoul, which does not have atomic weapons. Ashton said deep U.S. budget cuts would not alter Pentagon efforts to make South Korean defense a priority. Pyongyang is angry over U.S.-South Korean war games and U.N. sanctions meant to punish it for its third nuclear test. It has threatened nuclear attacks on Washington, though it is not believed to have the weapons needed to do so. South Korean marines take a rest on their K-55 self-propelled howitzers during an exercise against possible attacks by North Korea near the border village of Panmunjom in Paju, South Korea, Thursday, March 14, 2013.

The Republican convention will stage a tableau of speakers who are expected to offer accounts of Mitt Romney's life in the church. For most of his political career, Romney has said his life in the church has nothing to do with politics. He has offered only clipped discussions of his religious views, privately worrying about the impact of his faith on his electability. He has changed course because of an urgent problem: voters who find him distant and unlikable have become a greater threat to his political fortunes than those who may be biased against Mormonism. In his speech on the convention night, Romney will testify about how faith has guided his life, according to Eric Fehrnstrom, a campaign strategist. Other speakers are expected to relate stories about how Romney helped church members whose children were sick or dying — crouching by a disabled infant's crib to pray for her survival, helping a teenager with incurable cancer write his own will.

A senior U.S. military official visiting Seoul warned Pyongyang over recent threats and reassured South Korea that military backing would not be hurt by a U.S. budget debate. Deputy Secretary of Defense Ashton Carter told reporters Monday that Pyongyang's threats would deepen Washington's defense commitment to Seoul, which does not have atomic weapons. Ashton said deep U.S. budget cuts would not alter Pentagon efforts to make South Korean defense a priority. Pyongyang is angry over U.S.-South Korean war games and U.N. sanctions meant to punish it for its third nuclear test. It has threatened nuclear attacks on Washington, though it is not believed to have the weapons needed to do so. South Korean marines take a rest on their K-55 self-propelled howitzers during an exercise against possible attacks by North Korea near the border village of Panmunjom in Paju, South Korea, Thursday, March 14, 2013.

President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday the first rally since his inauguration. The President tweeted an announcement for the rally set for Saturday in Melbourne, Florida. "Join me in Florida this Saturday at 5pm for a rally at the Orlando-Melbourne International Airport!" Trump tweeted. An administration official said Trump would rally supporters at an airport hangar there, the same venue where he held a rally in September. The official said Trump is slated to arrive at the rally by landing at the airport on Air Force One and disembarking in front of the crowd, just as he did during the campaign. White House press secretary Sean Spicer said on Wednesday the event was a campaign rally and directed questions about it to "the campaign." He said Trump's campaign was paying for it but did not offer further details. Trump indicated in a form sent to the Federal Election Commission on Inauguration Day that he intended to run for President again, but noted it did not constitute the formal announcement of his 2020 candidacy. Last week, the Office of Special Counsel issued guidance for federal bureaucrats regarding the re-election effort.

This week's testimony by Mark Zuckerberg, the social network's chief executive, revealed limited understanding of Facebook's operations and how it works. Members of Congress raised concerns about Facebook's privacy and data collection policies. The testimony addressed how computers work. The questions did not produce a unified theory of Facebook's troubles or suggestions of how they might be solved. Some lawmakers have said technological illiteracy is the problem, that some older and tech-phobic lawmakers are fundamentally incapable of regulating Facebook properly. The biggest obstacle to regulating Facebook is not Congress's computer literacy, which gave Zuckerberg the upper hand this week. The biggest obstacle is a lack of political will and an unwillingness to identify the problems they are trying to fix.

President Donald Trump places his hands on former adviser Steve Bannon, whom White House Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said was not close to the president. Former acting Solicitor General Neal Katyal expressed skepticism, stating that Trump's strategy is sound and that Bannon's opinions are not disclosure violations. Katyal said Bannon's statements are in the public interest and that Trump is the most public figure in the public interest.

Gov. Sam Brownback of Kansas was confirmed to an ambassadorship on Wednesday after a six-month wait. The Senate voted 49-49 along party lines on the nomination of Mr. Brownback, a Republican who has grown unpopular in Kansas, to be ambassador at large for international religious freedom. Vice President Mike Pence cast the tiebreaking vote. Many religious leaders praised Mr. Brownback's confirmation and said he could use his political experience to help religious minorities, including Christian and Yazidi communities in the Middle East. "He has been a consistent, vocal, competent and impassioned advocate for these issues," said the Rev. Johnnie Moore, a Southern Baptist minister who served on the evangelical advisory board for President Trump's campaign. "It was all very logical to us that he would be the nominee, and we were thrilled by it." Many Democrats and gay rights advocates opposed the nomination of Mr. Brownback, who ended anti-discrimination protections for gay state workers in 2015.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman is "considering going to Singapore," his agent Darren Prince told CNN. Rodman's agent said that while he is considering making the trip, "no plans or flights have been made yet." The US President is expected to meet with the North Korean leader on June 12. White House press secretary Sarah Sanders announced on Tuesday that the exact location for the meeting will be the Capella Hotel on Singapore's Sentosa Island for a historic diplomatic meeting. The White House and State Department did not immediately respond to CNN requests for comment. A senior administration official told CNN that Rodman is not part of anything the White House team is doing at the summit. A State Department official told CNN: "We have no comment on Dennis Rodman's private travel. He's not a representative of the US government." Rodman has traveled to North Korea in the past and has struck up an unlikely friendship with the North Korean leader.

A Gallup poll released Monday shows Hillary Clinton's favorability rating below 60 percent for the first time since 2008. Fifty-eight percent of the public views Clinton favorably, while 39 percent see her unfavorably. That is down from 66 percent favorability in a mid-2012 Gallup poll, although still above her numbers during the 2008 primary. Gallup's Andrew Dugan writes: "This poll shows only slight changes in the public's overall assessment of Clinton, with her unfavorable rating now marginally higher than at any time since 2008." Among self-described independents, 52 percent view Clinton favorably, down 11 points from 63 percent in April. Clinton was also down 4 points among Republicans, although her numbers rose 2 points among Democrats. The Gallup survey is the latest of several polls to show Clinton's numbers declining amid controversy over her handling of Benghazi, as well as speculation about her plans for 2016. HuffPost Pollster, which includes all publicly available polling, shows her numbers dropping about 4 points since January. The Gallup poll surveyed 1,529 voters by phone between June 1 and June 4.

Montana Democrats need a U.S. Senate nominee. Actor Jeff Bridges has a home in Paradise Valley. In an interview on Howard Stern's radio show Monday, Bridges said his wife is not a fan of the idea of him running. "Don't even think about it," he said. Pratt, who lives in Billings, started a petition on Change.org encouraging Bridges to run. The petition attracted more than 1,100 signatures. "I look down and see this thing, Jeff Bridges for senator, and I say what?" said the actor. Sen. John Walsh (D-Mont.) dropped out of the race last week amid plagiarism allegations. Montana Democrats will gather at a Saturday convention to choose his replacement. Rep. Steve Daines (R) is favored to win the seat.

Speaker Paul Ryan appeared on "The Lead" with Jake Tapper on Thursday afternoon. Ryan said: "We do not always nominate a Lincoln and Reagan, but we hope that that person advances the principals of our party and appeals to a wide vase majority of Americans ... Saying that we're unified does not unify us, but actually taking the principles that we believe in and running a campaign that the Republicans can be proud about, and that can actually appeal to the majority of Americans. That's what takes it unify the party. ... I think conservatives want to know does he share the values and our principles and the government and the role of the executive. It's the constitution. There are a lot of questions that they're going to want answers to and myself included."

Republican Sen. Jeff Flake posted a photo Tuesday showing a check with his signature on it addressed to Democratic candidate Doug Jones. Flake's Twitter account posted the image of the $100 check along with the caption "Country over Party." The Arizona Republican, who has announced he is not running for re-election, attended a meeting with President Donald Trump and other Republican senators at the White House earlier Tuesday, where he was seated next to the President. In that meeting, Trump again expressed support for Moore in the special election set for next week. Flake said later Tuesday the President was "wrong" for backing the GOP candidate, who faces multiple allegations of sexual assault from several decades ago. "I do think the President is wrong here. I think it will have negative impacts for the party in the long term," he told reporters. CNN's Kristin Wilson and Phil Mattingly contributed to this report.

A South Carolina man, 24-year-old Michael Vines, was arrested over the weekend and charged with illegally possessing firearms. Firefighters saw Vines toss a handgun into the grass, according to The Smoking Gun. Authorities charged Vines with driving under a suspended license, driving too fast for conditions, and unlawful carrying of a firearm. The handgun police accused Vines of carrying was a fully loaded Smith & Wesson .38-caliber revolver. Vines is prohibited from owning a gun because of a rap sheet that includes multiple narcotics convictions. Vines has a tattoo of a handgun prominently displayed on his forehead. Greenville police referenced Vines' display of ink in a Facebook post, stating that "the real weapon was placed in property and evidence."

Donald J. Trump held his first of three rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, on Saturday. The aircraft is one of the biggest toys in national politics. After waiting more than an hour in an airport hangar, Trump used it to keep children happy. At the outset at the rally, Trump said he would let small children "run through the plane" as he talked. He said quickly, "Because the parents will damage it." The aircraft moved low past the crowd as the theme from the movie "Air Force One" blared, prompting "ooohs!" from the crowd. Trump had used similar procedures in Arizona months earlier. The rally did not fill the area created for attendees, although hundreds were on hand.

Mission Hospital released a statement to The Huffington Post stating that Billy Graham returned to his home in Montreat today following a two-day stay at the hospital, where he was admitted for pulmonary-related tests and observations. Chief Medical Officer William R. Hathaway said, "Mr. Graham was alert and in good spirits during his stay. We are pleased with the results of Mr. Graham's evaluation." WCNC reported that Graham, 95, was hospitalized in North Carolina for respiratory problems. Mark DeMoss, a spokesperson for the Graham family, said Graham should return home in a couple of days. Graham was at Mission Hospital a month ago for pulmonary testing prior to his birthday party. DeMoss told WCNC, "Mr. Graham is in the hospital with a respiratory congestion issue, similar to what he had a few weeks ago. As was the case then, we expect he will be able to return home in a day or two.

The Supreme Court issued a unanimous rebuke to President Obama on Thursday, saying he had overreached in issuing recess appointments during brief breaks in the Senate's work. The justices said Obama violated the Constitution in 2012 by appointing officials to the National Labor Relations Board during a break in the Senate's work when the chamber was convening every three days in short pro forma sessions in which no business was conducted. Those breaks were too short, Justice Stephen G. Breyer wrote in a majority opinion joined by the court's four other justices. At the same time, the court largely reinstated an arrangement between the executive branch and the Senate, in which recess appointments were allowed during more substantial breaks. Justice Breyer said such appointments generally remained permissible so long as they were made during breaks of 10 or more days. Although there may be few immediate practical consequences of the ruling, given the recent overhaul of the Senate's filibuster rules, the decision was nonetheless momentous, involving a constitutional adjudication of the balance of power between the president and the Senate.

The New York Daily News posted its Friday cover on Twitter late Thursday. The headline referenced former FBI Director James Comey's memoir, A Higher Loyalty: Truth, Lies, and Leadership, which is out next week. Comey said Trump had asked him to look into reports that he was filmed watching prostitutes urinate in a Moscow hotel suite. Comey said Trump denied the incident happened but wanted proof to assure first lady Melania Trump. The anecdote is in Comey's book. The Daily News has frequently used its front page to criticize the president. In February, it depicted Trump with NRA-branded tape over his mouth on one cover and criticized him for golfing during the funerals of the Parkland, Florida, mass shooting victims in another. It has also depicted him as Dr. Evil, a clown, and a racist, and called his actions "treasonous."

President Obama is traveling to the Union Depot in St. Paul, Minn., on Wednesday to call for new spending on transportation infrastructure, an issue that remains stalled in Congress. The president will call on lawmakers to pass a four-year, $302 billion surface transportation reauthorization bill that would repair and modernize the nation's roads, bridges, railways and transit systems, according to a fact sheet provided by the White House. To fund the initiative, Obama will propose dedicating $150 billion in "one-time transition revenue from pro-growth business tax reform," officials said. Funding for many transportation projects is due to expire later this year, according to the White House, putting more than 700,000 jobs in jeopardy. Obama will also launch a $600 million competition through the Transportation Department's existing TIGER grant program, which funds a range of infrastructure projects. TIGER stands for Transportation Investment Generating Economic Recovery. The grants, according to officials, will go to projects that will have a significant impact on a region, promote better job access and financial opportunity, save energy and fuel and spur economic development.

Former President Barack Obama had not finished his speech at the 2020 Democratic National Convention before President Donald Trump criticized him. Obama said the current president "hasn't grown into the job because he can't." "The consequences of that failure are severe. 170,000 Americans dead. Millions of jobs gone," Obama said. "Our worst impulses unleashed, our proud reputation around the world badly diminished, and our democratic institutions threatened like never before." In response, Trump posted in all caps: "In response, Trump revisited a criticism he often lobs at his predecessor: He followed that claim, which he has made many times despite there being no evidence anything like that occurred, with another all-caps tweet criticizing Biden. Several reports published during the Democratic primary that cited sources close to Obama said he purposefully stayed out of the race. Biden told reporters in April he had asked Obama not to endorse him in the race, saying "whoever wins this nomination should win it on their own merits."

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) said Thursday that Democrats are coalescing behind former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. When USA Today's Susan Page asked if the Democratic party is coalescing behind Clinton, Pelosi responded, "I think so; I think so." She said, "There's a great deal of excitement about the prospect that she would run." Pelosi clarified that she was not making an endorsement but added, "But I am gauging, I'm gauging. I'm encouraging people to think about it, so in case she asks us, we have something to say to her." Pelosi has previously expressed support for the idea of Clinton running for president. She said in May that she is praying for Clinton to run, and in an interview with the San Francisco Chronicle last year, she said Clinton was the Democrats' best "shot" for 2016. Clinton has not announced her plans for 2016. A super PAC supporting her candidacy has recently announced support from Senator Claire McCaskill (D-Mo.), who recently announced that Ready For Hillary has her support.

Caitlyn Jenner posted her first tweet at 12:17 p.m. on Monday. Four hours and three minutes later, she set a new Guinness World Record for the fastest time to gain 1 million followers on Twitter. In doing so, Jenner broke the previous record, held by President Obama, who earned the title when he began his @POTUS account in May. It took Obama just under five hours to break the record, set in 2014 by Robert Downey Jr. Jenner's debut on Twitter as Caitlyn broke the president's record. Administration officials such as senior Obama advisor Valerie Jarrett tweeted "nice to meet you." As of this writing, Jenner's first tweet — a photo of the Vanity Fair cover showing her with the quote, "Call me Caitlyn" — has been re-tweeted more than 180,000 times. News of Jenner's new name, she used to be known as Bruce, prompted 1.5 million tweets, according to Twitter, peaking at 11,000 tweets a minute.

Bob Dylan, the recipient of the 2016 Nobel Prize in literature, will not attend a Wednesday meeting with President Obama, a White House spokesman said Wednesday. The president is slated to meet with the other winners of the honor in a closed-to-press confab. Dylan did not initially return the Nobel committee's calls after the award was announced. He later proclaimed himself to be honored. Dylan will not attend the actual award ceremony. A representative for Dylan did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Dylan did receive Obama's praise in person. Obama tweeted last month: "Congratulations to one of my favorite poets, Bob Dylan, on a well-deserved Nobel."

Political analyst David Gergen, who has been a White House adviser to four presidents, said in an appearance on CNN's "Newsroom" that President Trump's campaign-style rally speech was "the most divisive speech I've ever heard from a sitting American president." The speech began with attacks on the press and covered Trump's tax plan, jobs, the yet-to-be-built wall, trade, and other topics Trump had touted throughout his 2016 campaign. Gergen said Trump played to his base and treated his other listeners and other people who had been disturbed about him or oppose him, basically as "I don't care, I don't give a damn what you think, because you're frankly like the enemy." Gergen said he thought the speech was "deeply disturbing."

A letter to the editor responded to a front-page article titled "Obama to 'Put Everything I've Got' Into Gun Control" published on the front page on Jan. 17. The writer stated that it has become fashionable of late to lament the unbridgeable divide over guns in the country. The writer said President Obama's critics charge that his recent action on gun control puts him at odds with all gun owners and enthusiasts. The writer said they believe the reality is different. The writer stated Americans are far from poles apart on the issue of gun control. The writer said Americans recognize that all things entail some measure of risk as well as benefit and legislate regulations accordingly. The writer said guns divide them because they fall in the gray area, disagree as to whether their utility outweighs their risk, and lack data to inform their opinions. The writer said for decades the gun lobby has done its best to suppress all research on firearms and their dangers. The writer also said President Obama said on Wednesday, "We don't benefit from not knowing the science of this epidemic of violence." The writer said his promise to back research into this area is encouraging.

Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel on Tuesday ordered the American military to review its policies concerning hairstyles popular with black women. Hagel told critics of new Army regulations banning large cornrows, twists and dreadlocks that he takes "very seriously" concerns that military rules on hair have unfairly targeted black women. Responding to a complaint lodged by the 16 women of the Congressional Black Caucus, Hagel said he had given the secretaries and military leaders of the Army, Air Force, Navy and Marines three months to review comprehensive military regulations as they pertain to black women "to ensure standards are fair and respectful of our diverse force." Hagel's order raises the possibility that the Pentagon will go beyond the initial request of the black caucus that he overturn the Army's new hair rules. A Pentagon spokesman said Hagel is "opening the aperture" on all of the services, which black servicewomen have said for decades have forced them to conform to norms based on the hair of white women.

Former first lady Barbara Bush was admitted Saturday to Methodist Hospital in Houston, Texas, for routine tests, spokeswoman Jean Becker said. "Mrs Bush is in for some routine tests, not an emergency of any kind," said Jim Appleby, spokesman for former President George H.W. Bush. The former first lady had not been feeling well for about a week, Becker said. Bush, 84, is expected to stay at the hospital for a day or two. Details on the testing were not immediately available. Becker, the chief of staff for former President George H.W. Bush, said her hospitalization is "not serious at all." Last year, Bush underwent open-heart surgery during which doctors replaced her aortic valve with a biologic valve. She spent nine days in the hospital afterward. Becker said her recent hospitalization is "not related" to the surgery. In November 2008, Bush underwent surgery for a perforated ulcer.

Conservative billionaire Charles Koch, the Koch Industries CEO, said in an interview that aired Sunday that Donald Trump's proposed temporary ban on Muslims entering the country is "antithetical to our approach." Koch said he has a problem with Trump's support of using a database to track Muslims in the country. "That's reminiscent of Nazi Germany. I mean that's monstrous, as I said at the time," the Koch brothers said. Despite his strong feelings about Trump's stance, Koch said he and his brother David will still not "put a penny" toward the "Never Trump" movement to stop the real estate mogul from securing the Republican nomination, even though they have been asked to contribute. The Koch brothers have not spent money for or against any particular GOP candidate in the primary. "That's not what we do," Koch said. "What we're trying to do is build alliances to make the country better. Like we have one with the White House on criminal justice reform. You do it by trying to find areas where you can work with everybody."

California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, the House minority leader, told reporters Thursday that Alabama's new state law banning almost all abortions goes too far. McCarthy said the law, which does not allow exceptions for abortions in cases of rape and incest, "goes further than I believe." He said he believes in "exceptions for rape, incest and life of the mother." McCarthy would not take a stand on whether the Supreme Court should strike down the measure, which he described as the strictest abortion law in the nation, if a challenge were to reach the court. Opinion polls show widespread opposition to overturning the high court's Roe v. Wade decision, which could return the issue back to the states. Republicans struggled to win over suburban women in last year's midterm elections and the controversy over abortion restrictions could prove politically troublesome. Republicans have been on the offensive this year trying to link congressional Democrats to late-term abortion measures pushed by some of the party's most liberal forces in state legislatures such as New York's.

In the past hours, Ukraine's Parliament voted to remove Viktor Yanukovich from office. Yanukovich fled his office and opposition protesters took control of his residence. Parliament voted to free jailed former prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko. The newly-installed interior minister declared that security police are to cease actions against protesters. Police are rallying to the opposition. Events are moving quickly, much more so than was anticipated yesterday when Yanukovich's government and opposition groups agreed to cease fire and negotiations. Today's events suggest a much larger power shift and change in national direction, one away from the influence of Putin. Reports and details continue to emerge. There remains a great deal to be sorted out before peace has come to Ukraine.

Hillary Rodham Clinton arrived in Vineyard Haven, Mass., on Wednesday. Hundreds of admirers waited in rain for a glimpse of the woman who they hope will be the next president. Lily Richards, a 17-year-old high school senior from Greenfield, Mass., whose high school thesis paper argued for Mrs. Clinton's election as president, said: "When I heard Hillary was going to be here, I literally started crying. Oh my God, I have to go." President Obama is vacationing at a sprawling shingled home, where he is receiving friendly waves from locals when his motorcade passes. After six years, energy in the area appears to be shifting from Obama toward Mrs. Clinton as the former secretary of state moves away from the president's orbit toward her own political future.

The US supreme court justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg on Wednesday underwent a heart procedure at a Washington hospital after reporting discomfort following routine exercise, a court statement said. Ginsburg, 81, was resting comfortably after having a stent placed in her right coronary artery and is expected to be discharged from MedStar Washington Hospital Center within 48 hours, the statement said. She reported discomfort after routine exercise on Tuesday night, according to the court statement. Ginsburg, the oldest member of the nine-justice court, has previously survived serious bouts with cancer in 1999 and 2009.

The United States has a new charge d'affairs in Libya to oversee diplomatic efforts following Ambassador Chris Stevens' killing, the State Department announced. Laurence Pope arrived Thursday in Tripoli to take on the role, the State Department said. With no ambassador in the country, Pope will handle those duties. State Department spokeswoman Victoria Nuland said Pope "looks forward to working with the Libyan government and the Libyan people during this historic and challenging time, as we build strong economic, social, political, and educational bridges between our two people." Nuland said in a written statement: "We will continue to assist as Libya builds democratic institutions and broad respect for the rule of law -- the goals that Ambassador Stevens worked hard to achieve." Pope, who was born in 1945, is coming out of retirement to take the job. A speaker of Arabic and French, he spent decades in the diplomatic ranks, beginning in 1969, before retiring in 2000. He held some senior posts, including director of Northern Gulf Affairs, associate director for counterterrorism, and political adviser to the commander of U.S. Central Command.

Sen. Ted Cruz said at the CBS Republican presidential debate in South Carolina that the Supreme Court has 80 years of precedent for not confirming justices in an election year. Cruz argued that the vacancy should be filled by the next president in 2017. Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy was nominated by former President Ronald Reagan in 1987 and confirmed by the Senate in 1988, an election year. After moderator John Dickerson interjected to note the error, Cruz, a former Supreme Court clerk, paused and said he had gotten his history wrong. The audience booed. Sen. Marco Rubio had made a similar point prior to Cruz, but he correctly distinguished between the nomination and successful confirmation of a Supreme Court justice. "It's been over 80 years since a lame duck president has appointed a Supreme Court justice," he said.

FBI Director James B. Comey and N.S.A. Director Adm. Michael S. Rogers appeared before the House Intelligence Committee on Monday. The hearing was transcribed by the Federal News Service. Comey said members of the committee thanked him for including him in the hearing. He said he was honored to be representing the people of the FBI. He said he hoped they had shown through their actions and words how much the FBI value their oversight of its work and how much they respect their responsibility to investigate those things as important to the American people. He said they showed both were being taken very seriously. Comey said their practice is not to confirm the existence of ongoing investigations, especially those investigations that involve classified matters, but in unusual circumstances where it is in the public interest, it may be appropriate to do so as Justice Department policies recognize. He said this was one of those circumstances.

President Obama on Thursday renewed his call for an immigration overhaul, telling an audience of activists at the White House that the fate of a bipartisan Senate bill now rests with Republicans in the House. "Anyone still standing in the way of this bipartisan reform should at least explain why," Obama said to applause in the East Room. "If House Republicans have new and different additional ideas for how we should move forward, then we should hear them. I will be listening." The Senate passed legislation in June by a vote of 68-32. The vote addressed Obama's plans to improve border security, require employers to verify the immigration status of their workers, and provide a path to citizenship for 11 million undocumented immigrants. White House strategists hoped the vote would prompt action in the House, where Republicans had resisted similar calls for an overhaul of the system. The effort stalled this summer, with many House Republicans expressing dissatisfaction with the increases in border security and saying they do not support any plan that would allow people in the country illegally to eventually become citizens.

The Senate on Thursday voted 100-0 to approve the nomination of Charlotte mayor Anthony Foxx as Transportation Secretary. The unanimous vote was a rarity for a Cabinet appointee. Foxx's confirmation process was smooth and drew national attention when his city hosted the 2012 Democratic National Convention. At 42, Foxx will be the youngest member of the Obama Cabinet and will replace Ray LaHood at the helm of DOT. Foxx's confirmation leaves two Cabinet nominees pending in the Senate: Tom Perez for Secretary of Labor and Gina McCarthy for Environmental Protection Agency. McCarthy's nomination was already meeting with Republican resistance in the Senate. Her nomination might face additional hurdles after President Obama revealed a climate-change agenda that has been noted by Republicans. Juliet Eilperin reported: "Now that the president is proceeding with regulating greenhouse gas emissions from existing power plants, Senate Republicans are likely to be even tougher on McCarthy, who informed them in April the agency was not drafting such regulations."

Gen. Keith Alexander, the Director of the National Security Agency, offered to resign after former NSA contractor Edward Snowden revealed himself as the source of leaked agency documents, according to a Wall Street Journal report. The Obama administration declined the offer. One former defense official told the newspaper that officials were concerned that Alexander's resignation would give Snowden a win. The report comes about a month after Reuters reported Oct. 16 that Alexander was expected to leave the agency by March or April, citing anonymous officials. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney confirmed a day later that Alexander, who has led the agency for eight years, would leave his post in March. Snowden leaked classified documents to The Washington Post and The Guardian in June detailing the agency's telephone and Internet spying programs. He fled to Hong Kong and then Moscow, where he is currently residing. White House National Security Council spokeswoman Caitlin Hayden declined to comment on the report, pointing instead to Carney's Oct. 28 statement that President Barack Obama has "full confidence" in Alexander.

Dave Chappelle praised fellow comic Michelle Wolf for "speaking truth to power" during her performance Saturday night at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner. Wolf's routine drew criticism from President Donald Trump and his supporters who said she made jokes directed at the administration, including jokes about White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders. Chappelle said he did not know who those people think they are that she can't say that to them because they offend people all the time. He said for many people, it is cathartic to watch that woman speak truth to power like that. He said the routine was "grounded in her truth" and that he respected Wolf's artistry. He said he knows how hard it is to do what she did in front of that lame-ass crowd.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad faced international condemnation at the United Nations on Thursday as Syrian forces blocked U.N. monitors from investigating a massacre site in a village near the city of Hama. Special emissary Kofi Annan acknowledged that his six-point plan for a political transition in Syria has reached a dead end, with both sides refusing to implement it. Annan said a reinvigorated diplomatic push would be required to avert a full-fledged civil war, and he warned for the first time that any party blocking a political transition should face unspecified "consequences."

The Senate voted to move forward on the Violence Against Women Act. Nebraska Republican Deb Fischer voted yes. Wisconsin Republican Ron Johnson voted yes. Ohio Republican Rob Portman voted no. Iowa Republican Chuck Grassley spoke on the Senate floor to urge a yes vote on the motion to proceed. House Republicans objected to the bipartisan Senate bill because they did not like its protections for immigrants, Native Americans, or LGBT people. They passed their own version of the law last year. Republican leadership refused to allow the bipartisan bill that had already passed the Senate to come to a vote. The question remains whether John Boehner and Eric Cantor will continue blocking a bipartisan bill because it offers legal protections to groups they dislike. The article urges Congress to reauthorize the expanded, bipartisan version of the Violence Against Women Act.

The Air Force said Thursday that it had suspended 92 officers at Malmstrom Air Force Base, nearly half of the nuclear launch crew there, in what it described as a cheating scandal. The Air Force acknowledged a "systemic problem" in the culture of the team entrusted to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. Air Force Secretary Deborah Lee James said a "climate of fear" in the ballistic missile force might have encouraged launch officers to share answers to monthly proficiency tests. She said the nation's nuclear arsenal remained safe. For now, the 92 officers who have been suspended and decertified are barred from the underground missile capsules from which ICBMs are launched. The remaining launch crew members at the Montana base — just under 100 — will now perform extra duty on 24-hour standby, Defense Department officials said, and will spend at least 10 days a month in the missile capsules, up from eight. "This situation remains completely unacceptable," Ms. James said in her second news conference in two weeks to discuss the case.

The director of the Defense Intelligence Agency, Lt. Gen. Michael T. Flynn of the Army, and his civilian deputy, David R. Shedd, will retire by early fall, the agency said in an email to its employees on Wednesday. The two men are stepping down at a time when the Defense Intelligence Agency is shifting its priorities from providing intelligence to troops in Iraq and Afghanistan to working more closely with the C.I.A. to gather and distribute information on global issues like the proliferation of weapons and rising powers like China. In a statement, Pentagon spokesman Rear Adm. John Kirby said that Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel "appreciates the service of these two dedicated and professional leaders," and that the retirements had been planned "for some time." Two senior American officials said tensions had flared between General Flynn and some of his Pentagon colleagues who balked at changes he wanted to make, including cuts to what he viewed as outdated intelligence programs in favor of devoting shrinking resources to newer threats, including in the digital realm.

Former Florida Gov. Charlie Crist (D), a former Republican, said racism is a "big reason" why he left the GOP. Crist told Fusion's Jorge Ramos the GOP is now seen as "anti-women, anti-minority, anti-women, anti-gay, anti-education, anti-environment." Crist said he left the Republican Party because leadership "went off a cliff." Ramos suggested "the moment" Crist decided to leave the Republican party was when he realized he would lose to now-Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) in the 2010 Senate race. Crist denied the claim, blaming the GOP's attitude toward working with President Barack Obama instead. "I couldn't be consistent with myself, and my core beliefs, and stay with a party that was so unfriendly toward the African-American president. I'll just go there," Crist said, saying anti-Obama "activists" were "intolerable." "I couldn't take it anymore," Crist added.

The U.S. House of Representatives approved a new North American trade deal on Thursday that includes labor and automotive content rules but leaves $1.2 trillion in annual U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade flows largely unchanged. The House passed legislation to implement the U.S.-Mexico Canada Agreement 385-41, with 38 Democrats, two Republicans, and one independent member voting no. The bipartisan vote contrasted with Wednesday night's Democrat-only vote to impeach U.S. President Donald Trump. The House vote sends the measure to the Senate, but it is unclear when the Republican-controlled chamber will take it up. Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell has said that consideration of the measure would likely follow an impeachment trial in the Senate, expected in January. The USMCA trade pact, first agreed upon in September 2018, will replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. Trump has vowed for years to quit or renegotiate NAFTA, which he blames for the loss of millions of U.S. factory jobs to Mexico.

It has been seven months since Bob Filner, a member of Congress, left Washington to become mayor of San Diego. The move was described as promising to shake up a City Hall that had been ruled by Republicans for close to 20 years. On Tuesday, employees and constituents accused Filner of sexual harassment. He faced calls from his supporters to step down and the exodus of some top staff members from City Hall. His former fiancée urged him to quit, detailing what she said was sexually inappropriate behavior by the mayor when they were dating. She announced last week that she had ended their engagement. San Diego has been introduced to terms such as the "Filner headlock," a description of how the mayor allegedly handled women he was trying to embrace.

John Dean, who served as White House counsel to President Richard Nixon, issued a warning for an attorney serving another president. Dean said former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, personal attorney for President Donald Trump, has crossed a line. Dean, who ultimately turned on Nixon and helped bring him down, said Giuliani was no longer a lawyer but a co-conspirator. Dean said Giuliani could face legal trouble. Giuliani has made media appearances in recent days in which he alternately denied and admitted asking Ukraine to investigate former Vice President Joe Biden on behalf of Trump. In a White House summary of a conversation released on Wednesday, Trump pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to work with Giuliani on those investigations. Earlier this week, Giuliani claimed the State Department called and asked for his help with Ukraine. The State Department denied that and described Giuliani as a "private citizen" who does not speak on behalf of the U.S. government.

An independent inquiry into the attack on the United States diplomatic mission in Libya that killed four Americans on Sept. 11 criticized the State Department for a lack of seasoned security personnel and for relying on local militias to safeguard the compound. The investigation into the attack on the diplomatic mission and the C.I.A. annex in Benghazi that resulted in the deaths of Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans also faulted State Department officials in Washington for ignoring requests from the American Embassy in Tripoli for more guards for the mission and for failing to make sufficient safety upgrades. The panel also said American intelligence officials had relied too much on specific warnings of imminent attacks, which they did not have in the case of Benghazi, rather than basing assessments more broadly on a deteriorating security environment. By this spring, Benghazi, a hotbed of militant activity in eastern Libya, had experienced a string of assassinations, an attack on a British envoy's motorcade and the explosion of a bomb outside the American Mission.

Rachel Maddow criticized Republican presidential candidate Carly Fiorina on her show Monday night. Fiorina, who announced her candidacy on "Good Morning America," told host George Stephanopoulos that she would make a good commander-in-chief because she "understand[s] technology, which is a tool to reimagine government and re-engage citizens in the process of government." Maddow pointed out that if one visits carlyfiorina.org, the site displays more than 30,000 sad faces, one for each person laid off during Fiorina's tenure at Hewlett-Packard. Fiorina received a $21 million severance package when she was removed. Maddow said: "It has been said once before in her political career. It will be said again: Carly will now disappear."

On Sunday, residents of Yarnell, Ariz., were told they could return home after a deadly wildfire engulfed their town for nine days. On Tuesday in Prescott, the neighboring town, residents and family mourned 19 members of their firefighting force that would not be coming home. At a memorial service for the Granite Mountain Hotshots who died in last week's fire, Vice President Joe Biden joined Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer, Sen. John McCain and Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano to speak to 1,000 of the Hotshots' family members and alumni. Biden quoted Psalm 122:1 before recalling his own family tragedy. Weeks after he was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1972, Biden's wife and one-year-old daughter were killed in a car accident in Hockessin, Del. His two sons survived, rescued by firefighters. "I didn't have the privilege of knowing any one of these heroes personally," he said of the Hotshots. "But I know them... I know them because they saved the life of my two sons."

New Jersey state Sen. Donald Norcross (D) announced Tuesday afternoon that he will run for the seat of retiring Rep. Robert Andrews (D-N.J.) hours after Andrews said he will resign from Congress. In a statement, Norcross said: "I am running for Congress because South Jersey needs someone who is going to stand up for us in Washington, D.C., as Rob Andrews has done for more than two decades. I have spent my career fighting for middle-class families, senior citizens and workers." Norcross, the brother of longtime South Jersey power-broker George Norcross, is a heavy favorite to succeed Andrews. He also received early backing Tuesday from state Senate President Stephen Sweeney, Camden Mayor Dana Redd, and Andrews himself. At his retirement news conference, Andrews said he hoped Norcross would run. The seat leans Democratic, meaning the Democratic primary should determine the winner.

Rick Gates, the former right-hand man to Paul Manafort, President Trump's campaign chairman, is being cross-examined by defense lawyers in Manafort's trial on bank and tax fraud charges in Alexandria, Virginia. Defense lawyers attacked his credibility. Gates admitted to having an affair about a decade ago, but he denied using company money for his trysts. Prosecutors led him through a clinical examination of his and Manafort's business dealings, including how he hid income to avoid taxes. It is unclear whether Manafort will take the stand in his own defense. His lawyers would not say. Prosecutors said they expect to wind up their case this week. Kevin Downing, the lead defense lawyer, began cross-examination Tuesday by asking Gates's credibility, demanding an exact accounting of when he lied to the government and pleaded guilty to the charge of doing so. Gates seemed to struggle to articulate that timeline, prompting Judge T. S. Ellis III to intervene.

Three likely Republican presidential contenders — Senators Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio, and Rand Paul — appeared at a candidate forum in late January. They said they considered "the increasing gap between rich and poor" to be a problem. On the question of whether the government should intervene, Cruz and Paul rejected that approach. Rubio agreed with them. Cruz said that when "government takes over the economy," "it freezes everything in place. And it exacerbates income inequality." He proposed lowering taxes and loosening regulations instead. A Pew Research Center poll from January 2014 surveyed about 1,500 adults. The poll found 69 percent of Americans consider inequality a problem, 69 percent of them, and almost half of Republicans say the government should act "to reduce the gap between the rich and everyone else."

The Washington Post printed a story on November 1 alleging that U.S. Sen. Robert Menendez (D-N.J.) engaged with Dominican prostitutes. The Daily Caller cited conflicting evidence and stated it would continue investigating the story. The Caller is actively pursuing the story, has investigators on the ground in the Dominican Republic, and will continue to report new facts as they emerge, whether or not they support its earlier reporting. An investigation by the Dominican National Police has charged that three women who filmed a videotape alleging Menendez had engaged prostitutes was a sponsored affair. The participants received several hundred dollars apiece for their participation. The Daily Caller has not independently verified the identities of the women involved in the Dominican National Police investigation but will continue to investigate the case. The article states that "investigating the case" beats "publishing a retraction and apology."

Before President Obama left the White House on Tuesday morning to fly to an event in Albany, several aides intercepted him in the Oval Office. Within minutes, the president would endorse same-sex marriage on Wednesday. Several aides described the decision and his subsequent announcement in a scheduled network television interview as a wrenching personal transformation. The announcement followed 48 hours of speculation after Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. embraced the idea of same-sex unions in a Sunday talk show interview. Advisers said Obama had intended since early this year to define his position before Democrats nominate him for re-election in September. Many of the president's allies believed he would not do so, citing his strong support from gay voters for having ended a ban on openly gay people in the military and disavowing a federal law defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

Representative Chris Cannon, a member of Congress, lost his bid for a seventh term in a Republican primary on Tuesday. The primary focused on whether he was conservative enough for Utah's Third District. The first-time candidate was Jason Chaffetz, a former Brigham Young University football player who served as chief of staff to Republican Governor Jon Huntsman Jr. Cannon, 57, had hoped his name recognition, campaign cash, and a pool of more moderate voters would propel him again to the Republican nomination. An endorsement from President Bush, who remains popular in Utah, had also been expected to help, as it did in 2006. Chaffetz carried the district, which covers all or parts of seven counties in central and western Utah, including southern suburbs of Salt Lake City. With almost 99 percent of ballots counted, Chaffetz had nearly 60 percent of the votes, leading Cannon by 27,266 to 18,208.

A Washington Post poll conducted by telephone April 29-May 2, 2013, among a random sample of 1,000 adults in the Commonwealth of Virginia, including users of both conventional and cellular phones, asked whether registered voters would vote. The poll included a click "detailed view" to see interactive results by political and demographic groups, including Democrats ages 18-39. Sampling, data collection, and tabulation were performed by Abt-SRBI of New York. Sampling, data collection, and tabulation were conducted by Abt-SRBI of New York. The results from the full survey have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. The error margin is four points for the sample of 887 registered voters and five points for the sample of 663 likely gubernatorial election voters. Sampling, data collection, and tabulation were produced for the Washington Post by Capital Insight.

Republicans are concerned about the impact of a debt ceiling increase on U.S. financial markets. House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) has had conversations with top Wall Street executives, asking how close Congress could push to the debt limit deadline without sending interest rates soaring and causing stock prices to go lower, people familiar with the matter said. Boehner spokesman Michael Steel said Tuesday night that he was not aware of any such conversations. Republicans have made demands in exchange for raising the debt limit.

Former acting director and deputy director for the CIA, Morell, endorsed Secretary Clinton. In an op-ed in the New York Times, Morell described the Secretary's actions while in charge of the State Department as: "I also saw the secretary's commitment to our nation's security; her belief that America is an exceptional nation that must lead in the world for the country to remain secure and prosperous; her understanding that diplomacy can be effective only if the country is perceived as willing and able to use force if necessary; and, most important, her capacity to make the most difficult decision of all — whether to put young American women and men in harm's way." Morell also said: "In the intelligence business, we would say that Mr. Putin had recruited Mr. Trump as an unwitting agent of the Russian Federation." Comments on the story are closed.

Gallup reported that a quarter of Americans view both major-party presidential candidates unfavorably. The figure is more than twice as high as those who disliked both Mitt Romney and Barack Obama in 2012. The article stated that if Donald Trump is the most poorly viewed major-party presidential candidate of all time and Hillary Clinton is in second, there must be some overlap between those two groups. Gallup estimated that a full one-quarter of American adults view both Trump and Clinton unfavorably, a figure more than twice as high as those who disliked both Mitt Romney and Barack Obama in 2012. The article also stated that 4 percent of Americans viewed both Trump and Clinton favorably. The article suggested that the upper-right quadrant of the top graph may grow as Clinton gains support at Trump's expense. It suggested that a third dimension could be added to show Americans' feelings about a third-party alternative to the two least-popular candidates on record.

President Obama has taken full control of the health care negotiations, casting himself for the first time in the role of mediator between the House and Senate during a 72-hour marathon of talks that have turned his White House into a de facto Congressional conference. Mr. Obama spent more than six hours with Democratic leaders on Wednesday, slipping in and out of health care talks to coordinate a response to the earthquake in Haiti. He spent much of Thursday in health care talks, ducking out in the evening to address House Democrats and attend his daughter Malia's band recital, where she plays flute, and then returning to the negotiating table until 1 a.m., shortly before the group recessed for the night. He was back at it Friday afternoon, holed up once again in the Cabinet Room from 1 p.m. to 3:45 p.m., at which point the White House announced that Mr. Obama was done holding or attending health care meetings, at least for now. Officials are waiting for cost analysis from the Congressional Budget Office.

Rep. Ted Lieu and Rep. Don Beyer Jr. have referred Jared Kushner to the Department of Justice for criminal investigation. The referral follows reports that Donald Trump ordered Kushner to receive top-secret security clearance despite recommendations from the White House counsel and the CIA not to give him access to sensitive government secrets. The two congressmen cited Kushner's false statements on security clearance forms and in public interviews as reasons for the referral. They requested an immediate investigation to determine whether Kushner is criminally liable for his false statements. In a letter, which can be read in full below, Lieu and Beyer detail inconsistencies in Kushner's responses on the SF-86 form he had to fill out while seeking clearance. Kushner repeatedly failed to detail contacts he had with foreign officials, including meetings with Russian officials. The pair note this is a violation of federal law and punishable by up to five years in prison. Rep. Lieu and Rep. Beyer further contend the investigation is critical because it is a matter of national security.

David Wildstein, the former Port Authority of New York and New Jersey executive at the center of the New Jersey bridge scandal, does not want to testify before state lawmakers on Thursday. He will file a lawsuit to avoid the subpoena. According to the Record, Wildstein's lawsuit argues that the subpoena served to him is invalid for a number of reasons. The suit questions everything from Wisniewski's signature on the subpoena to Wisniewski's ability to issue a subpoena for investigative purposes. Christie is scheduled to testify under oath tomorrow. Bob Somerby of the Daily Howler recently posted an article about how Rachel Maddow was wasting her energies reporting the TOTAL NON-STORY of Bridgegate. Somerby wrote that Rachel Maddow is an extremely non-serious pseudo-journalist.

President Hamid Karzai spoke before thousands of Afghan leaders on Thursday in Kabul, Afghanistan. He had just come to an agreement with American leaders on a security deal that would commit the two countries to a lasting military alliance, and which would define his legacy. He convened the assembly that would decide the deal's fate. After a speech in which he described his relationship with the United States as one of mutual distrust, he told the gathering, known as a loya jirga, that even if it approved the deal, he would wait until after the April presidential elections to sign it. The declaration surprised both American and Afghan officials. It put at risk an American deadline to have an agreement signed this year. It served notice that even with his leadership set to expire next year, Karzai intended for the United States to continue working through him at every turn until then.

Twitter blocked President Trump from Twitter for at least 12 hours, according to a report. The tweet stated that three tweets from the president had been removed and that the account would remain locked for 12 hours following the removal. The tweet also stated that if the tweets were not removed, the account would remain locked. The article questioned whether Trump would comply or whether Twitter would permanently suspend him. The tweet prompted further discussion about what action could be taken and how it would be done given the republican leadership. The article noted near-universal condemnation of domestic terrorists and their enablers in right-wing media, Congress, and the White House. The article also posed the question of whether Trump could be removed until January 20, and whether the republican party could be put on the defensive and be wound further for enabling the insurrection and for attacking America.

President Donald Trump said gun control "had little to do" with the shooting at a Pittsburgh synagogue Saturday that killed 11 people. He said the death toll would have been much lower had the synagogue hired an armed guard. Trump told reporters that if the Tree of Life synagogue had an "armed guard inside ... they would have been able to stop them," referring to suspected gunman Robert Bowers. Police said Bowers was armed with an assault rifle and handguns. Twitter responses criticized Trump for blaming the synagogue for failing to have a guard and pointed out that four of the six people wounded in the attack were police officers, all armed. They criticized him for his refusal to consider how gun laws affect gun violence in America and for his apparent aim to put even more firearms in people's hands. The idea of armed guards in places of worship drove Twitter users particularly bonkers.

Voters in Albuquerque on Tuesday defeated a ballot question that sought to ban abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy. The referendum was the first of its kind in the country for a municipality. The vote was marked by record turnout and aggressive tactics by volunteers on both sides. The volunteers sought to capitalize on controversy and passion surrounding the issue to drive voters to the polls. Political strategists said the vote demonstrated their message on abortion resonated among Hispanics, a demographic that accounts for nearly half of the residents in Albuquerque and New Mexico and is one of the fastest-growing populations in the country. Sam Bregman, chairman of the New Mexico Democratic Party, which campaigned against the ban, said in an interview: "This was a clear counterpunch to the Republicans and right-wingers who came from out of state to push their agenda on us."

Michigan lawmakers are considering hiring a state Title IX ombudsman and requiring minor patients to be advised of their rights amid criticism of how Michigan State University handled complaints against former sports doctor Larry Nassar. The proposals were among a number outlined Monday by Democrats in the Legislature, where majority Republicans also have introduced or are working on bills after more than 200 women and girls said in court that Nassar had sexually assaulted them with his ungloved hands under the guise of medical treatment. The ombudsman would work in the Michigan Department of Civil Rights and be "dedicated to listening and believing victims," said Rep. Erika Geiss, a Democrat from Taylor. Geiss said just one in five female victims of sexual assault ages 18 to 24 report it to law enforcement, some due to fear of retaliation. The ombudsman would ensure that survivors are given needed help and support, particularly after the Trump administration scrapped Obama-era guidance on investigating campus sexual assaults in favor of instructions that allow universities to require higher standards of evidence.

President Donald Trump visited Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, over the weekend. He said he wanted to get a three-month head start on his annual physical, due in February. Stephen Colbert's "Late Show" team speculated on a different reason for Trump's visit, specifically an issue with his "quid pro hole." Trump's medical visit was also the subject of speculation and cracks by Trevor Noah on "The Daily Show." Noah said, "That's not a thing. It's not like, 'Yeah, today we can just cup the balls and then in March I'll come back and cough.'" Noah also said it might be tough for any doctor to properly examine Trump.

President Bush spent Tuesday evening watching election returns at the White House. In the early hours of Wednesday, Senator John Kerry refused to concede Ohio, and the president remained in limbo. At 12:45 a.m., after Fox News and then NBC called Ohio for Bush, senior staff members watching election returns in the Roosevelt Room hurried to the White House residence. The move was intended to finish finishing touches on the president's victory speech and prepare for his arrival at an election night party at the Ronald Reagan building on Pennsylvania Avenue. Senator John Edwards, the Democratic vice-presidential nominee, made a public appearance in Boston saying the Democrats would fight on. Senior staff and the president remained in the White House residence at 2:45 a.m. Since early Tuesday, surveys of voters leaving polling sites had shown Senator John Kerry beating Bush nationally and in crucial swing states.

J.D. Scholten, a Democrat who nearly defeated Rep. Steve King (R-Iowa) in 2018, announced Monday that he will seek to challenge King again. Scholten, a former baseball player, launched his run Monday with a video narrated by Kevin Costner. Last fall, Scholten lost to King by 3% of the vote, the closest margin for any of King's challengers during his nine terms in Congress. After a long history of promoting racist and white nationalist rhetoric, as documented by HuffPost's Chris Mathias last year, King has faced consequences. In January, after a New York Times interview in which he condoned white supremacy, GOP leaders removed him from congressional committees. Scholten is the first Democrat so far to announce a run in the race against King, who represents Iowa's fourth congressional district. Several Republicans have announced primary challenges against King.

The foreign ministers of the European Union approved an arms embargo against Venezuela on Monday as part of what they called "restrictive measures" to pressure the administration of President Nicolás Maduro to strengthen the rule of law and democracy. The ministers also established the legal framework for sanctions, including travel bans and the freezing of assets, against government officials, a step the Trump administration has taken against dozens of Venezuelan government officials, including Maduro. The ministers did not name specific officials who might be subject to such penalties, saying they still hoped Venezuela could find a "peaceful negotiated way" out of its economic and political crises. "The primary responsibility for ending the crisis in Venezuela lies in the country," the ministers said in a statement. "The E.U. calls upon the government to urgently restore democratic legitimacy, including through free and fair elections, and on the opposition to continue engaging in a united manner towards a negotiated solution to the current tensions, in the interest of the country."

Israel said on Tuesday it would name a new community on the Golan Heights after U.S. President Donald Trump as an expression of gratitude for his recognition of its claim of sovereignty over the strategic plateau. Israel captured the Golan from Syria in a 1967 war and annexed it, a move not recognized internationally. The United States broke with other world powers last month when Trump signed a decree recognizing Israeli sovereignty there. "All Israelis were deeply moved when President Trump made his historic decision," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement made on the Golan. He added that, after the Jewish Passover festival, he would "bring to the government a resolution calling for a new community on the Golan Heights named after President Donald J. Trump." Trump's Golan move followed his decision in December 2017 to recognize Jerusalem as the Israeli capital, breaking with decades of U.S. policy over the status of a city contested by the Palestinians.

Speaker Pelosi named six Democratic members to a Republican Select Committee focused on dismantling women's health. The Democrats on the panel are Reps. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois, Jerrold Nadler of New York, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Jackie Speier of California, Suzan DelBene of Washington, and Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey. The Democrats are Reps. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois, Jerrold Nadler of New York, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Jackie Speier of California, Suzan DelBene of Washington, and Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey. Republicans included four women among their eight members of the panel. Democrats have women as five out of six members.

President Donald Trump posted two tweets early Wednesday morning addressing special counsel Robert Mueller's Russia investigation. Iran's official IRNA news agency reported Tuesday that Kavous Seyed-Emami, a dual Iranian and Canadian citizen, was in custody for passing information on the country's missile bases to the CIA and Mossad and planning to create an environmental crisis. IRNA quotes Tehran prosecutor Abbas Jafari Dolatabdi as saying Seyed-Emami and a network of people installed cameras in strategic areas of the country pretending to observe environmental issues but, in fact, were sending images and information to foreigners. Dolatabdi said Seyed-Emami hosted one of two U.S. intelligence officers during their visit to Iran. He did not elaborate. On Monday, Iran said Seyed-Emami took his own life.

Former Sen. Bob Dole (R-Kan.) was lifted out of his wheelchair Tuesday to give a final salute to former President George H.W. Bush. Dole, a former political rival of Bush, paid tribute to the 41st president earlier this week, describing Bush as a "cherished servant leader" who "answered the call to serve whenever the nation needed him." Bush's spokesman, Jim McGrath, described the salute as "a last, powerful gesture of respect from one member of the Greatest Generation, Senator Dole, to another." The 95-year-old Dole, who was seriously wounded during a 1945 battle in Italy, told CNN that under Bush's presidency, "three-fourths of Congress were veterans and we would stick together and work across the aisle." He also said, "And President Bush was a bipartisan president. So we got quite a lot done."

Legislation to avert furloughs at the Federal Aviation Administration has been delayed because of a typo in the bill, ABC News and CNN report. The Reducing Flight Delays Act Of 2013, which would authorize the FAA to use $253 million to fund air traffic controllers, lacks an "s" in the word "s" in the bill's "s" in the word "s." With lawmakers in recess, the bill will receive a procedural correction and be sent to the president's desk for signing Tuesday, according to ABC. The typo illustrates how quickly members of Congress moved to avert flight delays caused by sequestration cuts before they left for recess. The Senate passed the bill without a roll-call vote Thursday evening, and the House passed it by a 361-41 margin Friday morning. The FAA announced it was suspending employee furloughs on Saturday and said the nation's air traffic system would be normal by Sunday evening. Beyond the FAA and travelers dependent on it, those dependent on Meals on Wheels programs, Medicare's prescription drug program, and Head Start programs have not been spared from the impact of sequestration cuts.

The United Nations Security Council ordered new economic sanctions against North Korea on Thursday for its third nuclear test last month, unanimously approving a resolution negotiated with China. North Korea said Friday it was nullifying all agreements of nonaggression and denuclearization with South Korea and was cutting off the North-South hot line. It was unclear how North Korea's leader, Kim Jong-un, would react to the rebuke. His government has threatened to terminate the 60-year-old armistice that brought a halt to the Korean War and that has kept a cold peace on the peninsula since, and South Korean officials said they were on the alert for any possible attack by the North. Any military action or response could end up involving American forces that have remained in South Korea as it has turned from war-ravaged ruin into one of the most advanced industrialized powerhouses.

President Donald Trump tweeted on Thursday morning that it was "so wonderful" to greet some of those injured by a heavily armed gunman who opened fire on the crowd at Sunday's Route 91 Harvest Festival. Nearly 60 people were killed and more than 500 were hurt. Trump visited Las Vegas on Wednesday and met with police officers and doctors who responded to the attack. He said the trip was something he "will never forget." Trump's use of "wonderful" drew criticism on Twitter, with some users criticizing him for "making a tragedy sound like good news." Elaine Duke, the acting secretary of homeland security, called the federal response to Hurricane Maria tearing into Puerto Rico a "good news story."

Former Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid, 78, had surgery on Monday to remove a tumor from his pancreas at Johns Hopkins Cancer Center. The former senator from Nevada, who served in Congress from 1983 to 2017, is slated for chemotherapy treatment following the surgery. A family statement read: "His doctors caught the problem early during a routine screening and his surgeons are confident that the surgery was a success and the prognosis for his recovery is good." Reid's family said he is in "good spirits" after the surgery and feels grateful to his team of doctors. The news of Reid's diagnosis and surgery was first reported by KLAS-TV reporter George Knapp on Twitter and confirmed by an unnamed source to The Nevada Independent. A previous version of the article stated that Reid served in Congress from 1982 to 2016. In fact, Reid began his first term in 1983 and finished his final term in 2017.

President Trump's proposal to add $54 billion to the Pentagon budget next year would represent a 10 percent increase for a department that receives more of taxpayers' money than any other part of government. The outgoing Obama administration had forecast a $35 billion increase for the Defense Department in fiscal year 2018, so Mr. Trump's share of the proposed increase over and above that figure is $19 billion, according to budget analysts. The proposed Pentagon increase has been met with criticism from military spending hawks. White House officials said Mr. Trump will call for a significant cut in foreign aid, including programs that military officials say contribute to global stability and are seen as important in helping avoid future conflicts. Senior administration officials acknowledged on Monday that there were few specifics attached to the bigger budget number proposed for the Pentagon, so it is not yet possible to assess how many more troops, warships or jet-fighters the Pentagon will be able to field with the $54 billion.

Former Republican presidential candidate George Pataki endorsed Marco Rubio for the party's presidential nomination on Tuesday, saying he believed the U.S. senator had a broad-based campaign and the ability to unite Americans. Pataki, a former New York governor who suspended his presidential bid in late December, said in an interview on Fox News that Rubio's experience in Congress will help him lead the military and stand up to threats from abroad. "I have no doubt that Marco Rubio is ready today to lead this country, to serve and lead as our president, and to bring us together," he said. Pataki, 70, said he plans to campaign for the 44-year-old senator from Florida. "He's someone who understands not just New England or the Northeast; he understands this country," Pataki said. "I think he has the staying power and the vision to win not just the nomination, but most importantly, you have got to win the election. And I think he will."
