Edward Snowden, who leaked classified documents related to NSA tactics, was fired Tuesday by Booz Allen Hamilton, where he had worked as a contract employee, the company confirmed in a statement. Booz Allen Hamilton is a consulting firm that receives nearly all of its funding from the federal government. The company released a statement on Snowden's firing Tuesday: Booz Allen can confirm that Edward Snowden, 29, was an employee of our firm for less than 3 months, assigned to a team in Hawaii. Snowden, who had a salary at the rate of $122,000, was terminated June 10, 2013 for violations of the firm's code of ethics and firm policy. News reports that this individual has claimed to have leaked classified information are shocking, and if accurate, this action represents a grave violation of the code of conduct and core values of our firm. We will work closely with our clients and authorities in their investigation of this matter. Snowden claimed he made roughly $200,000, according to The Guardian.

The White House announced Monday that it is putting the same minds that rescued HealthCare.gov to work on other government technology challenges with the launch of a "U.S. Digital Service." The team will be led by Mikey Dickerson, a former Google engineer widely credited with playing a central role in salvaging the HealthCare.gov site after its launch. The idea behind the USDS is to institutionalize the approach that saved the health care site and apply it to the work of the government before disaster strikes. The launch follows months of discussion. In testimony before the Senate's Homeland Security Committee in May, U.S. Chief Information Officer Steve Van Roekel said the new team would have "centralized, world-class capability" and be "made up of our country's brightest digital talent." Van Roekel said: "Think of this as [a team of] management consultants that helps you understand your gaps."

A new NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll shows Barbara Bush and Hillary Clinton tied for the title of America's favorite first lady from the past 25 years. Bush and Clinton each received 27 percent support in the poll, tying for first. Current first lady Michelle Obama received 24 percent, and former first lady Laura Bush received 17 percent. The results were divided by political and demographic subgroups. Democrats preferred Obama to Clinton by a 3-point margin. Among Republicans, Barbara Bush favored her daughter-in-law by 9 points. Obama was the favorite of 58 percent of African-Americans surveyed, while Clinton was the favorite of 30 percent of those respondents. The poll also found that among Latinos surveyed, 45 percent preferred Clinton and 29 percent preferred Obama. Among whites, Barbara Bush was the favorite with 33 percent, followed by Clinton with 24 percent. The NBC/WSJ poll was conducted April 23-27 among 1,000 adults, including 300 cell-phone-only respondents.

Department of Homeland Security officials decided in recent months not to grant an application for American citizenship by Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of two brothers suspected in the Boston Marathon bombings, after a routine background check revealed he had been interviewed in 2011 by the F.B.I., federal officials said Saturday. Mr. Tsarnaev died early Friday after a shootout with police. Officials said that at the time of his death, his application for citizenship was still under review and was being investigated by federal law enforcement officials. It had been previously reported that Mr. Tsarnaev's application might have been held up because of a domestic abuse episode. Officials said that the record of the F.B.I. interview raised red flags and halted, at least temporarily, Mr. Tsarnaev's citizenship application. Federal law enforcement officials reported on Friday that the F.B.I. interviewed Mr. Tsarnaev in January 2011 at the request of the Russian government, which suspected that he had ties to Chechen terrorists.

President Obama traveled to Fort Bliss on Tuesday before his Oval Office speech on Iraq. He thanked Americans who most shouldered the burdens of what he described as a tragic, pointless war. The conflict has been one of the few rays of light in the conflict since Vietnam, when soldiers were scorned for decisions made by politicians. President George W. Bush attempted to make Iraq an invisible, seemingly cost-free war. He refused to attend soldiers' funerals and hid their returning coffins from the public. Obama has improved veterans' health care and made the Pentagon budget more rational. On Tuesday night, he said: "At every turn, America's men and women in uniform have served with courage and resolve." He added: "There were patriots who supported this war, and patriots who opposed it. And all of us are united in appreciation for our servicemen and women, and our hope for Iraq's future."

John W. Hinckley Jr., who tried to assassinate President Ronald Reagan in 1981, will be allowed to live permanently with his elderly mother in Williamsburg, Va., leaving the psychiatric hospital where he has been imprisoned for several decades, a federal judge ruled on Wednesday. Judge Paul L. Friedman of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia wrote in his opinion that Hinckley, 61, no longer posed a danger to himself or others. The release should begin no sooner than Aug. 5, the judge said. Although Hinckley has been living part time in Williamsburg for years, family and friends of Reagan said they were outraged that he would be allowed to reside there permanently. "I think it's terribly sad and wrong," Patti Davis, one of Reagan's daughters, said in a telephone interview. In a blog post on her website, Davis wrote that she had long been haunted by the shooting.

"I had very much led a deliberately private life for a long time," the former first daughter, 33, said, "and now I'm attempting to lead a purposely public life." "I'm also grateful to live in a city and a state and a country where I really believe in my elected officials, and their ethos and their competencies. Someday, if either of those weren't true, and I thought I could make more of a difference in the public sector, or if I didn't like how my city or state or country were being run, I'd have to ask and answer that question."

On Friday, nearly six months after his escape, Joaquín Guzmán Loera, the Mexican drug lord known as El Chapo, was captured again after a gun battle near the coast in his home state of Sinaloa, Mexican officials said. President Enrique Peña Nieto announced, "Mission accomplished: We have him." The arrest ended a manhunt involving every law enforcement agency in the country and assistance from the United States. The marines, Mexico's most-trusted military force, captured the fugitive in an early morning raid that left five people dead, the Mexican authorities said. An American official described the raid as "a Mexican op, planned and executed by Mexico."

Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid has introduced an amendment that would ban gun ownership by people convicted of misdemeanors under the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act, a 1994 law meant to prevent violence and harassment at abortion clinics. The amendment is a response to last week's shooting at a Planned Parenthood clinic in Colorado, where three people were killed and nine were injured. Reid said the shooting in San Bernardino only strengthened his resolve. He addressed his colleagues from the Senate floor Thursday morning, saying they are "complicit through our inaction. And if we continue to fail to act we'll be complicit today and every day into the future." The Senate will begin voting on amendments to the repeal bill this afternoon.

The Nimitz, the guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton, and other 5th Fleet personnel continued their search on Monday, Rebarich said. She declined to identify the sailor, citing Navy policy. The Nimitz, whose homeport is Bremerton, Washington, has been in the Arabian Sea since late July. It replaced the aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, which had spent months in the Arabian Sea during its deployment that saw the carrier break the Navy's previous at-sea record. Navy officials have limited port calls due to the coronavirus pandemic. The Nimitz's arrival in the Mideast saw Iran conduct a live-fire drill targeting a mockup aircraft carrier resembling it. The drill underlined the threat of military conflict between Iran and the U.S. after a series of incidents last year led to an American drone strike that killed a top Iranian general in Baghdad. Tehran responded to that strike by firing ballistic missiles that wounded dozens of American forces in Iraq.

A letter to the editor responded to a New York Times article titled "Trump Says Kentucky Derby Ruling Was 'Not a Good One'." The letter stated that stewards of the Kentucky Derby reviewed evidence and determined that the horse that came in first had competed unfairly and should be disqualified. The letter writer said President Trump objected to this. The writer said this objection reflects a worldview in which rules and fairness do not matter as long as you win, clear evidence of malfeasance, whether in a video replay or in a special counsel's report, be damned. The writer said the Kentucky Derby is a longstanding American tradition whose stewards took seriously their responsibility to ensure a just outcome. The writer said they wish members of Congress could act as decisively as the stewards of the Derby.

The Presidential Debate Commission announced Monday that it will cut off microphones during Thursday's debate while President Donald Trump and Democrat Joe Biden deliver their opening two-minute answers to each of the debate topics. The 90-minute debate is divided into six 15-minute segments, with each candidate granted two minutes to deliver uninterrupted remarks before proceeding to an open debate. The open discussion portion of the debate will not feature a mute button, but interruptions by either candidate will count toward their time in the second and final debate Thursday. The commission's announcement followed a contentious opening between the two presidential contenders that featured frequent interruptions, most by Trump. The commission faced pressure from the Trump campaign to avoid changing the rules, while Biden's team sought a more ordered debate. In a statement, the commission said it had determined it was appropriate to adopt measures intended to promote adherence to agreed upon rules and inappropriate to make changes to those rules.

During an MSNBC interview with Andrea Mitchell, former National Security Adviser Susan Rice said that investigations into Russia's influence in the 2016 elections "are very important and very serious." Rice rejected any suggestion that the Obama White House surveilled either Trump or his team. "The notion, which some people are trying to suggest, that by asking for the identity of the American person is the same is leaking it — that's completely false," Rice said. "There is no equivalence between so-called unmasking and leaking." Rice also said the sitting president has no personal authority to order surveillance of any American, rendering Trump's claims implausible. Her appearance was met with immediate Twitter responses from the White House.

It's like he's saying to the Russians, 'I know you don't like blind dates but these missiles they're really nice, really smart. Just come, no pressure. It's just a launch.'"

Eric Cantor's primary defeat against David Brat on Tuesday means that House Republicans will lose one of their best fund-raisers and a crucial link to some major donors the party is otherwise not close to. Mr. Cantor's leadership PAC, which he uses to dole out campaign money to his House colleagues and to Republican candidates, has raised more money since the beginning of 2013 than any other run by a member of Congress. It brought in more than $3.5 million from last year until April 30. Figures for May will be available by June 20. Even as he raised millions for his own race, Mr. Cantor pushed hundreds of thousands of dollars to his colleagues and to his local party. Part of his fund-raising success is due to his position as majority leader, and his successor will have similar sway. Mr. Cantor has also shown an ability to raise money from donors some Republicans struggle to attract — and that will be harder for the party to replace.

During his first State of the Union address Tuesday, President Donald Trump mentioned the words "immigrants" and "immigration more than any other president in the last 100 years since President Woodrow Wilson started delivering the State of the Union as a speech instead of a written report. The article noted that words and phrases were used in this year's State of the Union speech and in speeches and annual addresses past. Every square represents one instance and the quote from that speech can be accessed by hovering over a square. The analysis includes annual addresses to Congress and State of the Union addresses. It includes written addresses where oral addresses are not available (1919, 1920, 1924, 1932, 1946). The 1946 address was a lengthy written address, which may skew some results.

The author wrote for the first time that they have written President Obama at the White House. The author wrote: "Thank you for your diligent work of behalf of the American people over the last six years. In the next two, you will have challenges keeping Congress from impeding your, and our, agenda to make the USA a better place. I think you are a truly great president, and although I do think you could have done more, sooner, I'll not quibble. I write this to offer my support of $50 to buy ink for your veto pen that I hope you use aggressively over the next two years. Where can I send my $50? I would be proud knowing the very ink flowing from your pen was paid for by me and other supporters in our joint effort to stop the spread of injustice, intolerance, ignorance, and ineptitude. I voted for you twice and would again. I am a firefighter in Austin, Texas and wish you the best in keeping down the flames of hate. Thank you for your wisdom and service."

Gary D. Cohn, the chief White House economic adviser, is convening senior climate and energy ministers from about a dozen nations in New York next Monday for a breakfast in New York, the White House confirmed Tuesday. The breakfast will be held against devastation in the United States and the Caribbean from two hurricanes that scientists say may have been made more ferocious by warming trends. The event comes as the Trump administration has declared it will withdraw from the global Paris agreement while also telling nations it remains open to continued discussions. Invitations were sent to officials from the world's largest economies. The event is billed as "an opportunity for key ministers with responsibility for these issues to engage in an informal exchange of views and discuss how we can move forward most productively," according to the invitation. The note says the group will be kept small and include ministerial-level officials only.

Donald Trump held a cabinet meeting before a worldwide audience. As reporters were being ushered out of the room, Trump declared to all in attendance that "there has never been a president as tough on Russia as I have been." The article reported that worldwide laughter was audible as the words came out of his mouth. The article stated that if Trump does not believe the Russians are engaged in cyber warfare and are actively working to interfere in the 2018 elections, he is not doing anything to stop them. The article also stated that National intelligence officials should be walking out the door today demanding Trump's resignation.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on two high-profile gay marriage cases this week. The chart was presented by Pew Research Center. It was the result of a question asking people to name the Chief Justice of the United States from a handful of options. Less than three in ten people were able to name John Roberts as the current Chief Justice. More than half did not know who it was. Nearly one in five people named Thurgood Marshall, who was deceased and never Chief Justice, while four percent chose Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, who is not on the Supreme Court.

A CBS/NYT poll conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday found a divide on President Obama's response to the Ferguson shooting. Forty-one percent of Americans are satisfied with how Obama is responding to the situation, while 34 percent are dissatisfied. Twenty-five percent do not have an opinion. African-Americans were more likely to approve of the president than whites, whose attitudes split along party lines. Missouri Gov. Jay Nixon received weaker reviews overall. Only a quarter of blacks nationally are satisfied with Nixon's actions, while nearly half said Nixon's performance in the aftermath of the shooting was not satisfactory. Among whites, a third were satisfied and a third were dissatisfied.

A video surfaced Wednesday showing President Trump visiting the University Medical Center of El Paso following a mass shooting. The video shows Trump talking to medical staff about crowd sizes at political rallies earlier in the year. As he exchanges pleasantries with doctors and others at the hospital, he pauses to reminisce about rallies he and Texas Democrat Beto O'Rourke held in El Paso in February focused on immigration and border security. "That was some crowd," Trump says of his event. "We had twice the number outside. And then you had this crazy Beto. Beto had like 400 people in a parking lot, and they said his crowd was wonderful." Trump told aides on Air Force One that news cameras were not with him in the hospital on Wednesday and that coverage of the trip was being dominated by his foes.

Bill Maher called President Donald Trump's close relationship with Fox News host Sean Hannity a "violation" on Friday's broadcast of "Real Time." Maher discussed the courtroom revelation that Hannity was the "mystery" client of Trump's personal attorney Michael Cohen. Maher acknowledged that he "got" that Hannity "obviously carries Trump's water every day on the air." Maher also addressed the revelation that Hannity reportedly talks with the president every day. Maher said, "I mean, this is such a violation of what the Fourth Estate is supposed to be. It's not supposed to be a branch of the First Estate. Can you imagine if they found out that (former President Barack) Obama was talking to Rachel Maddow every day?"

Top U.S. diplomat Rex Tillerson and Turkey's Tayyip Erdogan had a meeting on Thursday about improving ties strained recently over their policies on Syria, in a meeting following weeks of rhetoric from Ankara. Tillerson arrived in Turkey on Thursday for two days of what officials said would likely be uncomfortable discussions between the allies, whose relations have frayed over a number of issues, particularly U.S. support for the Syrian Kurdish YPG militia, which Turkey considers as terrorists. Turkey launched an air and ground assault last month in Syria's northwest Afrin region to drive the YPG from the area south of its border. Ankara considers the YPG to be an arm of the PKK, a banned group that has waged a decades-long insurgency in Turkey. The militia is the main ground element of the Syrian Defence Forces (SDF), which the United States has armed, trained and aided with air support and special forces to fight Islamic State.

House Government Oversight Committee Chairman Darrell Issa shut off the microphone and walked out of the room when Maryland Rep. Elijah Cummings, the committee's top Democrat, criticized the GOP's IRS investigation. Cummings said he would like to use his time to make brief points, stating that for the past year, the central Republican accusation had been made. Issa cut off the mic. Cummings said: "We're done. Close it down."

President Barack Obama signed into law Friday a final bill authored by former Rep. Gabrielle Giffords. Giffords was wounded in an Arizona shooting a year ago. She took part in the signing ceremony at the White House. She resigned from Congress last month as she continues to recover from a gunshot wound to the head. The legislation increases the penalties for using ultra-light aircraft when smuggling drugs into the country. The small, single-seat planes are an increasingly favored tool that smugglers use to fly at night and then release their haul without detection. Obama said he told Giffords he expected to see more of her in the months and years to come. "I'm confident that, while this legislation may have been her last act as a congresswoman, it will not be her last act of public service," Obama said in a statement released by the White House. Giffords stepped down on the day the House passed her bill by a vote of 428-0.

President Obama and Hillary Clinton participated in a joint "60 Minutes" interview on Sunday. During the interview, interviewer Steve Kroft asked Obama, "What's the date of expiration on this endorsement?" Obama responded, "Oh, Steve. Everyone in this town is talking about it!" Clinton laughed. Obama said, "Steve, you guys in the press are incorrigible. I literally got inaugurated four days ago, and you're talking about elections four years from now!" Clinton added, "As you know, Steve, I am still secretary of state. So I'm out of politics. And I'm forbidden from even hearing these questions."

On Saturday, Donald Trump criticized Fox News for Sunday interviews with former FBI Director James Comey and Representative Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). Both men are being interviewed by Chris Wallace on "Fox News Sunday." Trump said Fox News was trying "sooo hard to be politically correct." He said "only pro Trump Fox shows do well" and added: "Rest are nothing." He also asked: "How's Shep doing?" — referring to former Fox News host Shepard Smith, who frequently criticized Trump and left the network in October. Trump also criticized MSNBC. Twitter critics did not let the president get off easy.

A letter to the editor responded to a May 30 news article titled "White House Asked Navy to Hide McCain Warship" that raised two possibilities. The first possibility is that President Trump's denial is a lie. The writer said this would not be surprising, because Trump lies continually and has no act of shabby vindictiveness to which he will not stoop. The writer said this is one of the vanishingly rare cases in which he is telling the truth. The writer said this would mean Trump does not have a grip on what is happening in his own White House and has created a climate of appalling small-mindedness and indifference to the political neutrality of the armed forces. The writer said neither possibility suits the dignity of a proud democracy and that Trump should make America great again.

President Obama summoned the heads of some of the nation's largest financial institutions to the White House on Friday and urged them to accept responsibility for their industry's excesses. The 13 chief executives emerged from the 90-minute meeting pledging to cooperate with the administration's efforts to shore up the banking industry and the broader economy. Administration officials and the bankers presented a unified message to the nation: We're all in this together. The White House had asked the banks on Thursday to provide broad, public endorsements of the administration's financial recovery program, according to bank officials. With the White House in the backdrop, one executive after another offered support for the president's efforts in several television interviews coordinated by the administration.

An Army sergeant who served as a sexual assault prevention and response coordinator at Fort Hood, Texas, is under investigation for allegations of pandering, abusive sexual contact, assault and maltreatment of subordinates, Pentagon officials said late Tuesday. The inquiry comes as the White House, the Pentagon and the armed services are dealing with the problem of sexual assault in the military. The Pentagon released a survey last week estimating that 26,000 people in the armed forces were sexually assaulted last year, up from 19,000 in 2010. A separate report recorded 3,374 sexual assault reports last year, a lower number than the survey, suggesting that many victims are not reporting the crimes. The noncommissioned officer under investigation had been working as an equal opportunity adviser and sexual harassment/assault response and prevention program coordinator with a battalion of troops — about 2,000 soldiers — assigned to the Army's III Corps at Fort Hood when the allegations surfaced, the Pentagon said in a statement.

Donald Trump said in a Wednesday interview with the conservative outlet the Daily Caller that "this Russia thing" was on his mind when he fired then-FBI Director James Comey. Trump associated the Russia probe with his appointment of acting Attorney General Matthew Whitaker. "I knew him only as he pertained, you know, as he was with Jeff Sessions," Trump said in response to his "thinking" about the attorney general position. "And, you know, look, as far as I'm concerned this is an investigation that should have never been brought. It should have never been had. It's something that should have never been brought. It's an illegal investigation."

Michelle Obama said her daughters, Sasha, 9, and Malia, 12, have certain restrictions that other children do not have because of Secret Service security issues. During an interview on NBC's "Today Show" on Wednesday, she said she is "not a big fan of young kids having Facebook." She added that Facebook is "not something they need." She added that it may be replaced when they get older. "It depends on when we leave and how old they are," Obama replied to a question about whether the girls would join the social networking site after the Obamas left the White House. Facebook's rules do not permit users under 13 years of age to use the site.

Thursday marked the fourth night of protests following the death of 16-year-old Kimani Gray, who was shot and killed by NYPD officers outside his best friend's house in East Flatbush, Brooklyn. Police maintain Gray was armed and pointed a weapon at officers. Dozens of demonstrators have been arrested, and a police officer suffered a wound to his face after being hit by an object. Mayor Michael Bloomberg said a "full and fair" investigation into the shooting would be conducted and urged community members to abstain from violence. "I understand that there's anger in the community, but the way to get answers is not through violence or law-breaking," Bloomberg said. "We cannot tolerate that, and we will not tolerate that." HuffPost Live examined Gray's death to ask whether NYPD officers are too disconnected with the communities they serve to protect.

The nation's top auto safety regulator, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, will test blame on General Motors when he testifies on Tuesday before a House subcommittee looking into the ignition problem of Chevrolet Cobalts and other cars. In written testimony filed in advance, David Friedman, the acting administrator, argues that "G.M. had critical information that would have helped identify this defect." Formal written testimony is usually not read in its entirety at a hearing but becomes part of the official record and gives indications about the tack witnesses will take in the question-and-answer session that follows. Mr. Friedman is scheduled to testify before the House Energy and Commerce subcommittee on oversight and investigations. The other witness is Mary T. Barra, the chief executive of General Motors, who is expected to strike an apologetic tone but not provide answers to why G.M. failed to act for more than a decade to fix the problem.

Robert M. Gates wrote in his book "Duty" that Hillary Rodham Clinton has fared better than either President Obama or Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Gates wrote that Obama could be cynical and controlling, and that Biden had an unerring capacity to be wrong on big issues. Gates wrote that Clinton was, in his words, "smart, idealistic but pragmatic, tough-minded, indefatigable, a very valuable colleague, and a superb representative of the United States all over the world." Gates paints a less flattering picture of Clinton as secretary of state, and not just because of his well-publicized claim that she confessed to opposing the Iraq troop "surge" for political reasons during the 2008 Democratic primaries.

As the White House was affected by the Monica Lewinsky scandal in January 1998, aides offered advice to President Bill Clinton's speechwriting team on how to use the State of the Union address that month to rebuild public confidence in the president. Minyon Moore, the president's public liaison, wrote in a memo: "Please recognize, I am in no way suggesting that he use his speech to discuss our current situation head-on. I am simply stating that we cannot take his supporters for granted, nor his detractors, and they need to be reassured on several fronts." Moore suggested that Mr. Clinton invoke God "as the underpinning for his policy and thought process." Her memo was among roughly 2,500 pages of documents from the Clinton White House years that were made public on Friday by the National Archives. More of the 30,000 documents will be released over the next several weeks.

The author wrote that when Trump is not threatening voters by threatening them with graphic visions of invading brown-skinned rapists, robbers, and murderers entering their homes, he claims he is solely responsible for the current strength of the economy. The author proposed a non-tribal, non-prevaricating look at the economy to determine whether Trump is the real deal or just another con-man. The author wrote that the economy cannot be judged by his claims about the stock market or economic statistics or even the unemployment rate. The author said the economy is worse, not better under Trump. The author then posed the question: is your living standard better or worse than it was on January 20, 2017?

The White House says President Barack Obama will not say "Mission accomplished" in his speech Tuesday night about the end of the U.S. combat role in Iraq. Seven years ago, President George W. Bush stood on an aircraft carrier to declare an end to major combat operations in Iraq. A banner proclaiming "Mission Accomplished" flew nearby. The Bush White House expressed regret that sign as the war dragged on and U.S. deaths mounted. "You won't hear those words coming from us," Obama spokesman Robert Gibbs said. Instead, Gibbs said, Obama will talk about what is involved in the U.S. troop drawdown and the changing mission in Iraq. However, Obama does plan to call Bush on Tuesday before delivering his Oval Office address, Gibbs said, though he would not say what Obama's message to his predecessor would be. Obama also called Bush last year before delivering a speech laying out the Iraq withdrawal timeline.

Puerto Rico's Department of Education said Wednesday that a U.S. judge issued an arrest warrant for the agency's boss but later withdrew it after officials pledged to submit documents related to a federal investigation. The department said the unidentified documents sought by the court are from 2011 to 2013, before Julia Keleher was appointed education secretary in December 2016. The documents are being sought as part of an investigation into a school tutoring program, officials said. The department's statement contradicted an earlier interview published by the newspaper Primera Hora that quoted Pedro Fortier of the U.S. Marshals Service as saying an arrest warrant was not issued. Fortier did not return messages for comment. Lymarie Llovet, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney's office, also said that an arrest warrant was issued. She added that the documents in the case are sealed and that she had no further details.

This week, the Obamas welcomed a new member to the first family — a 14-month-old female Portuguese Water dog called Sunny. In an interview with CNN's Chris Cuomo on Friday, the president revealed details about the new puppy. "Bo was getting lonely," the president said when asked why they got Sunny. "[He] was getting a little down in the dumps inside the house." With Sunny around, 4-year-old Bo has a playmate. Sunny (left) hangs out with Bo Obama. First Lady Michelle Obama, meanwhile, is in "full parenting mode," the president said -- especially because little Sunny has already had a few accidents in the White House. The president did not seem concerned. "We live in rental housing. We didn't have to put down a deposit," he said. "But we are making sure that it gets cleaned up for the next occupant."

The Federal Communications Commission will double the amount of money it devotes to adding high-speed Internet connections in schools and libraries over the next two years, officials said Saturday. The increase is in an effort to meet President Obama's promise to provide broadband service for an estimated 20 million American students in 15,000 schools. Financing for the new spending will come from restructuring the $2.4 billion E-Rate program, which provides money for "advanced telecommunications and information services" using the proceeds of fees paid by telecommunications users. The proportion that goes to broadband service in schools and libraries will increase to $2 billion a year from $1 billion. Obama referred to the changes during his State of the Union address last week. The changes will not require any additional taxes or assessments, according to an F.C.C. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity because a formal announcement was being planned for this week.

Sixty years after the Supreme Court outlawed "separate but equal" schools for blacks and whites, civil rights advocates say American schools are becoming increasingly segregated. First lady Michelle Obama said Friday that "many young people are going to schools with kids who look just like them." "Today, by some measures, our schools are as segregated as they were back when Dr. King gave his final speech," Obama told 1,200 graduating high school seniors Friday in the city that gave rise to the Brown v. Board of Education case. In a speech that was part commencement address, part policy pronouncement and part journey into her own past, Obama said that Brown's advances were being reversed. "Many districts in this country have actually pulled back on efforts to integrate their schools, and many communities have become less diverse," she said, leading to schools that are less diverse.

A blaze at the William J Clinton Birthplace, a National Historic Site in Hope, Arkansas, early Christmas morning is suspected to be arson, authorities said. The fire, which damaged the birthplace of Bill Clinton, began at about 3.20 a.m., according to Hope Fire Department Chief Dale Glanton. Glanton said it does not appear the building was set on fire by accident. As of the time of writing, no area churches or their nativity scenes were set ablaze, lending to the appearance of graffiti at the scene.

A special agent with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Homeland Security Investigations unit, Kelton Harrison, was shot and wounded early Tuesday while on surveillance in a criminal investigation in northern Hidalgo County, Texas, officials said. Special Agent Harrison was listed in stable condition by mid-afternoon after being taken to a local hospital where he underwent surgery for a gunshot wound, ICE spokeswoman Nina Pruneda said in a statement. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the special agent and his family," she added. The shooting happened early in a brushy area just outside Hargill, Texas, ICE said. The FBI field office in San Antonio said Tuesday it was involved in an investigation that the agency called an "AFO" or assault upon a federal officer. A spokesman for the FBI, Erik Vasys, would not offer any more details. The Texas Department of Public Safety, the Texas Rangers and the Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office were also assisting the case, ICE said.

President Donald Trump posted on Twitter early Saturday that there was "great support coming from all sides" for border security and his promised U.S.-Mexico border wall. Trump is refusing to end the partial government shutdown unless Democrats grant him federal funding for the wall he originally told voters Mexico would pay for. Democratic lawmakers, including House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, have said they do not endorse the wall idea. Talks between Trump's White House and congressional staffers are set to continue Saturday as they attempt to negotiate an end to the shutdown, the Associated Press reported. Trump followed up with another tweet in which he suggested Democrats "could solve the Shutdown problem in a very short period of time." He wrote: "All they have to do is approve REAL Border Security (including a Wall)!" He added: "This would be so easy to do!"

David Axelrod, a former top adviser to President Obama, said Sunday that it was a "mistake" for Obama to say in a speech last week that his policies are effectively on the ballot in the midterm elections this fall. "I wouldn't put that line there," Axelrod said on NBC's "Meet The Press." In a Thursday speech, Obama said: "I am not on the ballot this fall. Michelle's pretty happy about that. But make no mistake: These policies are on the ballot. Every single one of them." Republicans began running attack ads using the words to tie Democratic congressional candidates to the president, who polls show is unpopular. Axelrod added, "Understand, if you read the speech, the context of the line was the things he's pushing forward — minimum wage, pay equity, infrastructure — and he said these are on the ballot." Axelrod concluded, "It was a mistake."

Former President Jimmy Carter announced Sunday that his most recent scan shows he is cancer free. Carter, 91, made the announcement near the beginning of Sunday School class at Maranatha Baptist Church in Plains. A close friend and fellow church member Jill Stuckey said by phone from Maranatha, where Carter was teaching to about 350 people, many of them visitors, that Carter said he had gotten a scan this week and the cancer was gone. Stuckey said the church, many of them visitors, erupted in applause. In August, Carter said doctors had found four small melanoma lesions on his brain. The discovery followed the removal of a lesion on his liver that took about ten percent of the organ. He said he would receive four drug treatments, along with radiation therapy, and that he would cut back significantly on his schedule.

Republican candidate Scott Brown spoke at a campaign rally in Boston on the eve of the special election to fill the Senate seat left by the late Edward M. Kennedy. He stated, "With your help, our dream of depriving millions of health care is within reach." He also said, "Let's send a message, Massachusetts!" and "Let's tell people across the country that if they want health coverage, they are shit out of luck!" An aide to Brown said internal polling indicates the Republican's anti-healthcare message may be catching on: "Right now, Scott is showing a double-digit lead among people who describe themselves as douchebags." The article also referenced a Huffington Post article by Roy Sekoff on The Ed Show on Tuesday evening regarding the Massachusetts Senate race between Democrat Martha Coakley and Republican Scott Brown.

A dispute over the White House account of the attack on the American diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, flared up on Friday, with a disclosure of e-mails that show the White House was more deeply involved in revising talking points about the attack than officials have previously acknowledged. The e-mails, which the administration turned over to Congress, show the White House coordinating an intensive process with the State Department, the C.I.A., the F.B.I. and other agencies to obtain the final version of the talking points, used by Susan E. Rice, the ambassador to the United Nations, in television appearances after the attack. The State Department, in particular, pushed to remove references to Al Qaeda and Ansar al-Sharia, the Libyan militant group suspected of carrying out the attack, as well as warnings about other potential terrorist threats from the C.I.A., which drafted the initial talking points.

President Obama announced this morning that he would assign the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Susan Rice to the role of national security advisor, a position left open when Tom Donilon resigned from the post. In her new role, Rice will work directly with President Obama from the White House as his senior advisor on national security matters and operates from the White House Situation Room during times of crisis. Rice's name was floated last year as a possible lead contender to become secretary of state when Hillary Clinton retired from the role. Republicans in the Senate said they would not confirm her for that position, citing what they described as perceived missteps in the Benghazi matter. Other conservatives called Rice a "black radical." Environmentalists also disapproved of Rice for State and accused her of being invested in creating the Keystone XL oil tar sands pipeline, which they strongly oppose. Rice has also been accused of enabling massive violence throughout Africa.

The United Nations Security Council moved closer on Tuesday to expanding sanctions on North Korea for its nuclear and ballistic missile activities. The United States and China introduced a resolution that would target North Korean bankers and overseas cash couriers, tighten inspections of suspect ship and air cargo, and subject the country's diplomats to invasive scrutiny and increased risk of expulsion. The measure was drafted in response to the third North Korean underground nuclear test three weeks ago. China, North Korea's major benefactor, participated in drafting the language. It would be the fourth Security Council sanctions resolution on North Korea, which has defied the previous measures with increasing belligerence. A vote was expected on Thursday. North Korea vowed to scrap the 1953 armistice that halted the Korean War and threatened to attack the United States with what the North Korean government news agency called an arsenal of diverse "lighter and smaller nukes."

CNN host Jake Tapper was on vacation on Monday when a chyron appeared at the bottom of the screen during a segment led by guest host Jim Sciutto about Donald Trump's transition into the White House and whether the president-elect needs to distance himself from what he called the racist and Nazi-sympathizing "alt-right." The chyron characterized recent comments made by white nationalist Richard Spencer. Tapper responded on Twitter, saying he was "furious" and that the chyron was "unacceptable," as it would imply the worst about the segment. Scuitto also tweeted that he was upset over the chyron after the show. A CNN spokesperson told The Huffington Post, "It was poor judgment, and we very much regret it and apologize."

Energy Secretary Rick Perry is working his way to the White House exit according to two people familiar with his plans who spoke to Bloomberg. One person said Perry has not fully made up his mind. Another said his "exit isn't imminent." Perry spokeswoman Shaylyn Hunes said, "He is happy where he is serving President Trump and leading the Department of Energy." Other sources insist he is greasing the skids for his departure. That includes preparing his deputy, Dan Brouillette, to take over according to Bloomberg's sources. The article states that part of Perry's motivation in seeking to leave before the end of Trump's first term is a desire to build his income before retiring.

A letter to the editor responded to a May 17 news article titled "Trump Rants on Unauthorized Migrants: 'These Aren't People, These Are Animals'." The article described immigrants as "animals," "losers," "crazy," and "psycho." The letter writer stated that nothing President Trump says is a surprise anymore, but the article continues to draw attention. The letter writer said funding cuts in education, infrastructure, conservation, and early childhood programs continue to be made. The letter writer said Trump continues to undermine what is left of civil relationships and directs the focus of Americans, both Democrats and Republicans, away from the real priorities and toward daily drama. John N. CORBIN, CARY, N.C., wrote that Trump seems adept at directing the focus of Americans, both Democrats and Republicans, away from the real priorities and toward daily drama.

An envelope containing the compound ricin and addressed to President Donald Trump was intercepted earlier this week before it could reach the White House, law enforcement officials said Saturday, according to several news outlets, including The Associated Press. The FBI, Secret Service and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are reportedly investigating the package's source. Ricin is a highly toxic substance found in castor beans. As little as one milligram of it can kill an adult, according to a Cornell University fact sheet about the compound. There is no known antidote. It is unclear whether the package — which investigators believe was sent from Canada — was intercepted before it reached the White House mailroom, The New York Times reported. The White House mailroom is located at a remote site elsewhere in Washington. Packages containing ricin have, in the past, been intercepted en route to other political figures, including former President Barack Obama and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

Cambridge Analytica, an upstart voter-profiling company, secured a $15 million investment from Robert Mercer, a wealthy Republican donor, and recruited his political adviser, Stephen K. Bannon. The firm had promised tools that could identify the personalities of American voters and influence their behavior. It did not have the data to make its new products work.

A special Minnesota panel of three judges from three separate courts ruled that Al Franken, a Democrat, won the most votes in his 2008 Senate race against incumbent Republican Norm Coleman. The ruling on Monday is not expected to be the final decision because Coleman previously announced plans to appeal to the State Supreme Court, which has 10 days to do so. That appeal could mean a delay of several more weeks in seating Minnesota's second senator. After a statewide recount and a seven-week trial, Franken is 312 votes ahead. He gained more votes from the election challenge than Coleman, the candidate who filed it. A special Minnesota panel of three judges from three separate courts ruled that Al Franken, a Democrat, won the most votes in his 2008 Senate race against incumbent Republican Norm Coleman. The ruling on Monday is not expected to be the final decision because Coleman previously announced plans to appeal to the State Supreme Court, which has 10 days to do so. That appeal could mean a delay of several more weeks in seating Minnesota's second senator. After a statewide recount and a seven-week trial, Franken is 312 votes ahead. He gained more votes from the election challenge than Coleman, the candidate who filed it. The state law Coleman sued under required three judges to determine who got the most votes and is therefore entitled to an election certificate. That certificate is being held up pending appeal.

President-elect Donald J. Trump has expressed skepticism about climate change and appointed fossil fuel advocates to his cabinet. Bill Gates, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft, announced on Monday the start of a billion-dollar investment fund to invest in transformative energy research and development to reduce emissions that cause climate change. The fund would supplement and build on basic research already underway at government labs that may be threatened by the incoming administration. Gates said he expected the president-elect to recognize that government funding of basic research would eventually be good for business, jobs, infrastructure and other economic elements that Trump campaigned on. "It's a good deal," Gates said.

United Nations experts contend North Korea has been shipping supplies to the Syrian government that could be used in the production of chemical weapons. The evidence comes as the United States and other countries have accused the Syrian government of using chemical weapons on civilians, including recent attacks on civilians in the Damascus suburb of eastern Ghouta using what appears to have been chlorine gas. The supplies from North Korea include acid-resistant tiles, valves and thermometers, according to a report by United Nations investigators. North Korean missile technicians have also been spotted working at known chemical weapons and missile facilities inside Syria, according to the report, which was written by a panel of experts who looked at North Korea's compliance with United Nations sanctions. The report highlights the potential danger posed by any such trade between Syria and North Korea, which could allow Syria to maintain its chemical weapons while also providing North Korea with cash for its nuclear and missile programs.

House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) presided over his first Capitol Christmas tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday. He held a moment of silence for the victims of the mass shooting in San Bernardino, California, and asked for prayers. "We are all thinking about the current and ongoing tragedy in California today," he said. "Please keep the victims and families in your prayers right now." A day earlier, Ryan had urged Congress to prioritize mental health reform in response to last week's mass shooting at a Planned Parenthood clinic in Colorado. He did not mention steps related to gun control, such as mandating background checks and closing loopholes that make it easy to buy guns. "I'm sure that members of both parties have lots of ideas in this area, but we should make this a priority to prevent the violence to protect our citizens," he said, calling mental illness a "common denominator" in gun violence.

On Wednesday, Seth Meyers criticized Steve Bannon after Republican candidate Roy Moore lost Alabama's Senate race despite Bannon's support. Meyers said, "Bannon made mistake after mistake." Before the special election on Tuesday, Bannon appeared at a Moore rally and criticized MSNBC host Joe Scarborough for not getting into prestigious universities like Bannon did. Scarborough, a former congressman from Florida, is an alumnus of the University of Alabama. Meyers asked, "How stupid do you have to be to insult the University of Alabama in Alabama?" He added, "Who do you think they're going to support? 'Roll Tide' or someone who looks like he literally rolled up in the tide."

President Barack Obama and presumptive Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney are tied in Ohio, according to a poll released Thursday by Quinnipiac University. Obama leads Romney 45-44. When voters are asked whether they would vote for an Obama-Biden ticket or a ticket with Romney and Sen. Rob Portman (R-Ohio), who many speculate will be Romney's vice presidential nominee, the two are tied at 45-45. In a poll on Feb. 15, the firm had Obama up 46-44 over Romney, and with the addition of vice presidents, he was up 47-43. Other recent polls in Ohio have shown Obama with a slightly larger edge. The state has voted for the winner in every presidential election since 1960. There remains a substantial gender gap in Ohio polling, with men voting 50-40 for Romney and women voting 49-38 for Obama.

The Senate on Thursday confirmed the nomination of Sylvia Mathews Burwell to be secretary of health and human services, which will make her responsible for delivering health insurance to more than one-third of all Americans. Burwell was confirmed by a vote of 78 to 17. All the no votes were cast by Republicans. 24 Republicans joined 52 Democrats and two independents in voting for confirmation. Burwell, 48, has been director of the White House Office of Management and Budget since April of last year. White House officials said President Obama selected her because he wanted a proven manager to carry out the health care law, which got off to a rocky start under Kathleen Sebelius as health secretary. Senator Tim Kaine, Democrat of Virginia, said Thursday that she had brought "a more businesslike approach" to the White House budget office and that she would do the same at the Department of Health and Human Services.

At the Ligueros Club in Cartagena, Colombia, prostitutes dressed in lingerie wait for a bell to ring signaling the arrival of men on the prowl. American investigators seeking to determine the late-night activities of a group of Secret Service agents and military personnel assigned to President Obama's recent visit to Colombia have begun searching for as many as 21 women who are believed to include prostitutes and to have spent the night with the security officers, American security officials say. After uncovering evidence of misconduct, investigators for the Secret Service are seeking to interview women who are said to have accompanied 11 agents — including snipers and explosives experts — to their hotel rooms after a night of heavy drinking, said Representative Peter T. King, the chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security.

A federal appeals panel in Manhattan ordered the release on Monday of key portions of a classified Justice Department memorandum that provided legal justification for the targeted killing of a United States citizen, Anwar al-Awlaki. Intelligence officials contend al-Awlaki had joined Al Qaeda and died in a 2011 drone strike in Yemen. The unanimous three-judge panel, reversing a lower court decision, said the government had waived its right to keep the analysis secret in light of numerous public statements by administration officials and the Justice Department's release of a "white paper" offering a detailed analysis of why targeted killings were legal. Judge Jon O. Newman wrote for the panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit that whatever protection the legal analysis might once have had has been lost by public statements of public officials at the highest levels and official disclosure of the D.O.J. White Paper.

Almost a decade ago, an Arab diplomat likened the relationship between the United States and Saudi Arabia to a Catholic marriage "where you can have no divorce." There can be estrangement. The Obama administration is assessing the newly reconstituted House of Saud after the death of King Abdullah on Friday. Saudi Arabia's new king, Salman, 79, inherits policies put in place by the more assertive brother he is succeeding and conflicts that in recent years have characterized relations with Washington. On issues from Iran to the Arab Spring, from Syria to domestic issues within Saudi Arabia like the recent flogging of a journalist, there have been significant differences between American officials and the Saudi royal family.

At an event at George Washington University today, Nancy Pelosi praised Bernie Sanders and said he could win the nomination. Pelosi said, "It would be fabulous to have a woman president. You can't ask somebody to vote for somebody because of their gender." Pelosi said she voted with Sanders and against DOMA in 1996. She said, "[Hillary Clinton] is a very qualified person who happens to be a woman, but I haven't endorsed anybody yet. Bernie Sanders was my colleague in the House. We voted against DOMA, you know, against all of those things people are subjecting to scrutiny now. He's fabulous, and he has a very important tonic for the country and for the Democratic Party because he has ideas." Pelosi said, "He might win the nomination. I don't know that because in terms of the demographics of how popular she is in the minority community."

United States Customs and Border Protection officers used tear gas on Sunday at three locations near the border crossing in Tijuana, Mexico. A number of migrants tried to cross into the United States at the Tijuana River and were met with a law enforcement blockade with barbed wire and tear gas. In a widely viewed photograph, a woman can be seen pulling her family away from tear gas fired by Customs and Border Protection officers. Others crossed the Tijuana River on their way to El Chaparral, a port of entry on the Mexico side of the border, to evade the police blockade. Migrants also met tear gas and law enforcement officials at a set of train tracks near the San Ysidro crossing. The United States shut down the crossing in both directions in response to the migrants' attempt to cross.

The Senate voted Monday to approve Seema Verma, President Donald Trump's nominee for administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, 55-43. The confirmation comes as congressional Republicans advance their efforts this week to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, an overhaul that would entail significant involvement from CMS. The health care bill currently moving through the House plans to eliminate Medicaid expansion after 2020. An ally of Vice President Mike Pence, Verma has been working on health care policy for more than a decade and developed an alternative Medicaid plan in Indiana under former Republican Gov. Mitch Daniels that received significant support from conservatives. When the Affordable Care Act became law, Verma helped Pence, then the Indiana governor, tweak the Healthy Indiana Plan, sell it to the Obama administration as the vehicle for Medicaid expansion, and then dramatically scale it upward. Pence championed the program as a conservative alternative to Obamacare's main vehicle for expanded coverage.

President Obama intends to use his State of the Union address to put a difficult year behind him and reassert command before the capital is consumed with election-year politics. After five years in office, Obama has come to feel acutely the limits on his power and the shrinking horizons before him. His nationally televised speech to Congress on Tuesday is a critical opportunity to drive an agenda that may yet shape his legacy. Obama realizes that he has little chance of major legislative victories this year, with the possible exception of an overhaul of immigration law that Republicans are also making a priority. As a result, aides said, he will present a blueprint for "a year of action" on issues like income inequality and the environment that bypasses Congress and exercises his authority to the maximum extent.

Jeb Bush, a Republican donor he ran into recently, said, "Seriously, what's this guy's problem?" According to accounts provided by several sources close to Bush, Bush described Donald Trump, a publicity-seeking real estate developer, as "a buffoon," "clown," and "asshole." Bush also described Trump as "a publicity-seeking real estate developer" and "a buffoon," "clown," and "asshole."

The American Health Care Act, which was narrowly passed in the House last week, would worsen Obamacare's problems rather than fix them, according to a Congressional Budget Office analysis of a previous iteration of the legislation. The bill would end Obamacare's individual mandate, already too weak as a policy mechanism, and impose a fee on those who go without coverage and want to re-enter the insurance market, creating an incentive for relatively healthy people to remain uncovered. As a result, instability in Obamacare's exchanges as insurers scale back around the country would only be increased. It is unclear what health policy problem this bill would solve.

Conservative members of the House rebelled against their leadership on Thursday to scuttle an emergency spending measure that addressed the migrant crisis at the southern border, pushing the issue to a showdown on Friday as lawmakers prepared to leave for a five-week recess. The failure of the Republican border bill, coupled with the Senate's inability to bring a Democratic alternative to a vote, emphasized how the prospects of a broad immigration overhaul — which at the beginning of the 113th Congress held great bipartisan promise — have ground to a halt. The struggle to deal with immigration became more urgent with the arrival of tens of thousands of children at the border. The effort was driven by more conservative Republicans who balked at further government spending and President Obama's approach on deporting the migrants.

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) said Tuesday that he is considering running for another term in 2016, when he would be 80 years old. On KFYI-AM in Phoenix, host Barry Young asked if he was saying he might run again. McCain said: "That would not be wrong." The New York Times' Mark Leibovich, who is in Arizona following McCain, tweeted the news. McCain, the 2008 GOP presidential nominee, is in his fifth term. He has never taken less than 56 percent of the vote and easily dispatched a primary challenge in 2010 from former congressman J.D. Hayworth. If he runs again, McCain will likely find himself targeted by tea party groups.

Many Twitter users reacted to Democrat Joe Biden's win over President Donald Trump by using the phrase "You're fired." The phrase had been a recurring phrase from Trump's "The Apprentice" days before Biden's win in Pennsylvania. Before Biden's win, Twitter users used the phrase four years in the making. The race was not called until Saturday. After the race was called, users posted the phrase in Trump's face. George Takei tweeted the phrase and said in another tweet he had wanted to say it since before Trump became president. Some users posted the phrase in response to Trump.

Rep. Heath Shuler (N.C.) formally launched his bid Monday to oust Speaker Nancy Pelosi (Calif.) as the leader of House Democrats, beginning to ask lawmakers to support his more centrist campaign to be minority leader. "I'll be running," Shuler said after votes Monday, in his most definitive declaration yet that he will oppose Pelosi. Shuler hails from the Blue Dog Coalition, whose Democratic ranks were roughly halved by midterm elections two weeks ago. Many consider his effort a protest candidacy that will give the remaining moderate Democrats an alternative to voting for Pelosi, whose popularity plummeted during the fall elections amid thousands of campaign commercials that portrayed her in a negative light. The leadership elections for House Democrats are Wednesday morning, and the caucus expects to ratify the same slate of current leaders who oversaw its ranks for the past five years after Pelosi negotiated a deal to keep all her lieutenants at the leadership table.

Jim Gandy, chief meteorologist on WLTX in Columbia, S.C., incorporates links between bad weather and climate change into his daily broadcasts. In an interview, Gandy said: "In Columbia, the only thing that separates us from hell in the summertime is a screen door. And all of the climate models indicate that it's going to get worse if we don't do something about it." On Tuesday, Gandy was among eight weather broadcasters invited to interview President Obama and spend the day at the White House. The guests included Al Roker of the "Today" show and local weathermen and women from Chicago, Miami, Seattle and other cities. The administration said the guests were there to spread the word contained in a new report, the National Climate Assessment, that the warming climate is causing sweeping change across the United States.

CBS News correspondent Weijia Jiang was walking with other reporters outside the White House on Friday morning when President Donald Trump asked her to be "quiet." Trump said she was "so... she's so obnoxious." The president then turned to someone nearby and pointed back at Jiang. Trump said, "She's so... she's so obnoxious." The article notes that Trump added another "quiet" before calling her "obnoxious."

Caroline Kennedy, the daughter of President John F. Kennedy, is likely to be the next United States ambassador to Japan, according to people familiar with the appointment process. The vetting of Ms. Kennedy by the White House is almost complete, and an appointment could be announced in the coming weeks, along with the names of several other choices for important diplomatic posts. Ms. Kennedy, 55, was an early supporter of President Obama in the 2008 presidential election and offered backing as he battled Hillary Rodham Clinton for the Democratic nomination. She also served as a co-chairwoman of Mr. Obama's 2012 re-election campaign. The diplomatic assignment would vault Ms. Kennedy, a lawyer and the author of 10 books, into public life that her family has embraced for several generations, including in the diplomatic corps. Ms. Kennedy's grandfather Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. served as ambassador to Britain from 1938 to 1940.

House Speaker John Boehner told reporters Tuesday that the Obama administration is not helping Congress get to the truth over the IRS' scrutiny of conservative groups and the agency's recent revelation that it lost emails related to that probe. Boehner said: "When you look at the president, his own remarks when this IRS scandal unfolded almost a year ago, he said that he would fully cooperate -- he and his administration. They've not only not fully cooperated, they haven't done a damn thing to help us get to the truth of what really happened." The IRS says it lost some emails by Lois Lerner, who headed the division that processes applications for tax-exempt status. The agency blames that on Lerner's computer crashing. Republicans have said they do not believe the IRS explanation. Boehner said: "Listen, I grew up in a bar. This doesn't pass the straight-face test."

Democrats have an opportunity to move in different directions following the conclusion of Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation and Barr's subsequent letter to Congress. The author wrote that Democrats should praise Mueller for his work but stress that the Special Counsel was appointed by Trump's Justice Department to investigate President Donald Trump. The author wrote that Democrats should demand the report be made public in its entirety without delay and criticize Attorney General William Barr's unilateral decision not to pursue obstruction charges against the President. The author wrote that Democrats should tell the country the investigation is over and focus on continuing to do the job the American people have elected them to do. The author wrote that Democrats should continue to investigate Trump, his family, and his administration but remain low-key. The author wrote that Trump will bluster and brag about "no collusion" and that another shiny object will come along soon enough to distract him. The author wrote that Trump is vulnerable and beatable in the 2020 election and that Democrats should focus on that.

The article reports that President Obama is expressing outrage or anger over the Senate Republican open letter to Iran but letting it hang out there. Obama initially called the letter "somewhat ironic to see some members of Congress wanting to make common cause with hardliners in Iran." In an upcoming interview with Vice News, Obama continues: "I'm embarrassed for them. For them to address a letter to the ayatollah, who they claim is our mortal enemy, and their basic argument to them is 'don't deal with our president 'cause you can't trust him to follow through on an agreement."

President Donald Trump on Friday defended former aide Rob Porter, wishing him well in his future endeavors without mentioning the two ex-wives who have accused Porter of physical and emotional abuse. Trump's comments came at a time of national conversation about the mistreatment of women. They came amid White House finger-pointing about who knew what and when about the severity of the spousal abuse allegations. Trump said Porter, who resigned when the abuse allegations became public this week, had "worked hard" at the White House and wished him well. "It's a, obviously, tough time for him. He did a very good job when he was in the White House. And we hope he has a wonderful career," Trump said in his first comments on the allegations against the onetime West Wing star. "He said very strongly yesterday that he's innocent," Trump added.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel is the homeland "only of the Jewish people." The statement came ahead of April's election. Netanyahu addressed "slightly confused people" after Israeli actress Rotem Sela defended the rights of Israel's Arab population. Arabs comprise about 20 percent of Israel's 9 million residents and have full citizenship rights but have faced decades of discrimination. On Saturday, Sela wrote on Instagram: "When the hell will someone in this government tell the public that Israel is a country of all its citizens." Netanyahu responded: "Israel "is the national state, not of all its citizens, but only of the Jewish people."

The Senate on Wednesday unanimously approved sanctions intended to limit Pyongyang's ability to finance warheads and missiles. The legislation targets those who knowingly do business with North Korea to benefit its nuclear weapons program and authorizes $50 million to broadcast messages directly to people in the isolated nation. Senator Cory Gardner, a first-term Republican from Colorado and a co-sponsor of the bill, said the measure mandates the sanctions rather than leaving them up to President Obama's discretion and imposes the first punitive measures in response to a violation of the nation's cybersecurity infrastructure. Gardner said the measure is the first of its kind and he believes it will be a model for sanctions against other cyber-perpetrators around the globe.

Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder (R) will endorse Mitt Romney for president at a luncheon on Thursday, according to two sources with knowledge of his decision. MIRS news reported Wednesday evening that the two men will appear together at a luncheon Thursday for a "major announcement." A source confirmed that Snyder will be endorsing the former Massachusetts governor. Snyder is the early favorite in the Michigan Republican primary but may face a tough race against former Pennsylvania senator Rick Santorum. Snyder is in his first term. He won an open seat race in 2010 but has encountered early difficulties, and his approval rating has suffered some because of it. Snyder made his endorsement official in a Detroit News editorial published Thursday. "Mitt understands the challenges confronting Michigan as few Americans do," Snyder wrote. "I hope all Michiganians will join me in supporting the candidacy of this favorite son of our great state."

Former White House phsyician Dr. Connie Mariano said Chris Christie called her and yelled at her. Mariano said she worried his weight would lead to a heart attack or stroke in office. She said Christie told her to "shut up," even though he had made his weight a public issue by eating donuts on David Letterman's show. Mariano said, "It was essentially the tone of the press conference only louder. It was hard to get anything across." Mariano told 3TV, "I don't think he realized who he was talking to," adding that it is common for medical experts to weigh in on the health concerns of potential presidential candidates. "I think I'm qualified to make a comment." Mariano said she had previously supported Christie.

A Missouri state senator was arrested on Monday night outside the police department of the city of Ferguson, authorities said, in another night of protests following the fatal police shooting of an unarmed black teenager in August. State Senator Jamilah Nasheed was taken into custody by Ferguson police officers, said St. Louis County Police spokesman Brian Schellman. Further details were not immediately available. CNN footage broadcast by television station KSDK showed Nasheed shouting "No Justice" with replies of "No peace" from several protesters as she was handcuffed along with another man. KDSK reported that Nasheed was arrested after standing in the street and blocking traffic, then failing to move despite repeated warnings from police. Demonstrations have occurred in the St. Louis area almost daily since the Aug. 9 killing of unarmed black teenager Michael Brown by white police officer Darren Wilson.

Six additional Internal Revenue Service workers lost emails sought by congressional investigators when their computers crashed, investigators announced Tuesday. The employees may have been trying to cover up political targeting of Tea Party organizations. The revelation follows the news last week that Lois Lerner, the former chief of the I.R.S. division that grants tax-exempt status to organizations, had also lost two years' worth of files when her computer crashed in mid-2011. The loss of records has heightened Republican concerns that the tax agency conducted politically motivated reviews. "Plotlines in Hollywood are more believable than what we are getting from this White House and the I.R.S.," said investigators Representative Dave Camp, Republican of Michigan, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, and Representative Charles Boustany Jr., Republican of Louisiana, chairman of the Ways and Means oversight subcommittee.

President Donald Trump criticized the cable network on Tuesday. Trump posted on Twitter criticizing an interview that Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum conducted with Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), who had quit the 2020 race earlier this month. Swalwell sits on both the House Judiciary and Intelligence Committees that will hear former special counsel Robert Mueller's testimony on Wednesday. Trump followed up his tweet three minutes later with another praising Sean Hannity. Hannity, a Fox News primetime host, joined Trump on stage at a political rally before the 2018 midterms and has vowed to stump for Trump during his 2020 reelection campaign. Last month, Trump criticized Fox News after it released a poll showing him trailing many of his potential 2020 Democratic rivals. In May, he criticized the network for covering the Democrats.

A gun accidentally went off inside a kindergartner's backpack at a school in Memphis, the Shelby County Board of Education said Thursday, but no one was injured. In a statement, the board said the child had brought a firearm to school and it discharged while students waited for the opening bell in the cafeteria. School staff took possession of the backpack and local law enforcement responded. The situation is under investigation and classes continued as scheduled. The board said there is no evidence at this time of harmful intent; however, weapons of any kind are prohibited on campuses, and the student will be disciplined in accordance with the state's zero tolerance policy. The board said the safety of students and staff is of the utmost importance, staff is trained to handle emergency situations, and all students were kept safe and calm while the matter was handled. If the kindergartner is found guilty of an offense, he faces a 180-day suspension.

Senate negotiators resumed negotiations on immigration on Tuesday after Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York withdrew an offer to fully fund President Trump's proposed wall at the Mexican border. "The wall offer's off the table," Schumer told reporters at the Capitol a day after senators reached an impasse to end a three-day government shutdown. Schumer's decision to renege, made on Sunday but revealed publicly on Tuesday, marked another turn in the debate over how to shield from deportation hundreds of thousands of young immigrants brought to the country illegally as children. As part of a deal to end the shutdown, Senator Mitch McConnell, the majority leader, promised what he called a "fair and open" immigration debate on the Senate floor.

Former Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern was on life support and "no longer responsive" on Wednesday, two days after he was admitted to a hospice, his family said. The 90-year-old former U.S. senator from South Dakota suffers from a variety of ailments "that have worsened over recent months" due to age, the McGovern family said in a statement issued Wednesday afternoon. McGovern is best known for his 1972 run to unseat Richard Nixon on a platform that included ending the war in Vietnam. He lost 49 of the 50 states to the Republican incumbent, who resigned in the Watergate scandal less than two years later. McGovern won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1956 and was elected to the Senate in 1962. He returned to the Senate after his presidential campaign, but lost the seat in the Republican wave that accompanied Ronald Reagan's election to the White House in 1980.

President-elect Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood took an oath of office a day early on Friday in a televised speech to tens of thousands of supporters in Tahrir Square. The speech was delivered after the military's swearing-in ceremony. Morsi made a promise to work for the release of Sheik Omar Abdel Rahman, an Egyptian-born militant Islamist convicted after the 1993 World Trade Center attack of plotting to bomb several New York City landmarks. Morsi referred briefly to Abdel Rahman in the context of a vow to free Egyptian civilians imprisoned after military trials under the rule of the generals. "I see signs for Omar Abdel Rahman and detainees' pictures," he said. "It is my duty and I will make all efforts to have them free, including Omar Abdel Rahman."

Former Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern was on life support and "no longer responsive" on Wednesday, two days after he was admitted to a hospice, his family said. The 90-year-old former U.S. senator from South Dakota suffers from a variety of ailments "that have worsened over recent months" due to age, the McGovern family said in a statement issued Wednesday afternoon. McGovern is best known for his 1972 run to unseat Richard Nixon on a platform that included ending the war in Vietnam. He lost 49 of the 50 states to the Republican incumbent, who resigned in the Watergate scandal less than two years later. McGovern won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1956 and was elected to the Senate in 1962. He returned to the Senate after his presidential campaign, but lost the seat in the Republican wave that accompanied Ronald Reagan's election to the White House in 1980.

Twitter (TWTR) was offline for about an hour on Thursday afternoon. The company said some people may now be able to access the site again. In a statement Thursday afternoon, Twitter said it was "currently investigating issues people are having accessing Twitter." Users can continue to monitor the site's status at status.twitterstat.us. It is unclear at this time how extensive the outage was or its exact length. "The outage was due to an internal configuration change, which we're now fixing," Twitter said in an update posted to the status monitoring site. The outage coincided with the start of the White House's Presidential Social Media Summit. Twitter, along with Facebook (FB), was not invited to the summit, while a number of right-wing extremists were.
