Pfc. Bradley Manning on Thursday testified before a military judge in Fort Myers, Md. He said he provided vast archives of military and diplomatic files to the antisecrecy group WikiLeaks. He said he released the information to help enlighten the public about "what happens and why it happens" and to "spark a debate about foreign policy." Manning read a statement recounting his military career, including his appointment as an intelligence analyst in Iraq, which he said led to a wider debate about foreign policy. He said no one associated with WikiLeaks — an abbreviation he used to refer to the WikiLeaks organization — pressed him into sending any more information. He said he took full responsibility.

The article describes a scenario in which President Trump could enter a new Korean war. It states this would begin because the present approach of leaning on China to pressure North Korea will likely fail. It predicts Trump will grow angry at public snickering at the emptiness of his threats. At some point, U.S. intelligence will see a North Korean missile prepared for a test launch. Foreign Affairs describes a scenario in an essay by Philip Gordon imagining how Trump might drift into war by accident. The essay states: "He could do nothing, but that would mean losing face and emboldening North Korea. Or he could destroy the test missile on its launchpad with a barrage of cruise missiles, blocking Pyongyang's path to a nuclear deterrent, enforcing his red line, and sending a clear message to the rest of the world."

Sulaiman Abu Ghaith, a close associate of Osama bin Laden, told authorities after his arrest last year that the Sept. 11 terror attacks were a surprise to him, but that he had heard around Qaeda training camps in Afghanistan "that something big was going to happen," a federal agent testified on Thursday. The agent's testimony came in the trial of Abu Ghaith, 48, who later married Bin Laden's daughter and now faces charges that include conspiring to kill Americans and providing material support to terrorists. A prosecutor had told the jury that it would hear about Abu Ghaith's "confession," and that he had agreed, at Bin Laden's request, to make motivational speeches in Al Qaeda's training camps and, after Sept. 11, to make proclamations on behalf of the group.

U.S. District Judge Paul Oetken issued an order Friday allowing Lev Parnas, an associate of Rudy Giuliani, to begin sharing information with congressional investigators. Parnas, an associate of Giuliani charged with violating federal campaign finance laws, had sought permission from the courts earlier this week to turn over evidence to Congress that had been seized during the FBI's investigation into him. The House Intelligence Committee subpoenaed the materials, which include documents and the contents of a seized iPhone, in October. The information could still prove relevant to the impeachment investigation of Trump since Parnas was in regular contact with Giuliani, Trump's associate on the Ukraine scheme for which he has been impeached.

A new Pew Research Center poll shows 40 percent of Americans say the Obama administration has been dishonest about the deaths of four Americans in Benghazi, Libya. Thirty-seven percent say it has been honest. Twenty-three percent say they do not know. Among Republicans, 70 percent say the administration has been dishonest. Among independents, 48 percent say the administration has been dishonest, while 30 percent say it has been honest. In the same poll, 36 percent said Republicans have gone too far in their hearings on the matter, while 34 percent say the Republicans have handled the matter appropriately. Independents are evenly split. The poll also shows 56 percent of respondents are not following the issue closely or at all.

Vice President Joe Biden spoke at a Black History Month event on Tuesday. He discussed his basketball skills. He said he wanted to team up with former NBA player and Sacramento Mayor Kevin Johnson to take on President Obama. "I told the president, next game, I've got him," Biden said. "I may be a white boy, but I can jump." Biden also commented on Voter ID bills passed in Southern states including Alabama, Texas and North Carolina, saying such bills prove that racial hatred still exists. Opponents say such bills are aimed at discouraging black voters from showing up to the polls. "These guys never go away. Hatred never, never goes away," Biden said. "The zealotry of those who wish to limit the franchise cannot be smothered by reason."

During Saturday night's Republican presidential debate, Cruz said Ben Carson was "taking a break." Cruz said CNN reporters reported the same on television. Cruz said CNN political anchors Jake Tapper, Dana Bash, and Wolf Blitzer said the episode was highly unusual and highly significant. Cruz said CNN reporters reported the episode on television. Cruz said CNN political anchors Jake Tapper, Dana Bash, and Wolf Blitzer said the episode was highly unusual and highly significant.

Legislation to overhaul the nation's immigration laws would further strengthen the country's security system to guard against cases like the Boston Marathon bombings, Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday in the last of three hearings on a bipartisan immigration proposal. The Boston bombings — the two suspects in the case entered the country legally in 2002 under an asylum petition by their father — have been mentioned during the hearings. Some Republican senators and conservative commentators have urged caution on any new legislation until questions surrounding the bombings have been answered. Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina and a member of the bipartisan group of eight senators who wrote the legislation, has floated the idea of an amendment that would require immigrants, including refugees and asylum seekers, who are deemed potentially "high risk" to undergo a more comprehensive background check.

Secretary of State John Kerry accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel on Wednesday of thwarting peace in the Middle East. Kerry spoke in a manner that American diplomats have not heard from American diplomats during his four-year tenure. He said the Israeli government was undermining any hope of a two-state solution to its decades-long conflict with the Palestinians. Kerry said the American vote last week in the United Nations allowing condemnation of Israel for settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem was driven by a desire to save Israel from "the most extreme elements" in its own government. "The status quo is leading toward one state and perpetual occupation," Kerry said, his voice animated.

At 10:45 ET, police in Pittsburgh reported an active shooter near the Tree of Life Congregation Synagogue in Pittsburgh, Pa. Local media reports at least four people were dead, with several reports saying 7 or more. The Squirrel Hill area is one of Pittsburgh's largest Jewish neighborhoods and Tree of Life Synagogue is one of the largest congregations. More details are available. Police said the shooter is still active. Police told those in the area to shelter in place. Reports indicated the suspect in the shooting had surrendered. If in the area, do not take this as an all clear signal. More information is developing. ABC News reported that police in New York City are deploying protection to synagogues and Jewish locations throughout New York City. The article stated this appears to be a precaution and not a response to a known threat.

The newly appointed prime minister of the Palestinian Authority, Rami Hamdallah, submitted his resignation on Thursday after two weeks in office. It was not immediately clear if the president of the West Bank-based authority, Mahmoud Abbas, would accept the resignation. Analysts said the matter was primarily a domestic one that would not directly impinge on Abbas's ability to make decisions regarding Secretary of State John Kerry's peace mission. Analysts also said the image of chronic political instability could undercut crucial international support for the Palestinians, both financial and political, at a time when they are supposed to be pushing for statehood. Palestinians said they viewed the political drama as another setback for Abbas and his Fatah Party.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney said Tuesday in an interview on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360" that he has no regrets over his administration's decision to invade Iraq and topple Saddam Hussein. Cheney said, "It was the right thing to do then. I believed it then and I believe it now." He added, "No apologies." The Iraq War became an issue in the presidential campaign earlier this year when former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, brother of Cheney's former boss, George W. Bush, struggled to elucidate his position on the mission. After a week of questions, Jeb Bush said that "knowing what we know now, ...I would not have engaged. I would not have gone into Iraq." Later in August, the former Florida governor said that taking out Hussein "turned out to be a pretty good deal."

Secretary of State John Kerry visited Kiev on Tuesday with an offer of $1 billion in an American loan guarantee and pledges of technical assistance. He walked through a damp mist before stopping at improvised memorials where protesters were gunned down last month as they voiced opposition to what was then Ukraine's pro-Kremlin government. Kerry placed a lighted candle at one of the shrines, which were draped with flowers and photographs of some of the victims; met with religious leaders; and listened to Ukrainians who beseeched him for help. "We hope Russian troops will leave Crimea, and we also hope for your assistance," a Ukrainian woman told Kerry as he walked along Instytutska Street.

Bob Beauprez, a buffalo rancher and former congressman and community banker, defeated three rivals in a Republican primary election on Tuesday to become Colorado's governor in November, The Associated Press reported. With about 73 percent of the vote counted, Beauprez had 31 percent. His closest competitor, Tom Tancredo, also a former congressman, had 26 percent. Beauprez also beat Scott Gessler, the secretary of state, and Mike Kopp, an Army veteran and former state senator. The candidate with the highest profile was Tancredo, a conservative who had built a national profile for comments and staunchly opposing illegal immigration.

White House press secretary Jay Carney said Wednesday that the president does not have an opinion on the announcement that the U.S. Postal Service will stop delivering mail on Saturdays. Carney said the Republican-controlled House had not passed legislation designed to help the USPS. "We put forward a year and a half ago a series of proposals for reform of the postal service that would put it on much more firm financial ground and it passed the Senate," Carney said. "Unfortunately the House failed to take it up. So it would be our preference that that comprehensive package of reforms be implemented for the sake of a stronger future postal service." Carney said the USPS is an independent agency and that the White House only learned of the change, which takes effect in August, on Tuesday. Polling in recent years shows that a majority of Americans support halting Saturday mail delivery to help the Postal Service deal with its financial problems.

New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio said Monday that everyone must follow laws but he would not question his drivers' judgment after video footage showed his official vehicle breaking several traffic laws while he sat in the front seat. De Blasio said, "no one is above the law." He said he would not second-guess the police officers who drive him or question their security protocols. The mayor also said he does not believe the video undermines his recently launched traffic safety campaign. WCBS-TV reported the mayor's two-SUV caravan speeding and running stop signs Thursday. De Blasio did not answer questions Friday about the incident. He deferred then to Police Commissioner William Bratton, who said he was not "overly concerned" by the footage. De Blasio did not have any public events over the weekend.

An effort to provide emergency aid for American ranchers and farmers affected by a year of drought, frost and other calamities collapsed on Thursday as members of Congress departed for their five-week August recess. The legislation remained unfinished as they returned to campaign for re-election. After refusing to consider a sweeping five-year farm measure, House Republican leaders worked through a short-term $383 million package of loans and grants for livestock producers and a limited number of farmers. The measure passed 223 to 197, a narrow margin for a bill that has an impact on so many states. Democrats objected to the way the farm legislation has been handled and some Republicans objected to the costs. Democratic leaders in the Senate, which had already passed a bipartisan five-year bill, refused to take up the House measure, and faulted House Republican leaders for failing to consider the broader legislation in time.

Florida Gov. Rick Scott (R) is postponing a strategy meeting he had scheduled with Donald Trump in New York on Monday to monitor a storm approaching his state. Melissa Sellers, a spokesperson for Scott's political organization, said Sunday that the governor plans to stay in Florida. On Sunday, the National Hurricane Center issued a Tropical Storm Warning for parts of the Florida Gulf Coast. Sellers told The Washington Post last week that Scott intended to meet with Trump to talk about general election strategy in Florida, which is seen as a key battleground. Scott has said he is not interested in being Trump's vice presidential running mate. Sellers said that as of now, there is no date set for a re-scheduled meeting. Trump spokeswoman Hope Hicks said, "We should have a new date in the next few days."

Donald Trump shared a 30-second clip on Twitter on Friday that was reportedly created by a pro-Trump meme maker. The clip was based on a Time magazine cover and accompanying video from 2018 that argued why "Trumpism will outlast Trump." It ended with Trump standing behind a lectern bearing the sign "Trump 4Eva." Time tweeted its original version to the president. The clip was posted amid escalating U.S. tensions with Iran and a new rape allegation against Trump, which the president has denied. The tweet received negative responses from other users. A correction was issued stating that an earlier version of the story referred to the video as "doctored." The video is a different version from Time's but made to look similar.

Paul Ryan said he has no complaints regarding the way Mitt Romney has deployed his running mate. "Never once has the campaign asked me to stop something or do something differently or not do anything," Ryan told the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel. Last week, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker (R) suggested the Romney campaign was restraining Ryan. Ryan responded to criticism that the Romney campaign needs to be more bold. "A, we still have a ways to go. We still have a lot left that we're planning on doing. B, I think that's just what conservatives do by nature. I think that's just the nature of conservative punditry is to do that — to kind of complain — about any imperfection they might see," Ryan said.

President Donald Trump spoke at a rally in Louisville, Kentucky, on Monday. According to reports, Trump raised free agent quarterback Colin Kaepernick's inability to land a job with a team. Trump previously called Kaepernick disrespectful for taking a knee during the national anthem to protest racial injustice before games last season. The president referenced a Bleacher Report story in which an unidentified team general manager estimated that 10 percent of teams were reluctant to sign Kaepernick over fears Trump would tweet about them. "There was an article today … that NFL owners don't want to pick him up because they don't want to get a nasty tweet from Donald Trump," the president said. "Do you believe that?"

Sen. Dick Durbin called on the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate the death of suburban Chicago woman Sandra Bland, who was found hanged to death in a Texas jail cell earlier this month. Durbin wrote a letter to Attorney General Loretta Lynch urging the investigation into "the arrest, incarceration, and death of Sandra Bland, a constituent of mine from Naperville, Illinois." The letter was dated Jul 25, 2015 at 9:21 PM PT.

Republican leaders have made new references to President Obama's background or cultural influences. The article reports that Republican leaders believe the coming elections are more than a referendum on the administration's economic policies. The article also states that conservatives are also trying to make the fall campaign about the president himself and the kind of societal change he represents. The Republican Senate primary in Delaware this week was the latest in a series of conservative insurgents to challenge the party establishment. The article states that such primaries have threatened to reopen longstanding rifts within the party. The article argues that the increased focus on Obama's personal history is probably less about persuading the electorate as a whole than about unifying the disparate strands of the conservative base.

White House Press Secretary Jay Carney said Wednesday he had no idea whether singer Beyonce was lip-syncing when she sang the national anthem at President Obama's second inauguration. Carney said, "As powerful as this office is, we don't control the weather," and noted that pre-recordings were made as a precaution, just as they were for the 2009 inauguration. In response to several more questions on the issue, Carney said, "I'm glad you guys are focused on the important issues of the day here." A spokesman for the Marine Corps band said that the music accompanying Beyonce was pre-recorded. Carney could not say whether Beyonce was lip-syncing or actually singing, referring reporters to the Presidential Inaugural Committee and the singer herself.

President Donald Trump's reelection campaign removed an advertisement on Monday that promoted the Trump administration's first 100 days. The 30-second advertisement, which promoted the administration's accomplishments during the first 100 days, was deleted and replaced with an advertisement that featured the president shaking hands with National Security Advisor Lieutenant General H.R. McMaster after he accepted the job at Mar-a-Lago. McMaster was wearing his Army uniform at the time. The advertisement may have violated Defense Department rules barring active-duty members of the military from participating in political advocacy in uniform.

The White House released a text of President Obama's speech on Thursday on national security issues. The text read: "Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. Thank you all for being here. Let me just acknowledge the presence of some of my outstanding Cabinet members and advisors. We've got our Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton. We have our CIA Director Leon Panetta. We have our Secretary of Defense William Gates (sic); Secretary Napolitano of Department of Homeland Security; Attorney General Eric Holder; my National Security Advisor Jim Jones. And I want to especially thank our Acting Archivist of the United States, Adrienne Thomas. I also want to acknowledge several members of the House who have great interest in intelligence matters. I want to thank Congressman Reyes, Congressman Hoekstra, Congressman King, as well as Congressman Thompson, for being here today. Thank you so much."

The Obama administration opened its appellate defense of the 2010 health care act on Tuesday before three randomly selected judges who each had been appointed by Democratic presidents, including two named by President Obama. The 14 members of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, the first appellate court to review the law, are evenly divided as appointees of Democratic and Republican presidents. The odds of drawing three Democratic appointees in the computerized lottery are roughly 10 to 1. Lawyers do not learn the makeup of the panel until the day of the hearing. The party of the appointing president is not necessarily predictive of a federal judge's leanings. In five decisions in lower courts, three Democratic-appointed judges have upheld the Affordable Care Act while two Republican-appointed judges have ruled that its central provision — the requirement that most Americans obtain health insurance — is unconstitutional.

The U.S. ambassador to Israel did not attend Wednesday's arrival of Secretary of State Mike Pompeo in Israel as he was feeling unwell and had been advised to keep away, the U.S. State Department said. Pompeo landed at Ben Gurion Airport for a one-day visit during which he will meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his designated coalition partner, Benny Gantz. The envoy, David Friedman, tested negative for the coronavirus, a State Department spokeswoman said. Friedman experienced "mild upper respiratory symptoms" and was therefore asked by medical staff to avoid proximity to Pompeo, media added, quoting a statement from the U.S. embassy in Israel. Pompeo said on Twitter after his arrival that topics to feature in talks will be the virus pandemic outbreak and regional tensions with Iran.

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell sharply last week and a gauge of factory activity hit an eight-month high in early November, the Labor Department said. Other data released on Thursday showed that wholesale prices fell for a second month in October, the latest sign of a lack of inflation pressure, giving the Federal Reserve some leeway as it considers when to begin tapering its bond-buying program. Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 21,000 to a seasonally adjusted 323,000, the Labor Department said. Economists had forecast a drop in the newly jobless to 335,000, and some said that the Veterans Day holiday last week could have contributed to some of the decline. The department said no special factors affected the data, which covered the survey period for the government's report on employment in November.

Sen. Marco Rubio's 12-year-old daughter, Amanda, was released from Miami Children's Hospital Sunday evening after a golf cart accident Saturday. Rubio spokesman Alex Conant said in a statement: "She is recuperating from a concussion. Her condition has stabilized and should improve in the coming days. Her prognosis is good and she is expected to make a full recovery." The accident occurred in a private gated community. Amanda, the eldest of Rubio's four children, was a passenger in the golf cart. Conant added: "Senator and Mrs. Rubio are grateful for the many messages of support and prayers for their daughter. And grateful to the Miami Dade Fire Department and the staff at the Pediatric Trauma Center at Miami Children's Hospital for their excellent care."

Congress gave final approval Thursday to a $1.1 trillion spending bill that reduces budget cuts known at the sequester and guarantees the nation will not endure another government shutdown until at least Oct. 1. The bipartisan agreement to fund federal agencies through the rest of the fiscal year passed without fanfare. The Senate voted 72 to 26 to approve the measure Thursday evening after Republicans persuaded Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to drop a last-minute push to force another showdown over the Affordable Care Act, reprising the fight that closed the government for 16 days last fall. The House overwhelmingly approved the spending bill earlier this week, and the White House signaled that President Obama would sign it by Saturday, in time to prevent museums, agency offices and national parks from locking their gates when the current temporary funding measures expires.

Baltimore Mayor Catherine Pugh has asked the Board of Ethics to grant her an exemption from city ethics rules requiring officials to obtain approvals before soliciting private funds for community programs and events. The rules require officials to obtain approvals before soliciting private funds for community programs and events. City Solicitor Andre Davis has asked the board to grant Pugh the exemption so she does not have to make requests to the ethics and spending board each time she seeks private funds for the Baltimore City Foundation. The rules are meant to avoid conflicts of interest. Davis called Baltimore "a poor city" and questioned the constraints on the mayor's ability to solicit monetary assistance. He said the five-member board has not made a decision. Ethics board member Stephan Fogleman said he has questions about the request. Referencing former Mayor Sheila Dixon's theft conviction, he stressed the need for transparency in city affairs.

The campaign of presumptive 2016 Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump sent out an emergency email Saturday morning with a goal of raising $100,000 by the end of the day, for a campaign expected to cost in the hundreds of millions. The Clinton campaign launched a multi-million dollar advertisement campaign against Trump following his comments about the Orlando shooting. The Trump campaign appealed to Republican donors at the same time that the party appeared to be shunning him.

President Obama woke up in Havana on Tuesday to news that explosives had ripped through an airport and a subway in Brussels. He began a morning briefing on the terrorist attacks with officials in Washington inside a specially equipped secure communications room. An expression of condolence and support for the Belgian people was inserted at the last minute into his speech to the Cuban people. "We stand in solidarity with them in condemning these outrageous attacks against innocent people," Obama said in the Gran Teatro de la Habana. "We will do whatever is necessary to support our friend and ally Belgium in bringing to justice those who are responsible."

President Obama is giving serious consideration to speeding up the withdrawal of United States forces from Afghanistan and to a "zero option" that would leave no American troops there after next year, according to American and European officials. Mr. Obama is committed to ending America's military involvement in Afghanistan by the end of 2014, and Obama administration officials have been negotiating with Afghan officials about leaving a small "residual force" behind. His relationship with Mr. Karzai has been deteriorating. Last month, the United States began peace talks with the Taliban in Qatar. Mr. Karzai repudiated the talks and ended negotiations with the United States over the long-term security deal needed to keep American forces in Afghanistan after 2014.

Iran has extended its influence around the region by supporting Shiite opposition groups and conducting military operations in a handful of countries. Saudi Arabia is leading a coalition of Arab countries in military operations against the Houthi movement in Yemen. The formation of the coalition led to the creation, announced March 29 at an Arab summit in Egypt, of a unified Arab military force to counter Iranian influence and Islamic extremism. The article also included the question: "U.A.E. BAHRAIN, QATAR, U.A.E. Which Countries Are Fighting ISIS in Iraq?" The United States and Iran both have military operations against the Islamic State in Iraq, though American officials insist they are not cooperating with Iran. Jordan has conducted airstrikes as part of an American-led operation, which includes many other Western countries as well.

Seth Meyers said on Monday's broadcast of "Late Night" that he knows what may have happened to the notes that President Donald Trump reportedly seized from his interpreter following his 2017 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Meyers said: "Now we don't know what Trump did with those notes, but we do know that in her tell-all book former Trump aide Omarosa said she saw Trump trying to destroy evidence by eating a piece of paper in the Oval Office." White House aides later denied Omarosa Manigault Newman's claims. Meyers said: "We for real have a president who might one day say, 'If you want my notes you will need a search warrant for my belly.'"

The resignation of Democratic state senator Phillip P. Puckett on Monday, after serving 16 years in the Senate, set off charges of an unseemly deal and threatened Gov. Terry McAuliffe's chances of expanding Medicaid under the president's health care law. Democrats accused Republicans of masterminding Puckett's resignation by promising him a plum job and speeding the appointment of his daughter to a state judgeship. Over the weekend, reports that Puckett was resigning to take a job on the Virginia tobacco commission angered his fellow Democrats, who saw the hand of Republican officials who control the commission.

President Obama and Judge Sonia Sotomayor made remarks on her selection for the Supreme Court on Tuesday, as released by the White House. Obama said: "Of the many responsibilities granted to a President by our Constitution, few are more serious or more consequential than selecting a Supreme Court justice. The members of our highest court are granted life tenure, often serving long after the Presidents who appointed them. And they are charged with the vital task of applying principles put to paper more than 20 [sic] centuries ago to some of the most difficult questions of our time. So I don't take this decision lightly. I've made it only after deep reflection and careful deliberation. While there are many qualities that I admire in judges across the spectrum of judicial philosophy, and that I seek in my own nominee, there are few that stand out that I just want to mention."

Jennifer Willoughby and Colbie Holderness testified at a White House hearing about their experiences with Rob Porter, their former husband. Porter had become a top White House aide. On Friday, President Donald Trump said Porter "did a great job while he was at the White House. And we hope he has a wonderful career." Trump added that Porter had maintained his innocence. On Saturday, Trump tweeted that "lives are being shattered and destroyed by a mere allegation." Porter's resignation was announced Wednesday, hours after a photograph was published of Holderness with a black eye allegedly inflicted by Porter. Trump's staff secretary called the allegations from his former spouses "outrageous" and "simply false."

Florida's Republican presidential primary began with a heavy showing and may be headed for a clear victory over former House Speaker Newt Gingrich on Tuesday. Pollster.com aggregated all polling data on the race. The chart shows relative momentum among each candidate heading into the vote. Romney has risen since losing in South Carolina on Jan. 21; Gingrich has dropped precipitously. The chart asks whether Romney's large lead in the Florida polling makes a double-digit victory a necessity for his campaign to end the race between now and the end of February, or whether a Romney win in Florida — of any size — is enough.

Gov. Mike Pence of Indiana said he would support legislation to clarify the intent of a new state law that has drawn criticism over concerns that it could allow discrimination against gay people. In an interview on Saturday with The Indianapolis Star, the Republican governor said he had been in discussions with legislative leaders over the weekend. He expected that a clarification bill would be introduced this week to the religious objections law he signed on Thursday. Pence declined to provide details but told the newspaper that making gay and lesbian Indiana residents a protected legal class was "not on my agenda." He has disputed claims that the law allows state-sanctioned anti-gay discrimination, as some Indiana businesses, convention organizers and others have argued, and said that he did not anticipate "the hostility that's been directed at our state."

South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley (R-S.C.) will announce Monday that she is appointing Rep. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) to replace outgoing Sen. Jim DeMint (R-S.C.) in Congress, the New York Times reports. DeMint, who was elected to a second term in 2010, announced earlier this month that he will leave Congress in January to become president of the Heritage Foundation, a DC-based think tank. Scott, who is backed by Tea Party groups, has represented South Carolina's 1st congressional district since 2011. If appointed, he will become the state's first African American senator since the 19th century. He will also be the first black Republican in the Senate since Edward Brooke left his Massachusetts seat in 1979. DeMint's replacement will hold the seat until a special election is held in 2014.

Tim Pawlenty is running for the vice presidential nomination as Mitt Romney's running mate. Some believe Rick Santorum is poised to perform well in Minnesota, Pawlenty's home state. The Romney campaign has sent the former governor on a seek-and-destroy mission. Pawlenty, who in his brief run for the nomination was reluctant to attack, has called Santorum unqualified to be president. Pawlenty is walking a fine line in his try-out for a spot on the ticket. Presidential nominees often need and want an attack dog, but if the dog snarls and bites too much, it will stay in the pound.

President Obama will soon release a new budget. Progressives are angry over proposed cuts to Social Security; conservatives are denouncing the call for more revenues. House Republicans will block anything Obama proposes. The budget is best seen not as policy but as positioning, an attempt to gain praise from "centrist" pundits. The real policy action at this point is in the states, where the question is, How many Americans will be denied essential health care in the name of freedom? The question is also raised: how many Republican governors will reject the Medicaid expansion that is a key part of Obamacare. The answer is, nothing. When it comes to politics, it is a different story.

Ciamak Morsadegh, director of the Dr. Sapir Hospital and Charity Center in Tehran, lit another cigarette and reminisced about his wife leaving Iran for the United States after he insisted on staying. Morsadegh said that unlike thousands of other Jews he has never thought about leaving the Islamic Republic, for the simple reason that Iran is his home. "I speak English, I pray in Hebrew, but I think in Persian," said Morsadegh, a surgeon who is also a member of Parliament. "I am Iranian. Iranian-Jewish." Last week, the government of President Hassan Rouhani donated $400,000 to the Dr. Sapir Hospital. Morsadegh was not among the recipients.

Rumors surfaced Wednesday night that Rep. Renee Ellmers (R-N.C.) was romantically involved with Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), and that this could be at least part of the reason McCarthy backed away from running for speaker of the House. McCarthy denied this, and Ellmers reportedly has, as well, though she has declined to speak to the press. The press searched for Ellmers. A reporter identified her as Rep. Ann Wagner (R-Mo.). Wagner responded to questions about emails linking her to McCarthy.

On Friday, President Obama addressed the Trayvon Martin-George Zimmerman tragedy during a press briefing. During the briefing, Obama said: "You know, when Trayvon Martin was first shot I said that this could have been my son. Another way of saying that is Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago." The article reported that Obama's statement contrasted with the burial of a black boy. It said the two were inextricably linked by biases, with one expressing pains and peril while the other no longer could. The article characterized Obama's statements as pedantic and personal.

George Mason University recently renamed its law school after the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia. The school first announced it would change the name to The Antonin Scalia School of Law, or ASSoL, after receiving an anonymous $30 million donation on March 31. Observers commented on the acronym's similarity to a vulgarity, with many tweeting not a fan of the conservative justice. The school acknowledged the issue in a letter to its students and alumni, writing, "The name initially announced -- The Antonin Scalia School of Law -- has caused some acronym controversy on social media. The Antonin Scalia Law School is a logical substitute." The school's name change will go into effect July 1, pending final approval by the State Council of Higher Education for Virginia.

A freshman House Republican, Rep. Joe Walsh of Illinois, said he still cannot vote for the deficit-reduction proposal pushed by Speaker John Boehner, although he called it "a step in the right direction." Walsh said he does not think the Boehner proposal or a rival plan offered by Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid are sufficient. Asked if he could vote later Thursday in the House for the Boehner program, Walsh replied, "Right now, I can't." The tea party-backed lawmaker said he is still thinking about it. Walsh said lawmakers are "obsessed" with the Aug. 2 default deadline. He said chances of getting deficit-reduction right would be better if Congress were not wedded to the default deadline, saying "we've got plenty of revenues in August to service our debt."

President Obama placed a call to Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany last Thursday. He had a busy agenda: to consult with a close ally and mobilize Europeans to put more pressure on Russia to end its covert incursions in Ukraine. A day earlier, a young German intelligence operative had been arrested and had admitted that he had been passing secrets to the Central Intelligence Agency. Merkel chose not to raise the issue during the call. White House officials said the president was kept in the dark about the spying operation at a delicate moment in American relations with Germany. White House officials questioned who in the C.I.A.'s chain of command was aware of the case and why that information did not reach the Oval Office before the call.

Secretary of State John Kerry called Saturday's attack on at a shopping mall in Kenya's capital "an enormous offense against everybody's sense of right and wrong." Kerry, who is in New York for meetings at the United Nations, described the attackers as "ruthless and completely reckless terrorists." He spoke Sunday with Somalia's foreign minister and U.N. ambassador. The Somalia-based, al-Qaida-linked group al-Shabab has claimed responsibility for the attack on the upscale Westgate Mall in Nairobi. State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf said U.S. law enforcement, military and civilian personnel in Nairobi are providing advice and assistance to Kenyan authorities. Harf said five Americans were among the scores of people injured in the attack by Islamic extremists, but the U.S. has no reports of any American deaths.

Mayor Julián Castro of San Antonio is nominated as secretary of housing and urban development, replacing Shaun Donovan, who will become the president's new budget chief. Both nominations require confirmation by the Senate. President Obama officially nominated Castro on Friday. Obama said of Castro, "He's become a leader in housing and economic development," calling him an "all-star who has done a fantastic job in San Antonio." Castro's political options in Texas have become limited by the state's conservative politics, and while the housing secretary rarely has a high profile in Washington, he will be able to reach a much wider audience there.

The chairman of the Federal Reserve, Ben S. Bernanke, and most other Fed officials signaled Wednesday that they remained cautious about easing back too quickly on efforts to stimulate the economy. Some Fed policymakers suggested the central bank could begin reducing its monthly purchases of government bonds as early as next month. Most still want continued evidence of an upswing in the job market and a decline in unemployment first, according to minutes of the most recent meeting of the Fed's policy arm released Wednesday afternoon. Confusion on Wall Street over the Fed's intentions led to a day in the stock market. The major indicators were up in the morning after Mr. Bernanke testified to a Congressional committee but then fell sharply after the meeting minutes were disclosed.

Rush Limbaugh has not been a fan of Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton. Limbaugh has given his blessing to her selection as the next secretary of state. He called it "a brilliant stroke" by President-elect Barack Obama, who opposed Clinton for the Democratic nomination. Limbaugh weighs in on the new administration as one of Barbara Walters' "10 Most Fascinating People of 2008," which airs Thursday on ABC. Limbaugh said: "You know the old phrase, 'You keep your friends close and your enemies closer?' How can she run for president in 2012? She'd have to run against the incumbent and be critical of him _ the one who made her secretary of state." On Monday, Obama announced Clinton as his nominee for secretary of state. ABC is owned by The Walt Disney Co.

Gov. Chris Christie on Friday announced the resignation of the chairman of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, David Samson, the highest-ranking public official to step down during lane closings at the George Washington Bridge. Samson, an éminence grise in New Jersey politics and an adviser to Christie, had been under criticism for his role in the lane closings since January. Emails suggested he was more concerned about the political ramifications for Christie than drivers stuck in traffic. That was followed by accusations about conflicts of interest between his role at the Port Authority and his law practice. With those conflicts under investigation by federal authorities, Samson declined to cooperate with an internal investigation Christie had commissioned.

White House officials are pushing to resurrect a Republican health care bill before President Trump's 100th day in office on Saturday, April 29. Some members of the president's team have grown consumed by that deadline, worrying that appraisals of the president's tenure will be brutal and hoping that a last push on health care might bring a measure of salvation. Congress usually cannot take on two big things at once. At the same moment, Trump will hit his 100th day on Saturday, April 29, Republican congressional leaders face a deadline: Much of the federal government will run out of money. Reaching agreement to keep the government open past midnight on Friday will be the first priority of Republican leaders when Congress returns Monday from a two-week recess.

An American service member was killed and four others were wounded after a skirmish on Monday in Nangarhar Province in eastern Afghanistan, the Pentagon said. The episode took place in Achin, near the Pakistan border, in an area where a number of ambushes and strikes have occurred in recent months. The Pentagon did not indicate whether the episode involved the Taliban or members of the Islamic State, but both groups have been active in the area. Gen. John W. Nicholson Jr., the commander of the Afghanistan war effort, said in a statement: "We are deeply saddened by the loss of one of our own. At this very difficult time, our heartfelt sympathies go out to the families and friends of our fallen and wounded brothers." Defense Department officials said they would have more information after they have notified family members.

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont has 15 percent among Democrats, with 11 percent for Vice President Joseph Biden and 3 percent each for former U.S. Sen. James Webb of Virginia and former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley. Another 7 percent are undecided. An August 2007 poll of Iowa put Clinton one point behind Barack Obama and tied with John Edwards. A late February Quinnipiac poll had pegged Clinton at 61 percent in Iowa. This is the latest poll showing Clinton's polling numbers holding up, with a NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll showing her favorability declining but stronger than that of top Republicans and a New York Times/CBS News poll showing her favorability rising.

Former Vice President Joe Biden remains the Democratic frontrunner but remains ahead in polls. On Tuesday, Rosie O'Donnell, a television personality, told CNN's Chris Cuomo that Biden should sit out the 2020 election. O'Donnell said Biden should "be an elder statesman" and utilize his decades of experience to advise whoever ends up taking on President Donald Trump. She said Biden's ideas and beliefs are "antiquated" and he "is not the future of the Democratic Party." O'Donnell also said Biden is not the future of the Democratic Party. She also backed Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Kamala Harris (D-Calif.).

Global powers prepared for an 11th-hour effort to revive the peace effort in Syria. Kofi Annan, the special envoy and mediator who called the meeting, said on Friday he was optimistic that the talks in Geneva would yield an acceptable result despite Russian calls for changes in his settlement ideas. "I think we are going to have a good meeting" on Saturday, Annan told Reuters television in Geneva as senior officials held preparatory talks in advance of the weekend encounter of foreign ministers, including Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton. "I am optimistic," he said. The talks would end "with an acceptable result," he said, despite news reports suggesting that differences between Russia and other Western and Arab nations at the Geneva meeting had raised new obstacles to an agreement.

The jury weighing the fate of former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell and his wife Maureen is set to deliberate Wednesday for a second day after hearing a set of instructions. The seven men and five women jurors had no questions in open court on Tuesday afternoon during their first five and a half hours of deliberation. In instructing the jury on Tuesday morning, Judge James R. Spencer rejected arguments defense lawyers had made last week to narrowly define what must be proved to convict the McDonnells, who are accused, separately and together, of two counts of conspiracy, three counts of bribery, six counts of extortion and related secondary charges.

Rick Santorum, who won the state in 2012 but finished with just one percent of the vote in 2016, is ending his campaign, CNN reports. According to CNN's sources, Santorum plans to endorse another candidate. The article notes that New Hampshire is not Santorum's kind of state and he is polling any better in South Carolina. Santorum is not polling any better in South Carolina. The article suggests the campaign may have whipped Santorum's brain into too frothy of a mixture. Comments are closed on the story.

If Republicans in Congress and the Obama White House fail to resolve their differences in time, the federal government will begin a partial shutdown at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, with all but essential services curtailed or closed entirely. A few weeks later, another deadline will arrive when the government bumps up against its legally authorized borrowing limit. If Congress does not vote to increase the debt limit, it could set off severe financial problems for the government as it scrambles for the cash it needs to meet its commitments. Two distinct issues could affect the shutdown: the government could be forced to scale back operations beginning Tuesday if Congress and the administration do not agree on extending federal spending authority; about 800,000 employees would be involuntarily furloughed, while others would possibly have to work without pay.

The Tribune reported that Senator Mark Kirk (R-IL) suffered a stroke but has been successfully treated and resting comfortably. His office released a statement: "On Saturday, Senator Kirk checked himself into Lake Forest Hospital, where doctors discovered a carotid artery dissection in the right side of his neck. He was transferred to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in Chicago, where further tests revealed that he had suffered an ischemic stroke." The statement said: "Early this morning, the senator underwent surgery to relieve swelling around his brain stemming from the stroke. The surgery was successful. Due to his young age, good health and the nature of the stroke, doctors are very confident in the Senator's recovery over the weeks ahead."

The motion to overturn the Federal Communications Commission and save net neutrality passed the Senate. Senators Lisa Murkowski and John Kennedy joined Susan Collins and the entire Senate Democratic caucus and voted to overturn the FCC and save net neutrality. The resolution now goes to the House, where supporters will need to secure 24 votes from Republicans to pass the rollback, assuming all Democrats support. The resolution is still subject to a veto. The article states that most House members support net neutrality, and 99 senators are on record supporting it.

Mitt Romney's presidential campaign borrowed $20 million in August to pay for expenses before he could begin tapping general election dollars and is now $11 million in debt, a senior campaign official confirmed late Tuesday. Romney's campaign finance filings due to be released Wednesday will show the campaign with $15 million in debt, the official said, although the debt currently stands at $11 million. The National Review Online first reported the campaign's debt Tuesday night. Romney has raised hundreds of millions of dollars in general election funds but his campaign could not legally tap those funds until after he officially was nominated at the Republican National Convention. Through the summer, he could only spend primary dollars, and once that money dried up the campaign was forced to borrow money to pay its bills.

President Donald Trump on Saturday awarded a Purple Heart to an Army sergeant recently wounded in Afghanistan. The medal was awarded during a ceremony at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, outside Washington. Sgt. 1st Class Alvaro Barrientos was wounded in action on March 17 in Afghanistan during what is now America's longest war. The White House did not release Barrientos' hometown. Trump said, "Congratulations on behalf of Melania and myself and the entire nation. Tremendous," mentioning his wife. It was Trump's first visit as president to the military hospital.

Throughout most of 2015, the administration of Gov. Rick Snyder told residents of Flint, Mich., that their tap water was safe to drink. Emails released on Thursday suggest the state was concerned about its own employees' exposure to the city's water as early as January of last year, even arranging for purified water to be provided at a state office building there. The emails depict an exchange that month between employees of two state departments expressing concern about the water's safety within the Michigan government long before Mr. Snyder acknowledged to residents in the fall that there was a problem. The correspondence — between employees of the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality and the Michigan Department of Technology, Management and Budget — was obtained by Progress Michigan, a liberal advocacy group. The news was reported on Thursday by The Detroit Free Press.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor, a Virginia Republican, criticized the new nuclear deal with Iran, saying he believes it "bodes very, very ominously for the region and U.S. security." The arrangement announced Sunday gives Tehran six months to increase access to its nuclear sites in exchange for keeping the central elements of its uranium program. Cantor told "CBS This Morning" Monday that the terms are softer than those already in several U.N. resolutions. In a twist on a Ronald Reagan statement about arms control, Cantor said the attitude toward Iran should be "mistrust and verify." Reagan famously said he favored arms pacts with the Soviet Union if there was a "trust-but-verify" standard.

President Barack Obama's nominee for health secretary, Sylvia Mathews Burwell, is being praised by Republicans as she makes her first appearance before a Senate committee. Senator John McCain (R-Ariz.) introduced Burwell to the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee on Thursday. McCain praised Burwell for agreeing to lead HHS, saying the job was like "taking over the Titanic after it hit the iceberg." Senior committee Republican Sen. Lamar Alexander criticized "Obamacare" and cited Burwell's reputation for competence. The comments indicated Burwell could be headed for confirmation even while she is called upon to defend the health law.

MSNBC posted a tweet on Wednesday night that referred to conservatives as "animals" and to a 2013 Cheerios advertisement featuring an interracial family. The tweet stated: "Maybe the rightwing will hate it, but everyone else will go awww: the adorable new #Cheerios ad w/ biracial family." Following the tweet, MSNBC apologized. The apology stated: "Earlier, this account tweeted an offensive line about the new Cheerios ad. We deeply regret it. It does not reflect the position of msnbc. We are deleting the earlier offensive tweet. It does not reflect msnbc's position and we apologize."

On Tuesday, Democrat Steve Stern won New York's 10th Assembly District with 59 percent of the vote, becoming the 40th Democrat to win the seat. The district has not represented the state Assembly for over three decades. Hillary Clinton won the Suffolk-area seat 52 percent to 45 percent in the 2012 election. Barack Obama carried it 51 percent to 48 percent in 2012. The Daily Kos Special Elections Results tracker tracks this and every other legislative special election flip of the cycle. Republicans used the same tactic in the Virginia governor's race last year.

Former Pennsylvania Governor Tom Ridge appeared on MSNBC's "Hardball" Thursday evening to discuss his decision not to run for the Senate in 2010. He declined to say whether he would vote for the likely Republican nominee, Pat Toomey, against Arlen Specter. "It's called secret ballot," Ridge said. Ridge, described as a pro-choice moderate, criticized his party. "We have to reshape our message, reduce the decibel level -- we're too doggone shrill -- and be less judgmental about the people in the party that may disagree with us," he said. He reiterated the point later: "Our message became shrill. We became very divided over these social issues, and at some point in time, we'll have to be a lot less judgmental."

According to a new poll from Ipsos, 43 percent of Republicans hold the unconstitutional view that the president should be able to shut down media outlets he does not like. Thirty-six percent disagree with the statement that "the president should have the authority to close news outlets engaged in bad behavior." The poll also indicates 43 percent of Republicans think Trump has the right to demand their first-born. The article states that knowing a plurality of people in one of the major political parties believe the president should be able to violate the Constitution at a moment when the occupant of the White House appears to want to do just that is a scary prospect.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi announced at an evening news conference that the House is moving forward with an official impeachment inquiry of Donald Trump. The inquiry is expected to focus on Trump's efforts to pressure the Ukrainian government into opening an investigation into one of his potential 2020 election opponents. Pelosi said, "I can say with authority, the Trump administration's actions undermine our national security and intelligence." She noted the administration's refusal to turn over to Congress the contents of an "urgent" whistleblower report, as required by law, and demanded that report be released by Thursday. Pelosi said Trump's Director of National Intelligence "will have to choose whether to break the law or honor his responsibility to the Constitution."

Baptist minister Mark Walker (R) won the Republican runoff for U.S. House in North Carolina's 6th Congressional District on Tuesday. With nearly six out of 10 precincts reporting, the Associated Press called the race for Walker, who led Rockingham County District Attorney Phil Berger Jr., 57 percent to 44 percent. Rep. Howard Coble (R), 83, is retiring at the end of this term and endorsed Berger in the runoff and campaigned for him. Walker will be a heavy favorite in November. In the 5th District Democratic primary runoff, software developer Joshua Brannon defeated Gardenia Henley. Brannon will be a clear underdog against Rep. Virginia Foxx (R) in November.

Tea party groups have announced support for former state treasurer Shane Osborn in the Nebraska Senate primary. FreedomWorks is backing former state treasurer Ben Sasse. The Club for Growth and Senate Conservatives Fund has previously announced it will back Midland University President Ben Sasse. These groups have often been on the same page in certain races — they have all endorsed Sen. Thad Cochran's (R-Miss.) primary opponent, Chris McDaniel, — but there are also times when they do not join forces. The groups backing Sasse have spent more money on GOP primaries in recent years. The Republican primary in Nebraska is very likely to determine the successor to retiring Sen. Mike Johnanns (R-Neb.). The seat is not a top target for Democrats. Other GOP candidates include attorney Bart McLeay.

Fox News host Kimberly Guilfoyle has been close to the Trump family. She is currently dating Donald Trump, Jr., whose wife Vanessa Trump filed for divorce in early April. When not behind the Fox News desk, she has been jet-setting around with junior staff and Secret Service protection. The article questions whether Fox News has an obligation to disclose how close she is to the Trump family and whether she has an obligation to refrain from what it describes as obvious propaganda designed to bolster people she is in bed with. Former Fox News President Bill Shine is leaving to join the White House communications team. Fox News host Sean Hannity has nightly calls and dinners with Donald Trump.

A Quinnipiac University/New York Times/CBS News poll of likely voters in three battleground states, Colorado, Virginia and Wisconsin, found no sharp movement after the debate and the news last Friday that the unemployment rate in September had dropped below 8 percent for the first time since President Obama took office. The poll suggested that Romney had gained strength in a number of ways since last month and that Obama's best defense was the somewhat brighter economic outlook and voters continue to relate to him more than they do to his opponent.

Before Jonathan Bitecofer jetted off to Los Angeles for an appearance on "Cape Up," he discussed politics with me. Bitecofer said former vice president Joe Biden will be the Democratic presidential nominee. She said Democrats will win back the White House. She said Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Cory Gardner (R-Colo.) and Doug Jones (D-Ala.) are toast in their bids for reelection this November.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday criticized a federal appeals court one day after it refused to revive his U.S. travel ban on people from six Muslim-majority nations. On Monday, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals became the second federal appeals court to reject the Republican Trump administration's bid to undo a Hawaii federal judge's decision that blocked the temporary travel ban in a dispute headed to the U.S. Supreme Court. The three-judge panel said Trump's March 6 order violated existing immigration law but did not address whether it was unconstitutional discrimination against Muslims. Trump's 90-day ban targets travelers from Libya, Iran, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.

A Southern California man has been arrested after authorities say he sent an email threatening to kill Sen. Dianne Feinstein. Authorities say Craig Shaver of Lancaster sent a Sept. 30 email to the senator. Other details were not disclosed. Prosecutors said Thursday that Shaver, who has a 1991 grand theft conviction, attempted a criminal threat and accused him of being a felon in illegal possession of a revolver. He could face more than three years in prison if convicted. It was not clear whether Shaver has an attorney. Feinstein is the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee. She has received threats and abuse because some Republicans accuse her of trying to thwart the appointment of Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. A call to a Feinstein spokesman was not immediately returned.

The Nielsen ratings company reported Wednesday that 33.5 million people watched President Barack Obama's fifth State of the Union address, the smallest audience for the annual speech since Bill Clinton's last address in 2000. The audience was 37.8 million people. The 52.4 million people who watched his first address in 2009 were his largest audience. Sixteen networks aired the speech Tuesday night. The 6.5 million people who saw it on NBC gave NBC bragging rights over CBS, which had 6.4 million viewers. Nielsen reported ABC had 5.5 million viewers for the speech. It reported 3.7 million people saw Obama on Fox News Channel, 3.6 million on CNN, and 3 million on MSNBC.

The article reports that Attorney General Jeff Sessions threatened or offered to resign. Asked by ABC News if Sessions had threatened or offered to resign, Justice Department spokesperson Sarah Isgur Flores declined to comment. Sessions was one of President Trump's most reliable backers, shares Trump's contempt for civil rights and the rights of immigrants, and has been on the job for less than four months. The article states the relationship is already going to hell. The article suggests this does not matter how many sycophants and loyalists Trump surrounds himself with, regardless of how much assistance they give him or how slavishly they attempt to cater to his rapidly shifting whims, Trump is simply incapable of carrying out the duties of the office. Comments are closed on the story.

U.S. Capitol police arrested at least 80 people Thursday who were demonstrating against the proposed Republican health care bill. In a statement, police officials said they responded to 13 locations in office buildings on both sides of Congress beginning about 2 p.m. Twitter feeds showed videos and images of demonstrators who were handcuffed and flanked by police as some yelled through the hallways in protest of the bill. "After officers arrived at the numerous scenes, they warned the demonstrators to cease and desist with their unlawful demonstration activities," the statement said. "Those who refused to cease and desist were placed under arrest." Officers arrested 10 men and 11 women at House Office Buildings, while 22 men and 37 women were arrested on the Senate side. Officials did not identify which Congressional offices had been targeted.

President Trump has won preliminary approval to register 38 new trademarks in China for industries including restaurants and advertising. The trademarks cover business interests that could add to criticism over potential conflicts. As a businessman, Mr. Trump has amassed a vast portfolio of trademarks around the world. Those trademarks clash with the vision of a populist president who has espoused an "America First" strategy. China has been among the biggest targets for his business prospects. Including the latest batch, his companies have filed for at least 130 trademarks in China since 2005 for restaurants, bars, hotels, brokerage services, advertising and management consulting. As president, Mr. Trump has criticized China for its trade practices. On the campaign trail, he threatened to impose punitive tariffs against the country.

The chief of the police in Worcester, Mass., Chief Gary Gemme said Wednesday that the department has been reluctantly dragged into efforts to find a burial plot for dead Boston Marathon suspect Tamerlan Tsarnaev. A deal for the state prisons department to take the body has fallen through. The deal to bury the body at a prison site was reached on Monday, then "dissolved" on Tuesday. Gemme said efforts to contact state officials since then have gone unanswered. State corrections officials did not immediately return a message. Gemme said Worcester police are wasting precious resources providing security at the funeral parlor where the body is being kept. He said sending the body to Russia is "not an option." Gemme said: "We are not barbarians. We bury the dead."

The nonpartisan Tax Policy Center analyzed the presidential candidates' tax proposals. The analysis found that the tax cuts enacted by the Bush administration are, in effect, a fiscal poison pill aimed at future administrations. The tax cuts will not prevent a change in management, the Constitution states, but they will make it hard for the next president to change the country's direction. The analysis cited John McCain's early opposition to the Bush tax cuts, which he declared excessive and too tilted toward the rich.

President Obama is scheduled to release his budget tomorrow. The budget would include Social Security and veterans' disability benefit cuts in the form of the chained CPI. It would replace the $1.2 trillion sequester with $580 billion in revenue increases. The revenue increases would be revenue increases Republicans have consistently refused to accept. Republicans have negotiated $2.3 trillion in savings over the past few years. A truly balanced budget approach would be to get that revenue increase more in line with the spending cuts.

U.S. Capitol police arrested at least 80 people Thursday who were demonstrating against the proposed Republican health care bill. In a statement, police officials said they responded to 13 locations in office buildings on both sides of Congress beginning about 2 p.m. Twitter feeds showed videos and images of demonstrators who were handcuffed and flanked by police as some yelled through the hallways in protest of the bill. "After officers arrived at the numerous scenes, they warned the demonstrators to cease and desist with their unlawful demonstration activities," the statement said. "Those who refused to cease and desist were placed under arrest." Officers arrested 10 men and 11 women at House Office Buildings, while 22 men and 37 women were arrested on the Senate side. Officials did not identify which Congressional offices had been targeted.

Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. spoke at the Third International Regenerative Medicine Conference at the Vatican on Tuesday. He discussed his Roman Catholic faith and the need to develop new cures for cancer, a subject that has defined his final year in office. The conference is intended to highlight research advances with adult stem cells while largely avoiding the issue of research using fetal tissue or embryonic stem cells. Dr. Robin Smith, president of the Stem for Life Foundation and one of the organizers of the three-day conference, said in a welcoming speech Tuesday: "Most importantly, we want everyone to understand that no one has to choose between science and faith."

First Lady Michelle Obama channeled rapper Lil Jon in her latest effort to promote healthy eating, using his song "Turn Down For What" in a Vine posted by the White House Tuesday night. In the Vine, the first lady asks, "turnip, for what?" The Vine was a response to Vine user Alphacat, who, while doing a pretty good impression of the first lady's husband, President Barack Obama, asked how many calories Michelle Obama burned "every time you 'turn up'?" The two political figures are not the only political figures to use the song for the Rock the Vote campaign. The rapper recorded a video for "Turnout For What," featuring Lena Dunham, Fred Armisen and Natasha Lyonne.

Donald Trump told reporters Friday that "I am a young, vibrant man." He made the statement while with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Trump said, "I'm so young and vibrant that golf carts are the only vehicles where I get behind the wheel." He added, "I am a young, vibrant man. Now where's the bus back to the senior center?"

Trevor Noah criticized President Donald Trump's sons Eric and Donald Jr. on Wednesday night for complaining about Hunter Biden receiving favoritism because of his family name. Noah said he could understand why most people would complain about Hunter Biden getting a leg up in life via his last name, but what he could not understand was the Trump children doing it. Trump Jr. posted on Twitter Tuesday after he criticized Hunter Biden for acknowledging in an interview that he would not have acquired certain roles on the boards of companies had he not been the son of former Vice President Joe Biden. Noah said on Wednesday night's "The Daily Show": "If there was ever an example of people who got opportunities because of their names, it's these two."

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said she is not denying President Trump a platform. She said the goal is to get a date when the government is open and pay employees. She said she does not believe Trump thinks it is okay not to pay people who do work. She said her caucus does not either. The White House has not responded to Pelosi's letter. Pelosi urged Republican senators to call 202-224-3121 and tell them to reopen government.

The House on Wednesday passed a $410 billion omnibus spending bill that increases spending on domestic programs by an average of 8 percent in the current fiscal year, which began in October. The vote was 245-to-178. The bill was passed a week after President Obama signed a $787 billion measure, which he described as a reflection of Democratic priorities. The bill increases spending on domestic programs by an average of 8 percent in the current fiscal year, which began in October. On Thursday, Obama is scheduled to send his budget for the next fiscal year to Congress. He did not take a formal position on the bill passed by the House. A White House official said, "It's a big document. We are still reviewing it."

President Obama and Congress are ending the year as they began it, working on an economic stimulus package of tax cuts and spending. The latest effort is likely to raise the total cost of antirecession measures to the $1 trillion level that some economists had urged last winter. In a speech on Tuesday, Mr. Obama outlined proposals intended to promote job creation. They included incentives for small businesses to hire more workers, additional money to build roads and other construction projects, and rebates for homeowners who invest in energy-saving weatherizing improvements. Mr. Obama did not put a price on the proposals, which would add to the $787 billion Congress allocated last winter to revive the economy. He said the cost could be offset by some of the $200 billion in lower-than-expected spending on the bailout of financial institutions.

The White House announced it will cancel all public tours due to sequestration cuts, TPM reported Tuesday. The White House said in an email: "Due to staffing reductions resulting from sequestration, we regret to inform you that White House Tours will be canceled effective Saturday, March 9, 2013 until further notice. Unfortunately, we will not be able to reschedule affected tours." Staffers at the Capitol were also informed Tuesday that the building's West Front entrance will be closed starting next week to save money, the Washington Times reported. In January, President Barack Obama made headlines the day after his second inauguration when he and first lady Michelle Obama made a surprise appearance along the White House tour route. With the tours canceled, those wanting an inside look at the president's home will have to settle for an online interactive view of the White House.

The Senate passed a spending measure on Wednesday to keep the government financed through the end of September, resolving a budget fight as Congress moved quickly to the next budget. The Senate dealt with the most immediate financial concerns. The House of Representatives engaged in debate over the budget for the 2014 fiscal year that begins when the spending measure expires Sept. 30. The two parties hold views on economics, public spending and the role of government. As House Republicans moved ahead with their latest attempt to dismantle President Obama's health care overhaul — they voted on one measure that would do so on Wednesday and will vote on another on Thursday — Democrats held a news conference in the basement of the Capitol heralding the third anniversary of the law's passage.

Last week, President Obama said "the world has a responsibility to act" to help contain the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history. Obama announced the United States will devote significant new resources to curbing the spread of the disease in West Africa. "The reality is, this epidemic is going to get worse before it gets better," Obama said in announcing that the U.S. military will lead the fight against Ebola. "But right now the world still has an opportunity to save countless lives." Obama declared the epidemic a national security priority. "Ambassador Powell, working with leaders from across our government, is leading our efforts to build the coalition required to bring this epidemic under control," Psaki said in the State Department's statement. Powell previously served as the State Department's senior coordinator for avian influenza.

She said she does not believe Trump thinks it is okay not to pay people who do work. She said her caucus does not either. The White House has not responded to Pelosi's letter. Pelosi urged Republican senators to call 202-224-3121 and tell them to reopen government.

White House chief White House strategist Stephen K. Bannon said in an interview on Wednesday that news organizations had been "humiliated" by the election outcome and that the media should "keep its mouth shut and just listen for a while." Bannon said the media should be embarrassed and humiliated and keep its mouth shut and just listen for a while. He added, "I want you to quote this. The media here is the opposition party. They don't understand this country. They still do not understand why Donald Trump is the president of the United States."

New York Times columnists David Brooks and Bill Kristol sat down with Barack Obama last night. The paper's White House team has not had the opportunity to do so since Election Day. Unlike recent White House occupants such as George W. Bush and Bill Clinton, Obama has not provided The Times with the sort of pre-Inauguration interview the paper has come to expect. There is little expectation it will happen before Tuesday. "We would certainly like it to happen," said Times political editor Dick Stevenson, "but the days are running short at this point." Stevenson said that although The Times has put in multiple requests to the Obama team, and pointed out the historical precedent for this, they have had no luck securing a sit-down.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel heads to the White House on Friday for the seventh meeting since President Obama took office. The two men face a turning point in a relationship that has never been warm. By all accounts, they do not trust each other. President Obama has told aides and allies that he does not believe that Netanyahu will ever be willing to make the kind of big concessions that will lead to a peace deal. Netanyahu has complained that Obama has pushed Israel too far. The criticism was driven home during a phone call with Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton on Thursday morning, hours before Obama's speech, during which the prime minister reacted angrily to the president's plan to endorse Israel's pre-1967 borders for a future Palestinian state.

A letter to the editor responded to a Sept. 21 article titled "House Approves Stopgap Money, Setting Up Fight" that referenced House Republicans' attempt to eliminate spending for the Affordable Care Act. The letter writer stated that majority rule strikes at the heart of a fundamental principle of democratic governance: majority rule. The writer said Republicans are within their rights to repeal Obamacare if they can, and that this is fair. The writer said the Republicans' threat to shut down the government unless the majority accedes to their demands is unworthy of any representative of a country that bills itself as the world's greatest democracy. The letter also referenced a Sept. 20 news article titled "House Republicans Pass Deep Cuts in Food Stamps" in which Speaker John A. Boehner and other House Republicans said they want to encourage people to find work.
