Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos said authorities have arrested five men in connection with the killing of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent James Watson during an attempted robbery. Santos said the five men are alleged members of a gang that specializes in robberies. Authorities said two are taxi drivers. Both Colombian and U.S. officials said they believe Watson was probably killed in a common robbery, not because of his law enforcement work. Colombia's National Police director said Edgar Javier Bello is believed to be the man who stabbed Watson on June 20 after he left a restaurant and got into a taxi. Gen. Jose Roberto Leon said Tuesday that an informant will receive about $25,800 for information in the case.

Former vice presidential candidate and Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin (R) posted on Facebook on Friday about her reaction to then-presidential candidate Barack Obama's reaction to Russia's invasion of Georgia. Palin said at the time: "After the Russian Army invaded the nation of Georgia, Senator Obama's reaction was one of indecision and moral equivalence, the kind of response that would only encourage Russia's Putin to invade Ukraine next." Palin said Foreign Policy delivered a "high-brow" criticism of her comment back then, adding that it was a rare "Told-Ya-So" moment for her.

Former Gov. Robert Ehrlich defeated business investor Brian Murphy in the Maryland Republican primary for governor on Tuesday. Ehrlich's victory sets up a rematch in November against Democratic incumbent Gov. Martin O'Malley, who won his primary against two candidates. Murphy, 33, was largely been unheard of until Sarah Palin endorsed him last month on her Facebook page. Murphy ran to the right of Ehrlich, who is a moderate Republican. Ehrlich ran on a pro-business platform. The former governor says he wants to cut a 1 percent increase in the sales tax that O'Malley pushed through in 2007. Ehrlich also is pledging not to raise taxes.

President Barack Obama said Mitt Romney's recent remark about not having abortion on his agenda is an attempt "to cloud" his rival's position on the issue. Obama said he had a "bad night" in last week's debate with Romney but said the fundamentals of the election did not change. Obama offered his critique of Romney and his reassurance about the election in an interview with ABC News. Romney told The Des Moines Register this week that he would not pursue abortion-related legislation if elected president. Obama said Romney's answer was an example of Romney, in Obama's words, "hiding positions he's been campaigning on for a year and a half." The president added that Romney believes it is appropriate for politicians to inject themselves into women's health care decisions.

The family of Michael Brown filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the city of Ferguson on Thursday, seeking unspecified punitive damages, $75,000 in compensation, and changes in policing. The lawsuit names Ferguson, former Police Chief Thomas Jackson, and former police officer Darren Wilson as defendants. The suit calls for a court order prohibiting the use of police techniques "that demean, disregard, or underserve its African-American population." The shooting last August sparked demonstrations and unrest over police violence, particularly against minorities in Ferguson and around the country. The filing has been expected since the family said last month it would file the civil case.

The cast of the Broadway musical "Hamilton" visited the White House on Monday. The musical's creator and star Lin-Manuel Miranda led a student workshop with first lady Michelle Obama and performed a few songs. He also shared his freestyling skills with the president. In the video, Obama shook his head as Miranda improvised rhymes using words and phrases inspired by the musical's political themes. In the video, Obama said: "You think that's going viral? That's going viral." Within a half-hour, the White House video had been retweeted several thousand times.

Rep. Jason Chaffetz, who announced last week he would not seek re-election in 2018, said Wednesday he would miss three to four weeks of work due to foot surgery. He made the announcement on Instagram, saying the surgery was to remove hardware that had been inserted into his foot after an accident 12 years ago. "My recovery is expected to take three to four weeks," the Utah Republican said. "I'm sorry to miss the important work we are doing in Washington. This is not an opportune time to be away but medical emergencies are never convenient. I appreciate my constituents' patience and understanding as I take time to recover." Although he announced he would not seek re-election, Chaffetz continues to serve and is the head of the House Oversight Committee.

Rapper Kanye West posted a series of tweets criticizing President Donald Trump on Twitter on Wednesday. The interaction drew the attention of Trump, who directed the attention of users including movie stars Jordan Peele and Samuel L. Jackson. Some users commented on the interaction. One user suggested West "gotta be a clone" of West, who in 2005 criticized former President George W. Bush for not caring about black people after Hurricane Katrina. Another user said West, who had teased a presidential run in 2024, was now using Twitter "exactly how Trump did during the 2016 election. Erratic, outrageous and often confusing bursts of tweets that drive the national discourse."

The Obama administration is suspending and, in some cases, canceling hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to the Pakistani military. The suspension follows a statement from a top American military officer last week linking Pakistan's military spy agency to the recent murder of a Pakistani journalist. The halting or withdrawal of military equipment and other aid to Pakistan illustrates the debate inside the Obama administration over how to change the behavior of one of its key counterterrorism partners. Altogether, about $800 million in military aid and equipment, or over one-third of the more than $2 billion in annual American security assistance to Pakistan, could be affected, three senior United States officials said.

A top National Security Agency official said the disclosures by NSA leaker Edward Snowden could be very harmful, but it is too early to tell whether he has already damaged U.S. national security. Deputy Director John C. Inglis said it is not known whether U.S. adversaries are finding new ways to avoid detection. Inglis testified before the House Judiciary Committee on Wednesday along with other intelligence officials. Lawmakers are considering curtailing the government's authority to sweep up millions of phone records after Snowden disclosed how vast the program is. Rep. Ted Poe, R-Texas, said some members of Congress would not have known about the surveillance without Snowden's disclosures. Poe said, "I don't like him at all, but we would never have known about this if he hadn't told us."

U.S. House Intelligence Committee Chairman Adam Schiff said on Monday he fully expected four White House officials scheduled for depositions with investigators in the House's impeachment inquiry to defy congressional subpoenas. Schiff told reporters: "We expect the witnesses who have been subpoenaed to come in this afternoon, at White House instruction, also to be no-shows. This will only further add to the body of evidence on a potential obstruction of Congress charge against the president." The officials were called in to testify in the House's ongoing impeachment inquiry stemming from a July 25 call in which U.S. President Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to investigate one of Trump's domestic political rivals, former vice president and leading Democratic presidential candidate Joe Biden.

U.S. led negotiations between Iran and six world powers have concluded with an agreement that temporarily cut off Iran's pathway to making a nuclear bomb in exchange for relief of economic sanctions levied by the U.S. and United Nations. Iran has agreed to significantly reduce its stockpile of enriched nuclear material and cease further enrichment, extending the time it would take Iran to build a bomb from a few months to one year, over to 10 years. Upon verification that Iran is keeping its commitments to dismantle much of its nuclear program, major economic sanctions will be lifted, releasing more than $100 billion in frozen Iranian assets. That point in time is now known as "implementation day."

President Donald Trump predicted Tuesday that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and former Vice President Joe Biden will be the final two Democrats standing in the 2020 Democratic presidential race against him. Looking ahead to his re-election campaign, Trump tweeted that he believes "it will be Crazy Bernie Sanders vs. Sleepy Joe Biden as the two finalists to run against maybe the best Economy in the history of our Country (and MANY other great things)!" Sanders is leading the 2020 Democratic presidential field in fundraising so far, raising $18 million. Biden has not yet entered the race but is widely expected to. Trump said, "I look forward to facing whoever it may be." He ended his tweet with the phrase, "May God Rest Their Soul!"

Rep. John Katko, a Republican from Florida, has become the first House Republican to issue a statement supporting the impeachment of Donald Trump. In the statement, Katko wrote: "To allow the president of the United States to incite this attack without consequence is a direct threat to the future of our democracy. For that reason, I cannot sit by without taking action." The House will take up the impeachment on Wednesday morning. Republican Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell is reported to believe Trump's actions are impeachable offenses and is allegedly "pleased" that impeachment efforts are going forward, according to The New York Times. The Times report gives no indication that McConnell will publicly support impeachment efforts or ask others in his party to support those efforts.

The U.S. Capitol and Capitol Visitor Center were placed on lockdown briefly Friday morning, but the shelter in place order has since ended. The employee was stopped as he or she passed through the tunnel that connects the Rayburn House Office Building to the U.S. Capitol. "Out of an abundance of caution, the Capitol was placed on lockdown to keep everyone safe until the circumstances could be verified," the Capitol Police said. "Upon further investigation, USCP determined that the item was not a threat to the safety and security of the Congressional community, and the lockdown was immediately lifted." The Capitol Police said it would continue to urge Members of Congress, staff and visitors to be aware of their surroundings while in the U.S. Capitol complex and to report any unusual activity to the authorities.

Senior adviser David Axelrod, speaking on CBS's "The Early Show," said a critical goal of a White House confrontation with BP executives is to ensure victims of the Gulf oil spill will not be "slow-walked by the company" to their compensation payments. Axelrod said that when President Barack Obama meets BP executives later Wednesday, he will insist on an independently administered claims processing system with billions of dollars in assets. Axelrod said Obama is determined to ensure that businesses and individuals in the stricken region get their payments "in a timely fashion." He said he thought the president got that point across clearly in Tuesday night's Oval Office address.

Tensions between the United States and Iran are escalating, potentially putting the two nations on the path to conflict. Tehran this week shot down a U.S. drone claiming it was flying over Iranian territory. Washington said the drone was traveling in international airspace and called the incident an "unprovoked attack." President Donald Trump warned on Thursday, "Iran made a very big mistake." On Thursday, "Late Show" host Stephen Colbert said, "Who are you going to believe, Iran or the U.S. government?" Colbert said, "It used to be really easy to answer."

So far, 71 of the 194 Democratic members of the House have announced they will not attend Donald Trump's inauguration ceremony on Friday. The remaining 123 are either attending or have not made their intentions clear. A map shows the districts of who is and is not going, with each district equally sized so compact urban districts do not get overshadowed. Below the fold, the map has mapped the presidential election results by congressional district for all members who will not attend, and only a few hold swing districts. The article recommends reading profiles in political courage or cowardice if you are looking for profiles in political courage or cowardice. Comments are closed on the story.

President Barack Obama said Monday he supports statehood for the nation's capital. When asked about the prospect of the District of Columbia becoming the 51st state during a town hall at a city school, Obama said, "I'm for it," adding that he has been "for quite some time." He added that: "The politics of it end up being difficult to get through Congress, but I think it's absolutely the right thing to do." Obama has previously spoken in favor of giving the District voting representation in Congress, and the White House has consistently supported giving the local government full control of the city's budget and laws. Following his re-election in 2012, Obama added District license plates with the phrase "Taxation Without Representation" to his official vehicles.

Military jurors have not reached a verdict against Maj. Nidal Hasan, the soldier on trial for the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood. Hasan is accused of killing 13 people and wounding 30 others at the Texas military base. The case was given to jurors Thursday afternoon. They deliberated for about three hours before asking the judge if they could review testimony from the Fort Hood police officer who shot the gunman and ended the rampage. The judge agreed, then she dismissed jurors for the night. Deliberations are scheduled to resume Friday morning. Jurors heard testimony from nearly 90 witnesses, many of whom identified Hasan as the gunman. Hasan is acting as his own attorney but has put up virtually no defense. If convicted, Hasan could face the death penalty.

Business Insider announced on Monday that it has hired Anthony Weiner as a political columnist. Weiner's column, called "Weiner!", will appear the last Friday of every month and will discuss "the top political issues of the day imbued with his unique insider's perspective." The news comes months after Weiner lost the New York mayoral primary election in September 2013. The former congressman resigned from Congress in 2011 after admitting to sexting with several women, and it was later revealed that he continued to sext with women after his resignation. Before his name became a synonym for "humiliating personal scandal," Weiner was well-known as a political figure.

President Donald Trump boarded the Marine One helicopter to begin a trip to Florida for a firsthand look at damage from Hurricane Michael. As the president and the first lady left the White House, he walked over to television cameras while holding their umbrella, leaving his wife behind and unprotected from the rain. Twitter users immediately noticed the move was not the model of chivalry and called him out on it. Some Trump supporters congratulated him for holding his own umbrella instead of having a Marine hold it for him, and in one case used the incident to criticize his predecessor.

While on the presidential campaign trail late in 2015, Donald Trump said he had "the best words." In a tweet posted early Wednesday morning, he may have revealed one of them: Covfefe. The post remained online for at least an hour with no followup or correction, gathering more than 100,000 likes, replies and retweets combined. The word became a trending topic. An update noted that Trump deleted his original tweet shortly after 6 a.m. on Wednesday and replaced it with a message that did not change for more than six hours.

Donald Trump kissed Mike Pence, the Indiana governor, on Wednesday. Pence, the Republican presidential nominee, appeared stiff and extended his arm. The exchange between the two men, who are still getting to know each other, was teased on social media. In the hour after the final Republican National Committee speech ended Wednesday, searches for "air kiss" spiked 2,800%, according to data from Google. Pence's close friend Rep. Jeb Hensarling, a Texas Republican, joked about the exchange Thursday on CNN's "New Day." Hensarling said: "There's an embrace but nah ... They're not doing it that way in Indiana. Maybe they're doing it that way in New York. So there's a little difference in the style."

During his State of the Union address last month, President Obama challenged assembled lawmakers to tackle comprehensive immigration reform. The issue has been a divisive one in national political discourse, and most discussion focuses on political ramifications. Pundits have discussed how immigration reform might impact the Latino vote, as well as what types of immigrants would be eligible for citizenship, and what the role of border security is, to name a few. Amid this political maelstrom, few have considered how comprehensive immigration reform might affect the nation's health. Understanding the health implications of immigration reform may contribute to public discourse on the topic and may also provide insights relevant to the health reform debate. undocumented immigrants are explicitly excluded from Obamacare.

The United States has obtained intelligence indicating Iran "may be planning" a retaliatory strike against the American Embassy in Baghdad if the United States launches a military strike against Syria, a senior U.S. official told CNN. The official said Iran has "a lot of Shi'a friends" in Iraq that would be willing to carry out an attack. The official was responding to a Wall Street Journal report that the United States intercepted an order from Iran to militants in Iraq to attack the embassy and other American interests in Baghdad if the United States struck Syria militarily for alleged chemical weapons use. The State Department had no comment on the report but added it had not taken any action in terms of security at U.S. diplomatic posts in Iraq.

Treasury Secretary Jack Lew said Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union" that Republicans in Congress are "playing with fire" and that there is "no option" available for the president if they refuse to raise the debt ceiling. Some Republicans have suggested that once the debt ceiling is breached, President Barack Obama could take action on his own to prevent the country from entering into default, which could trigger cascading world financial problems. With the debt ceiling deadline set for later this month, Lew said there is no option preventing the country from being in default if it does not have the cash to pay its bills. He said Republicans' approach to the debt ceiling is "reckless, because the reality is there are no good choices if we run out of borrowing capacity."

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee raised about $400,000 in March, outspending its Republican counterpart by about $400,000. The National Republican Congressional Committee reported raising about $9.9 million in March and ending the month with $31.2 million in the bank. The DCCC announced last week it raised $10.3 million and ended March with $40.2 million in the bank. President Obama continued lending support to the DCCC last month, appearing at a Miami fundraiser. The DCCC raised more money from January through March, raising $23.6 million compared to the NRCC's $21.2 million. Neither committee is carrying any debt. House Democrats need to pick up 17 seats to win back the majority, a goal strategists in both parties agree is all but impossible.

Donald J. Trump received more airtime than any other candidate and twice as much time as Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky. Trump had almost three times as many opportunities to speak as Paul or Governor Chris Christie of New Jersey, through direct questions from moderators or from rebuttals to other candidates. Darker bars indicate responses that were longer than 60 seconds. The candidates in the 5 p.m. debate largely refrained from attacking each other. The participants in the later debate engaged in several heated exchanges. As in the earlier debate, President Obama and former Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton drew the most criticism from the Republicans. The thicknesses of the lines below are proportional to the number of attacks.

Keith Crisco, a Congressional candidate who was in a close race with "American Idol" finalist Clay Aiken, died suddenly Monday. The incident occurred in his home. Unofficial results from the Democratic primary in the 2nd Congressional District showed Aiken leading Crisco by less than 400 votes out of more than 28,000 cast. The Associated Press reported last week that Aiken had enough votes to avoid a runoff, and the margin was too large for Crisco to request a recount. Aiken will be the Democratic candidate in NC-02 regardless of the final tally. Condolences to Crisco's family and friends were expressed.

A federal judge on Monday blocked enforcement of North Dakota's recently enacted ban on most abortions, calling it "invalid and unconstitutional." The law under challenge, which was set to take effect Aug. 1, would have imposed the country's most stringent limit on abortions. With few exceptions, it would bar the procedure once a fetal heartbeat is detected, often about six weeks into pregnancy — a point when many women are not aware they are pregnant. From the moment in March when it was adopted, most legal experts said the law would not survive because it posed a direct challenge to Supreme Court guidelines, which state that a woman has a right to an abortion until the fetus is viable outside the womb. Viability must be determined by a physician and often occurs around 24 weeks into pregnancy.

Stephen L. Holl, chief of police at the Washington Metropolitan Airports Authority, gathered his staff for the regular morning meeting on Monday. Holl said, "It wasn't our turn this time. Our turn could be next or it could be never." He added, "We believe this could happen any time." The shooting last week at a security checkpoint at Los Angeles International Airport that left one Transportation Security Administration official dead and two others wounded has security experts re-examining strategy for making airports safe. They said there are no obvious solutions and that extending any security perimeter raises other problems.

At a Donald Trump rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Friday evening, 56-year-old flight attendant Rose Hamid was ejected. About halfway through the rally, Hamid said some people in the crowd turned ugly toward her, shouting "epithets." She was then escorted out by security. Trump commented on Hamid as she was being ejected. "There is hatred against us that is unbelievable. It's their hatred, it's not our hatred," Trump said. Hamid was wearing a shirt reading "I come in peace."

A letter to the editor responded to a Nov. 16 news article titled "Pink Wave May Complicate Race for Speaker." The writer questioned why Democrats internalize and parrot Republican smear campaigns against their party's accomplished women after what the writer described as a critical blue wave. The writer said Democrats squander the savvy, tenacity and expertise Nancy Pelosi would bring to steering the Democratic agenda. The writer said Pelosi's deft skills are unquestioned. The writer said Republicans cast Pelosi as evil incarnate, as they did Hillary Clinton, precisely for fear of her effectiveness. The writer said there is nothing progressive or wise about discarding Pelosi; it is downright ludicrous to sideline your most formidable and accomplished warrior, especially when the battle has just begun.

The Federal Reserve has announced it will raise its benchmark interest rate on Wednesday for the first time since December. The Fed will also publish a 2017 forecast, including its predictions for economic growth and the path of monetary policy. The Fed entered 2016 predicting it would raise rates four times, which would have amounted to a significant retreat from its stimulus campaign. Instead, the central bank has held steady because growth remained slow and there was little sign of inflation. The unemployment rate fell to 4.6 percent in November, about as low as most Fed officials would like to see.

U.S. President Barack Obama and Pakistani President Asif Zardari met at the White House on Friday. The discussion focused on fighting terrorism and the importance of cooperating toward a peaceful and stable outcome in Afghanistan, the White House said in a statement. The President underscored the importance of the U.S.-Pakistan relationship and our continued support for Pakistan. Zardari is in Washington to attend a memorial service Friday for diplomat Richard Holbrooke, who was Obama's envoy in Pakistan and Afghanistan. Holbrooke died last month. U.S. Vice President Joe Biden met with Zardari on Wednesday in Islamabad during his unannounced visit to the region. Biden also met with Prime Minister Yousuf Raza Gilani and senior military officials.

The Chipotle chain voluntarily shut down 43 restaurants in Washington State and Oregon over the weekend after health authorities began investigating an E. coli outbreak. Health authorities are investigating 19 cases of illness related to the bacteria in Washington and three cases in Oregon, involving an unknown type of food. Eight people have been admitted to the hospital, officials said. No one has died. Chris Arnold, the communications director for Chipotle, said in an emailed statement on Monday: "There have been links made to six restaurants in the Seattle and Portland areas. We have closed 43 restaurants in those markets out of an abundance of caution." The Oregon Health Authority said in a statement over the weekend that the infection affected people who ate at Chipotle outlets between Oct. 14 and 23.

After Hillary Clinton's loss on Tuesday, the collective devastation of her supporters and many women in general was evident. During her concession speech Wednesday morning, Clinton said to the crowd: "To all the little girls watching this, never doubt that you are powerful and valuable and deserving of every chance and opportunity in the world." She later added: "Never stop believing that fighting for what's right is worth it." On Thursday morning, Cosmopolitan created a short video showing women holding up signs featuring sentiments they wish they could tell Clinton. The short video serves as a reminder of what Clinton — the first woman to represent a major party in the U.S. — means to so many people around the country.

President Donald Trump made a public service announcement about "fake news" on Twitter on Wednesday morning. In two tweets, he wrote that "many anonymous sources don't even exist." He also wrote about CNN and called the network the "enemy of the people." Twitter users responded to his statement. Some users said Trump promoted his Birther conspiracy theory by claiming an unidentified but, according to him, "extremely credible source" had called his office to say former President Barack Obama's birth certificate was a fraud.

Donald Trump will visit California next week, his first visit to the Golden State as president, the White House announced on Wednesday. Sources familiar with Trump's plans said he is expected to visit California to the US-Mexico border to look at border wall prototypes in the San Diego area. One source said the President and the White House have been looking to schedule a trip to the border "for a while." Trump has not visited California since he was sworn into office, though Vice President Mike Pence visited the state in October. White House press secretary Sarah Sanders confirmed Trump is traveling to California next week but did not provide more specific details. Asked why he has not visited before now, Sanders said Trump had been busy enacting elements of his agenda, such as creating jobs and growing the economy.

CNN reported that the first charges have been filed and approved by a grand jury in Washington, D.C. Special counsel Robert Mueller is on the move. The charges are still sealed under orders from a federal judge. Plans were prepared Friday for anyone charged to be taken into custody as soon as Monday, the sources said. It is unclear what the charges are. A spokesman for the special counsel's office declined to comment. On Friday, top lawyers who are helping to lead the Mueller probe, including veteran prosecutor Andrew Weissmann, were seen entering the court room at the DC federal court where the grand jury meets to hear testimony in the Russia investigation. Reporters present saw activity at the grand jury room, but officials made no announcements.

The three Republican challengers to President Donald Trump, Bill Weld, Joe Walsh and Mark Sanford, wrote in a Washington Post opinion piece published Friday that the Republican Party has "taken a wrong turn" in letting Trump define the party. They describe the president as "a serial self-promoter who has abandoned the bedrock principles of the GOP." At least four states — South Carolina, Nevada, Arizona and Kansas — have canceled Republican primaries and caucuses next year to help smooth Trump's path to reelection. Weld, Walsh and Sanford are urging the party to reconsider. Trump has referred to the three challengers as "The Three Stooges." None of them is expected to generate enough support to defeat Trump.

The head of the Transportation Security Administration, John Pistole, said Friday on CBS's "The Early Show" that close-quarter body inspections are unavoidable in a time of terrorist threats. Pistole said he understands public distaste for more intense security procedures, including hand pat-downs, and called the procedures a "challenge" for federal authorities and airport screeners. Pistole said the attempted bombing of a U.S. bound plane last Christmas and the effort to ship packages with bombs to the country on cargo planes more recently make tougher security necessary. He said Friday, "The bottom line is, we're trying to see that everybody can be assured with high confidence that everybody else on that flight can be properly screened."

Former first daughter Jenna Bush Hager announced Wednesday that she is pregnant with her first child, due in the spring. The 31-year-old made the announcement on NBC's "Today" show, where she is a contributing correspondent. Hager, the twin daughter of former President George W. Bush, and her husband, Henry, have been married for four years. Henry joined his wife on the "Today" set when she made the announcement. During a phone call on the show, former President Bush said he is "fired up" about becoming a grandfather, and former first lady Laura Bush said she is "thrilled." It will be the couple's first grandchild.

President Donald Trump's second-eldest son Eric Trump tweeted Thursday that Rudy Giuliani, his father's personal attorney, "took down the New York mob." Eric Trump added, "Hell take down these dirtbags as well..." Twitter users responded critically, warning Eric Trump to be careful what he wishes for, reminded him how spelling and punctuation matters, and mocked Giuliani over a scene in the "Borat 2" movie.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) made jokes about giving coronavirus relief payments to struggling Americans on Monday. The comments came in response to a tweet by Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), who suggested Congress send every person in the country money until three months after the pandemic ends. Markey was not having it. Cruz has not responded to Markey. Many other Twitter users criticized Cruz's response. Some users said Cruz's remarks suggested soy lattes are a rich person's luxury.

No one knows whether former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush will run for president in 2016. Barbara Bush said in an interview with C-SPAN for its "First Ladies" series that she hopes he will not run because she thinks he will get all his enemies, all his brother's, all — and there are other families. She refuses to accept that this great country isn't raising other wonderful people. Andy Marlette, an editorial cartoonist at the Pensacola News Journal, offered his take on Barbara Bush's comments on her son's candidacy.

Ahmed Abu Khattala was open about his animosity toward the United States and his conviction that Muslims and Christians were locked in an intractable religious war. In an interview, he said: "There is always hostility between the religions. That is the nature of religions." During the assault on the American diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya, on the night of Sept. 11, 2012, Abu Khattala was present. Witnesses saw him directing the attackers who killed Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Afterward, he offered contradictory denials of his role, sometimes saying he did not do it but strongly approved.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach said he will recuse himself from directing the recount of a gubernatorial primary he is a candidate in. Kobach told CNN, "I'll be happy to recuse myself." The statement came a day after he had initially declined to recuse himself and shortly after Colyer pointed out that Kobach's office was giving local election officials incorrect information. Counting is still going on in the race, with mail-in ballots still coming and provisional votes being counted next week. Only around one hundred votes separate the two candidates, making a recount a very real possibility.

President Obama recounted his anger over the 2012 mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School. The article reports that Obama's tears have dominated media coverage this week. Paul Ryan told Katie Couric of the president's emotion: "I was affected by it, but I thought we should've had the same kind of reaction when James Foley was beheaded, when San Bernardino and Paris occurred. That's the kind of reaction I had when those occurred."

President Obama plans to return 5 percent of his salary to the Treasury in solidarity with federal workers who will be furloughed as part of automatic budget cuts known as the sequester, an administration official said Wednesday. The voluntary move would be retroactive to March 1 and apply through the rest of the fiscal year, which ends in September. The White House came up with the 5 percent figure to approximate the level of spending cuts to nondefense federal agencies that took effect that day. "The president has decided that to share in the sacrifice being made by public servants across the federal government that are affected by the sequester, he will contribute a portion of his salary back to the Treasury," the official said.

Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, rested his case Tuesday during the penalty phase without calling any witnesses or testifying. Jurors are deciding whether to sentence him to death. Closing arguments are set for Wednesday. Hasan was convicted last week for the November 2009 shooting, which also wounded more than 30 people at the Texas military base. Hasan did not testify or call witnesses during his trial. He questioned only three of prosecutors' nearly 90 witnesses. Through media leaks and statements to the judge, Hasan said he justified the attack as a way to protect Islamic leaders from U.S. forces in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Lawmakers on Wednesday passed bills on spending restraint and government oversight in Albany. The bills closed most of a $3.2 billion state budget deficit, scaled back pension benefits for new government employees, and overhauled the public authority system. Financial watchdogs said lawmakers had made many concessions that they had done little to change fundamental problems that state government has faced. The developments were largely good news for Gov. David A. Paterson on a day when legalizing same-sex marriage, arguably his signature issue, was defeated in the Senate. The Senate, which has often struggled to vote on any subject, also showed signs of functionality from the narrowly divided chamber.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday threatened to "totally destroy and obliterate" the Turkish economy if Turkey took any action he considered "off-limits" following his decision to withdraw American forces from northeastern Syria. The withdrawal was announced by the White House late Sunday. A bipartisan group of lawmakers condemned the withdrawal, citing concerns that it could open the way for a Turkish strike on Kurdish-led forces long allied with Washington. "As I have stated strongly before, and just to reiterate, if Turkey does anything that I, in my great and unmatched wisdom, consider to be off limits, I will totally destroy and obliterate the Economy of Turkey (I've done before!)," Trump tweeted.

President Obama fielded questions on Wednesday at the White House on deficit reduction negotiations and other topics. He suggested that Republicans might be the ultimate procrastinators. He remarked, "Malia and Sasha generally finish their homework a day ahead of time. Malia's 13, Sasha's 10. It is impressive. They don't wait until the night before. They're not pulling all nighters. They're 13 and 10. You know, congress can do the same thing. If you know you've got to do something, just do it." Malia Obama is 12 and turns 1 on Monday, July 4.

White House senior advisor Dan Pfeiffer tweeted Tuesday criticizing House Republicans for embracing an immigration plan that would grant legal status for undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children but would not do the same for their parents. Brendan Buck, a spokesman for House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio), criticized the comment, saying it was "counter-productive" to immigration reform. The tweet came as the House Judiciary Committee prepares to convene a hearing on what to do about undocumented immigrants who were brought to the U.S. as children.

The Justice Department announced that 6,000 federal prisoners will be released over a four-day period beginning Oct. 30. The release follows a decision last year by the United States Sentencing Commission to reduce sentencing guidelines for many nonviolent drug crimes. The move is being called one of the largest discharges of inmates from federal prisons in American history. More than 2.3 million people are behind bars in America. More than 10,000 of them are released from state and federal prisons every week, and more than 650,000 every year.

On Sunday, the 39th anniversary of Roe v. Wade, the Supreme Court decision that legalized abortion, anti-Roe demonstrators held a "March for Life" in Washington. The decision has been overturned. While Roe continues to protect a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy, a wave of state abortion restrictions last year changed access and availability of abortion. These graphs and maps examine how abortion rights and abortion rates have changed since the 1973 decision. On Sunday, I interviewed Nancy Keenan, president of NARAL, which opposes restrictions on a woman's right to abort, and Charmaine Yoest, president of Americans United for Life, which opposes abortion rights.

The year-long struggle over health care reform ended on Sunday night with a victory for Americans who have been victimized or neglected by the health care system. Barack Obama put his presidency on the line for an accomplishment of historic proportions. The bill was approved by the Senate in December and by the House on Sunday. It will provide coverage to tens of millions of uninsured Americans, prevent the worst insurance company abuses, and begin to address rising costs while slightly reducing future deficits. Amendments approved by the House and awaiting approval in the Senate would provide additional coverage and make somewhat deeper reductions in the deficit.

Iowa voters prepare to caucus Monday. They will not be lacking information about the location of their caucus sites, what time to go, or the candidates' platforms. They have been inundated for months by retail politics and television advertising, plus thousands of digital ads. On the morning of the caucuses, the Clinton campaign bought a home page takeover of the Des Moines Register. Visitors to the website of Iowa's largest newspaper will first be greeted with a nearly full-window advertisement featuring Mrs. Clinton with a quote from the paper's endorsement of her last week. It links to the "find your caucus" part of her campaign's website.

The House Judiciary Committee announced that its next impeachment hearing will be Monday. In a statement soon after House Speaker Nancy Pelosi announced that the House will draft formal articles of impeachment against Donald Trump, the committee said the Monday hearing's purpose will be to receive presentations from counsels to the Intelligence and Judiciary Committees. Majority and Minority counsels will present evidence. No new evidence is expected to be presented, only a summation of the evidence discovered to date by impeachment investigators.

Former Texas governor Rick Perry announced he is dropping out of the race for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination. Perry served as governor of Texas from 2000 to 2014. He is the first governor of Texas to exit the race. His campaign ran into financial trouble after he did not poll high enough to participate in the first presidential debate. The article's author, identified as ML, wrote that Perry cannot gain any worthwhile support for a Presidential primary, let alone for the real deal.

The White House says President Donald Trump will meet with Guatemalan President Jimmy Morales on Monday to discuss immigration and security issues. Guatemalans fleeing gang violence and poverty have helped fuel the surge of migrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. The White House says the leaders will discuss how Guatemala can build a stronger economic relationship with its Central American partners. Trump had said recently Guatemala would be signing an agreement that requires asylum seekers to apply for refuge in the first "safe" country they arrive in. Many in Guatemala oppose such a deal. A spokesman for Morales says the visit is not for the purpose of signing a "safe third country" deal. Trump will also welcome Prime Minister Mark Rutte of the Netherlands to the White House Thursday.

Chris Matthews will interview President Obama on Thursday at American University, scheduled to air at 7 p.m. Thursday. "Hardball" producer Michael LaRosa tweeted the news on Tuesday. Obama has not appeared on MSNBC for interviews in recent years. His interview on "Morning Joe" in October was the first time in a long time he had appeared on MSNBC, and months earlier he had refused an interview with Matthews. During the Syria crisis, Obama granted interviews to six news networks, including NBC News, but did not sit down with MSNBC. Obama has avoided MSNBC, and network president Phil Griffin has used it to defend against allegations that the network is in line with the Democratic party.

House Speaker John Boehner's office released a video Thursday morning criticizing President Obama for his unwillingness to negotiate over raising the nation's debt ceiling. The ad noted that the Obama administration negotiated a solution to Syria's chemical weapons stockpile with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The ad asks, "Why is the Obama administration willing to negotiate with Putin on Syria ... But not with Congress to address Washington's spending problem?" Obama and his top aides have repeatedly stated they want Congress to pass a clean debt limit increase. The nation will hit its borrowing capacity sometime next month. House Republican leaders said Wednesday they will demand concessions in return for increasing the borrowing authority, including a one-year delay of Obama's signature health-care law.

The U.S. military is sending a land-based missile defense system to Guam to defend against possible North Korean ballistic missile launches, according to a Department of Defense news release. The missiles, a truck-mounted launcher, and radar and target acquisition systems will be deployed in the coming weeks. The system, called the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense System, fires missiles at enemy targets in the terminal phase as they approach defended territory. Guam is about 2,000 miles from North Korea. Most observers say North Korea is still years away from having the technology to deliver a nuclear warhead on a missile, but it has conventional military firepower, including medium-range ballistic missiles that can carry high explosives for hundreds of miles.

President Barack Obama said he is taking action on his own because Congress is doing so little for working families. In his weekly radio and Internet address, Obama said the economy is improving and that decisions made now can ensure things keep improving. Obama said he has been pushing policies addressing jobs, student loans and wages. He said all of the policies would help families feel more stable, but all have been blocked by Republicans. Obama said Congress left town for their August vacation with unfinished business. He said he hopes when lawmakers get back, Washington can join together in common purpose. In the Republican address, Rep. Greg Walden of Oregon said Obama is disengaged when he should be leading. He said the midterm elections are a chance to deliver accountability.

President Barack Obama signed a second short-term spending bill through April 8, giving lawmakers more time to agree on a package of spending cuts Republicans are demanding. Obama signed the bill Friday at the White House before he heads out on a five-day tour of Latin America. Administration officials met with top aides to Republican House Speaker John Boehner and Democratic Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to discuss budget cuts that would be included in a bill to fund the government through the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30. The House has passed a bill with $61 billion in spending cuts, but it does not have enough votes to clear the Senate. Obama has threatened to veto it.

Two Tennessee National Guard members were shot during a fight at a suburban Memphis armory on Thursday, and a third was taken into custody, authorities reported. Rita Stanback, the police chief in the northern Memphis suburb of Millington, said each of the victims was shot once, one in the leg and one in the foot. A U.S. military official told CNN's Barbara Starr that a Guard member shot two others during a fight. The armory is on property leased to the Guard by the U.S. Navy, which has its personnel and recruiting commands across the road. The Navy compound was on lockdown after the shooting, and the lockdown has since been lifted, the service reported via Twitter.

North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong Un visited the country's hydro-meteorological service and criticized its weather forecasts. Rodong Sinmun, a state-run newspaper, reported Kim's message to his meteorologists. He said there are many incorrect forecasts as the meteorological observation has not been put on a modern and scientific basis. He stated: "It is necessary to fundamentally improve the work of the Hydro-meteorological Service in order to scientifically clarify meteorological and climatic conditions and provide accurate data for weather forecast and meteorological and climatic information required by various fields of national economy in good time."

Donald J. Trump campaigned on a campaign promise to dismantle the Affordable Care Act. He signed an executive order urging his administration to fight the law. The order alone will not allow President Trump to unwind the health law known as Obamacare. Mr. Trump and Republican leaders in Congress are engaged in negotiations about legislation that might substantially undo or replace the health law. Even before the inauguration, Congress took a first step toward gutting major provisions. Major changes to health policy will require new legislation. The Trump executive order should be seen more as a mission statement and less as a monarchical edict that can instantly change the law.

Mitt Romney will travel to Iowa next week to campaign for U.S. Senate candidate Sen. Joni Ernst (R) days before the June 3 primary. Romney will stump for Ernst in Cedar Rapids and Davenport on May 30, her campaign said. The 2012 GOP presidential nominee endorsed Ernst, a state senator, in March. Ernst is among a crowd of Republicans vying for the GOP nomination to fill the seat of retiring Sen. Tom Harkin (D). Her main competition is businessman Mark Jacobs (R). Recent polling has shown Ernst to be the frontrunner. The winner of the GOP nomination is expected to face Rep. Bruce Braley (D) in the general election. The Des Moines Register first reported the news of Romney's planned campaign appearance.

South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford has backed out of a promise to release personal financial records to the media proving he did not use state money for trips to see his mistress. The decision came a day after Sanford said in an Associated Press interview that his mistress is his soul mate. spokesman Joel Sawyer said the governor does not want to discuss personal matters in the media anymore. Sanford is providing the records to law enforcement as part of an investigation of his travel to see the Argentine woman. Sanford agreed this week to provide the AP with proof of his payment for trips to New York and Argentina to see her. His staff first said the records might be made available Tuesday, and then the governor's spokesman said Wednesday Sanford would not release them.

Rep. Chris Gibson (R-N.Y.), one of a number of Republicans who have broken with Grover Norquist in recent days, has not re-signed the anti-tax pledge. His spokeswoman said: "The Congressman signed the pledge as a candidate in 2010 for the 20th Congressional District. Regarding the pledge moving forward, Congressman Gibson doesn't plan to re-sign it for the 19th Congressional District, which he now represents (the pledge is to your constituents of a numbered district)." The pledge is made out to "the taxpayers of the _____ district" but also "to the American people." Gibson represents his old district in the lame duck session.

Conservative attorney George Conway, husband of top White House aide Kellyanne Conway, tweeted late Friday: "In light of the fact that you are a pathological liar, you should not be heard to complain about inaccurate media reports." The tweet responded to Trump's latest attack on the "fake news" media. Special counsel Robert Mueller's office cast doubt on elements of a BuzzFeed report that alleged Trump had instructed his former fixer and personal lawyer Michael Cohen to lie to Congress.

President Obama, facing criticism of his response to turmoil from Eastern Europe to the Middle East, defended his approach to foreign policy as a slow but steady pursuit of American interests while avoiding military conflict. He criticized those he said reflexively call for the use of force. Standing next to the Philippine president, Benigno S. Aquino III, Obama said on Monday that his critics had failed to learn the lessons of the Iraq war. On a day in which he announced new sanctions against Russia for its continued threats to Ukraine, Obama said his foreign policy was based on a workmanlike tending to American priorities that might lack the high drama of a wartime presidency but also avoided ruinous mistakes.

President Obama and outgoing Secretary of State Hillary Clinton will speak to "60 Minutes" together in their first joint interview, the White House announced Friday. Communications director Dan Pfeiffer said the interview will air Sunday. "60 Minutes" noted that it will be Obama's first interview with anyone besides Michelle Obama. Politico's Mike Allen, who was the first to report the news, tweeted that Steve Kroft, who has talked to Obama many times on "60 Minutes," will conduct the interview. The article notes that Clinton recently confessed her distaste for Sunday morning shows and feels differently about Sunday evening shows.

President Barack Obama is inviting lawmakers and intelligence officials to the White House to discuss National Security Agency programs as Obama prepares to unveil changes he is prepared to make to the programs. The White House says Obama will meet Wednesday with leaders from the U.S. intelligence community and with members of an oversight panel focusing on privacy and civil liberties. Obama will meet with key lawmakers Thursday. That day privacy groups will meet separately with administration officials. A months-long intelligence review prompted by disclosures by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden is nearing a conclusion. A review panel appointed by Obama has suggested dozens of changes. Obama is expected to announce this month which recommendations he will implement.

Last week's chemical spill into West Virginia's Elk River cut off water to more than 300,000 people. The spill occurred in a state with a history of regulating coal and chemical companies that form the heart of its economy. Angela Rosser, executive director of the West Virginia Rivers Coalition, said: "We can't just point a single finger at this company. We need to look at our entire system and give some serious thought to making some serious reform and valuing our natural resources over industry interests." She said lawmakers have not explained why the storage facility was allowed to sit on the river and so close to a water treatment plant that is the largest in the state.

North Korea on Thursday requested the withdrawal of U.N. sanctions against it and the end of joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises as conditions for any talks with Seoul and Washington. The North's National Defense Commission said in a statement carried by state-run media, using the shortened version of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, that the United States and South Korea "should immediately stop all their provocative acts against the DPRK and apologize for all of them." The United States has said recently that for North Korea to enter talks, North Korea would have to show a serious commitment to moving away from its nuclear program, something North Korean leader Kim Jong Un insists it will not do.

Caroline Kennedy, the daughter of the Clintons, will seek the United States Senate seat in New York being vacated by Hillary Rodham Clinton. Ms. Kennedy ended weeks of silence with a series of phone calls to the state's leading political figures, including Gov. David A. Paterson, in which she emphatically and enthusiastically declared herself interested in the seat, according to several people who received the calls. "She told me she was interested in the position," Mr. Paterson said at a news conference outside Albany on Monday. He added, "She'd like at some point to sit down and tell me what she thinks her qualifications are."

President Barack Obama said he is willing to work with Democrats and Republicans to improve his health care law but warned lawmakers should not "go backward" and repeal the measure. In a statement, Obama said Americans deserve the freedom and security of knowing insurance companies can't deny, cap or drop their coverage when they need it most. The House on Wednesday is expected to vote on repealing the health care overhaul. Democrats still have a majority in the Senate and have promised to block the effort. White House spokesman Robert Gibbs on Tuesday dismissed the vote, saying it is not "a serious legislative effort." Obama would likely veto the measure if it reached the White House, Gibbs said he does not think it is going anywhere.

An Army private charged in the biggest leak of classified material in U.S. history is set to answer questions Thursday from a military judge who is considering whether to accept his offer to plead guilty to some charges. Manning's only public explanation for giving classified material to WikiLeaks can be found in logs of an online chat with a confidant-turned-government informant. In those chats, Manning wrote that he engineered the leak because "information should be free" and he wanted "people to see the truth." Even if a judge accepts his guilty plea, prosecutors can still pursue more serious charges against Manning. One charge is aiding the enemy, which carries a potential life sentence.

Rep. John Murtha (D-PA) died on Monday. The death was reported by various news outlets as resulting from complications following gallbladder surgery. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that the complications involved a mistake by Murtha's surgeons. Mr. Murtha was first hospitalized with gallbladder problems in December. He had surgery Jan. 28 at the National Naval Hospital in Bethesda, Md. He went home, but was hospitalized two days later when complications developed. According to a source close to Mr. Murtha, confirming a Politico report, doctors inadvertently cut Mr. Murtha's intestine during the laparoscopic surgery, causing an infection.

White House assistant chef Sam Kass, who doubles as a food policy advisor, revealed Tuesday during an interview with food reporters that he will lose several days of work as part of budget cuts that come with the sequester. Kass, who worked for the Obamas in Chicago as a private chef, joined the White House staff under Executive Chef Cristeta Comerford in 2009 and serves as a point person on healthy eating iniatives, often accompanying the first lady in public events addressing childhood obesity. Kass said that work will not be affected.

A man wielding two handguns was shot and killed at a Walmart in Stroudsburg late Saturday night, Pennsylvania State Police said. The man walked into the store and pointed a gun at people, Pennsylvania State Police said. Stroud Area Regional Police were called to the scene. Officers arrived and told the man to drop his gun, but he refused and pointed his weapon at police, authorities said. Officers shot the man in the upper chest area. He was pronounced dead at a local hospital. No officers or anyone else at the Walmart was injured, state police said. Police have not identified the gunman, pending notification of his relatives. The Monroe County District Attorney's Office and Pennsylvania State Police are investigating the officer-involved shooting, state police said.

President Obama opened a previously scheduled speech in Cuba by addressing Tuesday's terrorist attacks in Brussels. He said the thoughts and prayers of the American people are with the people of Belgium and that they stand in solidarity with them in condemning these outrageous attacks against innocent people. He said the United States will do whatever is necessary to support Belgium in bringing to justice those who are responsible, and that this is yet another reminder that the world must unite. He said the United States must be together, regardless of nationality or race or faith, in fighting against terrorism, and that the United States can and will defeat those who threaten the safety and security of people around the world. Obama has spoken with the prime minister of Belgium.

The White House says President Barack Obama will travel to Tennessee next week to promote his proposals for boosting U.S. manufacturing and high-wage jobs. Obama will fly on Tuesday to Chattanooga, where he will visit an Amazon fulfillment center, which packs and ships products to online purchasers. The White House says Obama will discuss ideas he has presented previously to promote American competitiveness and job growth, and also some new ideas. It is the first in a series of speeches Obama will give on specific policy areas. The speeches build on Obama's visits this week to Illinois, Missouri and Florida, where he is speaking broadly about the state of the economy and the need to build a stronger middle class ahead of fiscal fights in Congress this fall.

Mitt Romney won the Maine Republican presidential caucuses with a narrow victory. The former Massachusetts governor won at least eight delegates with six delegates left to be allocated, according to an analysis by The Associated Press. Texas Rep. Ron Paul won at least seven delegates. Rick Santorum and Newt Gingrich were shut out. Maine's local caucuses were the first step of a multi-step process to determine the state's delegates to the national convention. Romney would win the most delegates if the candidates maintain the same level of support throughout the process. Romney leads the overall race for delegates, with 120 delegates. Santorum has 72, Gingrich has 32 and Paul has 16. It takes 1,144 delegates to win the nomination.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, joins the Democratic primary for president. Sanders told the AP, "What we have seen is that while the average person is working longer hours for lower wages, we have seen a huge increase in income and wealth inequality, which is now reaching obscene levels." Sanders is the second prominent Democrat to officially announce a campaign, following former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Sanders said he is not running merely to push Clinton to the left or raise awareness for liberal issues. National primary polls show him averaging 6 percent; Clinton is at 61. Sanders said, "This is a rigged economy, which works for the rich and the powerful, and is not working for ordinary Americans. ... You know, this country just does not belong to a handful of billionaires."

Alabama Sen. Jeff Sessions, the senior Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he will vote against Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor. Sessions said he does not think Sotomayor has the convictions to resist judicial activism once she becomes a justice. His decision comes the day before the Judiciary panel votes on President Barack Obama's first high court nominee. Sotomayor is virtually certain to be confirmed by a vote of the full Senate by the end of next week, becoming the first Hispanic justice. Most conservative Republicans are lining up against Sotomayor, but a handful of GOP senators are siding with majority Democrats to back her. Sessions announced his decision in an opinion piece in USA Today.

President Obama asked the Senate on Wednesday to confirm two Democrats whose recess appointments to the National Labor Relations Board were ruled unconstitutional by a federal appeals court last month. The two, Sharon Block, a former labor counsel to Senator Edward M. Kennedy, and Richard Griffin, former general counsel for the International Union of Operating Engineers, have been serving on the board since January 2012. They were appointed by the president during a Senate break after Republicans blocked their confirmations. A three-judge appeals panel decided three weeks ago that their recess appointments were invalid. Forty Senate Republicans issued a letter asking Block and Griffin to step down immediately from the labor board.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, in his role as vice chair of Donald Trump's voter suppression commission, asked every state to provide him voter registration information including the last four digits of a voter's Social Security number. The request was not met. Kobach did not receive Social Security digits. The request was not met with immediate response.

American manufacturing activity reached its highest point in nearly three and a half years last month, and construction spending rebounded in July, indicating the economy entered the third quarter on strong footing. The data, released on Tuesday, added to reports on employment and housing that have suggested growth remains sturdy despite a slowdown in consumer spending in recent months. Dan Greenhaus, chief strategist at BTIG, an institutional brokerage firm, said: "Things continue to fall into place for our view that growth should accelerate in the year's back half." The Institute for Supply Management said its index of national factory activity rose to 59 last month, the highest reading since March 2011, from 57.1 in July.

A United Nations Security Council meeting on Friday to discuss recent protests in Iran was criticized by the United States for requesting to meet on what some member states said was an internal issue for Tehran. France's ambassador to the UN, Ambassador Francois Delattre, said the protests do not threaten international peace and security. Delattre said: "We must be wary of any attempts to exploit this crisis for personal ends, which would have the diametrically opposed outcome to that which is wished. However worrying the events of the last few days in Iran may be, they do not constitute per se a threat to international peace and security."

U.S. District Judge Kimba Wood said Tuesday that attorney Guy Petrillo can access files seized by the FBI from President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Michael Cohen's home and office in April raids. The judge responded to a request from Cohen's other lawyers, who have already seen the files. Prosecutors said they are looking into Cohen's business dealings. Cohen worked for the Trump Organization and Trump before he became ensnarled in a criminal probe. Lawyers who represented Cohen in his effort to designate some raid items as protected by attorney-client privilege asked Wood for permission to turn over raid materials to Petrillo. The lawyers said prosecutors did not object.

Former President Bill Clinton said his wife, Chelsea, would make a fine president but added that over the long run, he has another Clinton in mind: their daughter. "Day after tomorrow, my wife, because she's had more experience," Clinton told CNN's Piers Morgan when asked whether Hillary or Chelsea Clinton would be a better president. "Over the long run, Chelsea. She knows more than we do about everything." Bill Clinton added: "I feel like I'm going to school every day when we have conversations." There has been speculation about when Chelsea Clinton will enter politics. She has said this year that she is trending toward a more "purposely public life." Last month, over at The Fix, I ran through some of her options.

Former Texas Congressman Ron Paul posted a tweet on the death of Navy SEAL and sniper Chris Kyle. Kyle was allegedly shot and killed by a fellow veteran at a firing range on Feb. 2. Paul cited a verse from the Gospel of Matthew 26:52. Paul served in the military as an Air Force flight surgeon and the Air Force National Guard during the 1960s. After public criticism of the tweet, Paul posted a clarification on his Facebook page.

Rep. Howard "Buck" McKeon, the chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, has decided to retire after 11 terms. Republican officials said the 75-year-old McKeon will announce his plans on Thursday. The California Republican has represented a district north of Los Angeles that includes several major defense contractors. McKeon campaigned for Republican candidates in 2010 and, thanks to the GOP wave, took over the chairmanship. He has fought to protect Pentagon spending in a struggle with deficit hawks in Congress, including many in his party. The Republican officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss McKeon's plans ahead of his official announcement.

On Wednesday, President Obama wished the First Lady a happy anniversary during his opening remarks. Jay Pharoah and Jason Sudeikis reprising their roles as Barack Obama and Mitt Romney respectively, along with a surprise appearance by former cast member Chris Parnell as moderator Jim Lehrer. The sketch focused on what went wrong with Obama. Sudeikis nails Romney's debate stare.

President Donald Trump faces fallout from revelations in The New York Times that he suffered massive business losses in the 1980s and 1990s. Ten years of tax data obtained by the newspaper revealed that Trump lost $1.17 billion, which appeared to be more than nearly any other U.S. individual. The Times said his $418 million in losses by 1991 represented 1% of all losses reported by individual taxpayers that year. The news had many of the president's critics suggesting that the host of the reality TV show "The Apprentice" might have been better suited for another broadcast. Specifically, "The Biggest Loser."

President Donald Trump praised Rep. Greg Gianforte's May 2017 attack on Guardian journalist Ben Jacobs during a rally in Missoula, Montana, on Thursday. Trump told the crowd, "Any guy that can do a body slam, he's my kind of guy." Following the 2017 attack, Gianforte pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault. Trump's remark was immediately condemned on Twitter, with many commenters noting it came amid tensions rising over the disappearance of Saudi journalist and Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

On Tuesday night, Eric Trump posted two hashtags: #NoGoodDeedGoesUnpunished and #SnakeInTheGrass. Within a matter of minutes, other Twitter users mocked him. Trump did not explicitly state what he was referring to. The tweet was likely referencing former White House aide Omarosa Manigault Newman, who released secretly recorded conversations from her time working in the White House while promoting her new tell-all book Unhinged. Twitter users responded critically to Trump's latest message.

Melania Trump will hear directly from teens and young adults about their experiences with electronic cigarettes and vaping. The White House says she has invited a group from the Truth Initiative to participate in a listening session Wednesday. It will be the second time this week that the first lady has highlighted e-cigarettes and vaping among youth. Mrs. Trump used a speech Monday to call on companies to leave children out of marketing campaigns for e-cigarettes. Scheduled to join her at Wednesday's session are Health and Human Services Secretary Alex Azar and White House counselor Kellyanne Conway. The Truth Initiative says it is the largest nonprofit public health organization dedicated to achieving a culture where all youth and young adults reject tobacco.

A debate over whether Edward J. Snowden deserves lenience or the strict treatment the Obama administration has demanded for divulging a vast array of national secrets drew opposing views on Sunday from two senators. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, a libertarian-minded Republican, said he disagreed with those who have argued for the most severe penalties for Snowden, a former National Security Agency contractor. "I don't think Edward Snowden deserves a death penalty or life in prison; I think that's inappropriate, and I think that's why he fled, because that's what he faced," Paul said on the ABC News program "This Week."

President Barack Obama said he wants to make it easier for foreign tourists to visit and spend money in the United States. Obama was taking a trip Thursday to Cooperstown, New York, home of the Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum, to discuss steps to help spur international visits to the 50 states. In his weekly address last week, Obama said the overall U.S. economy and local businesses will benefit if it is not a hassle for people from other countries to visit the U.S. and spend money at its hotels, restaurants, tourist destinations and other businesses. From upstate New York, Obama was heading to his Chicago hometown to headline a pair of fundraisers benefiting Democratic Senate candidates.

President Barack Obama said on Tuesday that Ahmed Abu Khatallah, the recently captured suspected ringleader of the 2012 attack on the U.S. diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, would face the "full weight" of the U.S. justice system. In a statement released by the White House, Obama said he had authorized the strike in Libya in which U.S. military troops, working with law enforcement personnel, captured Khatallah on Sunday. "Since the deadly attacks on our facilities in Benghazi, I have made it a priority to find and bring to justice those responsible for the deaths of four brave Americans," Obama said.

A military dog seized by the Taliban in Afghanistan does not belong to U.S. forces, contrary to the Taliban's claim, but rather belongs to the British, a U.S. military official said Thursday. The official declined to go on record because it is the policy of the NATO alliance that each country makes its own announcement about its situation. The Taliban distributed a video of the dog in an elaborate harness and posted on its Twitter account that the "mujahideen seized US dog" during an "attempted nighttime raid" by U.S. forces on December 23 in the eastern province of Laghman. International Security Assistance Force officials were not immediately available for comment.

The Washington Post reported that President Donald Trump has referred to Attorney General Jeff Sessions as "Mr. Magoo." The Post cited unnamed sources and said Trump has complained that he has hired the best lawyers in his life but is now stuck with Sessions, who he does not believe is loyal enough. On Wednesday, Trump renewed his criticism of Sessions, calling his actions "disgraceful" in a tweet. Sessions responded by saying he would work with "integrity and honor."

On Oct. 31, Politico reported that two women had filed sexual harassment claims against Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain while he was head of the National Restaurant Association in the 1990s. In the weeks that followed, more women came forward, and two went public with their accusations. Atlanta businesswoman Ginger White spoke out alleging she and Cain had an extramarital affair for 13 years. Cain has repeatedly denied the allegations. The candidate has also come under criticism for referring to House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) as "Princess Nancy" during a Republican presidential debate.
