Thousands of protesters gathered in Madison in reaction to Gov. Scott Walker's (R) new budget proposal. Wisconsin faces a $137 million budget deficit. Walker wants to curtail the collective bargaining rights of public employee unions, effectively preventing them from negotiating benefits, hours and working conditions. They would still be able to bargain over base wages, and Walker decided to exempt firefighters and police workers from his measure. Public workers would also have to contribute more money toward pension and health insurance plans. HuffPost Eyes and Ears contributors Matt Robison and Julia Meuse took photos of the protests in Madison.

Former Florida governor and potential 2016 presidential candidate Jeb Bush told Fox News Radio's "Kilmeade & Friends" on Thursday that he does not read the New York Times. Host Brian Kilmeade asked Bush for his response to a recent NYT article about members of the Christian right seeking an alternative contender. Bush responded, "I don't read The New York Times to be honest with you, so I guess you're going to force me to do so." The Washington Post has previously asserted that "it's dumb" for a politician to say they don't read the Times. New York Times reporters also pointed out that the article was "totally false."

On June 17, a white man entered a church in Charleston, S.C., and killed nine black people during a prayer meeting. Twenty-three days later, after a national outcry and a legislative debate, a Confederate battle flag similar to the one the gunman, Dylann Roof, waved in photos before the shootings was lowered from the grounds of the State House, where it had flown for more than 50 years. Crowds cheered and chanted as the flag was brought down and carefully folded just after 10 a.m. on Friday. Before the ceremony, reporters who were there said that though people who were both for and against the flag's removal attended the ceremony, the crowd was calm.

Four simultaneous missile launchings by North Korea on Monday occurred in Japan. According to the South Korean military, North Korea launched four ballistic missiles from its long-range rocket launch site on Monday morning. Analysts said the launches suggested North Korea could pose a more serious threat than indicated by previous tests. North Korea said on Tuesday that the tests were conducted by units "tasked to strike the bases of the U.S. imperialist aggressor forces in Japan in contingency."

Hillary Rodham Clinton plans to headline a California fundraiser for Terry McAuliffe, a longtime family friend running for governor in Virginia. The former secretary of state will attend the Beverly Hills fundraiser on Oct. 30. It will be hosted by longtime Clinton donors Haim Saban and his wife Cheryl. The former first lady has been helping McAuliffe in the final weeks before November's election. She was raising money for McAuliffe in New York on Tuesday and plans to appear at a "Women for Terry" event in Falls Church, Va., on Saturday. Democrats consider Clinton to be a strong contender for the 2016 Democratic presidential nomination should she decide to run. McAuliffe faces Republican Ken Cuccinelli in the November election.

Former United States senator Ted Stevens died Monday night in a plane crash at age 86. He helped shape modern Alaska with federal laws and billions in federal dollars. Stevens served in the Senate for 40 years, longer than any other Republican. He was known as a fierce and often hot-tempered advocate for his state. In October 2008, a federal jury in the District of Columbia found that Stevens had concealed more than $250,000 in gifts and convicted him on seven felony counts. Eight days later, he lost a bid for a seventh term to Mayor Mark Begich of Anchorage, a Democrat.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel called on all sides in the conflict in Ukraine to work toward the ceasefire envisaged by the Minsk accords, saying implementation of those agreements could lead to the lifting of EU sanctions against Russia. Speaking in the Russian town of Sochi after discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Merkel said there was no need to replace the Minsk process, which is designed to bring an end to the conflict between Moscow-backed rebels in Ukraine's east and the Kiev government. "For me the aim is to reach the point in the implementation of the Minsk accords where we can lift the European Union's sanctions against Russia," Merkel said.

President Donald Trump met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas during the second leg of his first foreign trip as president. Trump said he does not expect to emerge from his two-day visit to Israel and the West Bank with a deal in hand. He is the latest president to arrive at the visit with the goal of achieving Middle East peace. "During my travels I have seen many hopeful signs that lead me to believe that we can truly achieve a more hopeful future for people of this religion and for people of all faiths and all beliefs and frankly all over the world," Trump said, delivering remarks Monday evening alongside Netanyahu.

A GOP office in Hillsborough, North Carolina, was firebombed overnight with a swastika and the words "Nazi Republicans get out of town or else" spray painted on an adjacent building, according to local officials. Hillary Clinton responded to the incident. The NCGOP responded that at this point there is no evidence as to the perpetrators. Donald Trump weighed in. Law enforcement has no idea who was responsible for the bombing, or at least they are not yet saying. Comments on the story are closed.

On Monday, Post reporters provided updates from D.C. businessman Jeffrey E. Thompson's court hearing. A judge said the local charge carries a technical five-year sentence, while guidelines for the case range from probation to 12 months. The headline read: "TV campaign" and "GOTV" — get out the vote campaign. The prosecutor said Gray gave Thompson a $425,000 budget for a particular television campaign. The prosecutor said Thompson told him he would pay it secretly through adviser. The prosecutor said on request of Gray adviser, Thompson paid >$40,000 for home improvements for a close friend of Gray. Gray thanked Thompson for it.

Bernie Sanders' campaign said Tuesday it raised $3 million through online fundraising 24 hours after he nearly beat Hillary Clinton in the Iowa caucuses. The campaign raised the haul after Sanders gave his speech Monday night, campaign spokesman Michael Briggs said. The campaign's online fundraising comes as Sanders and Clinton square off in New Hampshire. Sanders has largely kept pace with Clinton in the money race throughout the campaign, logging $20 million in January alone, according to his campaign. The Sanders campaign has touted its online fundraising after events like Democratic and Republican debates and taunted the Democratic National Committee in December, saying it raised $1 million following a voter database breach.

Donald Trump posted on Twitter over the weekend about his possible impeachment, calls for civil war, and a demand to meet the whistleblower. Trump wrote: "Rep. Adam Schiff illegally made up a FAKE & terrible statement, pretended it to be mine as the most important part of my call to the Ukrainian President, and read it aloud to Congress and the American people. It bore NO relationship to what I said on the call. Arrest for Treason? Trump is in full-blown panic mode."

In the final leg of New Jersey's governor's race, both candidates are casting about for ways to save the state from financial doom as they confront the economic reality that will severely restrict the winner of Tuesday's voting. Democratic governor Jon S. Corzine says he may revisit his plan to lease the New Jersey Turnpike to raise cash — a proposal he abandoned last year in the face of intense opposition from lawmakers and voters. Republican challenger Christopher J. Christie says he can no longer fully restore property tax breaks for homeowners, given the uncertainty of the state's finances.

North Korea has increased its launch activities at Sohae Satellite Launching Station in North Korea, the satellite operator DigitalGlobe said Tuesday, citing recent satellite imagery of the facility. The increased activities came months after the Unha-3 rocket, launched from the same site in April, disintegrated shortly after takeoff and failed to put what North Korea claimed was a scientific satellite into orbit. The United States and its allies condemned the launching as a violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions that banned North Korea from testing technology that could be used to develop long-range ballistic missiles.

The U.S.-led coalition in Afghanistan formally ended its combat mission on Sunday, more than 13 years after an international alliance ousted the Taliban government for sheltering the planners of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on American cities. At a ceremony marking the end of the mission held at the ISAF headquarters in Kabul, U.S. General John Campbell, commander of the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF), said: "Today marks an end of an era and the beginning of a new one." He also said: "We will continue to invest in Afghanistan's future."

According to a CBS News story, also quoted in The Hill, the Secret Service has paid $35,000 to the Trump organization for golf cart rentals at Mar-a-Lago golf club. One purchase order reviewed by CBS News shows the Secret Service has spent $35,185 on golf cart rentals for the President's visit in Palm Beach County, Florida since the President's inauguration. The article states that whatever profit Mar-a-Lago receives from the Secret Service rentals presumably goes into the Trump trust and back into Trump's pocket. Comments are closed on the story.

Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign raised at least $45 million during its first quarter, her campaign told Bloomberg on Wednesday. The campaign said 91 percent of donations were of $100 or less. The haul from her campaign's launch in mid-April through June 30 is a record for primary money raised in a candidate's first quarter. President Barack Obama held the previous record for a campaign's first quarter, raising $41.9 million after launching his re-election bid.

Two reporters for The New York Times, David M. Halbfinger and David Kocieniewski, conducted wide-ranging interviews with the major-party candidates for governor of New Jersey, Jon S. Corzine, the Democratic incumbent, and Christopher J. Christie, his Republican challenger. The interview was edited. The first question was: "Given all the factors we know, and the uncertainties, what do you really think you can get accomplished in your next term?" The second question was: "The most important issue that impacts what you can get done is, are we going to get a national economic recovery that comes sooner and comes stronger to the state? I believe we've positioned ourselves for that."

After final negotiations that ran late into Thursday night, the House is expected to vote Friday on the Republican plan to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act. Lawmakers added additional changes on Thursday. The biggest change was a weakening of a federal requirement that health insurers provide essential health benefits, called essential health benefits. House Republicans had released several key changes to their plan on Monday, two weeks after its initial unveiling, in an attempt to appease both conservatives and moderates. The bill compares with the Affordable Care Act, with proposed changes to the original bill highlighted.

Before he was fired, FBI Director Comey had asked the Justice Department for vastly increased funding and staff for the Russia investigation. The question was whether Interim Director McCabe would ask for the same ramping up or was he giving a victory to Donald Trump in his attempt to obstruct justice by not ramping up the investigation the way Comey intended. Another question was asked: without the increased funding requested by Comey, how many years would it take for the FBI to complete its investigation? Eight? Should the FBI ramp up the Russia Investigation the way Comey intended? Comments on the story were closed.

BP earned $17 billion last year and ended the year with more than $8 billion in cash. The company faces short-term costs related to the oil well leaking millions of gallons into the Gulf of Mexico. Government, Gulf Coast residents, and investors have expressed concerns about BP's ability to meet obligations over the long term or survive the crisis intact. The ultimate cost of the disaster remains uncertain. Wall Street estimates range from $17 billion to $60 billion, including penalties, damages, and cleanup costs for the Deepwater Horizon disaster.

Michael D'Antonio, author of the book "Never Enough: Donald Trump and the Pursuit of Success" (St. Martin's Press), wrote in a CNN commentary on Monday that his father's $1 million loan got him started as a developer. The article stated that the loan was intended to show he is a self-made man and represented a new direction for the candidate. The commentary did not give Trump the credit he deserved.

Justice Clarence Thomas criticized New Jersey Democratic Sen. Cory Booker over a comment he made during Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh's confirmation hearing. During a conversation with the Federalist Society's Leonard Leo last week, Thomas said, "Honorable – if we could use that word about more people who are in public life, people who actually ask the questions at confirmation hearings, instead of 'Spartacus.'" The conversation aired on C-SPAN Wednesday and was filmed at the inaugural Gregory S. Coleman Memorial Lecture. The audience and Thomas both laughed following the comment.

Senator Marco Rubio has told colleagues and advisers he is considering running for president again in 2020 or 2024. As he and his team weighed a re-election campaign, they debated how well situated he would be in seeking the presidency from the Senate. Rubio set the record for doing the most half-assed Senate job and has announced he wants the job back.

A Muslim ninth grader named Ahmed Mohamed was arrested yesterday after school officials mistook his homemade clock for a bomb. After a friend posted a picture of Mohamed being arrested, his story received nationwide attention. #IStandWithAhmed immediately started trending as support poured in from all over the country. Ahmed was invited to the White House by President Obama via Twitter. The Huffington Post secured the formal invitation and security briefing from the White House to Ahmed Mohamed. On the second page, the White House briefed him on the security detail. The briefing also informed him there would be an itinerary.

Sixteen states filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging President Donald Trump's national emergency declaration for the southern border. The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The attorneys general from Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Virginia joined California Attorney General Xavier Becerra in the lawsuit. The attorneys general from Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Virginia joined the lawsuit.

A three-judge panel refused a request by Al Franken, the Democratic Senate candidate, to block a lawsuit over a recount in his contest. Franken led Republican candidate Norm Coleman by 225 votes in the recount, and Coleman is contesting the result. The judges' decision means the trial on Coleman's lawsuit will start Monday. Coleman argues that the recount process was flawed. He says that votes were double-counted in some precincts and that more absentee ballots should be admitted.

A shouting stenographer was removed from the House floor as lawmakers voted on a deal to reopen the government and avoid a debt crisis. The stenographer began shouting as the House approved the number of votes needed to pass the bill. According to reporters, she was yelling about God and Freemasons. An official house court stenographer took to the microphone and was screaming ab God. She was saying in the hall you can't serve two masters. Public Radio International's Todd Zwillich recorded the incident.

As classes began at a high school in suburban Pittsburgh on Wednesday morning, a 16-year-old student walked through the hallway stabbing and slashing students with two large knives, authorities said. An assistant principal tackled the student and he stabbed 20 students and a security guard and sent students running from the school, officials said. At least four students had serious wounds to the abdomen and torso but were expected to survive. The suspect, Alex Hribal, was treated for cuts to his hand at a hospital before he was taken into custody. He was charged as an adult on Wednesday with four counts of attempted homicide and 21 counts of aggravated assault.

Three new polls show a close race in Michigan. PPP's latest survey shows a small Santorum lead. A Mitchell Research poll shows Romney ahead. FiveThirtyEight's latest forecast gives Romney a 51 percent chance of victory. In recent days, Romney's super PAC has focused its ad campaign on attacks on Santorum. Ron Paul, who has been an ally of Mitt Romney in state after state, is launching a new statewide ad campaign in Michigan attacking Rick Santorum as well. Although their ads are different, the message is the same: attacking Rick Santorum's fiscal record from the right.

Mitt Romney will speak with Benjamin Netanyahu today. President Obama spoke with Netanyahu on the phone. Romney and Netanyahu have been friends for decades. Romney has accused Obama of ignoring the relationship between the U.S. and Israel. He has also criticized Obama for not taking a harder line on Iran. Obama has called it unacceptable for Iran to have a nuclear weapon; Romney has said that it is unacceptable for Iran to develop "nuclear capability." In one interview, Romney described his position and Obama's as the same. Netanyahu wants the U.S. to draw a "red line" that Iran cannot cross without facing an American attack.

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) said Sunday that he wants Vice President Joe Biden to participate in talks on raising the U.S. government's debt ceiling and ending the government shutdown. "I hope the president will become engaged. Maybe we need to get Joe Biden out of the witness protection program," McCain said on CBS's "Face the Nation." McCain said the Senate had not found a deal acceptable to both Republican and Democratic leadership. McCain noted that Biden has good relationships with many lawmakers. The vice president has mostly stayed out of negotiations over ending the shutdown, reportedly at the behest of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.).

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled that the State of Texas can enforce HB 2, an omnibus anti-choice law that mandates that legal abortion facilities meet the standards of ambulatory surgical centers and that doctors who provide abortions have admitting privileges at local hospitals. The law was opposed as medically unnecessary and dangerous by state- and national-level major medical associations. Anti-choice lawmakers claimed that HB 2 would increase the "health and safety" of Texans who seek legal abortion care. The law also bans abortion after 20 weeks and severely limits the provision of medication abortion.

The Chicago Sun-Times reported that President-elect Barack Obama's incoming chief of staff Rahm Emanuel had direct discussions about a U.S. Senate seat appointment with Gov. Blagojevich. Blagojevich is accused of trying to auction the seat to the highest bidder. Sources with knowledge of the conversations told the Sun-Times that Emanuel talked with the governor in the days following the Nov. 4 election and pressed early on for the appointment of Valerie Jarrett to the post. There was no indication from sources that Emanuel brokered a deal.

The Obama administration will prosecute Khalid Shaikh Mohammed and four other people accused of plotting the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks before a military commission rather than a civilian court, as it had previously planned. Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. announced on Monday that he has cleared military prosecutors at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, to file war-crimes charges against the five detainees in the Sept. 11 case. Holder had decided in November 2009 to move the case to a federal civilian courtroom in New York City, but the White House abandoned that plan amid political backlash.

A freight train derailed Tuesday afternoon just outside Baltimore in the Rosedale area, according to Baltimore area fire and police officials. The incident happened around 2 p.m. Emergency personnel were at the scene. Social media feeds from fire and police agencies said there was an explosion, smoke and fire and that several buildings collapsed in the warehouse area where the train derailed. No injuries were reported. As of 3 p.m., the National Transportation Safety Board said it was watching the situation to determine whether to send investigators to the scene. The train derailed in the 7500 block of Lake Drive and exits from I-95 and I-895 to Pulaski Highway were closed.

At least seven people were killed late Friday when an American drone fired three missiles at a house in northwestern Pakistan, according to an intelligence official, hours after Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif announced his cabinet. During his campaign, Sharif often criticized the United States for using drone aircraft to kill militants. The drones that struck Friday targeted a house in Mangroti village in the Shawal area of North Waziristan, the tribal region straddling the border with Afghanistan. The identities of the victims were not immediately known, but an intelligence official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described them as militants.

President Trump and Republicans have promised that their plan to overhaul the federal health care law will make medical coverage much more affordable. In April, Mr. Trump tweeted that premiums and deductibles would be "much lower." He also said the plan to replace the Affordable Care Act would protect people with potentially expensive medical conditions. As Senate Republicans unveiled draft legislation this week, they reiterated the goal of making it easier and cheaper for consumers to buy coverage than under the current law. "This plan will improve the affordability of health insurance," the Senate majority leader, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, wrote in an opinion piece on Friday.

Last night, Mitt Romney answered a question about his immigration stance and said he would respect Obama's Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals policy if elected into office. Many commenters commented on the announcement. The article asked whether the move was a desperate move by Romney and his team to gain Latino votes or whether Romney's shift from his self-deportation comments earlier in the year showed signs of an "evolving" Romney.

Federal and state investigators learned today that an additional chemical that was not previously identified was in the tank that leaked on Jan. 9 at Freedom Industries tank farm just upstream from West Virginia American Water's regional drinking water intake. The chemical, the company claims, has "low oral toxicity." Company officials told investigators that the "Crude MCHM" that spilled also contained a product called "PPH," which stands for polyglycol ethers, according to the U.S. Chemical Safety Board.

Mitt Romney praised the people of Poland for marching toward "economic liberty and smaller government" rather than "heeding the false promise of a government-dominated economy." In a speech Tuesday in Poland's capital, Warsaw, the Republican presidential candidate also praised Poland for its higher living standards and strong military. Romney's comments fit into his campaign's themes of smaller government, reduced federal spending, and fewer regulations on business. He said Poland is thriving because it sought to "stimulate innovation, attract investment, expand trade and live within its means." Romney said Poland's success is a reminder that "free enterprise can propel an economy and transform a society."

Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.) leads Harvard law professor Elizabeth Warren (D) by four points in the latest Boston Herald/UMass Lowell poll, after four polls in a row showing the Democratic challenger ahead. Brown leads by six points with registered voters and four points with likely voters in the survey, which has a 5.5 point margin of error. Unlike other recent surveys, this poll finds no convention bounce for Warren. Brown's lead with independents and his support among Obama voters are both larger. A third of Brown supporters are open to changing their vote; 19 percent of Warren backers say the same.

The official death toll from Washington's mudslide has increased to 27, with the Snohomish County medical examiner's office saying 19 victims have been positively identified, up from 24 dead with 18 identified on Monday. Workers are trying to improve the flow of the Stillaguamish River through the landslide at Oso to reduce flooding as they continue recovering bodies. The latest name to the list is 58-year-old Brandy L. Ward of Arlington. Like the rest she was killed by blunt force injuries in the March 22 slide.

Vietnam's foreign minister Pham Binh Minh arrived in North Korea on Tuesday ahead of a planned summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Vietnam's capital, Hanoi, on Feb. 27-28. No further details of his schedule have been released by his North Korean hosts. The two leaders held their first summit last June in Singapore. The United States is seeking a firm commitment on denuclearization from Kim.

EMILY's List announced it is spending $250,000 on a radio advertisement supporting Attorney General Martha Coakley (D). The advertisement is airing statewide with a concentration in the Boston market, a source said. In a statement, EMILY's List said the 60-second ad highlights state Sen. Scott Brown's record of voting with the Republican leadership 90% of the time and siding with special interests over Massachusetts families.

Pennsylvania Governor Tom Corbett (R) announced he will not appeal yesterday's federal district court decision striking down the state's exclusion of gay couples from marriage. The decision makes Pennsylvania the nineteenth state where same-sex marriage will be ongoing. Corbett explained his decision: "I have thoroughly reviewed Judge Jones' opinion in the Whitewood case. Given the high legal threshold set forth by Judge Jones in this case, the case is extremely unlikely to succeed on appeal. Therefore, after review of the opinion and on the advice of my Commonwealth legal team, I have decided not to appeal Judge Jones' decision."

A Wednesday afternoon lunch in which President Barack Obama discussed proposed energy legislation with Democratic senators has been postponed, an administration source said. The source said the meeting was rescheduled because of Obama's changing schedule and his expected remarks on the matter involving Gen. Stanley McChrystal. The lunch initially was to be a bipartisan meeting but was canceled, then rescheduled as a meeting with about half a dozen senators, but only Democratic ones, a source familiar with the schedule said. The lunch had been scheduled for 1:10 p.m. at the White House, that source had said.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Jan. 7 that JPMorgan Chase & Co officials will not be penalized as part of a settlement the bank is negotiating with federal authorities to resolve suspicions that it ignored signs of Bernard Madoff's Ponzi scheme. JPMorgan was not immediately available for comment by Reuters outside regular U.S. business hours. Madoff was convicted in 2009 of defrauding thousands of investors and is serving a 150-year prison sentence. JPMorgan has been accused of ignoring warning signs that Madoff's business was a fraud, often to win more fees and commissions for services they provided.

CNN and NBC News reported Monday that special counsel Robert Mueller told Attorney General William Barr some three weeks ago that his report would not be conclusive on the question of whether Donald Trump obstructed justice. CNN correspondent Laura Jarrett also reported that a definitive answer on obstruction was "not expected." Barr and Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, who oversaw most of the Russia investigation, had three weeks to plan for the summary they wrote in which they decided to unilaterally exonerate Trump, even though Mueller did not. It is unclear whether they had access to the full range of evidence Mueller laid out in his report.

President Obama said Thursday that he was not planning to significantly expand the war against the Islamic extremist movement anytime soon. His remarks came after days of debate inside the top levels of his national security bureaucracy about how, where, and whether to strike ISIS in Syria. Those deliberations, which included an intelligence assessment of America's potential allies in Syria, did not produce a consensus battle plan. Obama, who has long been reluctant to enter into the Syrian conflict, told reporters Thursday that "we don't have a strategy yet" for confronting ISIS on a regional level.

Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said Wednesday that he does not plan to serve in the next Obama administration if President Barack Obama wins a second term in November. Geithner said he was confident that Obama would be re-elected but added that he was also "confident that he is going to have the privilege of having another secretary of the Treasury." The comments came in an interview with Bloomberg Television.

The author wrote that they worry that if the United States does not pursue the Trans-Pacific Partnership, China will break the rules. The author stated that once the election is over, and trade is addressed, people will understand a couple of things they want to fix, but going forward they must build a global economy. The author also wrote that this comes on top of what the author described as Clinton's true colors leaking out in the Democratic Platform. The author wrote that Clinton was not believable when she announced her opposition to the Trans-Pacific Partnership she negotiated as Secretary of State, and that Bernie Sanders would have opposed the deal. The author concluded that fair traders are now left with Donald Trump.

MSNBC reported that Donald Trump will not participate in the FOX Debate on January 28. The reason cited is Meygan Kelly, who Trump hates and serves as moderator of the debate. The article stated that Roger Ailes is telling Trump to F himself and that it is time someone cut Trump down to size. As of the time of reporting, Trump said he would do a fund raiser for Vets instead. Comments on the story are closed.

Rhode Island House Speaker Gordon Fox says he is resigning from his leadership post and will not run for re-election, a day after federal and state authorities raided his Statehouse office and home. In a written statement sent Saturday evening, Fox says he will not let Friday's raids distract his colleagues from addressing the challenges facing the state. He says he wants to focus on his family and dealing with the investigation. The raids were part of an investigation by the U.S. attorney's office, FBI, IRS and state police. Officials have not said whom or what they are investigating.

Eric Trump tweeted four words during Monday's opening night of the Democratic National Convention: "This is absolutely terrible." The tweet prompted criticism from responders who assumed the tweet was about the DNC. One person commented: "The state of the union? Yes it is. This Presidency sure is. Can't end soon enough." Others mocked the lineup for next week's Republican National Convention.

Melania Trump addressed a cyberbullying summit in Rockville, Maryland, on Monday. She acknowledged that social media can be "destructive and harmful when used incorrectly." She posted a captioned tweet stating "#BeBest." Many Twitter users responded by highlighting the Twitter attacks her husband President Donald Trump launches at political rivals, celebrities, and anyone else who crosses him.

Protesters shouting about the Keystone XL pipeline interrupted President Barack Obama's speech on health care in Massachusetts on Wednesday. Obama said, "This is the wrong rally!" and "We had the climate change rally back in the summer." An update at 4:37 p.m. stated that Sophie Robinson and Shea Riester were named as protesters in a release from 350.org. The two shouted, "Mr. President, Reject Keystone XL! Stop Climate Change! For our generation, Stop the pipeline!"

Hillary Rodham Clinton's coming memoir about her tenure as Secretary of State will be titled "Hard Choices," her publisher said early Friday. The title addresses the dilemma Mrs. Clinton faced at the State Department carrying out President Obama's vision of diplomacy while bringing her own more hawkish stance to foreign policy discussions. As Mrs. Clinton emerges as a potential 2016 presidential candidate, she has been pushed to more clearly define her legacy as secretary of state. When asked recently at an event in New York what her proudest accomplishment was at the State Department, her response lacked specifics and drew criticism.

As Republicans prepared to campaign on a pledge to try to repeal the measure, Obama and the Democrats will work to keep voters focused on the new benefits rather than the size, cost or complexity of the bill. Democratic strategist Chris Kofinis said the real political battle over health-care reform begins after its passage. Kofinis said Republicans cannot let Republicans seize the message advantage, as they did during last summer's 'tea party' and town hall protests. For Democrats, Kofinis said they must take the initiative and aggressively sell this reform to the American people not for a few days, or weeks, but all the way through the election.

Following the primary election defeat of House majority leader Representative Eric Cantor of Virginia, the race to remake the Republican leadership may leave its top ranks more moderate. Representative Kevin McCarthy of California appeared all but certain on Thursday night to rise from majority whip, the No. 3 job, to majority leader after Representatives Pete Sessions and Jeb Hensarling of Texas withdrew from the race to succeed Cantor. Unless a new contender emerges before the leadership vote next Thursday, the new majority leader will have a less conservative voting record than the man he is replacing.

North Korea launched a rocket on Sunday that Western experts believe is part of a program to develop intercontinental ballistic missile technologies. The rocket blasted off from Tongchang-ri, the North's main satellite launch site near its northwestern border with China, a spokesman for the South Korean Defense Ministry said. President Park Geun-hye of South Korea called an emergency meeting of top national security advisers on Sunday to address the launch, her office said. South Korea, the United States and Japan also requested an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council.

Japan said on Saturday it was coordinating with the U.S. government for American citizens to leave the quarantined cruise ship Diamond Princess and return home on U.S.-chartered flights. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the Japanese government believes the steps taken by the United States will ease Japan's burden regarding the medical response to the situation and appreciates these measures. The United States said earlier on Saturday it would send an aircraft to Japan to bring back U.S. passengers on the Diamond Princess, where the most coronavirus infections outside China have occurred.

The U.S. government will hit the $16.4 trillion federal debt limit on Monday and turn to "extraordinary measures" to continue borrowing, the Treasury Department said Wednesday, beginning a countdown until Congress passes legislation to allow more borrowing or the government defaults on its debt.

A man helping campaign for U.S. Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson died after being injured in a car accident in Iowa on Tuesday, according to a statement from a hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, released by Carson's campaign. Campaign volunteer Braden Joplin, 25, died in Nebraska Medical Center after being admitted in critical condition following the accident in Atlantic, Iowa, the statement said. Carson, a retired neurosurgeon, temporarily suspended his campaign and was traveling from South Carolina to Omaha where he was planning to meet with Joplin's family members and offer his condolences.

Donald Trump Jr. posted a question about the Democrats on Twitter. In the tweet, he praised his father's signing of a new trade agreement with China and asked people to "name a single Democrat accomplishment." The article noted that the Democratic-controlled House had just impeached his father over the Ukraine scandal. One commenter wrote, "I'd say that was a pretty big accomplishment." Other commenters highlighted the Democratic taking of the House in the 2018 midterms.

President Obama will make his first trip as president to Kenya and Ethiopia later this week. In 2008, the United States elected the son of a Kenyan economist to its highest office. Seven years later, the organization is seeking input from Africa on how Obama has done and what he should still try to accomplish. The questions include whether the president has lived up to expectations and whether he has made a difference in the lives of Africans. The organization may publish a selection of the responses with upcoming coverage. A submission form is no longer accepting submissions.

Wall Street Journal columnist Peggy Noonan described President Obama's decision to appear on five Sunday shows in one day as "boorish" during a Sunday show appearance on ABC News with George Stephanopoulos. Noonan, a former speechwriter, said: "He's doing it because he can. The media environment allows a modern leader to be something subtly damaging, and that is boorish. They get their face in your face every day all the time. It's boorish and it makes people not lean toward you but lean away from you, no matter what the merits of the issue."

The forces of President Bashar al-Assad of Syria have substantially increased their air attacks, according to American intelligence reports. The reports paint an increasingly dire picture of the war in Syria as top Obama administration officials met Wednesday to review military options to help the rebels reverse their deteriorating position. The Syrian military's use of warplanes and helicopters has increased. It carried out at least 500 air-to-ground attacks against rebels and civilians in May, according to the intelligence reports, which were described by officials who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to discuss them.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton began testifying before Congress on Wednesday morning. She cautioned against retreating from dangerous diplomatic posts and made an uncharacteristic display of emotion as her voice broke while she said she takes the issue of diplomat safety personally. The Post reported that Clinton is more popular than ever. American Foreign Service Association president Susan Johnson spoke about the dangers embassy workers face in an interview with Federal Diary columnist Joe Davidson.

Israel aircraft bombed a target in Syria overnight Thursday, an Obama administration official said Friday night. United States officials said they were considering military options, including carrying out their own airstrikes. American officials did not provide details on the target of the Israeli strike. In late January, Israel carried out airstrikes against SA-17 antiaircraft weapons, which Israelis feared were about to be moved to the Hezbollah Shiite militia in Lebanon. Israel has been worried that chemical weapons and advanced arms might be transferred to Hezbollah from Syria, and the Israeli military has made clear it is prepared to take action to stop such shipments.

White House Chief of Staff John Kelly denied a report that he called President Donald Trump an "idiot." Kelly told NBC News on Monday, "He always knows where I stand and he and I both know this story is total BS. I am committed to the president, his agenda, and our country." The report circulated online.

President Donald Trump tweeted several times over the weekend that he "won the election," despite the fact that he lost. Trump also made claims of voter fraud more than one week after President-elect Joe Biden was projected the winner of the 2020 election. Several world leaders congratulated Biden on his win, and several GOP lawmakers called him the president-elect. Some Republicans floated the idea that Trump still has a chance at a second term in office.

John Kerry, making his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa as secretary of state, made his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa as secretary of state on Saturday. He urged Nigeria to uphold human rights as it steps up its fight against Islamic extremists. "One's person's atrocity does not excuse another's," Kerry said when asked about reports of serious human rights violations by Nigerian forces. "We defend the right completely of the government of Nigeria to defend itself and fight back against terrorists," he added. "That said, I have raised the issue of human rights with the government."

President Barack Obama was late for his speech at American University in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday and blamed printer toner for the delay. He apologized for the slight delay and said, "I apologize for the slight delay; even presidents have problems with toner." He then smiled as the audience laughed at his comment. Obama is delivering a speech at the university, one of many such events over the next several weeks to build support in Congress for the Iran nuclear deal.

A shooting at Santa Fe High School in Santa Fe, Texas, killed at least eight people Friday morning and injured one police officer. Politicians posted tweets and statements offering variations of the now-standard "thoughts and prayers." Survivors responded with candor. They said they were horrified by the shooting and to politicians they accused of enabling it. President Donald Trump said he would record their reactions.

More than 100 law officers continued a nationwide manhunt for an armed bank robber suspected of shooting two Tupelo, Mississippi, police officers, one of them fatally, the FBI said Thursday. The bank robbery in Tupelo turned into a shootout Monday afternoon, and the robber or robbers escaped and remain at large, the FBI said. The FBI, local banks and business are offering a more than $150,000 reward for the identification and capture of the bank robber, the FBI said. The suspect was driving a gray sedan as he fled eastbound on Carnation Street in Tupelo, the FBI said.

Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder (R) live-tweeted Sunday night's Democratic presidential debate in Michigan. He defended his administration's choices that led to nearly 100,000 Flint residents drinking poisonous water. Snyder tweeted that he is "taking responsibility" for the crisis and argued that the choice to use corrosive water from the Flint River was "never about money." He tweeted: "This was a failure of government at all levels that could be described as a massive error of bureaucracy."

A gunman holding hostages in the Lindt Chocolate Cafe in Sydney's central business district is said to be demanding an ISIS flag and a phone call with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. Photographs from local media showed people with their hands pressed against the glass with the writing on the flag in the window. The incident prompted concern that the crisis in Sydney could be linked to Islamic extremists. Australia, which is part of the international coalition fighting ISIS in the Middle East, said in September that it had foiled a plot by Islamic militants to carry out a public execution.

Financial markets ended slightly lower Thursday, for their first loss in a week. The market was headed for its first loss in a week of nominal highs. The escalating conflict in Ukraine, earnings and profit outlooks from retailers weighed down the market, eclipsing some good news in the United States on the economy and labor market. Erik Davidson, deputy chief investment officer at Wells Fargo Private Bank, said the key driver was largely the Ukraine news and uncertainty about what that means. President Petro O. Poroshenko of Ukraine said Russian forces had entered his country. He called an emergency meeting of the nation's security council.

Iranian President Hassan Rouhani said Wednesday he wants to extend health insurance coverage to 5 million of his country's uninsured. In a tweet, Rouhani referred to his plan as "RouhaniCare." Rouhani, in contrast to his predecessor Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, has sought inroads with the West and, in particular, the United States. His English language Twitter account is often topical and plays to that Western audience. Rouhani is also in nuclear negotiations aimed at reining in his country's ability to produce a nuclear bomb.

Early results from Iran's presidential election showed reformist-backed candidate Hassan Rouhani in the lead. Official figures showed Rouhani with 51% of the five million ballots counted so far, ahead of second-placed Tehran mayor Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf on 17%. If Rouhani maintains that margin, he will avoid a run-off vote. Electoral officials said turnout was high among the 50 million Iranians eligible to vote on Friday for a successor to Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

Funeral services for Rev. Clementa Pinckney are scheduled for today and are open to the public. Thousands are expected to attend, including President Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, Vice President Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, a congressional delegation, and many other leaders from around the country. President Obama has written and delivered the eulogy for Beau Biden, son of Vice President Biden, according to aides. He also wrote the eulogy for Rev. Clementa Pinckney himself.

North Korea has been open about its ultimate military goal: the country and its leader Kim Jong Un want a nuclear weapon placed on top of an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States. The regime has recently shown significant advancements in its internationally condemned nuclear program and exchanged escalating threats with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration. Former President Barack Obama warned his successor about Kim, and North Korea has become one of the Trump administration's most pressing international concerns.

U.S. Representative Michele Bachmann (R-MN) announced on her Facebook page that she plans to form an exploratory committee for a presidential run in 2012. She has not filed with the Federal Election Commission to make the decision. Last week, the blog featured quotes from Bachmann. The blog then volunteered potential running mates for her campaign. The blog invited readers to vote for potential running mates.

Kansas Sen. Pat Roberts (R) won his re-election bid, defeating Independent candidate Greg Orman in the midterm elections, according to CBS and Fox News. Roberts was also battling Democrat Chad Taylor until September 2014, when Taylor withdrew from the race and requested his name removed from the ballot. After a dispute between Taylor and Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, the state Supreme Court ordered Kansas to remove Taylor's name.
